# THE HARVARD ORIENTAL SERIES
<note>The Harvard Oriental Series (HOS) was founded in 1891 by Charles Rockwell Lanman and Henry Clarke Warren. It is one of the most prestigious academic collections of translated and edited Sanskrit and Pali texts, designed to make Asian philosophy and literature accessible to Western scholars.</note>

## VOLUME SEVENTEEN

Harvard Oriental Series, Volume Seventeen <term>HOS Vol. 17</term> <note>Volume 17 of this series, published in 1914, contains the definitive English translation of the "Yoga-System of Patañjali" by James Haughton Woods. It includes the Yoga-Sūtras along with two major commentaries: the Bhāshya and the Tattva-Vāicāradī.</note>

<summary>The official title page for the seventeenth volume of the Harvard Oriental Series, a landmark collection in the field of Indology and South Asian studies.</summary>

<meta>This page follows the Table of Contents and begins the author’s Preface, moving from the organizational outline of the book into the translator's personal justification and methodology for the work.</meta>

b [Harvard Oriental Series, Volume 17]

# PREFACE

**1. Reasons for taking up the work.** — It is with some hesitation that one attempts to translate into English the texts of a complex system that, with the exception of the <term>aphoristic rules</term> <note>original: "sūtras"; the foundational, brief statements of the Yoga system.</note>, have never been translated in Europe or America. However, the historical significance of these texts is profound. They act as a bridge between the philosophy of ancient India, the fully developed schools of Indian Buddhism, and the religious thought found today across Eastern Asia. This importance encourages the attempt. This system, when combined with the <term>logic school</term> <note>original: "Nyāya"</note> and the <term>metaphysical school</term> <note>original: "Vaiçeṣika"</note> and applied to the simple, practical teachings of early Buddhism, serves as an essential introduction to the logical and philosophical masterpieces of <term>Great Vehicle Buddhism</term> <note>original: "Mahāyāna"</note>.

**2. Difficulties of comprehending the work.** — Even after reading these passages a dozen times, the meaning of certain paragraphs remains elusive—such as the first half of the <term>commentary</term> <note>original: "Bhāṣya," specifically referring here to the commentary attributed to Vyāsa.</note> on section iii. 14. Even more difficult are the individual technical terms, even when their general literal meaning seems clear after a basic analysis. This remaining difficulty is inevitable as long as one is not fully immersed in the specific type of "emotional thinking" that reaches its peak in a spiritual object of aesthetic meditation.

**3. Difficulties of style.** — The <term>commentary</term> and, even more so, the <term>Exposition of Truth</term> <note>original: "Tattva-vāiçāradī," a highly influential sub-commentary by the 10th-century scholar Vācaspati Miçra.</note> are masterpieces of philosophical writing. They are not merely a loose collection of notes. Their extremely shortened and disconnected word order is a deliberate choice. The <term>school of interpretation</term> <note>original: "Mīmāṅsā," which focused on the precise analysis of Vedic texts.</note> first analyzed the <term>meaning of individual words</term> <note>original: "padārtha"</note>; then, in a separate section, the <term>meaning of the sentences</term> <note>original: "vākyārtha"</note>; and finally, and most comprehensively, the <term>deeper implication</term> <note>original: "bhāvārtha"</note> of the sentences as a whole. Wherever a full sentence structure was missing in the original, I have added the necessary words in brackets to create a clear statement. However, much remains obscure in the sections regarding the <term>deeper implication</term> of the <term>commentary</term>. In these parts, many outside technical terms are quietly introduced under the pretense of explaining the text. In this way, arguments are made against opponents whose names are never explicitly mentioned.

<summary>In this preface, the translator explains the historical importance of the Yoga system as a link between ancient Hindu philosophy and later Buddhist thought, while acknowledging the immense difficulty of translating its dense, technical style.</summary>
<keywords>Preface, Yoga philosophy, translation methodology, commentary, Harvard Oriental Series, technical terminology, Indian logic, Buddhism</keywords>

Preface

### Preface

creeps into the argument. The allusions are suggestive, but obviously elusive. The passage at section 3. 14 might be quite simple if we had before us the text which it criticizes.

**4. Translation of technical terms.**—A system whose subtleties are not those of Western philosophers suffers disastrously when its characteristic concepts are compelled to masquerade under assumed names, fit enough for our linguistic habits, but worn out even for us by reason of frequent shifting of meanings. Each time that <term>the Spirit-Self</term> <note>original: "Puruṣa"; the pure, eternal consciousness that remains a silent witness to all experience.</note> is rendered by the word "soul", every psychologist and philosopher is misled. No exact equivalent is found in our vocabulary. The rendering "Self" is less likely to cause misunderstanding. Similarly, and in accordance with the painstaking distinctions made at the end of section 2. 5, it is most important to remember that the term <term>undifferentiated-consciousness</term> <note>original: "a-vidyā"; though literally "non-knowledge" or "ignorance," the author argues it represents a positive state of clouded awareness.</note>, although negative in form, stands for an idea which is not negative, but positive. Bearing in mind the express instructions of the text, I have adopted "undifferentiated-consciousness" as the translation of <term>ignorance</term> <note>original: "avidyā"</note>.

Another word, which Professor Garbe discussed more than twenty years ago (in his translation of the <term>Commentary on the Exposition of the Sāṁkhya System</term> <note>original: "Sāṁkhya-pravacana-bhāṣya"</note>, page 70, note 1), is <term>aspect</term> <note>original: "guṇa"; traditionally "quality" or "strand," the author views these as the fundamental components of nature.</note>. I prefer to translate this term by "aspect" rather than by "constituent", because, in addition to the meanings "quality" and "substance", it often seems to have the grammatical value of "subordinate" as correlated to <term>the primary source</term> <note>original: "pradhāna"; the fundamental, unmanifested matter of the universe.</note>. Three other words—<term>purity and light</term> <note>original: "sattva"</note>, <term>energy and movement</term> <note>original: "rajas"</note>, and <term>inertia and darkness</term> <note>original: "tamas"</note>—seem untranslatable, unless one is content with half-meaningless word-for-word parallels. In another case I have weakly consented to use "Elevation" as equivalent to <term>highest discernment</term> <note>original: "prasaṁkhyāna"</note>; the original word denotes the culmination of a series of concentrations; the result is the merging of the Self in the object of contemplation.

**5. Punctuation.**—**1.** Quotations from the <term>Aphoristic Rules</term> <note>original: "Sūtras"</note> are enclosed in single angular quotation-marks (‹ ›). **2.** Quotations from the <term>Commentary</term> <note>original: "Bhāṣya"</note> are enclosed in double angular quotation-marks (« »). **3.** Quotations from authoritative texts are enclosed in ordinary double quotation-marks (" "). **4.** Objections and questions by opponents, and quotations from unauthoritative texts, are enclosed in ordinary single quotation-marks (' '). Hyphens have been used to indicate the breakdown of long compound words. A half-parenthesis on its side is used to show that two vowels are printed in violation of the rules of smooth vowel blending <note>original: "rules of euphonic combination (Sandhi)"; refer to Lanman's Sanskrit Reader, p. 289.</note>.

He also provides a guide to the specialized punctuation used to distinguish between foundational rules, commentaries, and opposing viewpoints.</summary>

# Preface

**6. Texts and Manuscripts.**—The text of the <term>concise rules</term> <note>original: "sūtras"; the short, thread-like aphorisms that form the foundation of Indian philosophical systems.</note> of the Yoga system, like that of the rules of all the other five systems, except perhaps the <term>Atomist school</term> <note>original: "Vaiçeṣika"; one of the six orthodox schools of Indian philosophy, known for its analysis of the physical world.</note>, is well preserved; and there is an abundance of excellent printed editions. The most accessible and the most carefully elaborated of these books is the one published in the <term>Anandashrama Series</term> <note>original: "Ānandāçrama"; a famous Sanskrit research institute and publishing house in Pune.</note> and edited by Kashinatha Shastri Agashe. Variants from twelve manuscripts, mostly southern, are printed at the foot of each page; and Bhojadeva’s <term>Gloss</term> <note>original: "Vṛtti"; a type of short commentary that explains the meaning of the sūtras.</note> is appended; also the text of the rules by itself and an index thereto. Another <margin>X</margin> edition, in the Bombay Sanskrit Series, by Rajaram Shastri Bodas, is also an excellent piece of work. I have, however, made use of the edition by Swami Balarama (Calcutta, <term>Vikrama Era</term> <note>original: "Samvat"; a traditional Indian calendar system starting in 57 BCE.</note> 1947, A. D. 1890; reprinted¹ in Benares A. D. 1908) because it is based on northern manuscripts and because of the valuable notes in the editor’s <term>scholarly commentary</term> <note>original: "tippaṇa"</note>. Of manuscripts, I have collated, with the kind permission of the Maharaja, during a charming week’s visit at Jammu just below the glistening snows above the Pir Panjal, two of the oldest manuscripts in the library of the Raghunath Temple. In Stein’s Catalogue these are numbered 4375 and 4388 and the former is dated <term>Vikrama Era</term> <note>original: "Samvat"</note> 1666 <note>equivalent to 1609 AD</note>. Two other manuscripts were lent me, one by the courtesy of the most learned Gangadhara Shastri, the other the very carefully written Bikaner manuscript, sent to me by the generosity of the Bikaner government, which proved to be extremely valuable for disputed readings in the <term>Clarification of Truth</term> <note>original: "Tattva-vāiçāradī"; an influential 9th-century commentary on Yoga by Vāchaspatimiçra.</note>. This latter manuscript seemed to be about a hundred and fifty years old and is described in Rajendralala Mitra’s Catalogue of Sanskrit Manuscripts in the Library of His Highness the Maharaja of Bikaner (Calcutta, 1880) under the number 569. An old <term>Sharada</term> <note>original: "Shāradā"; an ancient script used primarily in the Kashmir region.</note> manuscript, which, by the kind mediation of Mukundaram Shastri of Srinagar, was put into my hands, proved, upon critical examination, to have been so badly corrupted as, on the whole, not to be worth recording.

# INTRODUCTION

1. **Authorship of the <term>Yoga-sūtras</term> <note>The "Aphorisms on Yoga," the foundational text of the Yoga school of philosophy.</note>.—Identity of <term>Patañjali</term>, author of the sūtras, and of <term>Patañjali</term>, author of the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term> <note>The "Great Commentary," a famous work on Sanskrit grammar.</note>, not yet proved.** The opinion in India and in the West that the author of the <term>Yoga-sūtras</term> is also the author of the great grammatical comment upon <term>Pāṇini</term> <note>The ancient scholar who standardized Sanskrit grammar around the 4th century BCE.</note> has not been traced definitely any farther back than to the tenth century. The <term>Yoga-bhāṣya</term> <note>The earliest and most important commentary on the Yoga-sūtras, traditionally attributed to the sage Vyāsa.</note> (written about A.D. 650 to 850) makes no statement as to the authorship of the <term>Yoga-sūtras</term>, unless the benedictory verse at the beginning be regarded as valid proof that <term>Patañjali</term> wrote the sūtras. Still less is there any statement in the <term>Yoga-sūtras</term> about the author of the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term>. And conversely there is no reference in the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term> to the author of the <term>Yoga-sūtras</term>. On the other hand, there is ground for believing that the author of the Comment on <term>Yoga-sūtra</term> iii. 44 may have had the author of the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term> in mind when he quotes a certain formula and ascribes it to <term>Patañjali</term>. This is the only mention of <term>Patañjali</term> in the whole Comment. The formula is: "A substance is a collection of parts where the differences between those parts are followed by an inseparable unity" <note>original: "Ayutasiddha_avayava-bheda_anugataḥ samūho dravyam"</note>; and although it is ascribed to <term>Patañjali</term> <note>original: "iti Patañjaliḥ"</note>, it has not been found in the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term>. Nevertheless the <term>Yoga-bhāṣya</term> does here seem to contain an allusion, more or less direct, to the theory of the unity of the parts of concrete substances as set forth in the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term>. But the allusion is not direct enough to serve by itself as basis for the assertion that the <term>Yoga-bhāṣya</term> assumes the identity of the two <term>Patañjalis</term>. In other words, it does not justify us in assigning to the tradition of their identity a date as ancient as that of the <term>Yoga-bhāṣya</term> (eighth century). The allusion is, however, significant enough not to be lost out of mind, pending the search for other items of cumulative evidence looking in the same direction.

2. **Tradition of identity of two <term>Patañjalis</term> not earlier than tenth century.**—So far as I know, the oldest text implying that the <term>Patañjali</term> who wrote the sūtras is the same as the <term>Patañjali</term> who wrote the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term>, is stanza 5 of the introduction to <term>Bhojadeva</term>’s <note>An 11th-century polymath king known for his works on philosophy, grammar, and medicine.</note> comment on the <term>Yoga-sūtras</term>, his <term>Rājamārtaṇḍa</term> <note>Literally "The Royal Sun," a significant commentary on Yoga.</note>. This I would render as follows:

> Victory be to the luminous words of that illustrious sovereign, [<term>Bhoja</term>] <term>Raṇa-raṅgamalla</term> <note>A title meaning "the champion in the theater of war."</note>, who by creating his Grammar, by writing his comment on the <term>Patañjalan</term> [treatise, the <term>Yoga-sūtras</term>], and by producing [a work] on medicine called <term>Rājamṛgāṅka</term> <note>Literally "The Royal Moon," a medical treatise.</note>, has—like <term>Patañjali</term>—removed defilement from our speech and minds and bodies.

<summary>This page discusses the historical debate over whether Patañjali, the author of the Yoga-sūtras, is the same person as the Patañjali who wrote the great commentary on Sanskrit grammar. The author notes that evidence for this shared identity only clearly appears around the 10th century, notably in the works of King Bhoja.</summary>

## Introduction

Bhoja's Grammar, his comment called <term>Rājamārtaṇḍa</term> <note>The "Royal Sun," a famous 11th-century commentary on the Yoga-sūtras attributed to King Bhoja.</note>, and his medical treatise are all extant. The stanza must mean that <term>Patañjali</term> and <term>Bhoja</term> both maintained a standard of correct speech, Patañjali by his <term>Mahābhāṣya</term> <note>The "Great Commentary" on Sanskrit grammar.</note> and Bhoja by his Grammar; and that both made our minds clear of error, Patañjali by his <term>Yoga-sūtras</term> and Bhoja by his comment upon them; and that both made our bodies clear of impurities, Patañjali by his medical treatise and Bhoja by his <term>Rājamṛgāṅka</term> <note>A medical work, the name of which translates to "The Royal Moon."</note>.

This certainly implies that the writer of this stanza identified Patañjali of the <term>Yoga-sūtras</term> with Patañjali of the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term>. If the writer of the stanza of the introduction is the same as the <term>Bhojadeva</term> who wrote the <term>Rājamārtaṇḍa</term>, we may note that he is called <term>Raṇaraṅgamalla</term> <note>A title meaning "Champion in the Theater of War."</note> here, <term>Mahārājādhirāja</term> <note>A title meaning "King of Great Kings."</note> in the colophon in Mitra's edition, and Lord of <term>Dhārā</term> or <term>Dhāreçvara</term> in the colophon in the edition of Āgāçe. There were a number of Bhojadevas; but whichever of them the author of the <term>Rājamārtaṇḍa</term> may be, no one of them is earlier than the tenth century of our era.

The tradition of the triple activity of Patañjali as a writer on Yoga and grammar and medicine is reinforced as follows:

->*With Yoga for the mind, with grammar for speech,*<-
->*and with medicine for the body’s impurity,*<-
->*he who removed them, to that most excellent of sages,*<-
->*Patañjali, I bow with hands joined in reverence.*<-
<note>original: "Yogena cittasya, padena vācāṁ / malam, çarīrasya tu vaidyakena / yo ’pākarot, tam pravaraṁ munīnām / Patañjalim prāñjalir ānato ’smi."</note>

This is cited in Çivarāma’s commentary on the <term>Vāsavadattā</term> <note>A famous classical Sanskrit novel by Subandhu.</note> (ed. Bibl. Ind., p. 239), which Aufrecht assigns to the eighteenth century. The stanza occurs also in some MSS. just before the opening words of the <term>Mahābhāṣya</term> (Kielhorn's ed., vol. I, p. 503)—that is, not under circumstances giving any clue to its date. We may add that an eighteenth-century work, the <term>Patañjalicarita</term> <note>The "Acts of Patañjali," a hagiography of the sage.</note> (v. 25, ed. of Kāvyamālā, vol. 51), vouches for Patañjali's authorship in the fields of Yoga and medicine in the following <term>gīti</term> <note>A specific meter in Sanskrit poetry.</note> stanza:

->*Having composed the aphorisms on the science of Yoga,*<-
->*and the explanatory rules on the science of medicine,*<-
->*the sage Patañjali then*<-
->*promoted them to save this world.*<-
<note>original: "Sūtrāṇi yogaçāstre / vaidyakaçāstre ca vārttikāni tataḥ / kṛtvā Patañjalimuniḥ / pracārayām āsa jagad idaṁ trātum."</note>

As to the precise medical work of which Patañjali was the author or with which he had to do, all three stanzas leave us uninformed. Not so the following stanza from the introduction to the commentary on <term>Caraka</term> <note>One of the principal foundational texts of Ayurveda (Indian medicine).</note>, composed by <term>Cakrapāṇi</term>, who (according to Jolly’s book on Medicine in Bühler’s Grundriss, p. 25) wrote about 1060:

->*Through the Yoga of Patañjali, the Great Commentary, and the revision of Caraka,*<-
->*salutation to the Lord of Serpents, the destroyer of the defects of mind, speech, and body.*<-
<note>original: "Pātañjala-Mahābhāṣya-Carakapratisaṁskṛtaiḥ / mano-vāk-kāyadoṣāṇāṁ hantre ’hipataye namaḥ." The term "Lord of Serpents" refers to the belief that Patañjali was an incarnation of the celestial serpent Śeṣa.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the historical and literary tradition that credits Patañjali with expertise in three distinct fields: Yoga (mind), Grammar (speech), and Medicine (body). It examines various commentaries and verses, primarily from the 10th to 18th centuries, that support this "triple activity" and the identity of Patañjali as a universal scholar.</summary>

<header>Introduction</header>

This agrees in sense with the other stanzas, and in addition informs us that Patañjali's medical work consisted in a <term>revision</term> <note>Sanskrit: *pratisaṃskṛta*, meaning a refined or updated edition.</note> of the great compendium of <term>Caraka</term> <note>A foundational medical text of Ayurveda.</note>. Accordingly, the Bhoja-stanza appears to be the oldest external evidence thus far at hand for the tradition as to the identity of the two Patañjalis, and this tradition is not older than the tenth century, a thousand years and more after Patañjali the author of the <term>Great Commentary</term> <note>The *Mahābhāṣya* on Sanskrit grammar.</note>.

### 3. The identification of the two Patañjalis not confirmed by a comparison of philosophical concepts.

—Inconsistent use of terminology and conflicting definitions of concepts in the case of a single writer of two books are frequently explained by the fact that quite distinct subjects are discussed in the different works. In other cases the subject under discussion is the same and such an explanation of the inconsistency does not hold. An instance of the latter is the discussion of the nature of <term>substance</term> <note>Sanskrit: *dravya*.</note> in the Yoga-system and in the <term>Great Commentary</term>. In the commentary on Yoga-sūtra iii. 44 we have the following definition, “A substance is a collection of which the different component parts do not exist separately <note>original: *ayutasiddha_avayava-bheda_anugataḥ samūho dravyam iti Patañjaliḥ*</note>,” and the definition is attributed to Patañjali as being consistent with his sūtras. This quotation is of the most technical kind and is in the same style as the <term>Logic Sūtras</term> <note>The *Nyāya-sūtras*, which focus on formal reasoning.</note>. A similar use of language, for instance, is found in Logic Sūtra ii. 1. 32. On the other hand this phrase is not to be found in the <term>Great Commentary</term>, which however does repeatedly analyse the concept of substance. And, what is more important, nothing so precise as the formula attributed (iii. 44) to Patañjali is found in the Yoga-sūtras themselves. Yet substance is partially defined in Yoga-sūtra iii. 14, “A substance <note>Sanskrit: *dharmin*, the bearer of traits.</note> conforms itself to quiescent <note>past</note> and uprisen <note>present</note> and indeterminable <note>future</note> external-aspects <note>Sanskrit: *dharma*, or properties.</note>.” In this terminology <term>property-bearer</term> and <term>property</term> of the Yoga-sūtra are substitutions for <term>substance</term> and <term>quality</term> <note>Sanskrit: *dravya* and *guṇa*.</note> of the <term>Great Commentary</term>. In neither case is the description of substance discriminating. Yet such as it is, the difference is very slight. In the <term>Great Commentary</term> it is substance, we are told, which makes the difference in weight between iron and cotton of the same bulk and dimension (Kielhorn’s edition, vol. II, p. 366<sup>19</sup>); and it is that which causes the difference between penetrability and impenetrability. Or again it is that which does not cease to be, even when a succession of properties appears within it (vol. II, p. 366<sup>23</sup>). Of what kind then is this <term>form of being</term> <note>Sanskrit: *tattva*, or fundamental reality.</note>? The answer is that when the various reds and other properties of a <term>myrobalan fruit</term> <note>A small, sour fruit often used in Indian philosophical metaphors to illustrate an object that changes its color/state while remaining the same thing.</note>, for instance, successively appear within it, we have the right to call it a substance. In short a substance is a concretion of properties <note>original: *guṇa-sāndravo dravyam*</note>

It argues that differences in technical terminology—specifically the definition of "substance" (dravya)—suggest they may be different authors.</summary>

<page-num>xvi</page-num>
<header>Introduction</header>

...thus (Kielhorn, vol. II, p. 366^26); or, as it is put elsewhere, it is a <term>collection of properties</term> <note>Sanskrit: *guṇa-samudāya*</note> such that the various <term>states of being</term> <note>Sanskrit: *bhāva*</note> depend upon it (II. 200^14). This collection is loosely paraphrased as being a <term>group</term> <note>Sanskrit: *saṃgha*</note> or <term>mass</term> <note>Sanskrit: *samūha*, meaning an aggregate of parts</note> (II. 356^6).

In order, however, to make the comparison of the <term>property-holder</term> <note>Sanskrit: *dharmin*; the underlying entity that possesses characteristics.</note> of the Yoga-sūtras with the <term>substance</term> <note>Sanskrit: *dravya*</note> of the <term>Great Commentary</term> <note>The *Mahābhāṣya*, Patañjali’s work on grammar.</note>, we must assume that the interpretation of the Yoga-sūtras, as given in the Comment, correctly represents the concept in the mind of the author of the sūtras. There might well have been a series of redactions of the works of Patañjali, as of those of <term>Caraka</term> <note>The traditional author of a foundational medical text.</note>. The later interpretation, such as the formula in the Comment on iii. 44, might give us the original thought in more technical form. If this be so, we find a great similarity in the discussion of the relation of whole and parts in the two works. In the Comment on the Yoga-sūtra iii. 44 a <term>mass</term> <note>Sanskrit: *samūha*</note> is of two kinds: 1. that in which the parts have lost their distinctness, for example, ‘a tree’, ‘a herd’, ‘a grove’; 2. that in which the parts are distinctly described, for example, ‘gods and human beings.’ The second class has two subdivisions: 2^a. one in which the distinctness of parts is emphasized, for example, ‘a grove of mangoes’; 2^b. one in which the distinctness is not emphasized, for example, ‘a mango-grove.’ From another point of view a group is two-fold: 1. a group whereof the parts can exist separately, for example, ‘a grove’, wherein the trees exist separately from the aggregate whole; 2. a group whereof the parts cannot exist separately, for example, ‘a tree’ or ‘an atom’. The question now arises, To which of these kinds of groups does a substance belong? A substance (<term>substance</term>) is an <term>aggregate of generic and particular qualities</term> <note>Sanskrit: *sāmānya-viśeṣa-samudāya*</note>. This is the definition of substance from the point of view of its relation to its qualities. Furthermore, the substance is a group of the second subdivision of the second kind; it is ‘a collection of which the different parts do not exist separately’. This then is the resultant definition of substance according to the traditional interpretation of the Sūtras.

What now is the relation of whole and parts in the <term>Great Commentary</term>, with especial reference to the substance and its qualities? A <term>collection</term> <note>Sanskrit: *samudāya*</note> is loosely paraphrased as being a <term>group</term> or <term>mass</term> (Kielhorn, vol. II, p. 356^6). It is, etymologically at least, a <term>concretion of properties</term> <note>Sanskrit: *guṇa-sandrāva*</note> (II. 366^26). It is a collection of parts; the characteristics of the parts determine the characteristics of the whole (III. 3^14; <note>original: "avayavāir arthavadbhiḥ samudāyā apy arthavanto bhavanti"</note> "when the parts are meaningful, the collections also become meaningful" I. 217^16; I. 30^26-27; <note>original: "avayave kṛtaṃ liṅgaṃ samudāyasya viśeṣakaṃ bhavati"</note> "a mark made on a part becomes a distinguishing feature of the whole" I. 289^2 f; and I. 377^11). All these cases would belong to the first subdivision of the second kind of group, whereof the parts can exist separately.

<summary>This page compares the philosophical definitions of "substance" and "aggregates" in Patañjali's Yoga-sūtras and his Great Commentary on grammar, noting technical distinctions in how parts relate to the whole. These nuances help scholars determine if the two texts were written by the same author or represent different philosophical traditions.</summary>

<keywords>Patañjali, substance, dravya, Yoga-sūtras, Mahābhāṣya, philosophy of language, whole and parts, samudāya, guṇa, property-holder</keywords>

It concludes that the definitions differ enough to suggest two different authors.</meta>

<page-num>xvii]</page-num>
<header>Introduction</header>

Yet a <term>collection</term> <note>Sanskrit: *samudāya*</note> is not merely an assemblage of parts, but is a unity performing functions which the parts by themselves cannot perform—for example, a blanket, a rope, or a chariot, as compared with the individual threads, fibers, or chariot-parts (Reference: I. 220<sup>16–23</sup>). All these cases would belong to the second subdivision of the second kind of group, wherein the parts <term>cannot exist separately</term> <note>Sanskrit: *ayutasiddha-avayava*; a philosophical term for components that are inherently linked to the whole, like the color of a fruit or the threads in a cloth</note>. Such then are the different groups.

With regard to the <term>substance</term> <note>Sanskrit: *dravya*</note>, its relation to its <term>qualities</term> <note>Sanskrit: *guṇa*</note> is analogous to the relation of the parts to the group (Reference: I. 220, gloss 11). Just as a collection is <term>characterized by its parts</term> <note>Sanskrit: *avayavātmaka*</note> (Reference: III. 3<sup>14</sup>), so the substance is <term>characterized by its qualities</term> <note>Sanskrit: *guṇātmaka*</note> or is a <term>collection of qualities</term> <note>Sanskrit: *guṇa-samudāya*</note> (Reference: II. 200<sup>13</sup>). This last formula is given tentatively as a not quite final conclusion; yet the definition is not rejected. And elsewhere (Reference: I. 411<sup>15</sup>, II. 356<sup>17</sup>, II. 415<sup>13</sup>, and especially II. 366<sup>14–26</sup>), it is accepted as a working definition. Some qualities like sound, touch, color, and taste belong to all substances; they at least are present (Reference: I. 246<sup>ff</sup>, II. 198<sup>5ff</sup>). Nothing, however, is said about a <term>generic form</term> <note>Sanskrit: *ākṛti*; the "species" or universal shape that defines a category</note> being required to constitute a substance. At the most, it is true that when one asserts the reality of a species, one does not deny the reality of the substance; and conversely. For each person who makes the assertion, the reality of both is asserted. Either the species or the substance may be dominant in anything, and the other subordinate. It is only a matter of the relative emphasis in the use of words. But the word substance is used for a mass of particular qualities; it is not a concretion of species and qualities, but is contrasted with species. Accordingly, even if we admit that the formula ascribed to Patañjali in the Commentary on chapter iii, verse 13 is the correct rendering of the thought in the mind of Patañjali, the author of the Yoga-sūtra, it is not true that Patañjali, the author of the <term>Great Commentary</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Mahābhāṣya*, a foundational work on Sanskrit grammar</note>, when speaking of a substance means what is contained in this formula. And there is nothing here to indicate that the tradition which identifies the two Patañjalis must be correct.

### 4. Date of the Yoga-sūtras between A.D. 300 and A.D. 500.

—If Patañjali, the author of the *Great Commentary*, is not the author of the Yoga-sūtras, when were they written? The <term>argument</term> <note>original: "polemic"</note> in the Yoga-sūtras themselves against the <term>objectless</term> <note>Sanskrit: *nirālambana*; the school of Buddhist thought that denies the reality of external objects</note> school of Buddhists gives the answer. Very probably in the two Yoga-sūtras iii. 14 and 15 and certainly in iv. 14 to 21, this school is attacked. The idealism of the <term>Way of Consciousness</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Vijñāna-vāda*; a major school of Mahayana Buddhism that asserts that only consciousness is real</note> is attacked in iv. 15, 16, and 17. We cannot, it is true, maintain that the *Way of Consciousness* here attacked by the Sūtra must be the specific idealism of the philosopher <term>Vasubandhu</term> <note>A famous 4th- or 5th-century Buddhist monk and philosopher</note>. But the...

The probability that the idealism discussed is that of <term>Vasubandhu</term> <note>A famous 4th-century Buddhist philosopher</note> is high. This would place the earliest possible date for the text in the fourth century. While there were certainly idealists before him—just as there were philosophers of <term>yoga</term> before <term>Patañjali</term>—we have the significant authority of <term>Vācaspatimiçra</term> <note>A prominent 9th-century commentator</note> to support the likely theory that the school of <term>Vijñānavādins</term> <note>Buddhist "Consciousness-Only" idealists</note> is being challenged here by <term>Patañjali</term>. He accepts the interpretation of the Comment <note>The Yoga-bhāṣya</note> which suggests that a <term>Buddhist idealist of the destructive school</term> <note>original: "Vijñānavādinaṁ Vāināçikam"; p. 292^17, Calcutta ed.</note> was the target intended by the author of the <term>Sūtra</term>.

It is true that the <term>Sūtra</term> itself does not explicitly name this or any other school. Nevertheless, the fact remains that the <term>Sūtra</term> attacks a specific idealist position; the Comment explicitly describes that position; and <term>Vācaspatimiçra</term> identifies the opponent as a <term>Vijñānavādin</term>. Elsewhere, <term>Vācaspatimiçra</term> contrasts this school with other <term>Buddhist</term> schools, and it is unlikely he is referring to any "Consciousness-Only" tradition other than <term>Vasubandhu</term>’s.

If this is the case, it becomes clearer why <term>Nāgārjuna</term> (writing shortly before 200 AD)—the great teacher of <term>Voidism</term> <note>original: "Çūnya-vāda"</note>—does not mention <term>Patañjali</term> in the portions of the <term>Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way</term> <note>original: "Mūlamadhyamika-kārikās"</note> published so far. Yet, from Chinese translations of <term>Nāgārjuna</term>’s work, it is clear he was familiar with philosophical <term>yoga</term>. For example, in a Chinese translation^1 made in 472 AD of <term>Nāgārjuna</term>’s *Handook on the Heart of Skillful Means* <note>original: "Upāyakāuçalyahṛdaya-çāstra"; Nanjio, No. 1257</note>, eight schools of philosophers and logicians are listed:

1. **Fire-worshippers**
2. <term>Mīmāṁsakas</term> <note>Ritualists and hermeneuticists</note>
3. <term>Vāiçeṣikas</term> <note>The school of individualities or atomism</note>
4. <term>Sāṁkhya</term> <note>The dualist school of "Enumeration"</note>
5. <term>Yoga</term>
6. <term>Nirgranthas</term> <note>Jains, literally "the unattached"</note>
7. **Monists**
8. **Pluralists**

There was, therefore, a philosophical school of <term>Yoga</term> around 200 AD.^2 <term>Patañjali</term> was not unknown to <term>Buddhist</term> writers. However, there is no evidence that <term>Nāgārjuna</term> is referring to <term>Patañjali</term> the philosopher, who would have then lived before both <term>objectless</term> <note>original: "nirālambana"</note> schools. More likely, we may assume he refers to earlier authorities on <term>Yoga</term>, such as <term>Jāigiṣavya</term> or <term>Pañcaçikha</term>, both of whom are quoted in the <term>Great Commentary on Yoga</term> <note>original: "Yoga-bhāṣya"</note>.

Regarding the later time limit, a specific reference—if historically accurate—would confirm that <term>Patañjali</term> lived before 400 AD. In the <term>Great Chronicle</term> <note>original: "Mahāvaṁsa"; a historical poem about Sri Lanka</note>, chapter 37, verse 167, we find the words:

> *Arriving at a certain monastery, at night he rehearsed the system of Patañjali.*
> <note>original: "Vihāram ekam āgamma rattim Pātañjali-matam parivatteti"</note>

The verse refers to <term>Buddhaghosa</term> <note>The most important commentator of the Theravada Buddhist tradition</note>, who lived in the first half of the fifth century...

century. But unfortunately the <term>Mahāvaṁsa</term> <note>The "Great Chronicle" of Sri Lankan history</note> proper, the work of <term>Mahānāma</term>, ends, according to the judgment of Professor Geiger, at chapter 37, verse 50, at which point also the <term>ṭīkā</term> <note>A sub-commentary or technical manual</note> stops. The quotation therefore belongs to the <term>Cūlavaṁsa</term> <note>The "Lesser Chronicle," a later continuation of the Sri Lankan history</note>. And if, as Professor Geiger concludes, the work of Mahānāma is to be placed in the first quarter of the sixth century, the verse in question comes later, and probably later to such a degree that its value as evidence is almost nothing. If this be so, one can easily explain how it is that <term>Buddhaghosa</term> <note>A famous 5th-century Buddhist scholar</note> in the whole <term>Visuddhimagga</term> <note>The "Path of Purification," a major Buddhist treatise</note> and in the <term>Atthasālinī</term> <note>A commentary on Buddhist psychological ethics</note> makes no allusion to <term>Patañjali</term>.

Much more conclusive is the fact that <term>Umāsvāti</term> <note>An early and influential Jain philosopher</note> in his <term>Tattvārthādhigamasūtra</term> <note>The "Manual for Understanding the Nature of Realities"</note> ii. 52 refers to <term>Yoga-sūtra</term> iii. 22. There can be little doubt of the reference since Umāsvāti's <term>Bhāṣya</term> <note>A prose commentary</note> repeats (Bibliotheca Indica edition p. 53^13 and 65^3) two of the illustrations given in the <term>Yoga-bhāṣya</term> <note>The earliest commentary on the Yoga Sūtras</note>, of the fire set in the dry grass and of the cloth rolled up into a ball. Other references (Tattvārthādhigama-sūtra xii. 5 and 6 and ix. 44-46) are quite as likely allusions to ancient Jain formulae as to Patañjali. By how much Umāsvāti's date precedes that of his commentator, <term>Siddhasena</term>, cannot be said until the complete text of Siddhasena is published. The date for Siddhasena is set by Professor Jacobi (Journal of the German Oriental Society <note>original: "ZDMG"</note> 60. 289, Leipzig, 1906, reprint p. 3, A Jain Dogmatic System <note>original: "Eine Jaina-Dogmatik"</note>) at the middle or end of the sixth century. Umāsvāti precedes him; and Patañjali the philosopher would not be later than A.D. 500 and might be much earlier.

On the other hand I should guess that he is not much earlier. Because, for one reason, as Professor <term>Stcherbatskoi</term> <note>A Russian scholar of Buddhist logic</note> reports, <term>Dignāga</term> <note>A prominent Buddhist logician, active around 480–540 AD</note> (about A.D. 550 or earlier) seems to know nothing of him. And secondly because it is improbable that the <term>Yoga-bhāṣya</term> was composed very much later.

Other confirmatory evidence, somewhat later but more certain, would be the reference to <term>Yoga-sūtra</term> i. 33 in <term>Māgha’s</term> <term>Çiçupālavadha</term> <note>An epic poem titled "The Slaying of Shishupala"</note> iv. 55. Professor Hultzsch has kindly pointed out another reference at xiv. 62 of Māgha's poem. In respect of the date of Māgha, Professor Jacobi concluded (Vienna Journal for the Knowledge of the Orient <note>original: "WZKM"</note> vol. III, p. 121 ff.) that Māgha lived about the middle of the sixth century. But Mr. Gaurishankar Ojha's discovery of the <term>Vasantgaḍh inscription</term> dated <term>Vikrama</term> 682 <note>A year in the Hindu calendar equivalent to approximately 625 AD</note> adds new and most convincing evidence. Professor Kielhorn (News from Göttingen, philological-historical class <note>original: "Göttinger Nachrichten, philol.-histor. Klasse"</note>, 1906, Issue 2, p. 146) is of the opinion that Māgha, the grandson of a minister of the King <term>Varmalāta</term>, must be placed at about the second half of the seventh century.

Still later, <term>Gauḍapāda</term> <note>An early philosopher of the Advaita Vedānta school, c. 700 AD</note> (about A.D. 700), in his comment on the <term>Sāṁkhya-Kārikā</term> <note>The foundational verses of the Sāṁkhya school of philosophy</note> 23, quotes <term>Yoga-sūtra</term> ii. 30 and 32 and names Patañjali as the author.

The conclusion would be then that Patañjali's sūtras were written at some time in the fourth or fifth century of our era.

### 5. Date of the **Yoga-bhāṣya** <note>The "Commentary on Yoga," the oldest and most important commentary on Patañjali's Yoga Sutras, traditionally attributed to the sage Vyāsa</note> between A.D. 650 and A.D. 850.—Of this the limits are easier to fix. Three pieces of evidence help us to determine the earliest limit.

**A.** The Comment could not in any case be much earlier than A.D. 350. For (at the end of iii. 53 or 52) it quotes **Vārṣagaṇya** <note>An ancient and influential teacher of the Sāṅkhya philosophy</note> in the words

> Because there is no difference in form, obstruction, or genus, there is no separation of the root <note>original: "mūrti-vyavadhi-jāti-bhedābhāvān nāsti mūlapṛthaktvam iti Vārṣagaṇyah"</note>; thus says **Vārṣagaṇya**.

And again (iv. 13) the Comment quotes from a *teaching of the scriptures* <note>original: "çāstrānuçāsanam"</note> as follows:

> The supreme form of the Qualities <note>The three fundamental strands or energies of nature: sattva, rajas, and tamas</note> does not come within the range of sight; that which comes within the range of sight is as empty as an illusion <note>original: "Guṇānāṁ paramaṁ rūpaṁ na dṛṣṭipatham ṛcchati / yat tu dṛṣṭipathaṁ prāptaṁ tan māyeva sutucchakam"</note>.

Fortunately **Vācaspatimiçra** <note>A 10th-century polymath who wrote a sub-commentary on the Yoga-bhāṣya</note> offers us the information that this is an exposition of the teaching of the <term>Shaṣṭi-tantra</term> <note>The "Sixty Topics," a foundational but now lost work of the Sāṅkhya school</note>. And furthermore, in the <term>Bhāmatī</term> <note>Vācaspatimiçra's famous commentary on the Vedānta system</note> on <term>Vedānta-sūtra</term> <note>The foundational text of the Vedānta school of philosophy</note> ii. 1. 2. 3 (<term>Nirṇayasāgara</term> <note>A famous Indian publishing house</note> edition, 1904, p. 352, line 7 of the **Bhāmatī**), we are told that it is **Vārṣagaṇya**, the founder of the <term>Yoga</term> system, who said these words ("Therefore the Lord **Vārṣagaṇya**, the instructor of the Yoga-shastra, said: 'Of the qualities, the supreme form...'" <note>original: "ata eva yoga-çāstraṁ vyutpādayitā āha sma Bhagavān Vārṣagaṇyaḥ 'guṇānāṁ paramaṁ ...'"</note>).

Thus the Comment contains two quotations from **Vārṣagaṇya**. There is little reason to doubt that **Vārṣagaṇya** was an older contemporary of **Vasubandhu** <note>A famous Buddhist philosopher</note>. Professor **Takakusu**¹ by a combination of dates centering about the Chinese translation of **Paramārtha**'s Life of **Vasubandhu** estimated that **Vasubandhu** lived from about A. D. 420 till 500. Professor **Sylvain Lévi** (**Asaṅga**, vol. II, pp. 1 and 2) accepted the result of these discussions. But Professor **Wogihara**² had conjectured that the date of **Vasubandhu** must be set back. An elaborate confirmation of his suggestion is now offered by Monsieur **Noël Peri**,³ who places the death of **Vasubandhu** at A. D. 350; and by Mr. **B. Shiiwo**,⁴ who estimates that **Vasubandhu**'s life was from A. D. 270 to 350. This is a return to the fourth century, the date for **Vasubandhu** which **Bühler**⁵ favoured. Accordingly the **Bhāṣya** must in any case be later than A. D. 350.

**B.** Another kind of evidence which helps us to determine yet more closely the earliest limit is the fact that the <term>decimal system</term> <note>The numerical system using place value and zero</note> is used by way of

Having previously discussed Vārṣagaṇya, the author now uses the history of mathematics and literary citations by the poet Māgha to narrow the Commentary's date to between 650 and 850 A.D., before introducing the works of the 9th-century scholar Vācaspatimiśra.</meta>

illustration in the Comment on iii. 13. The oldest epigraphic <note>Relating to inscriptions on stone or metal</note> instance of the use of the decimal system <note>The base-10 numbering system using zero and place-value</note> is in the **Gurjara** <note>A dynasty in western India</note> inscription of A.D. 595. With one obscure and doubtful exception, there is no literary evidence of the use of the decimal system before **Varāhamihira** <note>A famous Indian astronomer and mathematician</note>, who lived in the sixth century. If we consider this kind of evidence alone, it is improbable that the Comment precedes the year A.D. 600; it is probably later.

**C.** There is evidence which determines that the earliest limit of the Comment is still later, as late as the seventh century. In the stanza iv. 55 of the *Śiśupālavadha* <note>The "Slaying of Śiśupāla," an epic poem</note> by **Māgha** (approximately <note>original: "circa"</note> A.D. 650), not only *Yoga-sūtra* i. 33 is referred to, but also the words of the <term>avatāraṇa</term> <note>An introductory preface or lead-in to a verse</note> in the Comment. In the Comment the <term>parikarma</term> <note>The purification or preparation of the mind</note> of the <term>citta</term> <note>The mind or consciousness</note> is enjoined. This is an uncommon term. Even if *citta-parikamma* <note>The version of this term in the Pali language, used in Buddhist texts</note> might be found in Buddhist books, the fact that it here immediately precedes the quotation from *sūtra* i. 33, makes it almost certain that such a mixture of terminology is impossible. In fact the stanza is full of specific yoga-terms in each line to such an extent that reference to any other system, much less to some heretical book, is quite excluded. The point is then that the words *citta-parikarma* together with the first word of the *sūtra* have been wrought into the metre of the poem as one word. The poet, as we saw, probably lived in the second half of the seventh century. If this is trustworthy evidence, the Comment cannot be earlier than A.D. 650.

**D.** The later limit is set by the date of **Vācaspatimiśra’s** *Nyāya Index*, A.D. 841—see below, page xxiii.

Accordingly the date of the *Bhāṣya* <note>The Commentary</note> would be somewhere between about A.D. 650 and about A.D. 850.

6. **Date of Vācaspatimiśra's Tattva-vaiśāradī about A.D. 850.**—In the verse at the close of his *Bhāmatī-nibandha*, **Vācaspatimiśra** gives the names of his works, seven in number:

> Through the *Nyāyakaṇikā*, the *Tattvasamīkṣā*, and the *Tattvabindu*; <note>original: "Yan Nyāyakarnikā-Tattvasamīkṣā-Tattvabindubhiḥ"</note>
> Through the treatises on Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga, and on the Vedāntas; <note>original: "Yan Nyāya-Sāṃkhya-Yogānām, Vedāntānām nibandhānaiḥ"</note>
> Great merit has been gathered; its abundant fruit by me <note>original: "Samacāisam mahat puṇyam, tat phalam puṣkalam mayā"</note>
> Is offered; now by this may the Supreme Lord be pleased. <note>original: "Samarpitam; athāitena priyatām Parameśvaraḥ"</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the general dating of the Yoga-bhāṣya (Commentary) to the specific life and timeline of its most famous sub-commentator, Vācaspati Miśra. The previous discussion established the 7th century as a starting point for the Commentary; here, we look at the 10th-12th century context of the scholar who explained it.</meta>

<page-num>xxii</page-num>
<header>Introduction</header>

The *Moonlight on Truth* <note>original: "kāumudī", referring to the Sāṁkhya-tattva-kaumudī</note> is on the Sāṁkhya <note>One of the six systems of Indian philosophy, focusing on the dualism between pure consciousness and matter</note> system; the *Expertise in Truth* <note>original: "Tattva-vāiçāradī"</note> is on the Yoga; the *Particle of Logic* <note>original: "Nyāya-kaṇikā"</note>, a gloss <note>A brief explanatory note or commentary</note> on the *Distinction of Injunctions* <note>original: "Vidhi-viveka"</note>, is on the Mīmāṁsā <note>The school of Vedic interpretation focusing on the logic of ritual and duty</note>; the *Drop of Truth* <note>original: "Tattva-bindu"</note> is on Bhaṭṭa's exposition of the Mīmāṁsā; the *Investigation of Truth* <note>original: "Tattva-samīkṣā"</note> and *The Luminous* <note>original: "Bhāmatī"</note> are both on the Vedānta <note>The school of philosophy based on the end of the Vedas, focusing on the nature of ultimate reality</note>.
In the same verse at the end of *The Luminous*, he speaks of himself as living under King **Nṛga**:
> Under that monarch of praiseworthy fame, the Illustrious **Nṛga**, this work was composed by me. <note>original: "tasmin mahīpe mahanīyakīrtāu Çrīman-Nṛge ’kāri mayā nibandhaḥ"</note>
Unfortunately there is (as Professor **Lüders** informs me) no epigraphical <note>Related to the study of inscriptions on stone or metal</note> record of this king and we cannot say when or where he lived. **Vācaspati Miśra** was a native of **Mithilā**,¹ the northern part of **Tirhūt**, and the latter part of his name would indicate, as **Fitz-Edward Hall** has pointed out, that he was a native of **Gangetic Hindustan** <note>The region surrounding the Ganges River in northern India</note>.
In the introduction to his edition of the *Aphorisms of Logic* <note>original: "Kusumāñjali"</note> (Calcutta, 1864, p. x), Professor **Cowell** thinks that **Vācaspati Miśra** lived in the tenth century. **Barth** (*Bulletin of the Religions of India*, 1893, p. 271) would set him at the end of the eleventh or beginning of the twelfth century. Professor **Macdonell** (*History of Sanskrit Literature*, p. 393) places him soon after A.D. 1100.
These judgements rest, more or less, upon the opinion that the *Royal Commentary* <note>original: "Rāja-vārttika"</note>, quoted by **Vācaspati Miśra** in his *Moonlight on the Principles of Sāṁkhya* on Verse <note>original: "Kārikā"</note> 72, was composed by, or for, **Bhoja Rāja**, called **Raṇaraṅga Malla** <note>A title meaning "Hero in the Arena of Battle"</note>, King of **Dhārā** (1018–1060). This opinion accords with the assertion of Pandit **Kāçīnātha Çāstrī Aṣṭaputra** of Benares College, who assured Dr. **Fitz-Edward Hall** that a manuscript of the *Royal Commentary* had been in his possession several years (**Hall's** edition of the *Commentary on the Sāṁkhya System*, 1856, p. 33). But the visible basis for this assertion—that the King in question is **Bhoja**—is not now at hand.
Similarly, Professor **Pathak** in his article on **Dharmakīrti** and **Shankarā-cārya** (see *Journal of the Bombay Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society*, vol. XXVIII, no. 48, 1891, p. 89, and also the table in the same Journal, p. 235, no. 49, note 74) is content to rest his conclusions as to the date of **Vācaspati Miśra** upon the fact that **Çribhāratī**, the pupil of **Bodhāraṇya**, in his edition of the *Moonlight on the Principles of Sāṁkhya* (Benares, Jāinaprabhākara Press, 1889, p. 182), prints, in a note at the end, the word **Bhoja** before the word *Royal Commentary*. Thus it would appear that this commentary is by **Bhojarāja** and that **Vācaspati Miśra**, who quotes it, must be later than **Bhojarāja**, that is, later than the tenth century. But we are not at all sure from other manuscript evidence that the word **Bhoja** should be read before the word *Royal Commentary*, and the date of this *Royal Commentary* is therefore undetermined.

¹ See the beginning of the *Summary of the Logic Sutras* <note>original: "Nyāyasutro-ddhāraḥ"</note> by **Vācaspati Miśra**: "By the illustrious **Vācaspati Miśra**, the learned master of the Lord of **Mithilā**" <note>original: "Çrīvāca-spatimiçreṇa Mithileçvarasūriṇā"</note> (**Haraprasād Çāstrī**, *Notices of Sanskrit Manuscripts*, Second Series, vol. II, p. 98).

<page-num>xxiii]</page-num>

# Introduction

By way of contrast, we now have the direct statement of <term>Vācaspati Miśra</term><note>A prolific 9th-century Indian philosopher who wrote influential commentaries on nearly every major system of Hindu thought.</note> that he finished his **Index of Logic Aphorisms** <note>original: "Nyāyasūcīnibandha"</note> in the year 898. For on the first page of this appendix to the **Commentary on Logic** <note>original: "Nyāya-vārttika"</note>, as given in the edition of the **Commentary on Logic** in the *Bibliotheca Indica* (1907), he says that he is about to compose an index for the **Logic Aphorisms** <note>original: "Nyāya-sūtras", the foundational text of the Nyāya school of logic.</note>:

->*By me, the illustrious Vācaspati Miśra, this index shall be composed.*<-
<note>original: "Çrīvācaspatimiçreṇa mayā sūcī vidhāsyate."</note>

And in the <term>colophon</term><note>A concluding statement in a manuscript or book, often providing details about the author, date, and location of completion.</note> he says that he made the work for the delight of the intelligent in the year 898.

->*This Index of Logic Aphorisms was made for the delight of the intelligent*<-
<note>original: "Nyāyasūcīnibandho 'sāv akāri sudhiyāṁ mude"</note>
->*By the illustrious Vācaspati Miśra, in the year eight-nine-eight.*<-
<note>original: "Çrīvācaspatimiçreṇa vasv-aṅka-vasu-vatsare." The Sanskrit words "vasu" (eight) and "aṅka" (nine) are traditional numerical symbols used to record dates.</note>

It remains to determine whether this year belongs to the era of **Vikramāditya** <note>The Vikrama era, beginning in 57–56 BCE.</note> or of **Śālivāhana** <note>The Śaka era, beginning in 78 CE.</note>. In the introduction to his edition of *Six Buddhist Nyāya Tracts* (*Bibl. Ind.*, 1910), **Mahāmahopādhyāya Haraprasād Shāstrī** gives the date as belonging to the second era, to **Śaka 898** (976 AD). He says (p. iii) that the author of the *Proof of Differentiation* <note>original: "Apohasiddhi"</note> "takes a good deal of pains in elaborately refuting the theory of **Vācaspati Miśra**," and that he does "not quote or refute **Udayana**, whose date is **Śaka 905 = 983 AD**." In his *Notices of Sanskrit Manuscripts*, second series, vol. II, p. xix, this distinguished scholar had come to the same conclusion with regard to the era to which this date of **Vācaspati Miśra** should be assigned.

This conclusion seemed doubtful to Mr. **Nilmani Chakravarti, M. A.**, in his valuable *Chronology of Indian Authors*, a supplement to Miss **Duff's** *Chronology of India* (*Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal*, vol. 3, 1907, p. 205). And one cannot refrain from thinking that the other era is presumably more likely for a Northern writer; and that more especially a great difficulty is created if only seven years are supposed to separate **Vācaspati Miśra** and **Udayana**. The difference between the two philosophers is of such a kind that one must assume a much longer interval between their writings. And furthermore, would it not be an extraordinary coincidence that the author of the *Proof of Differentiation* should be so minutely familiar with the work of **Vācaspati Miśra**, and yet not have the dimmest sense of the existence of **Udayana**, the light of a new dawn in the world of **Nyāya** <note>The Hindu school of logic and epistemology.</note>? Accordingly, the date of **Vācaspati’s** Logic-index would appear to be **Saṁvat 898 = 841 AD**; and the dates of his six other works, including the **Expertise in Truth** <note>original: "Tattva-vāiçāradī"</note>, may be presumed to be not many years earlier or later. We are therefore safe in making the statement that the date of the **Expertise in Truth** is not far from the middle of the ninth century, or approximately **850 AD**.

<summary>This page analyzes a dated colophon to establish that the philosopher Vācaspati Miśra lived in the 9th century, concluding his major works were written around 850 AD.</summary>
<keywords>Vācaspati Miśra, Nyāyasūcīnibandha, chronology, Indian philosophy, Nyāya, 9th century, Udayana, Vikrama era, Śaka era</keywords>

## BOOK THREE—SUPERNORMAL POWERS <note>This section, known as the "Vibhūti Pāda," describes the meditative techniques for achieving profound mental control and the resulting mystical abilities.</note>

# TRANSLATION OF THE APHORISMS ON YOGA <note>original: "Yoga-Sūtras"</note> WITHOUT THE COMMENT OR THE EXPLANATION

## BEING THE APHORISMS <note>original: "Sūtras"</note> TRANSLATED IN GROUPS, TOGETHER WITH GROUP-HEADINGS ADDED BY THE TRANSLATOR

### BOOK FIRST—CONCENTRATION <note>original: "Samādhi Pada"; the first of four chapters, focusing on the definition of Yoga and the mechanics of achieving deep meditative states.</note>

#### **Goal of Concentration**

**i. 1-4.** Yoga is the concentration which restricts the fluctuations <note>original: "vṛttis"; the constant modifications or "whirls" of the mind, such as thoughts, feelings, and perceptions.</note>. Freed from them, the Self <note>the true soul or pure awareness, distinct from the ego.</note> attains to self-expression.

> i. 1 Now the exposition of yoga [is to be made].
> i. 2 Yoga is the restriction of the fluctuations of <term>mind-stuff</term><note>original: "citta"; the collective mental apparatus including the intellect, ego, and subconscious.</note>.
> i. 3 Then the Seer [that is, the Self] abides in himself.
> i. 4 At other times it [the Self] takes the same form as the fluctuations [of mind-stuff] <note>meaning the soul mistakenly identifies itself with thoughts and emotions when the mind is not quieted.</note>.

#### **Forms of the mind-stuff**

**i. 5-11.** The fluctuations are all exposed to attack from the hindrances and are five in number: 1. sources-of-valid-ideas; 2. misconceptions; 3. predicate-relations; 4. sleep; 5. memory.

> i. 5 The fluctuations are of five kinds and are hindered <note>clogged by ego and desire, leading to suffering.</note> or unhindered <note>clarified and leading toward spiritual insight.</note>.
> i. 6 Sources-of-valid-ideas and misconceptions and predicate-relations and sleep and memory.
> i. 7 Sources-of-valid-ideas <note>original: "pramāṇa"; the means by which we gain correct knowledge.</note> are perception and inference and verbal-communication <note>reliable testimony or sacred tradition.</note>.
> i. 8 Misconception <note>original: "viparyaya"</note> is an erroneous idea not based on that form [in respect of which the misconception is entertained].
> i. 9 The <term>conceptualization</term> <note>original: "vikalpa"; a mental construct based on words that lacks a real-world object.</note> is without any [corresponding perceptible] object and follows as a result of perception or of words.
> i. 10 Sleep is a fluctuation of [mind-stuff] supported by the cause of the [transient] negation [of the waking and the dreaming fluctuations] <note>Yoga views sleep as a positive state of mental activity where there is an absence of other thoughts, rather than a total void.</note>.
> i. 11 Memory is not-adding-surreptitiously <note>retaining the impression.</note> to a once experienced object.

#### **Methods of restricting fluctuations**

**i. 12-16.** An orientation of the whole life with reference to one idea; an emotional transformation corresponding to this focused state.

> i. 12 The restriction of them is by [means] of practice and <term>passionlessness</term><note>original: "vairāgya"; the state of being free from worldly cravings or attachments.</note>.
> i. 13 Practice is [repeated] exertion to the end that [the mind-

<summary>This page defines Yoga as the mastery over mental "fluctuations" and begins a detailed taxonomy of the five types of mental activity, ranging from valid knowledge to memory. It establishes the foundational goal: allowing the "Seer" to reside in its true nature rather than being lost in thought.</summary>

<keywords>Yoga-Sūtras, concentration, mental fluctuations, mind-stuff, the Seer, valid knowledge, misconception, conceptualization, memory, practice, passionlessness</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the translation of the first book of the Yoga-Sūtras, picking up mid-sentence from the previous discussion on how to stabilize the mind. [mind-stuff] shall have permanence in this [restricted state]. i. 14 But this [practice] becomes confirmed when it has been cultivated for a long time and uninterruptedly and with earnest attention. i. 15 Passionlessness <note>original: "vairāgya"; the act of letting go of worldly desires.</note> is the consciousness of being master on the part of one who has rid himself of thirst for either seen <note>objects experienced through the senses in this world.</note> or revealed objects <note>rewards promised in sacred texts, such as a place in heaven.</note>. i. 16 This [passionlessness] is highest when discernment of the Self results in thirstlessness for qualities <note>original: "guṇas"; the three fundamental components of nature—equilibrium, activity, and inertia—which make up all material things.</note> [and not merely for objects].

### Kinds of concentration

**i. 17–18.** Four kinds of conscious concentration, and the concentration of subliminal-impressions alone.
> i. 17 [Concentration becomes] conscious [of its object] <note>original: "samprajñāta"; a state of meditation where the mind remains focused on a specific object or thought.</note> by assuming forms either of deliberation [upon coarse objects] or of reflection upon subtile objects or of joy or of the feeling-of-personality. i. 18 The other [concentration which is not conscious of objects] <note>original: "asamprajñāta"; a deeper state where the mind is completely still and no longer focuses on an object.</note> consists of subliminal-impressions only <note>original: "saṃskāras"; the latent mental imprints or "grooves" left behind by past experiences.</note> [after objects have merged], and follows upon that practice which effects the cessation [of fluctuations].

### Degrees of approach to concentration

**i. 19–23.** The worldly approach; the spiritual approach; the combinations of methods and intensities; and the devotion to the highest Self.
> i. 19 [Concentration not conscious of objects] caused by worldly [means] is the one to which the discarnate <note>original: "videhas"; beings such as gods who exist without physical bodies.</note> attain and to which those [whose bodies] are resolved into primary-matter <note>original: "prakṛti-layas"; those whose consciousness has merged back into the fundamental substance of the universe without reaching full liberation.</note> attain. i. 20 [Concentration not conscious of objects,] which follows upon belief [and] energy [and] mindfulness [and] concentration [and] insight, is that to which the others [the yogins] attain. i. 21 For the keenly intense, [concentration] is near. i. 22 Because [this keenness] is gentle or moderate or keen, there is a [concentration] superior even to this [near kind]. i. 23 Or [concentration] is attained by devotion to the <term>Lord</term><note>original: "Īśvara"; the Supreme Being or a specialized consciousness that serves as the ultimate spiritual ideal.</note>.

### Analysis of the highest Self

**i. 24–28.** Unique quality of the highest Self; proof of His existence; His temporal priority; His symbolical realization.
> i. 24 Untouched by hindrances <note>original: "kleśas"; the five causes of suffering, such as ignorance and attachment.</note> or karmas <note>actions and their resulting consequences.</note> or fruition <note>the ripening of the results of past actions.</note> or by latent-deposits <note>subconscious tendencies.</note>, the <term>Lord</term> is a special kind of Self. i. 25 In this [Lord] the germ of the omniscient is at its utmost excellence. i. 26 Teacher of the Primal [Sages] also, forasmuch as [with Him] there is no limitation by time. i. 27 The word expressing Him is the <term>Sacred Syllable</term> <note>original: "Praṇava"; the holy sound "Om".</note>. i. 28 Repetition of it and reflection upon its meaning [should be made].

### **Obstacles to the calming of the mind-stuff**

**i. 29-34.** The internal faculty is vulnerable to distractions. These can be overcome by focusing the mind on a single point, cultivating positive social attitudes, or practicing controlled breathing.

> i. 29 From this practice, the seeker gains a turning-inward of consciousness <note>original: "pratyak-cetana"; the realization of the inner self as opposed to external objects.</note> and the removal of various obstacles. i. 30 These mental distractions are the obstacles: illness, mental laziness, doubt, lack of focus, attachment to sensory objects, false perception, failure to reach a state of concentration, and the inability to remain in that state once it is achieved. i. 31 These distractions are accompanied by physical pain, mental distress, trembling of the body, and labored inhalation or exhalation. i. 32 To prevent these, one should practice focusing on a single principle <note>original: "eka-tattva"; a single truth or object of focus.</note>. i. 33 The mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the collective term for the mind, intellect, and ego.</note> becomes clear and calm by cultivating an attitude of friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, joy toward the virtuous, and neutrality toward those who do wrong. i. 34 Or, the seeker may reach a stable calm through the intentional exhaling and holding of the breath.

### **Attainment of Stability**

**i. 35-39.** Methods for achieving focus through specific sensory or mental objects.

> i. 35 Or, stability is gained when a specialized sensory perception arises, which binds the mind <note>original: "manas"; the central faculty that coordinates the senses.</note> to a state of steadiness. i. 36 Or, focus can be achieved by meditating on an inner light that is free from all suffering. i. 37 Or, the mind-stuff reaches a stable state by taking as its object of meditation a person who has completely mastered their desires. i. 38 Or, the mind-stuff can find stability by reflecting on the insights gained during dreams or deep sleep. i. 39 Or, one may reach stability through meditation upon any object that one finds truly helpful or inspiring.

### **Mastery and concentration**

**i. 40-47.** The definition of mastery and the different levels of mental absorption, where the mind becomes like a clear jewel.

> i. 40 The mastery of such a practitioner extends from the smallest atom to the greatest imaginable magnitude. i. 41 When the mental fluctuations <note>original: "vṛttis"; the constant "whirlpools" or movements of thought.</note> have died away, the mind-stuff becomes like a transparent jewel. It reaches a balanced-state <note>original: "samāpatti"; a state of total absorption where the mind takes on the shape of whatever it observes.</note> where the one who knows, the process of knowing, and the object being known all merge together. i. 42 In this state, a "balanced-state with deliberation" <note>original: "savitarka samāpatti"; a stage of meditation where the mind still mixes the word, the object, and the idea together.</note> is one where the mind is still confused by the relationship between the word used, the actual object, and the knowledge associated with it.

<summary>This page outlines the nine primary obstacles to mental clarity—such as illness and doubt—and provides various techniques for stabilizing the mind, including breath control, ethical attitudes, and focused meditation.</summary>

i. 43 When the memory is quite purified, that <term>balanced-state</term> <note>original: "samāpatti"; a state where the mind is like a clear jewel, reflecting the object of focus without distortion.</note>—which is, as it were, empty of itself and which brightens into conscious knowledge as the intended object and nothing more—is <term>super-deliberative</term> <note>original: "nirvitarka"; a deep state of focus that moves beyond words and logic.</note>. i. 44 By this same balanced-state, the reflective and the super-reflective states are also explained. i. 45 The subtle object also terminates in <term>unresolvable-primary-matter</term> <note>original: "aliṅga"; the most fundamental, formless state of nature.</note>. i. 46 These same balanced-states are the <term>seeded concentration</term> <note>original: "sabīja samādhi"; meditation that still has an object or a "seed" of thought to hold onto.</note>. i. 47 When there is the clearness of the super-reflective balanced-state, the practitioner gains internal undisturbed calm.

### Normative insight

**i. 48-51.** After-effects of concentrated insight efface after-effects of concentration upon objects.

i. 48 In this concentrated mind-stuff, the insight is <term>truth-bearing</term> <note>original: "ṛtambharā"; a state where the mind perceives the essential truth of things directly.</note>. i. 49 This has another object than the insight resulting from things heard or from inferences, inasmuch as its intended object is a particular <note>Unlike logic or learning, this insight reveals the specific, unique nature of an object rather than a general category.</note>. i. 50 The <term>subliminal impression</term> <note>original: "saṃskāra"; the deep-seated mental habits or "grooves" formed by past actions and thoughts.</note> produced by this super-reflective balanced-state is hostile to other subliminal impressions <note>Meaning it helps to overwrite and erase old, negative mental habits.</note>. i. 51 When this subliminal impression also is restricted, since all is restricted, the practitioner gains <term>seedless concentration</term> <note>original: "nirbīja samādhi"; the highest state where even the most subtle mental activity ceases.</note>.

# BOOK SECOND—MEANS OF ATTAINMENT

## Devices for weakening hindrances

**ii. 1-11.** Aids serviceable to the beginner who is on the path to concentration.

ii. 1 Self-castigation, study, and devotion to the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "Īśvara"; the supreme soul or the ideal model of consciousness.</note> are the <term>Yoga of action</term> <note>original: "kriyā-yoga"; the active discipline for those seeking to prepare their minds for deeper meditation.</note>. ii. 2 For the cultivation of concentration and for the attenuation of the hindrances. ii. 3 <term>Undifferentiated consciousness</term> <note>original: "avidyā"; a fundamental ignorance or lack of spiritual awareness.</note>, the feeling-of-personality, passion, aversion, and the will-to-live are the five <term>hindrances</term> <note>original: "kleśas"; the root causes of all human suffering.</note>. ii. 4 Undifferentiated consciousness is the field for the others, whether they be dormant, attenuated, intercepted, or sustained. ii. 5 The recognition of the permanent, of the pure, of pleasure, and of a self in what is impermanent, impure, pain, and not-self is undifferentiated consciousness (*avidyā*). ii. 6 When the power of seeing and the power by which one sees have the appearance of being a single self, this is the feeling-of-personality <note>original: "asmitā"; the ego-driven mistake of identifying the soul with the mind or body.</note>. ii. 7 Passion is that which dwells upon pleasure. ii. 8 Aversion is that which dwells upon pain. ii. 9 The will-to-live <note>original: "abhiniveśa"; the instinctive fear of death and the urge to cling to life.</note>, sweeping on by the force of its own nature, exists in this form even in the wise. ii. 10

These [hindrances when they have become subtile] are to be escaped by the inverse-propagation <note>This refers to the process of "involution," where mental distractions are traceed back to their origins and dissolved into their cause.</note>. ii. 11 The fluctuations of these should be escaped by means of contemplation.

### Karma

**ii. 12–14.** Origin of karma in hindrances; result of karma in state-of-experience, length of life, and pleasure or pain.

> ii. 12 The <term>latent-deposit of karma</term> <note>original: "karmāśaya"; the storehouse of merit and demerit from past actions that remains in the mind.</note> has its root in the hindrances and may be felt in a birth seen <note>the current life</note> or in a birth unseen <note>future lives</note>. ii. 13 So long as the root exists, there will be fruition from it [that is] birth [and] length-of-life [and] kind-of-experience. ii. 14 These [fruitions] have joy or extreme anguish as results in accordance with the quality of their causes whether merit or demerit.

### All is pain

**ii. 15.** Present and future and past correlations with objects result unavoidably in pain.

> ii. 15 As being the pains which are mutations and anxieties and <term>subliminal-impressions</term> <note>original: "saṃskāra"; the deep mental imprints or habits formed by past experience.</note>, and by reason of the opposition of the fluctuations of the aspects (*guṇa* <note>The three fundamental qualities of nature: lucidity (sattva), activity (rajas), and inertia (tamas).</note>),—to the discriminating all is nothing but pain.

### There is an escape

**ii. 16.** Only yogins <note>Practitioners of yoga who have developed spiritual sensitivity.</note> are sensitive to future pain. This may be avoided in that it has not expressed itself in actual suffering.

> ii. 16 That which is to be escaped is pain yet to come.

### Cause of pain

**ii. 17–24.** The Seer-sight relation implies 1. complexes of potential stresses between aspects (*guṇa*) and between sense-organs and elements, 2. the power of the Seer who is undefiled by aspects, 3. the actual correlation until the purpose of the Seer, which is to differentiate consciousness, is completed.

> ii. 17 The correlation of the Seer <note>original: "draṣṭṛ"; the pure consciousness or the Self.</note> and the object-of-sight <note>original: "dṛśya"; the world of matter and experience.</note> is the cause of that which is to be escaped. ii. 18 With a disposition to brightness and to activity and to inertia <note>The three Gunas.</note>, and with the elements and the organs as its essence, and with its purpose the experience and the liberation [of the Self],—this is the object-of-sight. ii. 19 The particularized and the unparticularized [forms] and the resoluble only [into primary matter] and irresoluble-primary-matter—are the divisions of the aspects (*guṇa*). ii. 20 The Seer who is nothing but [the power of seeing], although undefiled (*çuddha* <note>original: "shuddha"; pure, untainted by the qualities of nature.</note>), looks upon the presented idea. ii. 21 The object-of-sight is only for the sake of it [the Self]. ii. 22 Though it has

**ii. 23** The reason for the apperception of what the power of the property and of what the power of the proprietor are, is correlation. <note>This describes the "joint-working" or link between the "Seen" (the world) and the "Seer" (the soul).</note>

**ii. 24** The reason for this [correlation] is <term>undifferentiated-consciousness</term> <note>original: "avidyā"; often translated as spiritual ignorance or a failure to distinguish between the self and the non-self.</note>.

### The escape

**ii. 25.** A positive state of <term>Isolation</term> <note>original: "Kaivalya"; the state of ultimate spiritual freedom and detachment.</note> follows the ending of the correlation.

**ii. 25** Since this [non-sight] does not exist, there is no correlation. This is the escape, the Isolation of the Seer.

### Means of escape

**ii. 26-27.** The act of discrimination leading up to the act of insight.

**ii. 26** The means of attaining escape is unwavering discriminative discernment. **ii. 27** For him [there is] insight sevenfold and advancing in stages to the highest.

### Eight aids to yoga

**ii. 28-29.** To purify the aspects and to intensify intuitive thinking there are five indirect aids and three direct aids.

**ii. 28** After the aids to yoga have been followed up, when the impurity has dwindled, there is an enlightenment of perception reaching up to the discriminative discernment. **ii. 29** Abstentions and observances and postures and regulations-of-the-breath and withdrawal-of-the-senses and fixed-attention and contemplation and concentration. <note>These are the famous eight limbs of Yoga: Yama, Niyama, Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, Pratyāhāra, Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, and Samādhi.</note>

### First indirect aid : i. Five abstentions

**ii. 30-31.** The elements and degrees of morality in the form of prohibitions.

**ii. 30** Abstinence from injury and from falsehood and from theft and from incontinence and from acceptance of gifts are the abstentions. **ii. 31** When they are unqualified by species or place or time or exigency and when [covering] all [these] classes—there is the Great Course-of-conduct. <note>This implies that these ethical rules must be practiced universally, without exception.</note>

### Second indirect aid : ii. Five observances

**ii. 32.** Advances in morality in the form of voluntary action.

**ii. 32** Cleanliness and contentment and self-castigation and study and devotion to <term>the Lord</term> <note>original: "Içvara"; the supreme soul or spiritual guide.</note> are the observances.

### Results of the abstentions and observances

**ii. 33-45.** Persistent inhibitions of certain kinds reorganize an increase of activity of the opposite kind.

**ii. 33** If there be inhibition by perverse-considerations, there should be...
