# BOOK THIRD—SUPERNORMAL POWERS

## First direct aid : vi. Fixed-attention

**iii. 1.** The knower focuses the process of knowing upon the object to be known.
> iii. 1 Binding the mind-stuff <note>original: "citta," referring to the collective functions of the mind, ego, and intellect</note> to a specific place is fixed-attention <note>original: "dharana"</note>.

## Second direct aid : vii. Contemplation

**iii. 2.** A two-term relation between the process of knowing and the object to be known.
> iii. 2 The continuous flow of a single idea toward that place is contemplation <note>original: "dhyana"</note>.

## Third direct aid : viii. Concentration

**iii. 3.** A fusion of the knower and the process of knowing with the object to be known.
> iii. 3 This same contemplation, when it shines forth solely as the object itself, as if emptied of its own form, is concentration <note>original: "samadhi"</note>.

## Transition to seedless concentration

**iii. 4-10.** The direct aids in combination result in insight and restricted subliminal-impressions and the calm flow of the mind-stuff.
> iii. 4 These three practiced together upon a single object constitute constraint <note>original: "samyama"</note>. iii. 5 Through the mastery of this constraint, the light of higher insight <note>original: "prajna"</note> dawns. iii. 6 Its application is achieved in stages. iii. 7 These three are "internal" or direct aids compared to the previous five steps of yoga. iii. 8 Yet, even these three are "external" or indirect aids when compared to seedless concentration <note>A state of meditation where the mind is so still that no "seeds" of thought or objects remain</note>. iii. 9 The mutation of restriction occurs when the subconscious impressions of an outgoing mind disappear and the impressions of restraint appear, becoming part of the mind-stuff at the moment of control. iii. 10 The mind-stuff flows peacefully because of these ingrained habits of restraint.

## Mutations of substances

**iii. 11-15.** In the focused state the concentration holds two time-forms within the span of attention. Mutations are in fixed orders of subliminal-impressions <gloss>primordial nature</gloss> <note>original: "prakṛti"</note> in the restricted state.
> iii. 11 The mutation of concentration is the fading of many-centeredness and the rising of one-pointedness within the mind-stuff. iii. 12 Then, once more, when the thought that has just passed and the thought that has just arisen are exactly alike, the mind-stuff has reached a state of one-pointed mutation. iii. 13 By this, the changes in the external characteristics, the time-state, and the condition of both physical elements and the sensory organs are explained. iii. 14 The substance <note>The underlying reality or "subject" that remains while its qualities change</note> remains the same throughout its past, present, and yet-to-be-manifested qualities. iii. 15 The variation in the sequence of these changes is the reason for the variation in the transformations.

### Application of constraints to different orders of mutations

**iii. 16-52.** When a single <term>mutation<note>original: "parinama"; the process by which an object changes its state, appearance, or temporal condition</note></term>—whether of its outward form, its time-state, or its intensity—is understood, the entire sequence of change comes under the control of the practitioner's concentrated insight.

iii. 16 As a result of <term>constraint<note>original: "samyama"; the unified practice of fixed-attention, contemplation, and concentration</note></term> upon the three mutations [there follows] the knowledge of the past and the future. 

iii. 17 Words, the objects they represent, and the ideas associated with them are often confused because they are mistakenly identified as being the same. By practicing constraint upon the distinctions between these three, there arises the [intuitive] knowledge of the sounds and cries of all living beings.

iii. 18 As a result of direct perception of <term>subliminal-impressions<note>original: "samskaras"; the deep-seated mental habits or "seeds" left by past actions</note></term>, there is [intuitive] knowledge of previous births. 

iii. 19 [As a result of constraint] upon a presented-idea [there arises intuitive] knowledge of the <term>mind-stuff<note>original: "citta"; the collective functions of the mind including the intellect and ego</note></term> of another person. 

iii. 20 But [this intuitive knowledge of another's mind] does not include the object that the person is currently thinking about, since that object is not-in-the-field of the practitioner's own consciousness. 

iii. 21 As a result of constraint upon the outer form of the body, the power of the body to be perceived by others is suspended. When the light from the body is disconnected from the eyes of an observer, the <term>practitioner's<note>original: "yogin"</note></term> body becomes invisible. 

iii. 22 <term>Action<note>original: "karma"</note></term> is of two types: that which bears fruit quickly (advancing) and that which bears fruit slowly (not-advancing). As a result of constraint upon these actions, or by observing the signs of approaching death, there arises an intuitive knowledge of the time of one's own end. 

iii. 23 [As a result of constraint] upon friendliness and other sentiments, there arise great powers [of friendliness]. 

iii. 24 [As a result of constraint] upon various strengths, there arise powers like those of an elephant. 

iii. 25 As a result of directing the light of higher sensory activity, there arises [intuitive] knowledge of things that are subtle, hidden, or far away. 

iii. 26 As a result of constraint upon the sun [there arises the intuitive] knowledge of the various regions of the universe. 

iii. 27 [As a result of constraint] upon the moon [there arises the intuitive] knowledge of the arrangement of the stars. 

iii. 28 [As a result of constraint] upon the pole-star [there arises the intuitive] knowledge of the movements of the stars. 

iii. 29 [As a result of constraint] upon the "wheel of the navel" <note>This refers to the *manipura chakra*, an energy center located near the solar plexus</note> [there arises intuitive] knowledge of the arrangement of the physical body. 

iii. 30 [As a result of constraint] upon the "well of the throat" [there follows] the cessation of hunger and thirst. 

iii. 31 [As a result of constraint] upon the "tortoise-tube" <note>original: "kurma-nadi"; a subtle energy channel in the chest believed to govern physical and mental stability</note> [there follows] the absolute motionlessness of the mind-stuff. 

iii. 32 [As a result of constraint] upon the radiance in the head [there follows] the sight of the <term>Perfected Beings<note>original: "Siddhas"; semi-divine masters who have attained spiritual completion</note></term>. 

iii. 33 Or, as a result of spontaneous <term>vividness<note>original: "pratibha"; an intuitive "flash" of light or sudden spiritual insight that reveals truth without effort</note></term>, the practitioner discerns all things. 

iii. 34 [As a result of constraint] upon the heart [there arises] a consciousness of the nature of the mind-stuff. 

iii. 35 Experience consists of ideas that fail to distinguish between the <term>purity<note>original: "sattva"; the highest, most transparent quality of the mind</note></term> of the mind and the <term>Self<note>original: "Purusa"; the true, unchanging consciousness that is distinct from the mind</note></term>, which are in fact completely different. Since the pure mind exists for the sake of the Self, [intuitive] knowledge of the Self arises as the result of constraint upon that which exists for... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

iii. 53 As a result of this <note>The practice of "constraint" on moments and their sequence</note> there arises the deeper-knowledge of two equivalent things which cannot be distinctly qualified in species or characteristic-mark or point-of-space. <note>This refers to the ability to distinguish between two identical objects, such as two atoms, which normally cannot be told apart by the senses.</note> iii. 54 The [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination is a deliverer, has all things as its object, and has all times for its object, and is an [inclusive whole] without sequence. <note>This "delivering" knowledge (<term>tāraka-jñānam</term>) is described as a total, instantaneous realization that transcends the linear flow of time and space.</note> iii. 55 When the purity of the *sattva* <note>original: "sattva"; the quality of light, clarity, and harmony in the mind</note> and of the Self are equal there is Isolation. <note>original: "kaivalya"; the state of absolute freedom and liberation where the soul is no longer entangled with material nature.</note>

## BOOK FOURTH—ISOLATION
### Substances and subconsciousness

**iv. 1–13. Correspondence between imperceptible forms of substance and latent-impressions of concentrated states.**

iv. 1 Perfections proceed from birth or from drugs or from spells or from self-castigation or from concentration. <note>These "perfections" (<term>siddhis</term>) can be innate, chemically induced, or achieved through discipline and meditation.</note> iv. 2 The mutation into another birth is the result of the filling in of the evolving-cause. <note>Nature flows into new forms as obstacles are removed.</note> iv. 3 The efficient cause gives no impulse to the evolving-causes but [the mutation] follows when the barrier [to the evolving-cause] is cut, as happens with the peasant. <note>Just as a farmer opens a sluice-gate to let water flow naturally into a field, the yogin removes obstacles so that nature can evolve toward higher states.</note> iv. 4 Created mind-stuffs may result from the sense-of-personality and from this alone. <note>A highly advanced practitioner may create multiple bodies and minds from their own ego-sense.</note> iv. 5 While there is a variety of actions, the mind-stuff which impels the many is one. iv. 6 Of these [five perfections] that which proceeds from contemplation leaves no latent-deposit. <note>Unlike powers gained through drugs or spells, the results of meditation do not create new karmic debts.</note> iv. 7 The yogin’s *karma* is neither-white-nor-black; [the *karma*] of others is of three kinds. <note>original: "karma"; actions and their consequences. The three kinds for others are good (white), bad (black), and mixed.</note> iv. 8 As a result of this there follows the manifestation of those subconscious-impressions only which correspond to the fruition of their [*karma*]. iv. 9 There is an uninterrupted-causal-relation [of subconscious-impressions], although remote in species and point-of-space and moment-of-time, by reason of the correspondence between memory and subliminal-impressions. <note>Even across different lifetimes, our deep-seated habits and memories remain linked.</note> iv. 10 Furthermore the [subconscious-impressions] have no beginning [that we can set in time], since desire is permanent. <note>The will to live and the thirst for experience are seen as eternal forces driving rebirth.</note> iv. 11 Since [subconscious-impressions] are associated with cause and motive and mental-substrate and stimulus, if these cease to be, then those [subconscious-impressions] cease to be. iv. 12 Past and future as such exist; [therefore subconscious-impressions do not cease to be]. For the different time-forms belong to the external-aspects. iv. 13 These [external-aspects with the three time-forms] are phenomenalized [individuals] or subtile [generic-forms] and their essence is the aspects (*guṇa*). <note>original: "guṇa"; the three fundamental qualities—sattva (purity), rajas (activity), and tamas (inertia)—that make up all material reality.</note>

### Polemic against Idealism

**iv. 14–23. Knowledge of the stream of consciousness is impossible unless it be a permanent order as contrasted with a succession of transient appearances.**

iv. 14 The that-ness of a thing is due to a singleness of mutation.

iv. 15. Because, while the [physical] thing remains the same, the mind-stuffs are different, [therefore the two are upon] distinct levels-of-existence. <note>This verse argues against idealism; it suggests that because different people can perceive the same object differently, the object itself must exist independently of any single person's mind.</note> iv. 16 And a thing is not dependent upon a single mind-stuff, [for then in certain cases] it could not be proved [by that mind-stuff], [and] then what would it be? iv. 17 A thing is known or not known by virtue of its affecting [or not affecting] the mind-stuff. iv. 18 Unintermittently the Master of that [mind-stuff] knows the fluctuations of mind-stuff [and thus] the Self undergoes-no-mutations. <note>The "Master" refers to the <term>Puruṣa</term> (the true Self), which is unchanging and merely observes the constant changes within the mind.</note> iv. 19 It does not illumine itself, since it is an object-for-sight. <note>The mind is seen as a subtle material tool; it cannot see itself any more than an eye can see itself without a mirror.</note> iv. 20 And there cannot be a cognition of both [thinking-substance and thing] at the same time. iv. 21 If [one mind-stuff] were the object-for-sight for another, there would be an infinite regress from one thinking-substance to another thinking-substance as well as confusion of memory. iv. 22 The Intellect (*<term>citi</term>*) <note>original: "citi"; the power of pure consciousness</note> which unites not [with objects] is conscious of its own thinking-substance when [the mind-stuff] takes the form of that [thinking-substance by reflecting it]. iv. 23 Mind-stuff affected by the <term>Seer</term> <note>The pure conscious subject</note> and by the object-for-sight [leads to the perception of] all intended-objects.

## Complete Self-realization of the Self

**iv. 24-34.** All hindrances subside; all acts of the Self are spontaneous and free; absence of limitations which thwart one who wishes to attain the ultimate ideal of his own nature.

iv. 24 This [mind-stuff], although diversified by countless subconscious-impressions, exists for the sake of another, because its nature is to produce [things as] combinations. <note>Just as a house exists for the inhabitant and not for itself, the mind exists for the sake of the Self.</note> iv. 25 For him who sees the distinction, pondering upon his own states-of-being ceases. iv. 26 Then the mind-stuff is borne down to discrimination, onward towards <term>Isolation</term>. <note>original: "kaivalya"; the state of ultimate liberation.</note> iv. 27 In the intervals of this [mind-stuff] there are other presented-ideas [coming] from <term>subliminal-impressions</term>. <note>original: "saṃskāra"; the deep-seated mental habits or traces of past actions.</note> iv. 28 The escape from these [subliminal-impressions] is described as being like [the escape from] the hindrances. iv. 29 For one who is not usurious even in respect of Elevation, there follows in every case as a result of discriminative discernment the concentration [called] <term>Rain-cloud of [knowable] things</term>. <note>original: "dharma-megha-samādhi"; a state where virtue and knowledge shower down upon the practitioner, ending all struggle.</note> iv. 30 Then follows the cessation of the hindrances and of <term>karma</term>. <note>The cycle of cause and effect produced by actions is finally broken.</note> iv. 31 Then, because of the endlessness of knowledge from which all obscuring defilements have passed away, what is yet to be known amounts to little. iv. 32 When as a result of this the aspects (*<term>guna</term>*) <note>original: "guṇa"; the three fundamental qualities of nature—purity, activity, and inertia—that make up the physical and mental world.</note> have fulfilled their purpose, they attain to the limit of the sequence of mutations. iv. 33 The positive correlate to the moment, recognized as such at the final limit of the mutation, is a sequence. iv. 34 <term>Isolation</term> is the inverse generation of the aspects, no longer provided with a purpose by the Self, or it is the <term>Energy of Intellect</term> grounded in itself. <note>This final verse defines liberation as the state where the forces of nature retire, having completed their work, leaving pure consciousness to shine in its own light.</note>

<summary>This concluding section of the Yoga Sūtras explains the transition from mental discipline to total spiritual liberation (Kaivalya). It clarifies that while the mind is a complex mechanism of nature, it exists solely for the experience and eventual liberation of the unchanging Self.</summary>

# NOTICE TO THE READER

Patañjali's **Mnemonic Rules** or <term>Yoga-sūtras <note>Sanskrit: aphorisms or threads of thought</note></term> are divided into four books as follows :

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Book 1. Concentration** <note>original: Samādhi</note>, with 51 rules or *sūtras*, — | pages 1 to 100 ; |
| **Book 2. Means of attainment** <note>original: Sādhana</note>, with 55 *sūtras*, — | pages 101 to 200 ; |
| **Book 3. Supernormal powers** <note>original: Vibhūti</note>, with 55 *sūtras*, — | pages 201 to 296 ; |
| **Book 4. Isolation** <note>original: Kāivalya; the state of absolute freedom</note>, with 34 *sūtras*, — | pages 297 to 348. |

In all, there are 195 rules. Their extreme brevity is apparent when they are printed continuously, as at the end of the <term>Ānanda-āçrama edition <note>A famous series of Sanskrit texts published in Pune, India</note></term>, where the entire text of the rules occupies only between four and five pages.

The **Comment** or <term>Bhāṣya <note>The primary commentary attributed to Vyāsa</note></term>, usually after a brief <term>introductory paragraph <note>original: avatāraṇa</note></term> or phrase, takes up the rules, one by one, and gives first the text and then the meaning thereof.

**Vācaspatimiçra's Explanation** <note>Vācaspatimiçra was a 10th-century scholar who wrote the Tattva-vaiśāradī, a sub-commentary on Vyāsa's work</note> is of course in the first instance an explanation of the Comment ; but since the Comment comprehends also the Rules, it is in fact an explanation of both Rules and Comment. In the body of this volume, the Explanation is not put all together by itself, but is made to keep pace with the Comment, rule by rule.

### Meaning of the Differences of Type

The translation of the Rules is set in <term>pica type <note>A standard size of font, approximately 12 points</note></term> of full-faced <term>Clarendon style <note>A bold, heavy typeface used here to make the primary rules stand out</note></term> ;
The translation of the Comment is set in <term>pica type</term> of <term>Roman style <note>Standard upright type</note></term> ;
The translation of the Explanation is set in <term>long primer type <note>A smaller font size, approximately 10 points, used for secondary commentary</note></term> of <term>Roman style</term>.

Single angles (like these < >) indicate that the words which they enclose are taken from the particular Rule or **Yoga-sūtra** under discussion.
Double angles (like these « ») indicate that the words which they enclose are taken from the Comment or <term>Yoga-bhāṣya <note>The commentary on the Yoga-sūtras</note></term>.
Double quotation marks (“ ”) indicate that the words which they enclose are taken from some authoritative text.
Single quotation marks (‘ ’) indicate that the words which they enclose are the objections or questions of an opponent, or are a quotation from some unauthoritative text.
A half-parenthesis on its side (◡) is used between two vowels to show that they are printed in violation of the rules of <term>euphonic combination <note>Known as 'Sandhi' in Sanskrit, these rules govern how sounds change when words meet</note></term>.

Of this [sūtra] the first portion, the word <term>now <note>original: atha</note></term>, he [the author of the Comment] discusses in the phrase «The expression <now> indicates that a distinct topic commences here.» [The word <now> is used] as in [the sūtra] “ Now¹ this is the Light <note>original: Jyotis; referring to a specific Vedic ritual chant</note> ”. # Conditions required for a beginning [-i. 1]

Thus it is [by insisting upon the authoritativeness of the book] that [Patañjali] refuses to say that [the book may begin] immediately after his understanding the truth and his desire to announce. But if it be agreed that [the word <now> indicates] that a distinct topic commences, then when once yoga has been mentioned as the topic of the book, the student easily understands the announcement of the import of the book as a whole and is started into action. 

Now every one knows from <term>Revealed Scripture <note>original: Śruti; the most authoritative Hindu texts, like the Vedas</note></term> and <term>Tradition <note>original: Smṛti; remembered laws and teachings</note></term> and the Epics and the <term>Ancient Histories <note>original: Purāṇas</note></term> that concentration is the cause of final bliss [and that yoga is authoritative]. Some one might ask, ‘If the word <now> indicates that a distinct topic commences in all those works to which it is attached, then, if this is so, would not such an announcement ¹ as, “Now therefore the inquiry into the Absolute <note>original: Brahma</note> [is to be made]” also be included?’ To prevent this mistake [the commentator] uses the word <<here.>> 

[Again], some one cites the <term>Law-book of the Yogi Yajñavalkya <note>original: Yogiyājñavalkyasmṛti</note></term>, “The Golden Embryo <note>original: Hiraṇyagarbha; the primordial creator</note> and no other of ancient days is he who gave utterance (*vaktā*) to yoga” and asks how it can be said that Patañjali gives utterance to the authoritative book on yoga. In reply the author of the aphorism says <the exposition>: exposition in the sense of expounding something previously expounded. When then the word <now> signifies that here a distinct topic commences, then the point of the statement is quite consistent.

Accordingly he says, <<The authoritative work which expounds yoga ... as commenced>>. Here an objector interrupts, ‘The topic which is commenced here is not the authoritative work, but yoga in so far as it is taught.’ In reply to which, he says <<is to be understood.>> True, we are beginning yoga in so far as it is taught. But the instrument which is to teach this [yoga] is the authoritative work which deals with the same. Moreover the teacher’s activity has to do more immediately with the instrument than with the thing he works upon. Accordingly, with emphasis upon the activity of the author (*kartṛ*), we are to understand that the authoritative work which deals with yoga is commenced. But the topic commenced is that yoga only which is limited in its activity by an authoritative work. This is the real point. 

And one must suppose that the hearing of the word <now>, which means that a distinct topic has commenced, suggests—like the sight of a water-jar ² carried [on a girl’s shoulder at early morning]—another meaning, [namely,] it serves as an auspicious beginning.

Doubt as to the actual thing [yoga] is occasioned by doubt as to the meaning of the word [yoga]. This [doubt] he removes by stating that [<<yoga>> in the phrase] <<yoga is concentration>> is etymologically derived from the stem <note>original: yuj-a; from the Dhatupatha dictionary iv. 68</note> in the sense of concentration and not from the stem <note>original: yuj-i; vii. 7</note> in the sense of conjunction or union.

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the first aphorism of the Yoga Sūtras. # Book I. Concentration or <term>Samādhi <note>A state of intense concentration or meditative absorption where the mind becomes one with the object of contemplation.</note></term>

...in the words «But this.» The word **"and"** <note>original: ca</note> has the sense of **«but»** and distinguishes the whole from the part.—«Which belongs to all the stages» refers to the stages or states which are to be described: the **"Honeyed"** <note>original: Madhumatī; a stage of high spiritual insight</note> [iii. 48], the **"Honey-like"** <note>original: Madhu-pratīkā</note> [iii. 48], the **"Sorrowless"** <note>original: Viçoka</note> [i. 36], and the **"Residual Impressions"** <note>original: Saṁskāraceṣā</note> [iii. 9]. These belong to the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: citta; the collective mental functions including the subconscious and intellect</note></term>. In all these stages is found that <term>yoga <note>The practice of calming the mind to achieve liberation</note></term>, the more special mark of which is the restriction of the mind-stuff. 

But concentration is only a part of this and does not share this same special mark. The words «yoga is concentration» are a statement for etymological purposes only, used when one is not focusing on the difference between the whole and its parts. However, when referring to the practical purpose of what he calls «yoga,» he says it is the restriction of the fluctuations of mind-stuff: this is the stricter sense of the term. 

To those <note>The Vaiçeṣikas, a school of ancient Indian philosophy that focused on logic and physics</note> who hold the view that fluctuations are sensations inherent in the soul and that therefore the restriction of them would also involve the **soul** <note>original: ātman</note> in which they inhere—to these people, in rebuttal, he says it is «a quality of the mind-stuff.» The term **mind-stuff** <note>original: citta</note> he uses as a partial expression for the <term>inner-organ <note>original: antaḥkaraṇa; the internal faculty of processing thought</note></term> or the **thinking-substance** <note>original: buddhi; the higher intellect</note>. The point is that the **Absolutely-eternal Energy of Intellect** <note>original: citi-çakti; pure consciousness</note>, being immutable, cannot have sensations as its properties; but the thinking-substance can.

An objector says, ‘This may be so. But if yoga belongs to all its stages—why then! Sir, since you concede that the restless, the infatuated, and the distracted states also are stages of mind-stuff, and since there would be among these states a restriction of fluctuations, then "yoga" would have to include these states also.’ 

In replying to this difficulty, he makes clear which stages are to be included and which are not included in yoga by the words beginning with **«the restless.»** 

i. The **restless** <note>original: kṣipta</note>, incessantly thrown by the force of <term>rajas <note>the quality of energy, movement, and passion</note></term> upon this or that object, is excessively unstable; 
ii. the **infatuated** <note>original: mūḍha</note>, because of a preponderance of <term>tamas <note>the quality of darkness, inertia, and ignorance</note></term>, is filled with the fluctuation of sleep; 
iii. the **distracted** <note>original: vikṣipta</note> differs from the restless in that, although prevailingly unstable, it is occasionally stable—this instability being either natural or generated by diseases, languor, and other obstacles to be described later [i. 30]; 
iv. the **single-in-intent** <note>original: ekāgra</note> is the focused mind; 
v. the **restricted** <note>original: niruddha</note> mind-stuff is that in which all the fluctuations are restricted and in which nothing remains but **subliminal-impressions** <note>original: saṁskāra; the latent memories or tendencies left behind by past experiences</note>. 

In spite of the fact that certain fluctuations of the restless and the infatuated (the first two of these five stages) are restricted by each other, they are still far removed from being called "yoga." This is because these two states are not even indirectly causes of final bliss; in fact, they work against it. However, in the case of the **distracted** state, since it occasionally has stability when directed towards a real object, he denies that it can be yoga in the words «Of these stages.» When the mind is distracted, the concentration which is the occasional stability of the mind-stuff...

---

### 7] States of mind-stuff fit for Yoga [-i. 1]

...when directed to a real object, cannot properly be called <term>yoga <note>The practice of calming the mind to achieve spiritual liberation.</note></term>. Why [cannot this be called yoga]? Because it has come under the adverse influence of distraction, which is the opposite of this [yoga]. When fallen into the hands (<note>original: antargata</note>) of a troop of opponents, it is hard for a thing to be even what it is, and it is still harder for it to produce effects. Just as anyone can see that a seed which has fallen into the fire and stayed there three or four moments has not the power of sprouting, even if sown: this is the real meaning. 

If then concentration which has come under the adverse influence of distraction be not yoga, what then is yoga? To this he makes answer: "But that [state] which, when the mind is single-in-intent." By the word "real" (<note>original: bhūta</note>) he excludes [any] imaginary [object]. Since sleep, a fluctuation of <term>mind-stuff <note>original: citta; the collective functions of the mind including the subconscious.</note></term>, is also single-in-intent with regard to <term>inertia <note>original: tamas; the quality of darkness, heaviness, or stability.</note></term>—a real (<note>original: bhūta</note>) object, the peculiar (<note>original: sva</note>) [aspect of a substance <note>‘Aspect of a substance’ refers to the Sanskrit terms dharma (quality) or parināma (transformation).</note>] upon which it [sleep] depends (<note>original: ālambana</note>)—so he says "distinct" (<note>original: sad</note>); which means it is clear (<note>original: çobhana</note>), in which the <term>clarity <note>original: sattva; the quality of light, goodness, and purity.</note></term> [aspect] becomes evident in a very high degree. 

But that thing is not clear in which <term>inertia <note>original: tamas</note></term> is in preponderance, inasmuch as it, [the inertia,] is the cause of hindrances. Now the perception of a thing either by verbal communication (<note>original: āgama</note>) or by inference may, we grant, be luminous (<note>original: dyotanam bhavad api</note>); still, in so far as it is mediately known, it does not destroy <term>undifferentiated-consciousness <note>original: avidyā; spiritual ignorance or the primary cause of suffering.</note></term> which we directly experience. For in such [illusions as the sight of] two moons or a defective sense of orientation, [verbal communications or inferences] do not destroy undifferentiated-consciousness. 

Accordingly he uses the word "fully" (<note>original: pra</note>), because it means luminous to the full extent (<note>original: pra-karṣam</note>) and because it alludes to immediate perception [in the case of yoga]. The <term>feeling-of-personality <note>original: asmitā; the ego or 'I-am-ness'.</note></term> and the other hindrances have their root in undifferentiated-consciousness (<note>original: avidyā</note>). Furthermore, since knowledge (<note>original: vidyā</note>) destroys undifferentiated-consciousness (<note>original: avidyā</note>); and since, when knowledge emerges, the hindrances [arising] from undifferentiated-consciousness and so on are destroyed, inasmuch as they are contrary the one to the other, and inasmuch as [then] the cause [of the hindrances] would be destroyed; therefore he says "and causes [the hindrances] to dwindle." 

This, then, is the reason why [yoga] slackens the bonds which consist of <term>karma <note>The law of cause and effect based on one's actions.</note></term>.—And in this passage, by a figurative use of the cause for the effect, he employs the word "karma," whereas subtile-influences (<note>original: apūrva; the latent results of actions</note>) are intended.—The word "slackens" means brings [them] down from their operation. For later [ii. 13] he says, "So long as the root exists, [there will be] fruition from it." And finally it "sets before it as a goal the restriction [of all fluctuations]."—Moreover since this [yoga] conscious of objects is four-fold, he employs the words [beginning] "This [conscious yoga]." He describes [the yoga] not conscious of objects with the words "all the fluctuations." [In other words,] we know (<note>original: kila</note>) that sources-of-valid-ideas and other fluctuations (<note>original: pramāṇādivṛtti</note>) made of <term>passion <note>original: rajas; the quality of activity and motion.</note></term> and <term>inertia <note>original: tamas</note></term> are

### i. 2—] Book I. Concentration or <term>Samādhi <note>A state of deep meditative absorption or "putting together" of the mind.</note></term>

Every thing, inasmuch as it is made up of three aspects <note>These are the three "gunas" or qualities: purity (sattva), energy (rajas), and inertia (tamas).</note> and inasmuch as these aspects are not in equilibrium, has a multitude of <term>mutations <note>original: pariṇāma; the process of one state transforming into another</note></term> arising from a multitude of reciprocal antagonisms; and thus may consistently have many states. The commentator shows that the "restless" and other stages of the mind-stuff have, according to circumstances, a variety of subordinate states. 

«For . . . which is vividness.» 

The mind-stuff's <term>purity <note>original: sattva; the quality of light and clarity</note></term> is <term>purity</term> in its form as a mutation of the mind-stuff; and this purity, in its form as vividness, is thus shown to be a preponderance of the <term>purity</term> quality within the mind-stuff. In this mind-stuff, when <term>energy <note>original: rajas; the quality of movement and passion</note></term> and <term>inertia <note>original: tamas; the quality of darkness and stability</note></term> are somewhat less than the <term>purity</term>, and when those two are equal to each other, <term>then <note>original: tadā</note></term> the mind-stuff is that thing described in the Comment which acquires a fondness for supremacy and for objects-of-sense, such as sound and so on. 

Although the mind-stuff, under the predominance of <term>purity</term>, desires to meditate upon <term>reality <note>original: tattva; the "that-ness" or true principle of existence</note></term>, still, when that reality is concealed by <term>inertia</term>, it thinks that such supremacies as <term>atomization <note>original: aṇiman; the supernatural power to become as small as an atom</note></term> are the true reality and desires to meditate upon <term>them <note>original: tad</note></term>. It meditates for a moment, and then, caught by <term>energy</term>, although obtaining no permanence in its meditation on them, it gains nothing except a fondness for these things. But its natural inclination towards sound and other objects of sense is quite well known. Accordingly, in this way, the mind-stuff is said to be distracted.

While describing the restless mind-stuff, he alludes also to the "infatuated" state: 

«the very same . . . with <term>inertia <note>original: tamas</note></term>.» 

Now, when <term>inertia</term> suppresses <term>energy</term> and extends itself, then—since <term>energy</term> has become incapable of removing the <term>inertia</term> which covers the mind-stuff’s <term>purity</term>—the mind-stuff covered with <term>inertia</term> tends towards demerit and other forms of ignorance. 

«Non-perception» is declared to be misconceived perception [i. 8], and also to be sleep-perception [i. 10], which is <term>supported <note>original: ālambana; having a foundation or mental object</note></term> by a <term>cause <note>original: pratyaya; a mental concept or underlying intent</note></term> of a transient negation. And from this word comes the <term>suggestion <note>original: sūcitā</note></term> of the "infatuated" state also. 

A «failure of its own rightful supremacy» is an obstruction to one's will in every direction. Thus it is that mind-stuff becomes pervaded with demerit and other forms of ignorance. But when this same substance of the mind-stuff comes to have its quality of <term>purity</term> manifest, its cover of <term>inertia</term> removed, and is accompanied by <term>energy</term>, then it tends—as the author says—towards merit and perception and passionless and rightful supremacy, as he says in the phrase «dwindled away.» 

That substance of the mind-stuff is referred to where the covering—that is, the quality of <term>inertia</term>, that is, the "infatuated" state—has <term>almost entirely <note>original: prakarṣeṇa; thoroughly or prominently</note></term> dwindled. For the same reason, «it is illumined in its totality»: in <term>particular effects <note>original: viśeṣa</note></term> and <term>non-particular causes <note>original: aviśeṣa</note></term> and in the <term>manifest mark <note>original: liṅga; the "resoluble" components of nature</note></term> and the <term>unmanifest bearer <note>original: liṅgin; the "irresoluble" primary matter</note></term> [see ii. 19] and the Self. Still, it has not the capacity for merit and rightful supremacy since it lacks activity. With regard to this he says, «pervaded by <term>energy</term> only.» In other words, when <term>energy</term> is the active agent, merit and the rest do persist. ### Functions of the mind-stuff [—i. 2]

In the <term>honeyed stage <note>original: Madhubhūmika; a level of insight where the yogi gains a "sweet" or direct perception of reality.</note></term> and the stage of the <term>one whose light is insight <note>original: Prajñājyotis; a practitioner who has attained a high degree of clarity.</note></term>, both of whom have reached a state of concentration that is still focused on an object, the <term>purity <note>original: sattva; the quality of light, clarity, and goodness.</note></term> of the mind-stuff is included. He now describes the state of the mind-stuff of the fourth class of contemplators, the <term>one who has transcended the state of meditation <note>original: Atikrāntabhāvanīya; the highest level of yogi before final liberation.</note></term>, with the words "the same." Since the stain of the last vestige of <term>passion <note>original: rajas; the quality of activity and attachment.</note></term> is removed, the mind-stuff is grounded in itself. 

Now the gold of the <term>purity <note>original: sattva</note></term> of the <term>intellect <note>original: buddhi; the "thinking-substance" that makes decisions.</note></term>—when once the stain of <term>passion</term> and <term>inertia <note>original: tamas; the quality of darkness and lethargy.</note></term> is purified by the "crucible-cooking" <note>original: puṭa-pāka; a technical term for a process of intense purification through heat, like refining metal.</note>, which consists of practice and passionlessness—has withdrawn the organs that deal with the senses and is grounded in itself. It still has one <term>further task <note>original: para kārya</note></term> to perform: the discriminative discernment between the pure substance of the mind and the true Self. This discernment continues as long as its <term>purpose <note>original: adhikāra</note></term> is unfinished. With this in mind, the author says "the mind-stuff." 

The mind-stuff, which is now nothing more than this discernment between the mind's purity and the Self, moves toward the state of contemplation called the <term>Rain-cloud of Knowable Things <note>original: Dharma-megha-samādhi; a state where the yogi is showered with the highest truth before liberation.</note></term>. This state will be described later in book four, aphorism 29. He explains what is perfectly clear to <term>yogis</term> regarding this state: "this... is the highest." The mind-stuff, which acts as the discernment of the difference between the mind’s purity and the Self and lasts until the <term>Rain-cloud of Knowable Things</term>, is called the highest **Elevation** by contemplators. If one does not wish to distinguish between the mind and its properties, this **Elevation** may be seen as being the same as the mind-stuff itself.

To introduce the <term>Concentration of Restriction <note>original: Nirodha-samādhi; the state where all mental fluctuations cease.</note></term> as the reason for letting go of even this discernment and for accepting the <term>Power of Consciousness <note>original: Citi-śakti; the "Energy of Intellect" or the true, unchanging Self.</note></term>, he shows the excellence of consciousness and the lower value of even the highest insight with the phrase "the Power of Consciousness" and what follows.

Impurity consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Even pleasure and delusion bring pain to a person of discernment; therefore, like pain, they must be escaped. Furthermore, even exceptional beauty eventually ends, and thus it causes pain. Accordingly, the person of discernment must reject that as well. Since this impurity and this "ending" do not happen in the <term>Power of Consciousness</term>, which is the true Self, it is said to be "undefiled and unending." 

An objection is raised: "How can <term>this <note>original: iyaṃ; referring here to the Power of Consciousness.</note></term> be free from defilement if, by being aware of things that consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, it takes on their form? And how can it be unending if it accepts and rejects these forms?" 

In reply, it is said "it has objects shown to it." The <term>Power of Consciousness</term> is that to which various objects are merely shown. The objection would be correct if the consciousness took on the form of objects, just as the <term>intellect</term> does. However, it is only the <term>intellect</term> that <term>undergoes changes <note>original: pariṇatā satī; transforming or mutating in form.</note></term> to match the objects it perceives. The intellect shows the object to the <term>Power of Consciousness</term>, but the consciousness itself does not take their...

# Book I. Concentration or <term>Samādhi <note>A state of deep meditative absorption where the observer and the object of meditation become one.</note></term>
<meta>i. 2—</meta>

form. And when this happens, the <term>Self <note>original: Puruṣa; the pure, unchanging consciousness that is the true witness of our lives.</note></term> is then said to become aware of the objects. 

A skeptical voice asks, “How can the <term>Energy of Intellect <note>original: Citi-śakti; the power of pure awareness.</note></term>—unless it strikes upon the <term>thinking-substance <note>original: citta; the mental mirror or mind-stuff.</note></term> which has taken the form of some object—know that object? Or, if it does strike upon that object, how is it that it does not itself undergo a change into the form of that object?” 

To this, the author replies that the Self **does not unite** with objects. Union here implies a kind of contagion or "rubbing off" of qualities; the author’s meaning is that none of this occurs within the pure Intellect. If anyone asks why there is no such union of this Intellect with objects, the reply is that it **is immutable**. 

Mutation—which consists of the three-fold character of <term>external aspect <note>original: dharma</note></term>, <term>time-variation <note>original: lakṣaṇa</note></term>, and <term>intensity <note>original: avasthā</note></term>—does not belong to the Energy of Intellect also <note>original: api</note> in the same way that it belongs to the mind-stuff. The Intellect does not pass into a change in the form of an action, nor does it mutate to match the thinking-substance. The author will now show how it is possible for this Energy, even if it does not unite with objects, to still be conscious of them. 

This much is established: the Energy of Thought is unsullied by the <term>qualities of nature <note>original: guṇas; the fundamental forces of purity, activity, and inertia.</note></term>. However, it has been stated that even <term>discriminative discernment <note>original: viveka-khyāti; the highest form of intellectual understanding</note></term> is not unsullied, since its very essence is part of the thinking-substance. It is **therefore contrary** to this pure Energy of Intellect. The real meaning here is: if even this highest discernment is to be eventually set aside, then how much more should you reject the other mental fluctuations which are full of defects? For this reason, the introduction of the **Concentration of Restriction** is appropriate. 

And so he says, **“Hence . . . with this.”** The meaning is that the yogi restricts even the highest discriminative discernment through a "higher passionlessness," which is simply the complete calming of all perceptions.

Now, what kind of mind-stuff would it be that has all its fluctuations restricted? In reply, he says, **“[When it has reached] this state.”** He is speaking of the mind-stuff in the state of total restriction. 

He then explains what restriction itself is: **“This is the [so-called] seedless.”** The <term>latent deposit <note>original: āśaya</note></term> of <term>actions <note>original: karma</note></term>—which produces our hindrances, our birth, our length of life, and the nature of our experiences—is the "seed." That which is free from this is **“seedless.”** For this same seedless concentration, he provides the technical term used among practitioners of yoga when he says, **“In this state nothing [remains].”** 

He sums up with the words: “The yoga which we have defined as the restriction of the fluctuations of the mind-stuff is two-fold.” <note>Referring to the division between concentration with an object (Samprajñāta) and concentration without an object (Asamprajñāta).</note>

When the mind is in this unconscious or restricted state, what will then be the condition of the Self? For it is the very essence <note>original: ātman</note> of the Self to receive knowledge <note>original: bodha</note> reflected upon it by the <term>intellect <note>original: buddhi</note></term>. But in this case, there is a total absence of objects in the intellect to be reflected.

<summary>This page explains that pure consciousness (the Self) is immutable and does not "mix" with objects of the world, unlike the mind. It introduces the concept of "seedless" concentration, where all mental fluctuations and karmic tendencies are completely stilled.</summary>

<keywords>Self (Puruṣa), Energy of Intellect (Citi-śakti), thinking-substance (citta), mutation (pariṇāma), discriminative discernment (viveka-khyāti), Concentration of Restriction (nirodha-samādhi), seedless concentration (nirbīja-samādhi), karma, ātman</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Book I, following the definition of yoga as the restriction of mental activities. It transitions from defining the state of the mind to describing the resulting state of the Observer or Self.</meta>

<page-num>13</page-num>
# Consummation of Yoga. —i. 3

### 3. Then the Seer [that is, the Self] abides in himself.

At that time the <term>Energy of Intellect <note>original: citi-śakti; the power of pure consciousness or awareness.</note></term> is grounded in its own self, just as it is when in the state of <term>Isolation <note>original: Kaivalya; the ultimate state of liberation where consciousness exists independently of the material world.</note></term>. But when the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: citta</note></term> is in its emergent, active state, the Energy of Intellect—although it remains fundamentally the same—does not seem to be so.

To introduce the next <term>sūtra <note>A concise aphorism or rule.</note></term>, the commentator raises a question: “Since the mind is in this unconscious state [of deep meditation], what happens to the Self?” This question acts as an objection: “Now, the very essence of this Self is that it receives <term>knowledge <note>original: bodha</note></term> reflected upon it by the <term>thinking-substance <note>original: buddhi; the higher mind or intellect</note></term>, which constantly changes its shape to match one object after another. Thus, the Self is always experiencing something. But there can be no experience when the Self is deprived of the knowledge provided by the thinking-substance. After all, the very nature of this Self is this reflected knowledge, just as shining is the nature of the sun. Furthermore, this knowledge does not occur in a mind that contains only <term>subliminal impressions <note>original: saṁskāra; the latent memories or tendencies left behind by past actions.</note></term>. Since a thing cannot exist without its own nature, why does the Self not simply perceive the thinking-substance itself when it is in that state of quiet impressions?”

To this, the author replies: “There is a total absence of objects.” The <term>thinking-substance as such <note>original: buddhi-mātra</note></term> is not an object for the Self. It only becomes an object when it is fulfilling the two purposes of the Self: <term>discriminative insight <note>The ability to distinguish between the eternal Self and the temporary world.</note></term> and the enjoyment of worldly objects. Neither of these exists when the mind is in its restricted, meditative state. Thus, it is established that there are no objects for the Self to perceive at that time.

The rebuttal is also given in the aphorism: **3. Then the Seer [that is, the Self] abides in himself.** The words "in himself" mean that the qualities of being peaceful, cruel, or deluded—which we falsely project onto the Self—have stopped. For the Self’s <term>Intelligence <note>original: caitanya</note></term> is its own <term>true nature <note>original: svarūpa</note></term> and is not subject to conditions. In contrast, the knowledge produced by the thinking-substance takes on various forms, such as "peaceful" or otherwise. 

The Self is subject to conditions in the same way a crystal is. A crystal is naturally transparent and white, but it appears red if it is placed near a <term>China-rose <note>A bright red hibiscus; a standard metaphor in Indian philosophy for how the mind's proximity to the world colors our pure awareness.</note></term>. When the condition (the flower) is removed, the thing that was conditioned (the crystal) does not cease to exist; it simply returns to its natural state. This is the real point. 

And although the <term>Seer <note>original: draṣṭṛ; the witness or observer.</note></term> cannot actually be divided from his own <term>essence <note>original: svarūpataḥ; literally, "by nature," although the essential attribute cannot be divided from the Self.</note></term>, the author still uses a <term>predicate relation <note>original: vikalpya; a mental construction or verbal distinction.</note></term> by putting the words "in himself" (*svarūpe*) in the <term>locative case <note>A grammatical form indicating location, implying "within his own nature."</note></term> to make the meaning clear. The author of the Comment makes this same point by saying the Self is “grounded in its own self.” The phrase “at that time” refers specifically to the state of meditative restriction, not the state of active emergence. 

An objection is made: “This may be true. But if, while in the state of active emergence, the Energy of Intellect is not...”

<summary>This page explains that during deep meditation (nirodha), the Self (the Seer) rests in its pure, unchanging state of awareness, free from the "coloring" of the mind's thoughts and moods. It uses the metaphor of a clear crystal that only appears red when placed next to a red flower to explain how consciousness seems to change even though it remains immutable.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Book I of the Yoga Sutras, specifically moving from the state of the Self during deep meditation (restriction) to its appearance during normal, active consciousness (emergence). It addresses the philosophical problem of how an unchanging Self can appear to change.</meta>

<page-num>14</page-num>
<header>i. 3—] Book I. Concentration or <term>Samādhi <note>original: Samādhi; a state of intense concentration or meditative absorption.</note></term> [14</header>

...grounded in itself. If the Self were only grounded in itself while in the state of <term>restriction <note>original: nirodha; the state where the mind's activities are stilled.</note></term>, then it would imply that the Self undergoes <term>mutation <note>original: pariṇāma; change or transformation.</note></term> when it enters other states. On the other hand, if in the state of <term>emergence <note>original: vyutthāna; the active, distracted state of everyday consciousness.</note></term> it remained visibly grounded in itself, then there would be no difference between active life and meditative restriction.

In reply to this, the commentator says: "But when the mind-stuff is in its emergent state." The <term>Energy of Intellect <note>original: citi-śakti; the power of pure consciousness or awareness.</note></term>, because it is absolutely eternal, never deviates from its own nature. Accordingly, it remains the same in the state of restriction as it does in the state of emergence. 

Think of it like this: <term>mother-of-pearl <note>A common metaphor in Indian philosophy. A person might mistake a shiny shell for silver, but the shell's inherent nature (svarūpa) does not change regardless of whether the observer sees it correctly or is mistaken.</note></term> as such does not gain or lose any part of its being, regardless of whether the <term>perception <note>original: jñāna</note></term> which refers to it is the source of a <term>valid idea <note>original: pramāṇa; accurate knowledge.</note></term> or the source of a misconception. The observer, however, even though the object remains exactly the same, is under the illusion that it is not so. Compared with the concentration found in the state of restriction, even the concentration that remains "conscious of an object" is considered nothing more than a state of emergence.

How then does the Energy of Intellect seem different in the active state? The answer is: "Since objects are shown to it."

### 4. At other times it [the Self] takes the same form as the fluctuations [of mind-stuff].

In the emergent state of the <term>subliminal impressions <note>original: saṁskāra; the latent tendencies or memories that trigger thoughts.</note></term>, the Self appears to have fluctuations that are indistinguishable from the fluctuations of the mind-stuff itself. As we find in a <term>sūtra <note>A concise aphorism or rule.</note></term> by the ancient sage <term>Pañcaçikha <note>An early teacher of the Sāṃkhya school of philosophy.</note></term>: "There is only one appearance for both—that appearance is knowledge." 

The <term>mind-stuff <note>original: citta</note></term> acts like a magnet. As an object that is meant to be seen by the Self (acting as the Witness), the mind aids the Self simply by being near it. Thus, the relationship between the mind and the Self is like that between <term>property <note>original: svam</note></term> and a <term>proprietor <note>original: svāmin; an owner.</note></term>. Therefore, the reason why the Self seems to experience the changing thoughts and fluctuations of the mind is due to its beginning-less correlation with the <term>thinking-substance <note>original: buddhi; the higher intellect.</note></term>.

To introduce the next rule, the commentator asks: "How in that case?" Meaning, if the Energy of Intellect is actually unchanging, in what specific way does it take on an appearance of change? He provides the reason—"Since objects are shown to it"—and then repeats the core rule: **4. At other times it takes the same form as the fluctuations [of mind-stuff].** The phrase "at other times" refers to the emergent or active state...

state; ⟨the fluctuations [of mind-stuff]⟩ are the tranquil and the cruel and the infatuated <note>These correspond to the three qualities (gunas) of nature: sattva (tranquil), rajas (cruel/active), and tamas (infatuated/dull).</note>; «not distinguished» means not different. And so although the <term>Soul <note>original: ātman</note></term> has no misconceptions, it seems to have misconceptions; although not an experiencer, it seems to be an experiencer; although it lacks the discriminative discernment, it seems to be provided with it, [and] it shines forth by the discriminative discernment.² And this will be set forth in detail in this [*sūtra*] [iv. 22], “The <term>intellect <note>original: citi; pure consciousness.</note></term> which unites not [with objects] is conscious of its own thinking-substance when [the mind-stuff] takes its form [by reflecting it];” and in this [iii. 35], “Experience is undistinguished from a presented-idea on the part of the <term>sattva-aspect <note>The highest, purest quality of the mind, which is most capable of reflecting the light of the Self.</note></term> and of the Self, each absolutely unmingled [in the presented idea].” 

And this has been established in another system also <note>The Sāṃkhya system, which provides the metaphysical framework for Yoga.</note>. Accordingly with the words «and so» he introduces (*āha*) the *sūtra* of <term>Pañcaçikha <note>An ancient legendary teacher of the Sāṃkhya-Yoga tradition.</note></term> the <term>master <note>original: ācārya</note></term>, “There is only one appearance [for both],—that appearance is knowledge.” The question is raised, ‘How is there one appearance? considering that you say that the fluctuation of the thinking-substance—occupied on the one hand with the different kinds of things, and occupied on the other hand with insight, and perceptible as being unintelligent in so far as it is primary-substance—is appearance; and [considering that you at the same time say that] the Self’s <term>intelligence <note>original: caitanya; the fundamental light of awareness.</note></term>, which is different from this and which is the perception, is [also] appearance.’

## i. 4—] Book I. Concentration or <term>Samādhi <note>A state of deep meditative absorption where the mind becomes one with the object of contemplation.</note></term>

To this he replies [in the words of the ancient sage Pañcaśikha] «that appearance is knowledge.» When he says «only one», he says it with reference to <term>ordinary <note>original: laukika</note></term> knowledge, [which is] a fluctuation subject to origination and dissolution.¹ But <term>knowledge <note>original: khyāti</note></term> is not <term>intelligence <note>original: caitanya</note></term>, [which latter is] the very nature of the Self. On the contrary that [i. e. intelligence] is concerned not with <term>ordinary perception <note>original: lokapratyakṣa</note></term>, but rather with verbal-communication and inference. Consequently after [the author of the Comment] has shown that <term>undifferentiated-consciousness <note>original: avidyā; the primal ignorance that fails to distinguish between the eternal Self and the temporary mind.</note></term> is the original cause [of making wrong attributions] in the emergent state, he suggests that this [consciousness] is the cause of the contact [of the Self with the thinking-substance], and also that the relation between property and proprietor is the cause of experience. He makes this [series of assertions] consistent by saying «the mind-stuff.» Mind-stuff is the property of its proprietor, the Self: this is the connexion [of the statements]. 

The objection is made that <term>that-by-which-one-is-intelligent <note>original: cetana</note></term>, [namely,] the agent that is Master of the mind-stuff, accepts <term>aid <note>original: upakāra</note></term> afforded by the mind-stuff, whereas it is impossible that he [the Master of the mind-stuff should accept] aid afforded by this [mind-stuff]. The reason for this is that there is no correlation [of the Self] with this [mind-stuff], since [the Self] cannot be aided [by it]. But on the other hand (<term>ca</term>) if it be the case (-<term>tve</term>) that there is a connexion with this [mind-stuff] or that aid is accepted from it, one would have to admit that [the Self] enters into mutation. In reply to this objection he says «like a magnet; and, as an object suitable to be seen [by the Self as Witness], it gives its aid [to the Self] by the mere fact of being near it.» 

The mind-stuff is not in physical connexion with the Self, but is near it. [This] nearness, moreover, does not result from a correlation either spatially or temporally of the Self with it [the mind-stuff]. But the distinguishing characteristic [of this nearness] is [that the Self stands to the mind-stuff in a relation of] <term>pre-established harmony <note>original: yogyatā; a natural fitness or capacity for the two to interact despite their different natures.</note></term>. Moreover the Self has the capacity for being the experiencer [while] the mind-stuff has the capacity for being experienced. Accordingly [mind-stuff] is described «as an object suitable to be seen.» In other words it is described as an object-for-experience when it enters into mutations which have the forms of <term>various kinds of things <note>original: śabdādi; literally "sound and the rest," referring to all sensory objects.</note></term>. Although experience is a fluctuation in the form of sounds and of other [perceptible] things and is an <term>external aspect <note>original: dharma</note></term> of the mind-stuff, still it [experience] belongs to the Self, because the Self <takes the same form as the fluctuations:> [that is, because they result from the false supposition of an identity between mind-stuff and <term>intelligence <note>original: caitanya</note></term>: this is what is

It explains that the connection between the observer and the mind is a beginningless cycle, much like the relationship between a seed and its sprout.</meta>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>Five kinds of fluctuations [—i. 5</header>

is meant. Therefore, although there is no physical connection with the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: citta; the collective mental functions including intellect, ego, and sensory mind.</note></term>, it is still established that the Self accepts the assistance provided by it, and that the Self does not undergo any <term>mutation <note>original: pariṇāma; the process of change or transformation that affects matter but not the pure spirit.</note></term>. 

A question is raised: "We grant that the relationship between 'property' (the mind) and 'proprietor' (the Self) explains why we have experiences, and that this relationship depends on <term>undifferentiated-consciousness <note>original: avidyā; a state of spiritual ignorance where one cannot distinguish between the eternal Self and the temporary mind.</note></term>. But what causes this undifferentiated-consciousness itself? As everyone admits, no effect is produced without a cause. Is there a specific starting point for this ignorance in a person, as there is a start to sleep?"

While appearing to summarize, the author removes this doubt by explaining that the reason the Self experiences the <term>fluctuations <note>original: vṛtti; the 'whirlpools' or active states of the mind, such as thoughts and perceptions.</note></term> of the mind—whether they be peaceful, painful, or dull—is a correlation that has no beginning. This is because it is driven by an ignorance that is itself without a beginning. The <term>serial-order <note>original: santāna</note></term> of this ignorance and the <term>subconscious impressions <note>original: vāsanā; the latent tendencies left behind by past actions.</note></term> is like the cycle of seed and sprout: it is impossible to say which came first; they have always been in motion.

Furthermore, these fluctuations—for many such are found in the mind—must be restrained.

### **5. The fluctuations are of five kinds and are hindered or unhindered.**

The <term>hindered <note>original: kliṣṭa; literally 'afflicted,' these are mental states that lead to suffering and keep the soul bound to the cycle of rebirth.</note></term> fluctuations are those caused by the <term>hindrances <note>original: kleśa; the five spiritual afflictions, including ignorance and egoism, described in Book II, aphorism 3.</note></term>. These provide the soil in which the "deposits" of <term>karma <note>The law of cause and effect where actions lead to future consequences.</note></term> grow. 

In contrast, the **unhindered** fluctuations have "discriminative discernment" as their goal. This discernment allows the practitioner to see the truth of reality and thus stops the <term>task <note>original: adhikāra; the inherent 'duty' or purpose of material nature to provide experience to the Self.</note></term> of the <term>aspects <note>original: guṇa; the three fundamental qualities of nature: goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas).</note></term>. 

Even when unhindered thoughts occur within a stream of hindered ones, they remain unhindered. This is a reciprocal process: fluctuations produce corresponding <term>subliminal impressions <note>original: saṃskāra; deep-seated mental habits.</note></term>, and these impressions, in turn, create new fluctuations. In this way, the wheel of thoughts and habits rolls on ceaselessly <note>Compare Book IV, aphorism 11, page 288 of the Calcutta edition.</note> until the highest state of concentration is reached. When the mind operates this way and finally finishes its task, it either rests in its own true nature or is resolved back into its primary cause. 

Whether they lead to suffering or toward freedom, there are five types of these mental fluctuations.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the mind's activities. Having established that the Self’s experience is tied to mental fluctuations, the text now begins to categorize these fluctuations to make the practice of Yoga manageable. This moves into the commentary on Yoga Sūtra 1.5.</meta>

<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>i. 5-] Book I. Concentration or <term>Samādhi <note>original: samādhi; a state of deep meditative absorption where the mind becomes one with the object of contemplation.</note></term></header>

Let this be granted. Still, a person is only qualified for that in which they have the capacity. Furthermore, the restriction of <term>fluctuations <note>original: vṛtti; the active states or "whirlpools" of the mind, such as thoughts, perceptions, and memories.</note></term> is impossible unless one has a clear idea of what those fluctuations are. And yet, no one, even in a thousand years, could count them all. Numberless as they are, how then can they be restricted? In reply to this difficulty, the author introduces the <term>sūtra <note>original: sūtra; a concise aphorism or rule in Sanskrit literature.</note></term> whose purpose is to teach us their number and their nature with the words: <<Moreover these—for there are many such found in the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: citta; the total mental field comprising the intellect, ego, and sensory mind.</note></term>—must be restricted:>>

**5. The fluctuations are of five kinds and are hindered or unhindered.**

The fluctuations form a single whole. Of this whole, there are five parts, and of them, the first is the <term>source-of-a-valid-idea <note>original: pramāṇa; correct knowledge or accurate perception.</note></term>. Accordingly, there is a fluctuation which has the parts of this whole, namely five-fold, that is, consisting of five parts. And since these fluctuations are many—inasmuch as there are different mind-stuffs belonging to <term>Chāitra <note>original: Chāitra; a traditional placeholder name in Sanskrit texts, similar to "Person A" or "John Doe."</note></term> and to <term>Māitra <note>original: Māitra; another placeholder name, like "Person B."</note></term> and to other people—the use of the plural is consistent. 

What he wishes to say is this: Whether it is Chāitra or Māitra or anyone else—of all these without exception, the fluctuations are of exactly five kinds and there are no more fluctuations. And the word <<mind-stuff,>> which has a <term>collective sense <note>original: jātyabhiprāya; referring to the universal class or genus rather than a specific individual.</note></term>, is used in the singular, but is to be understood as plural: "mind-stuffs." 

He shows that there are differences of a subordinate kind which are useful in the pursuit of Yoga in the words <hindered or unhindered.> By the help of the unhindered fluctuations, the hindered should be restricted; and then the former should be restricted by the higher <term>passionlessness <note>original: vairāgya; the state of being free from worldly desires or attachments.</note></term>. He gives the explanation of this in the words <<caused by the hindrances>>; in other words, the fluctuations have the feeling-of-personality and the other hindrances as their cause of action. 

Another interpretation would be that, for a person whose chief end is to fulfill the purposes of the Self, those fluctuations which consist of <term>passion <note>original: rajas; the quality of energy, movement, and attachment.</note></term> and <term>inertia <note>original: tamas; the quality of darkness, heaviness, and ignorance.</note></term> act as hindrances insofar as they cause obstruction. <<Hindrance>> is used here in the sense <note>original: Pāṇ. v. 2. 127; a reference to Panini's grammatical rules regarding how a word describes its effect.</note> of having something hindered as its effect. This hindrance belongs to those fluctuations, and therefore they are called "hindered."

Since the action of those hindered fluctuations tends towards an increase of hindrance, it is they which are the field for the growth and accumulation of the <term>latent-deposits of karma <note>original: karmāśaya; the unconscious storehouse of past actions that dictates future experiences and rebirths.</note></term>. For this observer—namely, the thinking-substance whose chief end is to fulfill the purposes of the Self—decides definitely (<term>determination <note>original: ava-sāya</note></term>) by sources-of-valid-ideas and in other ways what the intended object is, and becomes attached to it or averse to it, and then accumulates latent-deposits of <term>deeds <note>original: karma</note></term>. Thus, hindered fluctuations become the soil for the propagation of accumulated merit and demerit. 

He explains the unhindered fluctuations by saying that they <<have discriminative discernment as their object.>> When the <term>purity <note>original: sattva; the quality of light, clarity, and goodness.</note></term> of the thinking-substance is cleansed of passion and inertia and flows calmly onwards, the clearing of the <term>insight <note>original: prajñā</note></term> is the discriminative discernment. By thus speaking of that which has discernment as its object, he partially describes that <term>discrimination <note>original: viveka</note></term> between the purity of the mind and the Self, which is the object of this insight. Accordingly, since the unhindered have as their object the discrimination of the difference between the purity of the mind and the Self, for—

<header>19] Mingling of fluctuations [-i. 6</header>

For this very reason, they obstruct the task of the aspects (<term>guna <note>The three fundamental qualities of nature: harmony, activity, and inertia.</note></term>). Now, the aspects have the task to develop products. Since, moreover, this development lasts until the end of discriminative discernment <note>The realization that the Self is separate from the physical and mental world.</note>, and since when the aspects have accomplished their task (<term>adhikāra <note>The inherent duty or authority of nature to provide experience for the soul.</note></term>), these unhindered fluctuations restrict their authority (<term>adhikāra</term>), for this reason, sources-of-valid-ideas and the other fluctuations are these unhindered ones.

[The objection is made:] “This may be true. But all living creatures have hindered fluctuations only, since there is nothing born that is free from desire. Furthermore, unhindered fluctuations cannot exist in the stream of hindered fluctuations. And even if those [unhindered fluctuations] could exist, they could not produce effects since they have fallen into the midst of obstructors. For this reason, the restriction of the hindered by the unhindered, and of these latter by the higher passionlessness, is nothing more than a wish.” 

In reply to that objection, he says, “in the stream of the hindered.” Practice and passionlessness are produced by devoting oneself steadily to verbal communications <note>Scriptures and teachings.</note> and to inferences and to the instruction of teachers. “In the midst of the hindered” [means] among [them]. That they occur there means that they are in themselves quite unhindered, although they occur in the stream of the hindered. Surely a <term>Brahman <note>A scholar or priest belonging to the highest social class in traditional Indian society.</note></term>, although he reside at <term>Çālagrāma <note>A sacred village on the Gandaki river known for its holy stones.</note></term> which is crowded with hundreds of <term>Kirātas <note>original: Kirātas; mountain-dwelling tribes often regarded as outsiders or "barbarians" by the orthodox scholars of the time.</note></term>, is not [on that account] a <term>Kirāta</term>. This is an example of what is meant by [occurring] in the midst of the unhindered. 

And in so far as they are found among the hindered, the unhindered—without being suppressed by the hindered—do after all, as gradually their own subliminal-impressions <note>The latent mental patterns or "seeds" left behind by past thoughts and actions.</note> come to fruition, suppress the hindered. “Corresponding” means that unhindered subliminal-impressions [are produced] by unhindered fluctuations. This is that wheel of fluctuations and subliminal-impressions which ceaselessly rolls on until the concentration of restriction [is attained]. 

Operating in this wise, the mind-stuff reaches the state of restriction and, coming [then] to consist of nothing but subliminal-impressions, abides in its own likeness (<term>ātmakalpena <note>Remaining in its own form, reflecting the purity of the Self.</note></term>): this is the superficial view. Or else—and this is the stricter view—it becomes resolved into primary substance <note>It returns to the unmanifest state of nature (Prakṛti) once its work is done.</note>.

—He joins together the meaning of <term>sūtras</term> [5 and 6] by the word “These.”—The word “five-fold” [literally, five times] is an expression of the sense merely; but it is not a literal rendering of the force (<term>vṛtti <note>Here referring to the grammatical function or meaning of a word.</note></term>) of the termination (<term>çabda</term>), because it is not taught [by <term>Pāṇini <note>The ancient authority on Sanskrit grammar.</note></term>, at v. 2. 42] that the termination <term>taya</term> (<term>tayap</term>) has the meaning of “kinds.”

«chiefly concerned with the ascertainment of the particular» he distinguishes that which relates to perception from that which relates to inference and to verbal-communication. In other words, although the genus itself does shine forth [into consciousness] in perception, still it is subordinated to the particular. This would also be a partial characterization of <term>direct experience</term> <note>original: "sākṣātkāra"</note>. And so even the discriminative-discernment receives its characteristic mark.—With the words «The result [of perception] is an illumination by the Self of a fluctuation which belongs to the mind-stuff» he denies that there is any contradiction in the result. An objector asks how an illumination which is found in the Self can be the result of a fluctuation situated in the mind-stuff? For surely when an axe¹ is busy with a <term>khadira-tree</term> <note>Acacia catechu; a hard-wooded tree used in Vedic rituals</note>, it is not chopping on a <term>palāça-tree</term> <note>Butea frondosa; the "flame-of-the-forest" tree</note>. In reply [Vyāsa] says «undistinguished.» For the illumination whose seat is in the Self is not produced, but is the result when the <term>pure intelligence</term> <note>original: "cāitanya"</note> is reflected in the mirror of the thinking-substance and assumes the form of that [thinking-substance] in so far as the fluctuation of the thinking-substance has the form of the object. And this [intelligence] in this [assumed] condition is undistinguished from the thinking-substance and has its being in the thinking-substance. Moreover since the fluctuation has its being in the thinking-substance there is ground for the relation of the source-of-the-valid-idea to the result in the fact that [both] have the same locus [namely, in the thinking-substance]. And this he says «we shall explain» in the passage "Self is conscious-by-reflection."

ii. After perception [and before verbal-communication], because [in the first place] verbal-communication depends upon inference, in so far as it obtains its <term>validity</term> <note>original: "sāmartyaṁ gṛhṇāti" — literally "takes its power"</note> from a knowledge of the <term>connective-power-of-words</term> <note>original: "sambandha"</note> resulting from an inference with regard to a <term>cognition</term> <note>original: "buddhi"</note> on the part of the hearer which [inference] is based on actions and so on, and [in the second place] because [in this <term>aphorism</term> <note>original: "sūtra"</note>] the inferred is followed-in-enumeration by verbal-communication,—[therefore] he gives the characteristic marks of inference, before [he gives those of] verbal-communication, in the words «subject-of-the-illation.» A subject-of-illation is a <term>subject</term> <note>original: "dharmin"</note> distinguished by <term>attributes</term> <note>original: "dharma"</note> which we wish to know. Things belonging to the same class with it [the subject-of-illation], [are] objects similar to the genus which is an attribute of the <term>major-term</term> <note>original: "sādhya" — the thing to be proved, like "fire" in a logic example</note>, [that is, objects that are] <term>similar instances</term> <note>original: "sapakṣa"</note>. «Which is present» in these [things belonging to the same class],—with these words he excludes [both] contrariety and lack of community as between an <term>attribute of the middle-term</term> <note>original: "sādhana-dharma" — the sign or reason, like "smoke" in a logic example</note> [and the attributes of the major]. Things belonging to different classes are dissimilar instances, and they are other than the similar instances, [that is,] contrary to them and containing the negation of them. «Absent» from these [things belonging to a different class].
