<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the three sources of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) according to the Yoga Sūtras. Having previously addressed perception, the text now transitions into the definitions and logical requirements for inference and verbal testimony (authoritative word), explaining how we derive knowledge from signs and trustworthy sources.</meta>

# Perception, Inference, and Verbal Communication [—i. 7]

Accordingly (<term>accordingly</term> <note>original: "tad"</note>) by this he rules out <term>over-inclusive uncertainty</term> <note>original: "sādhāraṇa-anaikāntikatva"; a logical fallacy where a reason is too broad and applies to things outside the intended group</note>. "Things-are-brought-into-relation"—this is how the word "relation" is used, referring to a <term>logical sign</term> <note>original: "liṅga"; an observable characteristic that allows one to infer something not currently seen, like smoke inferring fire</note>. Thus, by describing the <term>property of the subject</term> <note>original: "pakṣa-dharmatā"; the requirement that the logical sign must actually be present in the thing being discussed</note>, he avoids the <term>unproven fallacy</term> <note>original: "asiddha"; specifically the "nature-unproven" or "svarūpa" type, where the reason given does not actually exist in the subject</note>.—"Refers to that" means having a necessary connection with that, based on the <term>etymology</term> <note>The study of word origins</note> of the word "refers" (<term>object/sphere</term> <note>original: "vi-ṣaya"</note>). This is based on the <term>List of Roots</term> <note>original: "Dhātu-pāṭha"; a classical manual of Sanskrit verbal roots</note>, which states that "the root *si* means 'to bind' or 'to connect.'"

With the words "the ascertainment of the <term>genus</term> <note>original: "sāmānya"; the general category or universal nature of a thing</note>," he distinguishes the object of an inference from the object of a perception. Inference arises only when there is an awareness of a relation between two terms. Since we cannot easily grasp every specific particular relation, we discuss the "genus" or "general category," as it allows us to understand these relations more easily. For this, he gives an example in the passage beginning "Thus, for instance." The word *and* (<term>and</term> <note>original: "ca"</note>) following the word "Vindhya" carries a reason with it.

Because the <term>Vindhya range</term> <note>A major mountain range in central India</note> has no motion, it does not arrive at another place. Hence, as there is an <term>absence of motion</term> <note>original: "gati-nivṛttau"; literally 'the ceasing of movement'</note>, there is an absence of "getting" from one place to another. Conversely, because they *do* get from one place to another, the moon and stars—much like a man named <term>Chaitra</term> <note>A common name used in Indian logic examples, similar to 'John Doe'</note>—must have motion. Thus, the point is established.

iii. Regarding the <term>fluctuation</term> <note>original: "vṛtti"; a state or activity of the mind</note> which is <term>verbal communication</term> <note>original: "āgama"; knowledge derived from a reliable source or scripture</note>, he provides the distinguishing characteristic in the words "a trustworthy person" and so on. Insight, compassion, and the sharpness of the sense organs combine to create <term>trustworthiness</term> <note>original: "āptatva"</note>. A person whose life is guided by these traits is a trustworthy one. This is a person who has personally seen or inferred the truth of an object. Unless there is a spoken word, there is no way for another person to receive that seen or inferred object. Because this word is rooted in something seen or inferred, it is only through these two sources that the word's meaning becomes complete. "His knowledge passing over" to another person means that in the <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>original: "citta"; the field of consciousness</note> of the listener, a knowledge arises that is similar to the knowledge found in the mind of the trustworthy teacher. To achieve this transfer, "a thing is mentioned"—that is, it is made known—as a way for the listener to gain what is good and avoid what is harmful. 

The rest is easy. Verbal communication where "the speaker declares an incredible thing"—for example, "These same ten pomegranates will become six <term>cakes</term> <note>original: "apūpa"; traditional fried sweet cakes often used in ritual offerings</note>"—or communication regarding "a thing which the speaker has not seen or inferred for himself"—for example, "Let him worship at a shrine who desires heaven"—is communication that <term>wavers</term> <note>is unreliable or invalid</note>. 

An objector might say, "If that is true, then the communication of even great figures like <term>Manu</term> <note>The legendary first man and foundational lawgiver of Indian tradition</note> would 'waver' and be unreliable, for even they spoke of things (like the afterlife) which they themselves had not seen or inferred."

In reply he says, "but if the original utterer." ### 8. Misconception is an erroneous idea (<term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "jñāna"</note>) not based on that form [in respect of which the misconception is entertained].

Why is it not a source-of-a-valid-idea? Because it is inhibited by a source-of-a-valid-idea, for the reason that a source-of-a-valid-idea has as its object a positive fact. In such cases there is evidently an inhibition of the source-of-the-invalid-idea by the source-of-the-valid-idea, as for instance the [erroneous] visual perception of two moons is inhibited by the actual (<term>objective truth</term> <note>original: "sad-viṣaya"</note>) visual perception of one moon. This [fluctuation, namely, <term>misconception</term>] proves to be that [well-known] five-jointed <term>undifferentiated-consciousness</term> <note>original: "avidyā"; a state of spiritual ignorance or lack of awareness</note> [the joints of which are enumerated later in book ii. 3 in the words]:

> “Undifferentiated-consciousness and the feeling-of-personality and passion and hatred and the will-to-live are the hindrances.”

These same [are known] by peculiar technical <note>1 Compare the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, book i. chapter 5, verse 5.</note> designations: <term>Obscurity</term>, <term>Infatuation</term>, <term>Extreme Infatuation</term>, <term>Darkness</term>, and <term>Blind-Darkness</term>. These will be discussed in connection with the subject of the defilements of the mind-stuff.

**8. Misconception is an erroneous idea not based on that form [in respect of which the misconception is entertained].** The word "Misconception" indicates the thing to be characterized; the words "erroneous idea" and so on [give] the distinguishing characteristic. A form which appears [in consciousness] as an idea (<term>knowledge</term> <note>original: "jñāna"</note>) is un-based on that form, [or, to put it as does the sūtra,] "not based on that form." As, [to give another example in which the negation applies to the action <note>2 This is a case of <term>action-negation</term> (original: "prasajya-pratiṣedha"). ### Nature of misconception

...ridden] by the perception of the inhibition <note>The act of one idea being suppressed or replaced by a more accurate one</note> [of the one idea by the other idea]. An objector says, ‘If this be granted, the predicate-relation (<term>*vikalpa*</term> <note>often translated as conceptualization or verbal delusion; a mental state based on words without a corresponding reality</note>), in that it is not based on the true form, would also upon consideration prove to be a misconception.’ In reply to this he says «an erroneous perception.» For these words describe an inhibition familiar in common experience to everybody.¹ Now this [inhibition] occurs in misconception; but not in the predicate-relation, forasmuch as the business-of-life [is done] by this [predicate-relation], and because, on the other hand, only the learned kind of persons when they might be engaged in reflection would have in this matter any idea of an inhibition.

—[The author of the Comment] puts forward the objection «Why is it not a source-of-a-valid-idea ?» The point is that a previous [perception] should not be inhibited by a later [perception] which has incurred contradiction; on the contrary the later [perception should be inhibited] by just that previous [perception] which occurred first and has not incurred contradiction. He gives the rebuttal in the words «Because . . . by the source-of-a-valid-idea.» For this rule [of the <term>Mīmāṅsā</term> <note>A school of philosophy focused on the interpretation of rituals and logic</note>] applies (<term>*evam*</term>) when a later [perception] arises in dependence upon a previous. 

But in this present case two perceptions, each from its particular cause, in entire independence of each other, spring up. Accordingly the later [perception] does not attain to a rise [into consciousness] unless it has destroyed the earlier [perception]; and in fact its rise [into consciousness] has its being in the removal of that [previous perception] by inhibition. But it is not true that the rise [into consciousness] of a previous [perception] has its being in an inhibition of the later, for the reason that, at that time [the time of the earlier perception], this [later perception] does not yet exist. Hence the fact that [one perception] has not incurred contradiction is the reason why [another perception] is to be inhibited ; and [hence also] the fact that [a perception] has incurred contradiction [is the reason] why it should act as inhibitor. 

Consequently it is established that the source-of-a-valid-idea, because its object is a positive fact, can inhibit the source-of-an-invalid-idea. An example is given in the words «In such cases . . . . . by the source-of-the-valid-idea.» In order that it may be rejected, he shows the worthlessness of this [source-of-invalid-ideas, i. e., of undifferentiated-consciousness] in the words «This . . . that . . five.» So, undifferentiated-consciousness as a genus [exists] in five special-forms [literally, in five joints], namely, undifferentiated-consciousness, sense-of-personality, and so on. 

The mental-process (<term>*buddhi*</term> <note>the intellect or higher mind</note>) which [recognizes] the self in eight forms which are not the self, that is, in the undeveloped [primary substance] and in the Great [thinking-substance] and in the substance of personality and in the five subtile-elements (<term>*tanmātra*</term> <note>the underlying potential of sound, touch, color, taste, and smell</note>),—is undifferentiated-consciousness, the [so-called] Obscurity. Similarly the mental-process which [recognizes] welfare (<term>*çreyas*</term> <note>the highest good or spiritual bliss</note>) in forms where no welfare is, in atomization (<term>*aṇiman*</term> <note>the yogic power to become as small as an atom</note>) and the rest of the eight supremacies of <term>yogins</term>, is eight-fold, the [so-called] Infatuation. ...the property that it does not come into existence." — Many thinkers [of the <term>Mīmāṅsā</term> <note>a school of philosophy focused on ritual interpretation and the logic of language</note> and <term>Nyāya</term> <note>the school of logic and epistemology</note> schools] have advanced the assertion that there is no fluctuation [called] predicate-relation other than the source-of-valid-ideas or the misconception. **10. Sleep is a fluctuation [of mind-stuff] supported by the cause (<term>presented-idea</term> <note>original: *pratyaya*</note>, that is <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*; the quality of darkness or heaviness</note>) of the [transient] negation [of the waking and the dreaming fluctuations].¹**

And this [fluctuation] by [the operation of] connecting-memory becomes, upon awakening, a special kind of presented-idea (<term>presented-idea</term> <note>original: *pratyaya*</note>). How is it that one can reflect: "I have slept well, my mind is calm, it makes my understanding clear; I have slept poorly, my mind is dull, it wanders unsteadfast; I have slept in deep stupor, my limbs are heavy, my mind remains unrefreshed (<term>weary</term> <note>original: *klānta*</note>) and languid and as it were stolen [from my grasp]?" [The answer is:] the man [just after] awakening would of course not have this connecting-memory, had there not been [during sleep, some] experience of [this form] of a cause (<term>presented-idea</term> <note>original: *pratyaya*</note>, that is <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*</note>); nor would he have the memories based upon it and corresponding with it [at the time of waking]. Therefore sleep is a particular kind of presented-idea (<term>presented-idea</term> <note>original: *pratyaya*</note>); and in concentration it also, like any other presented-idea, must be restricted.

**10. Sleep is a fluctuation [of mind-stuff] supported by the cause of the [transient] negation [of the waking and the dreaming fluctuations].¹**

For, the word "fluctuation" given-in-the-topical [<term>aphorism</term> <note>original: *sūtra*</note> i. 5] is made-the-subject-of-an-assertion [here]. Because, with regard to sources-of-valid-ideas and misconceptions and predicate-relations and memories being fluctuations, there is no disagreement among investigators—therefore this word is-made-the-subject-of-an-assertion (<term>reiterated</term> <note>original: *anūdyate*</note>) [namely, that one of the fluctuations is sleep,] in order that this particular [fluctuation] may be mentioned. But as to whether sleep is a fluctuation or not, there is disagreement among investigators. Accordingly it must be expressly said that it is a fluctuation. And the fact that the matter-in-hand [namely, that one of the fluctuations is sleep] is made-the-subject²-of-an-assertion cannot serve as an express statement [to the effect that sleep is a fluctuation].

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on Sutra 1.10, which defines sleep (nidrā) as a mental fluctuation. It moves from the definition to a logical defense of why sleep is considered an active mental state rather than a total void, using the evidence of memory upon waking.</meta>

i. 10--]    Book I.  Concentration or Samādhi    [30

Consequently the word fluctuation is used [here] again. That fluctuation is called sleep, the object or support of which is a <term>cause</term> <note>original: *pratyaya*</note>, that is, a <term>cause</term> <note>original: *kāraṇa*</note>—the <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*; the quality of darkness and heaviness</note> which covers over the <term>lucidity</term> <note>original: *sattva*; the quality of light and clarity</note> of the thinking-substance—of the [transient] negation of the fluctuations of waking or of dreams. For the substance of the thinking-substance has three aspects <note>These are the three Gunas or qualities of nature: Sattva (lucidity), Rajas (energy), and Tamas (inertia)</note>; and when <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*</note>, the coverer of all the organs, preponderates over <term>lucidity</term> <note>original: *sattva*</note> and <term>energy</term> <note>original: *rajas*</note> and becomes <term>manifest</term> <note>original: *āvis*</note>, then, because there is no mutation of the thinking-substance into the form of an object, the Self, aware of a thinking-substance which consists of intensified <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*</note>, is in deep sleep and inwardly conscious. Thus it is explained.

[An objection:] why not consider sleep to be merely an absence of fluctuations, as in the case of <term>restricted isolation</term> <note>original: *kāivalya*; the final state of liberation where the mind ceases all activity</note>? He answers «This.» And this [fluctuation] by [the operation of] connecting-memory, that is, a remembrance which can be <term>made the basis of an argument</term> <note>original: *sopapattika*</note>, is a special kind of presented-idea. How [is the argument? He replies]: When <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*</note> is manifest in company with <term>lucidity</term> <note>original: *sattva*</note>, then the connecting-memory of a man just arisen from sleep is of such a kind that he reflects «I have slept well, my mind is calm, it makes my understanding clear;» clarifies it, in other words. 

But when <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*</note> is manifest in company with <term>energy</term> <note>original: *rajas*</note>, then the connecting-memory is of such a kind that he <term>reflects</term> <note>original: *āha*</note> «I have slept poorly,» in other words, my mind is dull and unfit for work. Why? Since it wanders unsteadfast. [The author of the Comment] describes the connecting-memory of a man [just] awakened, with reference to a sleep in which <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*</note>, preponderating altogether over <term>energy</term> <note>original: *rajas*</note> and <term>lucidity</term> <note>original: *sattva*</note>, <term>comes-quite-to-the-fore</term> <note>original: *samullāse*</note>, in the words «I have slept in deep stupor, my limbs are heavy, my mind remains unrefreshed and languid and as it were stolen [from my grasp].»

—In the words «. . . of course not have this . . .,» he gives a negative instance of the <term>middle-term</term> <note>original: *hetu*; the logical reason in an argument</note>, [that is, experience,] in order to show that the <term>major-term</term> <note>original: *sādhya*; the thing to be proven, here being the memory</note> does not exist. «Awakening» means just after awakening. «[Had there not been during sleep, some] experience of [this form] of a cause» means [had there not been] an experience of the cause of the [transient] negation of the fluctuation. «Based upon it» is said with reference to the time of waking. 

An objection is made that sources-of-valid-ideas and other fluctuations have their locus in the emergent mind-stuff and must be restricted because they are enemies to concentration; but that sleep, since it amounts to a fluctuation single-in-intent, is in no wise a foe to concentration. To this he replies with the words «And in concentration.» Sleep, to be sure, does amount to [a fluctuation] single-in-intent; but, because of its quality of <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*</note>, it is a foe to concentration-with-seed and to seedless-[concentration], [that is, concentration without subliminal-impressions]. And therefore it also must be restricted: this is the meaning.

<summary>This page argues that deep sleep is a positive mental state (fluctuation) dominated by inertia (tamas), proven by the fact that we can remember the quality of our sleep upon waking. It concludes that sleep must be restrained through practice because its dullness interferes with the higher stages of meditative concentration.</summary>

11. **Memory** <note>original: *smṛti*</note> is **not-adding-surreptitiously** <note>original: *asampramoṣa*; This implies that memory is the retention of an experience without "stealing" or adding new, false elements to it.</note> to a once experienced object.

Does the mind-stuff remember the presented-idea or does it [remember] the object? The presented-idea, if affected by the <term>object-known</term> <note>original: *grāhya*</note>, <term>shines-forth-in-consciousness</term> <note>original: *nirbhāsa*</note> in a form <gloss>1</gloss> of both kinds: both of the object-known and of the <term>process-of-knowing</term> <note>original: *grahaṇa*</note>, and gives a start to the corresponding <term>subliminal-impression</term> <note>The deep mental traces left by every experience, which later trigger memories.</note>. This subliminal-impression [of these two kinds changes into] its <term>phenomenal form</term> <gloss>2</gloss> by the operation of the <term>conditions-which-reveal-it</term> <note>original: *vyañjaka*</note>—that is to say, the subliminal-impression—and brings forth [in its turn] a memory which [also] consists of the object known and of the process-of-knowing. With regard to these two, in the case of the <term>intellect</term> <note>original: *buddhi*</note>, the form of the process-of-knowing is predominant; and in the case of memory, the form of the object-known is predominant. The latter [that is, memory] is of two kinds: those in which the things-to-be-remembered are imagined <note>original: *bhāvita*</note> or not imagined. In a dream, the things-to-be-remembered are imagined, whereas in waking life, the things-to-be-remembered are not imagined <note>In the yogic view, dreams are a form of memory where the mind constructs or "fantasizes" around stored impressions, while waking memory aims to accurately recall actual events.</note>. All memories arise out of an experience either of sources-of-valid-

---

<gloss>1</gloss> The object as such is not directly perceived, but only its **form** <note>original: *ākāra*</note> as reproduced in the **thinking-substance** <note>original: *buddhi-sattva*; the highest, clearest part of the human mind</note>, which in its turn reflects the image cast upon it by the Self.

<gloss>2</gloss> Literally, "possessing a manifestation of the manifester of itself." (1) The word **self** <note>original: *sva*</note> denotes some change or time-form or intensity [iii. 13] yet to be <term>manifested</term>. Anger or fear would serve as an example. (2) The word **manifesting agent** <note>original: *vyañjaka*</note> denotes the conditions which transform the hidden form into a visible phenomenon. The approach of a tiger would be a concrete example that triggers the hidden impression of fear. (3) The word **manifestation** <note>original: *añjana*, *prakāçana*, or *āvirbhāvaka*</note> is the presented-idea of the tiger. The discussion is not about things in themselves, but their <term>phenomenal forms</term>. A <term>manifested form</term> <note>original: *vyakti*</note> is, in the terminology of the philosopher **Vācaspatimiçra**, equivalent to a **fluctuation** <note>original: *vṛtti*</note>. And this manifested form is further conceived to be any change in a **substance** <note>original: *dharmin*</note> which realizes some **purposeful action** <note>original: *arthakriyākāritva*</note>. When we regard a substance and see it doing anything that interests us, we call it a "thing"—in other words, a **transformation** <note>original: *pariṇāma*</note> or a manifested form. Consequently, things do not simply arise and vanish from nothingness, as some Buddhists would argue; rather, our conscious experience temporarily isolates successive visible aspects of permanent underlying substances. In short, all phenomena are latent or hidden within the substance and become active or "fluctuating" under specific conditions.

It explains the technical process of how a subconscious impression is transformed into a conscious memory through the interaction of the intellect and external triggers.</summary>

**11. Memory** <note>original: *smṛti*</note> **is not-adding-surreptitiously** <note>original: *asampramoṣa*</note> **to a once experienced object.**

This not-adding-surreptitiously-to, which is the same as not stealing for, an object once experienced by means of <term>sources-of-valid-ideas</term> <note>original: *pramāṇa*</note> and other fluctuations is memory. For in the case of knowledge produced by nothing but a <term>subliminal-impression</term> <note>original: *saṃskāra*; the latent mental trace left by past actions and thoughts.</note>, the object which appeared in that experience which was the cause of the subliminal-impression, is the own peculiar [object of that knowledge]. But the appropriation of any object in addition to that [own peculiar object] is a surreptitious addition, that is, a stealing [from other experiences]. Why [is there any stealing at all]? Because there is similarity [between the subliminal-impression and other experiences].—Since this word «surreptitious adding» <note>original: *sampra-moṣa*</note> is etymologically derived ² from the root *muṣ* ‘to steal’. What he means to say is this: all sources-of-valid-ideas and other fluctuations give access <note>original: *adhi-gam*</note>, either by the generic or the special form, to a hitherto inaccessible object. But memory does not go beyond the limits of a previous experience. It corresponds with that [previous experience] or corresponds with less than that, but it does not correspond to [any experience] in addition to that. This fact distinguishes memory from other fluctuations.—He puts forth for discussion the problem «Does [the mind-stuff remember] the presented-idea?» Because experience <note>original: *anubhava*</note> directs itself towards the <term>object-known</term>, [therefore] the subliminal-impression resulting from it <note>original: *taj-ja*, meaning 'born of that'</note>, [that is, from experience,] since it has no [present] experience of its own, makes us remember only the object-known: this is one view of the case. [Another view is that the subliminal-impression makes us remember] only the experience [of knowing], for the reason that [subliminal-impressions] are derived solely from experience. After putting forth this problem, [the author of the Comment,] by way of bringing the two views into consistency, decides that remembrance must be of both kinds. In so far as it directs itself towards the object-known, [the subliminal-impression] is affected by the object-known. ### 12. The restriction of them is by [means of] practice and passionlessness.

The so-called river of <term>mind-stuff<note>original: *citta*; the collective term for the mind, intellect, and ego.</note></term>, whose flow is in both directions, flows towards good and flows towards evil. Now when it is borne onward to <term>Isolation<note>original: *kāivalya*; the ultimate state of spiritual freedom or liberation in Yoga philosophy.</note></term>, downward towards <term>discrimination<note>the capacity to distinguish between the eternal self and the temporary world.</note></term>, then it is flowing unto good; when it is borne onward to the whirlpool-of-existence, downward towards non-discrimination, then it is flowing unto evil. In these cases the stream towards objects is dammed by passionlessness, and the stream towards discrimination has its flood-gate opened by practice in discriminatory knowledge. Thus it appears that the restriction of the mind-stuff is dependent [for its accomplishment upon means] of both kinds, [practice and passionlessness].

With the word «now» he asks what is the means for restriction. He gives the answer in the [following] *sūtra*: **12. The restriction of them is by [means of] practice and passionlessness.** If the restriction is to be effected, then both [these] distinct activities, practice and passionlessness, must operate together, but not either one or the other separately.<note>Literally, there must be a simultaneous action (original: *samuccaya*) of practice and passionlessness, where both function as subordinate activities working together rather than as alternatives to each other.</note> Accordingly he says «The river of mind-stuff.» The words «borne onward to» [connote] a continuous connexion; «downward towards» [suggest] depth or bottomlessness.

Of these [two methods], he characterizes practice by telling what its <term>essential nature<note>original: *svarūpa*; the true form or defining characteristic of a thing.</note></term> is and what its purpose is, [and does so in the words]:

### 13. Practice is [repeated] exertion to the end that [the mind-stuff] shall have stability in this [restricted state].

The word "unfluctuating" means without fluctuations of <term>activity<note>original: *rajas*; the quality of energy, passion, and movement that can disturb the mind.</note></term> and <term>inertia<note>original: *tamas*; the quality of darkness, heaviness, and lethargy.</note></term>. It is with this end in view [that there is practice]. In the words "shall have stability" there is [a specific grammatical use of] the locative case expressive of the reason [for the action], as in the phrase “He kills the leopard for the sake of the skin.” He makes the word "effort" clear by a pair of synonyms: "a [consequent] energy, a persevering struggle." That this [effort] starts from a specific <term>will<note>original: *icchā*; a conscious intention or desire.</note></term> he declares in the words "with a desire of effectuating this." The word "this" refers to stability. In the words "the course-of-action-requisite thereto" he describes the goal of the effort. The [eight] means-of-attaining [this] stability are the [three] inner <term>limbs<note>original: *aṅga*; the components or branches of the yoga system.</note></term> and the [five] outer limbs, of which the first [two] are the abstentions and the observances [see Book ii. 30 and 32]. The sense is that the activity of the practitioner is occupied with the means [of the action], and not merely with the result.

### 14. But this [practice] becomes firmly grounded when it has been cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with dedicated devotion.

[Practice,] when it has been cultivated for a long time, cultivated without interruption, and carried out with self-discipline, with continence, with knowledge, and with faith—in a word, with dedicated devotion—becomes firmly grounded. In other words, it is not likely to have its object suddenly overpowered by a rising <term>latent impression<note>original: *saṃskāra*; the subliminal "grooves" in the mind left by past experiences.</note></term>.

An objection is made that practice is obstructed by these rising latent impressions, which have been the foes of practice since a time without beginning. How then does [practice] lead to stability? In reply he says, **14. But this [practice] becomes firmly grounded when it has been cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with dedicated devotion.** This same practice becomes a confirmed state only when provided with [these] three qualifications. And its goal, namely stability, is not suddenly overrun by rising latent impressions. But if, even after having done practice of this kind, a man should fail to persevere, then in the course of time he might be <term>overwhelmed<note>original: *abhibhūyeta*; to be conquered or suppressed by opposing forces.</note></term>. Therefore, one must not fail to persevere.

### 15. Passionlessness is the consciousness of being master on the part of one who has rid himself of thirst for either seen or revealed objects.

The <term>mind-stuff<note>original: *citta*; the field of consciousness containing thoughts, memories, and emotions.</note></term> (*citta*),—if it be rid of thirst for objects that are seen, such as women, or food and drink, or power,—if it be rid of thirst for the objects revealed [in the <term>Vedas<note>The ancient and sacred scriptures of India.</note></term>], such as the attainment of heaven or of the <term>discarnate state<note>original: *videha*; a state of existence without a physical body.</note></term> or of <term>resolution into primary matter<note>original: *prakṛtilaya*; a high state of meditation where the self seems to merge back into the fundamental substance of the universe, though without final liberation.</note></term>,—if, even when in contact with objects either supernormal or not, it be, by virtue of <term>Elevation<note>original: *prasāṁkhyāna*; the highest form of discriminative discernment.</note></term> (*prasāṁkhyāna*), aware of the inadequateness of objects,—[then the <term>mind-stuff</term>] will have a consciousness of being master, [a consciousness] which is essentially the absence of <term>immediate-experience¹<note>original: *ābhoga*; here referring to the mental "expansion" or "fullness" that comes from being engrossed in an object.</note></term> (*ābhoga*) [and] has nothing to be rejected or received, [and that consciousness is] <term>passionlessness<note>original: *vairāgya*; the state of being free from worldly attachments.</note></term>.

And inasmuch as the [three] preceding ones have their purpose fulfilled by this same [fourth form of consciousness], therefore these are not separately mentioned. Thus all is quite cleared up.

# Book I. Concentration or *Absorption*

...passionless with regard to [all] <term>fundamental qualities<note>original: *guṇas*; the three primary forces—sattva, rajas, and tamas—that constitute all material and mental phenomena.</note></term>, whether perceptible or not-perceptible. Thus, passionlessness is of two kinds. Of these [two], the latter is nothing but an undisturbed calm of perception [untouched by any objects whatsoever]. And at the rising of this [state, the <term>practitioner<note>original: *yogin*</note></term>] on whom this insight has dawned, thus reflects within himself: 

“That which was <term>to be attained<note>original: *prāpaṇīya*</note></term> has been attained; the hindrances which should have dwindled have dwindled; the close-interlocked succession of existences-in-the-world, which—so long as it is not cut asunder—involves death after life and life after death, has been cut.” 

It is just this uttermost limit of knowledge that is passionlessness. For it is with this that <term>Isolation<note>original: *kaivalya*; the ultimate liberation of the soul from matter and the cycle of rebirth.</note></term>, as they term it, is inseparably connected.

After describing the lower passionlessness, he tells of the higher: 

### 16. This [passionlessness] is highest when discernment of the Self results in thirst-lessness for the qualities [and not merely for objects].

Lower passionlessness serves as a cause of higher passionlessness. He points out the means to this [higher passionlessness] in the words “passionless on seeing the inadequateness of [all] objects whether seen or revealed.” By this [statement], the lower passionlessness has been set forth. “Practice in the vision of the Self” is the practice in that vision of the <term>Self<note>original: *Puruṣa*; the pure consciousness that is distinct from the mind and body.</note></term> who has become accessible through verbal communications, logical inference, and the instruction of teachers. [This practice] is a constantly reiterated performance—through this. 

Purity of this vision is a focusedness upon <term>lucidity<note>original: *sattva*; the quality of light, clarity, and harmony.</note></term> in so far as <term>passion<note>original: *rajas*</note></term> and <term>inertia<note>original: *tamas*</note></term> have been rejected. Resulting from this [purity] is that perfect discrimination between the qualities and the Self—to the effect that the Self is pure and exists from time-without-beginning, whereas the qualities [in respect of which it is not contaminated] are the opposite of this—by which [discrimination] the <term>thinking-substance<note>original: *citta*</note></term> of the practitioner is <term>satiated<note>original: *ā-pyāyita*; filled or strengthened.</note></term>. It is to such a practitioner that reference is made. Now these same words [“by this”] describe the concentration called the <term>Rain-cloud of Knowable Things<note>original: *dharma-megha-samādhi*; a high state of spiritual absorption mentioned in Book iv. 29 where wisdom falls like rain.</note></term>. 

A practitioner of such a kind as this is altogether passionless with regard to the qualities, whether their properties be developed or undeveloped—that is to say, even to the extent that he is passionless with regard to the discernment of the difference between <term>lucidity<note>original: *sattva*</note></term> and the Self, [for to this discernment] qualities are essential. “Thus,” that is, therefore, passionlessness is of two kinds. The first is when the <term>substance<note>original: *sattva*; here used as the fundamental 'stuff' of the mind.</note></term> of the mind-stuff has [all] its inertia washed away by the excess of its lucidity, and when the mind-stuff’s <term>lucid quality<note>original: *sattva*; used here as the specific quality of clarity.</note></term><note>This use of the word *sattva* is an intentional ambiguity in the original text. It refers both to the 'substance' of the mind-stuff and to the specific quality of clarity (sattva-guṇa) which dominates the mind in higher states of attainment.</note> is in contagion with a tiny stain of passion. <meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the highest form of passionlessness (vairāgya) as defined in the Yoga Sutras, Book I, Sutra 16. It explains the psychological state of a liberated practitioner who has moved beyond desire for even the most fundamental forces of nature (the guṇas) and achieved a state of pure perception.</meta>

->Undisturbed calm of the Self<-
->[-i. 16<-

Moreover, this state is common even to those who are content (<term>tāuṣṭika<note>Those who have reached a state of satisfaction through intellectual study or limited practice but have not yet attained final liberation.</note></term>).¹ For they too, by virtue of that same discrimination, have been merged back into <term>primary matter<note>original: *prakṛti*; the fundamental material cause of the universe.</note></term>. In this same sense it has been said in the <term>Sāṁkhya-kārikā<note>A foundational text of the Sāṁkhya school of philosophy, which provides the theoretical basis for Yoga.</note></term> (verse 45): “From discrimination results resolution into primary matter.” Among these—that is, of these two kinds of passionlessness—the latter is nothing but an undisturbed calm of perception. 

The use of the words “nothing but” indicates that this state of passionlessness is without any external object to cling to. For the mind’s pure essence (<term>sattva<note>The quality of clarity, light, and harmony.</note></term>) becomes such that it is untouched by even a particle of the stain of <term>passion<note>original: *rajas*; the quality of activity, restlessness, and desire.</note></term>. This state is the foundation for that kind of passionlessness. For this very reason, it is called the “undisturbed calm of perception.” Although the pure essence of the mind is by nature undisturbed, it sometimes experiences defilement from contact with passion and <term>inertia<note>original: *tamas*; the quality of darkness, heaviness, and ignorance.</note></term>. 

But when all defilement by passion and inertia is washed away by a stream of the undefiled water of practice and passionlessness, the mind’s essence becomes absolutely and undisturbedly calm. It reaches a point where nothing is left but this clear, undisturbed perception. The author shows its qualities so that we may be inclined to seek it. He says, “at the rising of this.” The meaning is: When this state arises, then the <term>yogin<note>A practitioner of yoga.</note></term>—on whom this insight has dawned—has achieved the present insight known as the <term>Rain-cloud of knowable Things<note>original: *dharma-megha-samādhi*; the highest state of concentration where wisdom falls like rain, extinguishing all remaining karma.</note></term>. 

“That which was to be found”—meaning <term>Isolation<note>original: *kaivalya*; the ultimate spiritual liberation where the Self is completely detached from matter.</note></term>—has been found. In this sense, he will say later (iv. 30), “Even while living, the wise man becomes liberated.” The reason is that what remains as mere subconscious impressions has had its root cut out from undifferentiated consciousness. This is the main point. 

How is it that Isolation has been found? It is because all the hindrances which should have dwindled—such as undifferentiated consciousness and the other four, together with their deep-seated <term>subconscious impressions<note>original: *vāsanā*</note></term>—have indeed dwindled. 

An objection is raised: there is a massive accumulation of merit and demerit (good and bad deeds); there is the endless cycle of worldly existences and the unbroken sequence of birth and death for all living creatures. How, then, can there be Isolation? 

In reply to this, he says the chain “has been cut.” That succession of lives, whose joints normally show no break, is tightly interlocked. These sections of the entire multitude of merits and demerits are closely bound together. No living being is ever free from this bond of birth and death; this is the cycle of worldly existence. But when the hindrances dwindle, this chain is cut. To this same effect, he will say later (ii. 12), “The <term>latent deposit of karma<note>The accumulated psychological and spiritual results of past actions.</note></term> has its root in the hindrances,” and (ii. 13), “So long as the root exists, there will be the ripening of its fruit.” 

Someone might ask: “Without the full maturity of the <term>highest discernment<note>original: *prasaṁkhyāna*</note></term> and the restriction of the 'Rain-cloud of knowable Things,' what is this 'undisturbed calm of perception'?” To this he replies: “it is the uttermost limit of knowledge.” Higher passionlessness is simply one form of this “Rain-cloud” state.

**17. [Concentration becomes] conscious [of its object] by assuming forms either of deliberation [upon coarse objects] or of reflection [upon subtile objects] or of joy or of the sense-of-personality.**

The second, [that is, reflection,] which has deliberation subtracted [from it] is [concentration] reflecting [upon subtile objects]. The fourth, [that is, the sense-of-personality,] which has this [joy] subtracted from it, is [concentration] which is the sense-of-personality and nothing more. All these kinds of concentrations have an object upon which they rest.

limit, they pass beyond or go beyond [the period during which] the fruit corresponding to the <term>subliminal-impressions<note>original: "saṃskāra"; deep-seated mental imprints or tendencies formed by past experiences that shape future behavior.</note></term> ripens. Yet once again they enter the round-of-rebirth. And so it has been declared in the <term>Vayu Purana<note>An ancient Sanskrit text belonging to the Purana genre, dealing with cosmology and mythology.</note></term>, “Ten periods of <term>Manu<note>A mythological figure in Hindu cosmology who presides over a specific age or "Manvantara."</note></term> the devotees of sense-organs remain here below; a full hundred, the worshippers of elements.”¹ Similarly those [whose bodies] have been resolved into <term>primary-matter<note>original: "prakṛti"; the fundamental, unconscious substance from which the material world evolves.</note></term>,—in so far as they have become identified with one or the other of the five fine-substances or the personality-substance or the Great [thinking-substance] or the undeveloped [primary-matter] by serving [one or the other] of these,—have their inner-organs permeated by <term>subliminal-impressions</term> from one or the other of these. After the body falls to pieces they are resolved into one or the other [of these] from the undeveloped [primary-matter] downwards. The words «with its task still undone» mean that its purpose is unfulfilled. For that mind would have its purpose fulfilled, if it could also generate the discernment of the difference <note>The realization of the distinction between the pure conscious Self (Purusha) and the material world (Prakriti).</note>. The mind, however, which has not generated the discernment of the difference has not fulfilled its purpose and its task is still undone. Thus, as he says, they experience a *quasi*-state of Isolation <note>A state resembling liberation (Kaivalya) but lacking the permanent separation of the soul from matter.</note>, during which the mind (<term>mind-stuff<note>original: "cetas"</note></term>), with its task still undone, is resolved into primary-matter. «But this lasts only till the mind-stuff, under the pressure of its [unfulfilled] task, returns [to the world].» Even after it has been reduced to a state of uniformity with primary-matter, it reaches the limit [of its time] and yet once again appears, that is, it becomes discriminated from this [primary-matter]. Precisely so after the rains are passed, a frog’s² body, after having been reduced to an earthy state, when sprinkled with water from the cloud, experiences once again the state of being a frog’s body. And in this same sense it has been said in the <term>Vayu Purana</term>, “But those who-identify-them-selves-with-illusions-of-personality (<term>ego-centered<note>original: "ābhimānika"</note></term>), remain a thousand [periods of Manu]; those who identify themselves with the thinking-substance, ten thousand, and from them fevers [of desire] have passed away; those who meditate upon undeveloped [primary-matter], remain for a full hundred thousand; but after attaining to the Self, who is out of relation with qualities, there is no tale of time.”¹ Thus inasmuch as this [state which is resolved into primary-matter] leads to a recurrence of births, its <term>discardability<note>original: "heyatva"; the quality of being something to be avoided or overcome.</note></term> has been established.

<header>i. 20 -] Book I. Concentration or <term>Samādhi<note>original: "Samādhi"; a state of intense meditative absorption where the practitioner’s mind becomes fully merged with the object of contemplation.</note></term></header>

[That concentration not conscious of objects, which is] caused by [spiritual] means is that to which <term>yogins<note>Practitioners of yoga who seek spiritual liberation through disciplined mental and physical effort.</note></term> attain. Belief is the mental approval [of concentration]; for, like a good mother,¹ it protects the yogin. For him [thus] believing and setting discrimination [before him] as his goal there is the further <note>original: "upa"; a Sanskrit prefix meaning "towards" or "approaching," here used to indicate a secondary or supporting attainment.</note> attainment of energy. For him who has reached the further attainment of energy mindfulness is at hand. And when mindfulness is at hand the mind-stuff is self-possessed and becomes concentrated. When his mind-stuff has become concentrated he gains as his portion the discrimination of insight, by which he perceives things as they really are. Through the practice of these means and through passionlessness directed to this end there [finally] arises that concentration which is not conscious [of any object]. But for yogins he describes a series of means for the attainment of concentration. 

**20. [Concentration not conscious of objects,] which follows upon belief [and] energy [and] mindfulness [and] concentration [and] insight, is that to which the others [the yogins] attain.** 

It might be objected that those who reflect upon sense-organs might also be just the persons to have belief. To this he replies in the words «Belief is the mental approval [of concentration].» This [approval], moreover, has as its object a reality which is quite accessible by verbal-communication or by inference or by the instruction of teachers. For it is this mental approval, [which is itself] an extreme delight [and] a great volition, [that is called] belief. Those who are under the illusion that the self is in such things as sense-organs, have not an extreme delight. Because it is a disapproval [of concentration which they feel]; the reason [for this disapproval is that] it has its origin in downright infatuation. This is the meaning.— Why does he speak of just this [particular] belief [in concentration not conscious of objects]? He replies, «for, like a good mother, it protects the yogin» from calamities which follow upon a deviation from the way. This is a particular kind of volition and it generates an exertion directed towards the object desired. So he says «For him [thus] believing.» The exposition for the words «for him» is in the words «setting discrimination [before him] as his goal.» [For such a man] «there is the further <note>original: "upa"</note> attainment of energy.» «Mindfulness» is <term>contemplation<note>original: "dhyāna"; the seventh stage of yoga, characterized by a continuous, unbroken flow of thought toward the object of meditation.</note></term>. «Self-possessed» is undistracted. «Becomes concentrated» means having <note>original: "yukta"; meaning yoked, joined, or disciplined.</note> the concentration of the [eight] aids to yoga. And by mentioning the concentration which is inseparably connected with the <term>restraints<note>original: "yama"; the five ethical rules of yoga, including non-violence and truthfulness (see Book II, sutra 30).</note></term> and with the <term>observances<note>original: "niyama"; the five personal disciplines of yoga, such as purity and contentment (see Book II, sutra 32).</note></term>, the restraints and the observances and the other [six aids] are hinted at.

# Nature of the <term>Içvara<note>original: "Īśvara"; the Lord, or a unique Supreme Self who acts as a spiritual guide and is untouched by the laws of karma.</note></term> — i. 24
### 7 [H.O.S. 17]

**devotion to the Içvara.** He <note>Referring to the commentator, likely Vyāsa or Vācaspati Miśra.</note> discusses the words "By devotion." By devotion [that is] by a special kind of adoration either mental or verbal or bodily. "He inclines," that is, He is brought near [to the practitioner] and favors him. "Profound-desire" is a wish for something yet to come, to the effect that this thing coveted by him may be his. By this means only and not by any other functional-activity. The rest is easy.

But it is now asked who is this [being] that we have called the Içvara, as distinct from the primary-substance <note>original: "prakṛti"; the material world or nature.</note> and the Self?

<margin>G. Justi. Development of the Idea of God, 3</margin>
**24. Untouched by hindrances or <term>karmas<note>Actions and their moral consequences.</note></term> or fruition or by latent-deposits, the Içvara is a special kind of Self.**

The **hindrances** are undifferentiated-consciousness <note>original: "avidyā" or ignorance; the root of suffering.</note> and the rest [ii. 3]. The **karmas** are good (*kuçala* <note>meaning "virtuous" or "skillful"</note>) or evil. The **fruition** is the consequences which these [evolve]. The **latent-deposits** (*āçaya*) are subconscious-impressions (*vāsanā*) corresponding to these [fruitions]. These [hindrances and karmas and fruitions and latent-deposits], although they are found in the central-organ (*manas* <note>the mind or coordinating faculty of the senses</note>), are attributed to the Self. For it is he <note>the individual soul or Self</note> that is said to be the experiencer of the results of these [in the central-organ]. Just as the victory or defeat which depends upon the combatants is attributed to [their] lord (*svāmin* <note>master or owner</note>). For, the Içvara is a special kind of Self who is untouched by this [kind of] experience.

Then there are those who have obtained Isolation; and those who are in Isolation (*kevalin* <note>a soul that has achieved absolute freedom and independence</note>) are many.¹ Now these by severing the three instruments of bondage² have obtained Isolation; and the Içvara's relation to this [Isolation] belongs neither to the past nor to the future, [but is eternal]. Thus it is not with Him as with the [ordinary] liberated [Self] that there has been expressly made known a starting point of bondage (*pūrvā bandhakoṭi* <note>original: "pūrvā bandhakoṭi"; literally the "prior limit of bondage," meaning a time when the soul was bound before it became free.</note>). Nor is it with Him, as it is with one [whose body] is resolved into primary-matter, that there is an end point (*terminus ad quem* <note>original: Latin phrase for "the limit to which."</note>), when bondage—

---

¹ According to the *Sāṁkhya-sūtra* i. 91-92 the Içvara should be classed as one of these.
² The three types of **bondage** (*bandhana*) would be 1. primary-matter (*prakṛti*), 2. its modifications (*vikāra*), and 3. sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). Compare the *Sāṁkhya-tattva-kaumudī* xliv. The three types of **ripening** (*vipāka*) are birth (*jāti*), length of life (*āyus*), and experience (*bhoga*) (ii. 13). These three are also the **obstacles** (*upasarga*) (Vācaspati-miçra, i. 29, Calcutta edition, p. 66¹⁴).

might recur. But He is at all times whatsoever liberated and at all times whatsoever the <term>Içvara<note>original: "Īśvara"; the Lord or Supreme Ruler.</note></term>.

But it might be asked, ‘That universally admitted eternal <term>superiority<note>original: "utkarṣa"; the state of being higher or more excellent than others.</note></term> of the Içvara which results from his assuming a <term>sattva<note>The quality of purity, brightness, and intelligence within nature.</note></term> of <term>perfect<note>original: "prakṛṣṭa"; meaning distinguished or of the highest quality.</note></term> quality—has that any proof [to authorize it], or is it without proof?’ [The reply is, His] <term>sacred books<note>original: "śāstra"; the authoritative scriptures of the tradition.</note></term> are its proof. [But then] again [it may be asked], what proof have the sacred books? [The reply is] they have their proof in the perfect quality of [His] sattva. Inasmuch as both [the sacred books and the superiority] reside in the Içvara’s sattva, there is a never-beginning relation between the two. From these [sacred books, therefore] this proves to be true that He is at all times whatsoever liberated and at all times whatsoever the Içvara. 

Now this His <term>pre-eminence<note>original: "aiśvarya"; the sovereignty, power, or lordship that defines the Īśvara.</note></term> is altogether without anything equal to it or excelling it. For, to begin with, it cannot be excelled by any other pre-eminence, because whatever might [seem] to excel it would itself prove to be that very [pre-eminence we are in quest of]. Therefore that is the Içvara wherein we reach this uttermost limit of pre-eminence. Nor again is there any pre-eminence equal to His. [Why not?] Because when one thing is simultaneously desired by two equals, the one saying ‘let this be new’ and the other saying ‘let this be old’, if the one wins his way, the other fails in his wish and so becomes inferior. And two equals cannot obtain the same desired thing simultaneously, since that would be a contradiction of terms <note>This is a logical argument for the uniqueness of the Lord: if two beings were equally omnipotent, their conflicting wills would lead to chaos; therefore, there can be only one supreme being.</note>. Therefore [we maintain that,] in whomsoever there is a pre-eminence that is neither equalled nor excelled, he is the Içvara, and He is, as we said, a special kind of Self.

He anticipates the objection that ‘the <term>universe<note>original: "viśva"; the totality of the created world.</note></term> is pervaded by animate and inanimate [beings] only and by nothing else. Consequently if the Içvara be inanimate, then He is the <term>primary substance<note>original: "pradhāna"; the root-matter or "Prakṛti" from which the physical world evolves.</note></term>, since what is evolved from primary substance also falls within primary substance. And by this hypothesis he could not be made inclined since he is inanimate. Or on the other hand, if he be animate, still,—since the Energy of Intellect is <term>indifferent<note>original: "audāsīnya"; a state of neutral detachment or "witness-consciousness" that characterizes the pure spirit (Puruṣa).</note></term> and since in so far as it is not in the round-of-rebirths it has no feeling-of-personality or other [hindrance],—how can the Energy of Intellect be inclined, [or] how can profound-desire [have anything to do with Energy of Intellect]?’

<summary>This page provides a logical defense of the Lord's unique supremacy, arguing that His pre-eminence is absolute and proven by scripture, while addressing the paradox of how a detached spiritual entity can be moved by a practitioner's devotion.</summary>

In alluding to this he says "But now . . . primary-substance." He gives the reply to this objection in the following aphorism:

**24. Untouched by hindrances or actions or the results of action or by subconscious traces, the <term>Lord<note>original: "Īśvara"; the supreme ruler or God in the Yoga system.</note></term> is a special kind of Self.**

"The <term>hindrances<note>original: "kleśas"; the five afflictions: ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life.</note></term> are <term>undifferentiated-consciousness<note>original: "avidyā"; spiritual ignorance or lack of insight.</note></term> and the rest," for it is these that, by the blow of various kinds of misery, hinder a person within the <term>round-of-rebirth<note>original: "saṃsāra"; the cycle of birth, death, and reincarnation.</note></term>. "Good or evil" are merit and demerit; and by a figurative expression they are called <term>actions<note>original: "karma"; the law of cause and effect where deeds determine future states.</note></term>, because they proceed from action. "<term>Fruition<note>original: "vipāka"; the ripening or outcome of past actions.</note></term>" is birth, length of life, and the [kind of] experience [ii. 13]. "Corresponding to these:" the subconscious impressions corresponding to the fruitions. These subconscious impressions are called <term>latent-deposits<note>original: "āśaya"; the stock of traces left in the mind by past experiences.</note></term> because they lie in the ground of the <term>mind-stuff<note>original: "citta"; the collective mental functions of intellect, ego, and sensory mind.</note></term>. 

For, until [that particular] action, [that is, some demerit], which <term>precipitates<note>original: "nirvartaka"; that which brings something to completion or produces a result.</note></term>¹ the birth [of an individual] as a young elephant, makes manifest an <term>impression<note>original: "bhāvanā"; a mental inclination or habit-force.</note></term> [latent in his mind-stuff] which is characterized by a previously [existing] and potential kind of <term>experience<note>original: "anubhava"; direct perception or feeling.</note></term> [proper to] a young elephant—for so long [that action] is not capable of [producing] the experience proper to a young elephant. Therefore it proves to be true that the impression which produces the experience of being born as a young elephant corresponds to the result of being born as a young elephant. 

It might be said: "Such things as hindrances, inasmuch as they are properties of the thinking-substance, can by no means whatsoever touch the Self. Accordingly, merely by mentioning the word 'Self,' the absence of any trace of these [hindrances] is established. Consequently, what need is there of the words 'hindrances or actions' and the rest?" 

In reply to this he says "These." These [hindrances and actions and results and latent impressions], although they reside in the <term>central-organ<note>original: "manas"; the coordinating faculty of the mind.</note></term>, are attributed to the Self who is in the round of rebirths. Why? "For it is he that is said to be the experiencer of the results of these [in the central-organ]." That is to say, he is the <term>thinker<note>original: "cetayitṛ"; the conscious witness or animator of the thought process.</note></term>. Consequently the Lord, because He is a Self, comes into relation with these. For this reason, [because these are only attributed to the Self], it is consistent to make a denial of this [relation]. This he does in the word "who." For the Lord is a special kind of Self who is untouched by this [kind] of experience, namely, that also found in the thinking-substance and common to the Selves in general.

It is "a special kind" in that it is specialized [and] discriminated from [all] other Selves. Desirous of pointing out what is not to be included in the words "a special kind," he first raises a <term>counter-objection<note>original: "paricodana"; a formal challenge in philosophical debate.</note></term> and then rebuts it in the words "Now these . . . have obtained <term>Isolation<note>original: "Kaivalya"; the state of absolute freedom or liberation from matter.</note></term>."

With this resolve the Exalted One reflects, and assumes a **purity** (*sattva*) of perfect quality. Although He is untouched by undifferentiated-consciousness, it appears as if He were under the illusion of identifying Himself with undifferentiated-consciousness and as if He were ignorant of the real nature of undifferentiated-consciousness. The authority of the sacred texts is granted because they are effective in practice. This effectiveness is beyond doubt because they never fail to achieve their intended purposes. [This authority is granted. He shows that it is not based merely on human trial and error.] For instance, consider the various medicinal herbs and the specific ways they are combined, or the sacred incantations where individual syllables must be precisely connected or excluded. No one using only ordinary human methods of proof could, even in a thousand lifetimes, discover these exact connections and exclusions. Furthermore, we cannot claim that these specific herbal or syllable combinations are simply a result of <term>tradition<note>original: "āgama"; oral or written transmission of sacred knowledge.</note></term> and that tradition is a result of these combinations in an endless, beginningless cycle. This is because the chain of transmission is broken during a <term>great mundane dissolution<note>original: "pralaya"; a periodic event where the physical and mental universe dissolves back into its primal state.</note></term>. There is no reason to say such a dissolution does not exist. The author will later explain in detail [in section iii. 13] that the world is an evolved form of the <term>primary-substance<note>original: "prakṛti"; the fundamental material and mental cause of the universe.</note></term> and is essentially identical to it. We clearly see a "diverse transformation" (such as curds) arising from a "uniform state" (such as milk). Similarly, milk or sugar-cane juice takes on various forms like curds or molasses. It is evident that any diverse transformation requires a prior uniform state. In the case at hand, the primary-substance can undergo diverse transformations by taking forms such as the Great Intellect and the sense of "I" (personality); occasionally, it can also return to a uniform state. This uniform state is the state of perfect balance within the primary-substance. This, in fact, is the great mundane dissolution. [Therefore, the dissolution is a reality.] [Returning to the argument that the authority of the sacred books cannot be found through simple human experience:] Accordingly, the Exalted One is primarily the author of the sacred incantations and the <term>Medical Vedas<note>original: "Ayurveda"; the ancient Indian system of medicine.</note></term>. Therefore, we must acknowledge that because the "stains" of <term>passion<note>original: "rajas"</note></term> and <term>inertia<note>original: "tamas"</note></term> have been removed from Him, the essence of His thinking-substance shines with universal knowledge.

To resume the argument. Because He intended to provide instruction regarding both earthly happiness and eternal liberation—matters that cannot be tested by human experience—the <term>Vedas<note>The oldest and most authoritative scriptures of ancient India.</note></term> as a whole were composed by <term>the Lord<note>original: "Īśvara"</note></term> and must be understood to originate solely from the perfect quality of His thinking-substance. In this state of superior <term>clarity<note>original: "sattva"</note></term>, there is no possibility of error or deception, which only arise from passion or darkness. It is thus established that the sacred books find their proof in the perfect quality of His nature.—[A further objection.] ‘This may be so. But if the sacred books prove His perfection only because they are the *result* of that perfection, then we would be using an <term>inference from effect to cause<note>original: "śeṣavat"; a logical process where one reasons backward from a result to its origin.</note></term>¹ . ...of the omniscient. It is possible for the seed of the omniscient to reach this absolute limit because it exists in varying degrees, just as in any ascending scale. He in whom the limit of thinking is reached is the omniscient, and He is a unique kind of <term>Self<note>original: "Puruṣa"; in this philosophy, the "Self" or "Soul" is pure consciousness, distinct from the mind and body.</note></term>. 

[If you object that this logical argument would also prove the omniscience of the Buddha or of the Jina <note>Referring to the founders of Buddhism and Jainism; the author is defending the unique status of the Hindu Lord (Īśvara).</note>, the reply would be this:] A logical inference exhausts its force <note>original: "upakṣaya"; meaning the logic has done its job once it proves a general category exists.</note> by bringing a general proposition to a conclusion, but it is powerless to prove a specific, individual instance. Therefore, the discovery of the [Omniscient] one’s specific name is [not a matter of logic, but is rather] to be sought out in sacred tradition <note>original: "verbal-communication"; refers to the Vedas and other authoritative scriptures.</note>, [which excludes those other cases, since their traditions are considered incorrect]. 

Although He is above all feelings of personal satisfaction, yet the gratification of living beings is a sufficient motive for the <term>Lord<note>original: "Içvara" or "Īśvara"; the Supreme Being or "Special Self" in Yoga philosophy.</note></term>. He may be understood as resolving, ‘By instruction in knowledge and in right-living, at the end of a world-age and at the great dissolution, I will lift up human beings who are caught in the whirlpool of existence.’ And likewise it has been said: <note>This quote is attributed to Pañcaçikha, an early teacher of the Sāṁkhya school of philosophy.</note> “The First Knower, assuming a created mind-body through compassion, the Exalted One, the Supreme Sage, declared this doctrine to <term>Āsuri<note>According to tradition, Āsuri was the first student of Kapila, the founder of the Sāṁkhya system.</note></term> who desired to know.”

After having mentioned the sacred books as a means of proving [His] power of action and of knowledge, the author now shows that logical inference is another way of proving [His] power of knowledge. This is stated in the words “Furthermore.” 

### **25. In Him [the Lord], the seed of the omniscient is at its utmost excellence.**

The author discusses [the aphorism] in these words: “This our...” In proportion to the degree to which the <term>darkness<note>original: "tamas"; the quality of ignorance, heaviness, or inertia that clouds the mind.</note></term> which covers the <term>purity<note>original: "sattva"; the quality of light, clarity, and intelligence in the mind-stuff.</note></term> of the thinking-substance has been removed, our own process of knowing things beyond the senses—whether they are in the past, future, or present, occurring separately or all together—may be described as being either small or great. This capacity is the seed [or] cause of the omniscient. Some people know a very little of the past or of other times, while another...

much, another still more. Thus with regard to objects to be known there is a [relative] smallness or greatness of the knowing-process. In this wise only the object of proof is described; now he gives the means of proof in the words “It is possible.” In the words “It is possible for the germ of the omniscient to reach this [uttermost] limit” there is a statement of the major term <note>In Indian logic, the "major term" is the property one seeks to prove (in this case, reaching the limit of omniscience).</note>. The limit is the reaching of the utmost excellence; it is that state higher than which there is no excellence. Accordingly it should not be urged that this is establishing what is already established. For [this higher than which there is no excellence, is established] only so far as it is a terminal-point. [For,] the logical reason (<term>hetu</term>), as he gives it, is “for it admits of degrees of excellence.” Whatever admits of degrees of excellence, all that is [capable of reaching] the utmost excellence. Similarly in the case of the <term>kuvalaya<note>A small water-lily berry.</note></term> berry and the <term>āmalaka<note>The Indian gooseberry, which is larger than the kuvalaya.</note></term> fruit and the <term>bilva<note>The wood-apple, the largest of the three examples.</note></term> fruit there is a size that admits of degrees. And in the soul (<term>ātman</term>) [there is a magnitude which has reached its] utmost excellence. Thus he shows that there is a concomitance [of terms] <note>Meaning that wherever there are degrees of a quality, there must be a state where that quality is maximized.</note>.—And when he says “as in the case of any ascending scale,” it is not relevant to object that there is a discrepancy in so far as the properties [of a substance], such as its magnitude, [form an ascending scale but do not reach utmost excellence]. For in the case of the whole, its magnitude does of course not excel the magnitude of the parts. But whatever magnitudes there are, each functioning by itself, from the smallest atom up to the final whole, may be so arranged that one may assert a progressive increase of magnitudes. But, because it is not finished as contrasted with the object to be thought, in so far as it has [successively] one or two or a multitude of objects, thinking may with reason be said to admit of degrees of excellence. Thus there is no discrepancy. He brings the discussion to a close in the words “He in whom the limit.”—It might be objected that there are many authors of sacred books (<term>tīrthakara<note>Literally "ford-makers"; a term used for the founders of various philosophical and religious sects, particularly in Jainism and Buddhism.</note></term>), Buddha and Arhata <note>A title for a Jina or Jain teacher.</note> and Kapila the Sage <note>The traditional founder of the Samkhya school of philosophy.</note> and many others. Why, by this line of inference, may they not be counted as omniscient? In reply he says “a general proposition.” Whence then can we be informed of his particular qualities? The reply is “the [Omniscient] one’s.” The point is that the pseudo-sacred-words composed by Buddha or by the others are not a Sacred Word (<term>āgama</term>). For they give instruction in the way of soullessness <note>The Buddhist doctrine of "Anātman," which denies a permanent, underlying self.</note> and of momentariness <note>The Buddhist doctrine that all things exist for only a single moment.</note>, both of which are contradicted by all sources-of-valid-ideas. The reason for this is that they are deceitful. A Sacred Word has as its distinguishing-characteristic the Revealed-Word (<term>çruti<note>The Vedas, considered to be of divine origin.</note></term>) and the Tradition (<term>smṛti<note>Literature based on the Vedas, such as law books and epics.</note></term>) and the Epics and <term>Purāṇas<note>Ancient texts containing mythology and cosmology.</note></term>. The Sacred Word (<term>ā-gama</term>) is that from which the [spiritual] means for [worldly] happiness and [final] bliss come to (<term>ā-gam</term>) or strike upon the thinking-substance. From this [Sacred Word] comes information as to [the Lord's <note>original: "Içvara's"</note>] particular qualities, such as His name—any particular name, for example <term>Çiva<note>Shiva.</note></term> or the Lord (<term>Içvara</term>)—which are firmly established in the Revealed Word and in the other books. Under the word “such as” (<term>ādi</term>) are included the sexpartite <note>Likely referring to the six divine attributes: knowledge, detachment, lordship, dharma, etc.</note>

### 27. The word expressing Him is the Mystic-syllable (<term>praṇava<note>The sacred sound 'OM', considered the primordial vibration of the universe.</note></term>).

The <term>Lord<note>original: Içvara</note></term> is the object expressed by the mystic syllable. The relation of this thing-to-be-expressed to the expressive-word is fixed. But the usage [as determined] by the Lord declares this its fixed meaning. Thus the [actual] relation of father and son is permanent, but the verbal statement that "that man is this man's father" is suggested [to the mind] by usage. And the usage with regard to the relation between expressive-words and things-expressed is made by [the Lord] to serve with a distinct reference to the power of expression which they had in former creations also. The authoritative sages maintain that the relation between a word and an intended-object is eternal in so far as the <term>consensus<note>original: sampratipatti</note></term> [the continuous transmission of meaning through successive generations of speakers] is eternal.

What else comes to him?

**29. Thereafter comes the right-knowledge of him who thinks in an inverse way, and the removal of obstacles.** Whatever obstacles there may be—such as disease and the rest—all these are removed by devotion to the <term>Lord</term>, and the practitioner comes to a vision of his own true self. He gains the right-knowledge which sees that just as the Lord is a Self—undefiled and undisturbed by hindrances, isolated and free from accidental changes—so he, too, is a Self that is conscious of its own thinking-substance.

What else comes to him? **29. Right-knowledge comes to that kind of thinking which was previously under the conditions of ignorance and was "inverted" (turned away from the truth). ### 31. Pain and despondency and unsteadiness of the body and inspiration and expiration are the accompaniments of the distractions.

Pain proceeding from self <note>original: "ādhyātmika," pain caused by one's own body or mind</note>, pain proceeding from living creatures <note>original: "ādhibhautika," pain caused by other beings</note>, and pain proceeding from the gods <note>original: "ādhidaivika," pain caused by supernatural or environmental forces</note>. Pain is that by which living beings are stricken down and for the destruction of which they struggle. Despondency is agitation of mind due to an impediment to the fulfillment of a desire. Unsteadiness of the body is that which makes it unsteady and makes it tremble. Inspiration is breathing which sips in the air which is outside. Expiration is that which makes abdominal air <note>original: "koṣṭhyam," air residing in the stomach or trunk</note> flow outwards. These are the accompaniments of the distractions. These occur in one whose mind-stuff is distracted. These do not occur in one whose mind-stuff is concentrated.

Not only the nine obstacles but also pain and the other accompaniments of these obstacles occur to this practitioner of yoga. So the commentator Vyāsa <note>The primary traditional commentator on the Yoga Sutras</note> recites the aphorism <note>original: "sūtra"</note> beginning with the word 31. Pain. Pain is that which is to be felt as unpleasant. Pain proceeding from self is bodily by virtue of sickness, or mental by virtue of such things as passion. Pain proceeding from living creatures is such as is generated by tigers. Pain proceeding from the gods is such as is generated by the baleful influence of planets. And this pain, inasmuch as living beings in general would feel it to be unpleasant, is to be rejected. Accordingly he says "by which . . . stricken down." The breathing which without volitional action sips in the air which is outside and drinks it or makes it enter—this inspiration is opposed to controlled exhalation <note>original: "recaka"</note>, which is accessory to concentration. The breathing also, which without volitional action makes abdominal air flow outwards and expels it—this expiration is opposed to controlled inhalation <note>original: "pūraka"</note>, which is accessory to concentration.

**32. To check them [let there be] practice upon a single entity.**

To check them <note>The "distractions" or obstacles to yoga mentioned in the previous sections.</note> let [the practitioner] train his mind-stuff <note>original: "citta," the collective term for the mind, ego, and intellect.</note> by making it rest upon a single entity.

But if this [mind-stuff when single-in-intent] is withdrawn from all [objects] and concentrated upon one [entity], then it may be said to be single-in-intent [and] hence not limited to one object after another. 

If, on the other hand,—[in the opinion] of him who maintains that the mind-stuff becomes single-in-intent as a stream of similar ideas,—singleness-in-intent be a property of the mind-stuff [conceived] as a stream, then the mind-stuff [conceived as] a stream could not be a single thing, because [as he insists] it changes from moment to moment. If however [it be maintained <note>As, for example, by the Buddhist philosopher Dharmakīrti.</note> that] singleness-of-intent is a property of an idea only in so far as it forms a part of the stream, then—whether it consist in a stream of similar ideas or in a stream of dissimilar ideas—it is all of it in nowise other than single-in-intent, inasmuch as it is limited to one object after another, and the fact that mind-stuff is distracted is unexplained. Therefore it may be said that mind-stuff is a single thing [and] has many intended objects [and] is stable.

Furthermore if ideas accidentally related and different in nature were produced by a single mind-stuff, then what a situation! One idea would be the remembrancer of a thing seen by another idea; and one idea would be later the experiencer of the latent-impression of <term>karma</term> <note>Karma: The accumulated effects of past actions that shape future experiences.</note> accumulated by another idea. Even if this could in some way be harmonized <note>original: "samādhīya." This word also has the meaning of 'concentrated' or 'brought into samādhi.'</note>, it would surpass [in falsity] the maxim of the Cowdung <note>A classic Sanskrit logical maxim used to point out an absurdity. It mocks the idea that two things are the same just because they share an origin, such as claiming cowdung is the same as milk simply because both come from a cow.</note> as a milky preparation.
