# One common substrate of ideas [—i. 32

Moreover, if the field of consciousness <note>original: "mind-stuff" or "citta"</note> is merely one idea following another in rapid succession, then [the Buddhist who holds this opinion] denies his own lived experience. How can the "I" in expressions such as "I am touching what I have seen" and "I am seeing what I have touched" exist within one undivided <note>original: "abheda"</note> foundation of ideas, if all those individual ideas have nothing in common? How could the realization "I am this undivided self"—which focuses on a single "I" and remains constant across absolutely different mental states—find a foundation <note>original: "āçrayet"</note> in one general pool of ideas? This sense of "I am this undivided self" is something any person can know through their own experience. 

Furthermore, the authority of direct perception cannot be overturned by any other source of knowledge. In fact, any other way of gaining valid ideas only comes into use because of perception. Consequently, the field of consciousness is a single, stable thing that can hold many different objects.

The author now introduces a <term>sūtra</term> <note>A "thread" of knowledge; a concise rule or aphorism in Indian philosophy.</note> which summarizes the meaning he has been establishing. He does this by saying, "Furthermore these." This "furthermore" refers to the meaning he has just stated. The flow of the argument is that he sums up the section by reciting this rule. The reason why these distractions must be restricted is stated in the phrase "the foes of concentration." Although the previous words beginning with "By devotion to the Lord" [i. 23] referred only to practice, in this case, passionlessness <note>original: "vairāgya" or detachment</note> must be considered a partner to this practice. Accordingly, he says "by the same two." By these same two methods already described—consistent practice and detachment—the distractions are to be restricted. The words "of these" refer to these two (practice and detachment); the words "the practice" refer to what is described next.

**32. To check them [let there be] practice upon a single entity.**

A "single entity" refers here to the Lord <note>original: "Içvara"</note>, as He is the primary subject of this discussion. According to the Destructionists <note>A term for those, often Buddhists, who believe that the self is not permanent but is destroyed and recreated every moment.</note>, the field of consciousness as a whole is always "single-in-intent"—meaning it is never actually distracted. If that were the case, their own teachings and the actions intended to support those teachings would be meaningless, as he says in the words "But one whose." [He is referring to one] who believes the mind is directed toward one object after another, whether one at a time or many. In that view, the mind would be limited in time, being present <note>original: "samutpanna"</note> only as long as the object of focus is vivid <note>original: "ābhāsa"</note>, ending right there and not moving elsewhere. One might ask, "Why not first take the first object and then afterwards take the next?" In reply, he says "and is momentary." Inasmuch as a moment is indivisible, it cannot contain within itself the relationship of "before" and "after." In our system, however, since the field of consciousness is not momentary, it can remain stable with regard to its object, whether that object is one or many. And since at each moment—insofar as one object is taken and another is left—[the field of consciousness can be]

<meta>This page continues the philosophical argument against the Buddhist school of "Momentariness." The previous page argued that our sense of self ("I am seeing what I touched") proves the mind is a single, continuous entity. This page refutes the idea that a mind made of disconnected, momentary flashes could ever practice concentration or carry the results of its actions.</meta>

...distracted. Consequently, by removing the fluctuations of distraction, single-pointed focus <note>original: "singleness-of-intent"</note> may be established upon the mind-field <note>original: "mind-stuff" or "citta"</note>. To show that teaching and practicing this is not a pointless exercise, he uses the words "But if." He summarizes by saying "hence not."

He then prepares to argue against a Destructionist <term>vaināśika</term> <note>A term used in classical Indian philosophy for those (primarily Buddhists) who believe all things are destroyed and replaced every moment.</note> by using the words "on the other hand... who." His point is that you cannot attempt to impose a single focus upon a mind that is, by definition, already single-focused and lasts only a moment. However, if we view the mind-field as a continuous sequence that has existed from a time without beginning—and is *not* merely momentary—then distraction can be removed and a single-pointed focus can be established. 

He takes these two possibilities and highlights the flaws of the first by saying "of him." In the Buddhist system, if concentration is supposed to be a property of the "mind-stream" or a series of mental events, then that stream is not a single unit; it does not persist across the different ideas as they arise one after another. Why is this so? Because in that system, whatever exists is entirely momentary, and nothing lasts longer than a flash—this is the core of their argument. 

He considers the second possibility with the words "If however." A specific idea, which is just one part of this conventional <term>sāmvṛta</term> <note>meaning "covered" or "relative" reality in Buddhist philosophy</note> stream, might be considered "real." For this reason, focusing on this one idea would be a quality belonging to just that part of the stream, something to be achieved through effort. He points out the flaw in this view by saying "all of it." 

Essentially, as long as an idea exists in reality, it is limited to one object at a time. Because it only exists during the clear appearance <term>ābhāsa</term> <note>the manifestation or "shining forth" of an object in the mind</note> of its intended object <term>yat</term>, and because it vanishes the moment that appearance is over, every thought is *already* single-pointed by nature. If this were true, the fact that the mind gets "distracted" would be impossible to explain. Yet, the whole purpose of practice is to remove this very distraction. 

He concludes by saying "Therefore." Because distraction exists, the mind must be a single, stable entity that can perceive many different objects over time. He explains this further by saying "Furthermore if." 

For just as Person A <note>original: "Chāitra"</note> cannot be the same person who remembers a book read by Person B <note>original: "Māitra"</note>, and just as Person A cannot enjoy the rewards of the subconscious imprints <term>karma</term> built up by Person B (with whom he has no connection, whether good or bad), so too a thing seen by one momentary thought-flash cannot be remembered by a completely different momentary thought-flash. Nor can the "fruit" or result of a subconscious deposit of action <term>karma</term> built up by one momentary idea be experienced by a different, later idea.

For example, in rituals such as the ancestor-offering <term>śrāddha</term> or the sacrifice for a newborn <term>vaiśvānara iṣṭi</term>, we see that the benefits of the ritual pass from one person to another (from the son to the parents, or the father to the son), even though the person receiving the benefit wasn't the one who physically performed the act. # Permanence of the ego

...mango-seeds that have been nourished with sweet juices [we see] that the fruition by an indirect process must become sweet. <note>This is an analogy: just as a seed's treatment affects the future fruit, the Buddhist argues that one momentary thought can pass its "flavor" or "impression" to the next thought in the sequence.</note> [Thus the effort of one momentary idea could find its result in another idea single-in-intent and indirectly related to it through a serial-order.] In reply to this he says **«Even if this could in some way be harmonized.»** The connection of thought is this. What shall we say is the difference between ideas resident in one serial-order and different ideas <note>original: "bhinnapratyayānām"</note> resident in another serial-order, so that—when [something] has been experienced or when [some] latent-impression of karma <note>original: "karmāçayasya"</note> has been heaped up by an idea resident in one serial-order—[another] idea belonging to the same serial-order should be the one to remember or to enjoy it and not an idea belonging to a different serial-order? For this that we call a serial-order is not such a [materially] real thing that it could [as such] distinguish the <term>unit-in-the-serial-order</term> <note>original: "santānin"; the individual momentary thoughts that make up the stream.</note> from [ideas] resident in other serial-orders. 

Furthermore, an imaginary distinction cannot consistently exert activity. Surely the Brahman-boy cannot cook with fire that he imagines to be present. Moreover, the relation of cause and effect is also nothing that is [materially] real [in this case of the two ideas, one of which appears in a series after the other has disappeared]. Because it is impossible that there should be in the present time a substrate for two things which are not co-existent, just as there cannot be [a substrate] for two things [separate in space] like the left horn and the other horn which do however coexist [in time]. For the past and the future cannot function as the present by <term>being-partially-in-relation-and-partially-out-of-relation</term> <note>original: "vyāsañj"; a technical logical term meaning to exist in multiple things simultaneously without being fully contained by any one of them.</note> [since momentariness is by hypothesis assumed]. 

Consequently, ideas are not under the limiting-conditions either of a serial-order or of a causal relation which is a part of their being; [and], because they are real, they cannot, in so far as there are no reciprocal contacts, be distinguished from other ideas whether resident in the same serial-order or in other serial-orders. This same line-of-reasoning is continued by an allusion to the cow-dung and the milk; cow-dung is milk, because it is a product of the cow, like milk, which both sides admit [to be a product of the cow]. <note>This is a "reductio ad absurdum" argument: if any product of a cow is "milk," then cow-dung is milk. Similarly, if any momentary idea in a series is the "same" as the others just because they share a "stream," the logic fails.</note> [The Buddhist argument] «surpasses» this [in falsity] because it is superior [in falsity] even to this [line-of-reasoning] in so far as it has the false appearance of being a line-of-reasoning.—And this [system of ours] cannot be charged [with the fault of] destroying what has been accomplished and accepting what has not been accomplished. <note>A classic logical trap: "krtanāśa" (losing the fruit of one's deeds) and "akrtābhyāgama" (receiving results for deeds one did not do). If the "I" changes every second, the person who acted is gone, and a new person suffers the consequences.</note> For [we hold that] it is mind-stuff that is the agent of actions;

<meta>This page continues the philosophical defense of a permanent, stable mind against the Buddhist theory that the mind is merely a series of momentary flashes. It specifically addresses how a single "mind-stuff" can experience, remember, and recognize its own past.</meta>

<page-num>70</page-num>
<header>Book I. Concentration or Samādhi</header>
<sig>i. 32-]</sig>

It is this mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"</note> that is connected with the pleasures and the pains generated by these actions. For the mind-stuff, when it is transformed by receiving the reflection <note>original: "chāyā"</note> of the pure intelligence <note>The Self or Puruṣa</note>, experiences pleasures and pains. Hence, there is a common supposition that experience belongs to the Self; this happens because of the assumption <note>original: "graha"</note> that the mind-stuff and the Self are identical. Such is the very nature of these mental pleasures and pains—which arise based on their own specific causes—that they themselves remember and experience the later consequences, while others do not remember them. This natural order of mental states should not be treated as an injunction <note>original: "niyoga"; a command in sacred law</note> where one says, "Let this be so" or "Let this not be so." Nor should it be a subject of cross-examination <note>original: "paryanuyoga"</note> where one asks, "Why is this not so?" 

To anyone who is not satisfied with what has already been said, the author speaks with the words: "Moreover . . . his own self." The idea of "I" is bound up with the mind-stuff. This mind-stuff is the underlying foundation for experiences and the memories of those experiences, which have the qualities of beginning and ending, no matter how varied they may be. How could this "I" be attached to fleeting ideas that are absolutely separate from itself? 

An objector might argue that because there is a distinction between two different causes—namely, 1. the actual process of knowing through perception and 2. memory—and because these involve two contradictory qualities (immediate perception versus indirect memory), the act of recognition <note>original: "pratyabhijñāna"; the "this is that same thing" realization</note> cannot be a single idea. They would argue there is no unity in the mind-stuff that contains these contradictory ideas. In response to this, the author says: "in one's own experience." The objector might reply that the distinction between causes and the presence of contradictory qualities should prevent this single experience. In reply, the author says: "Moreover . . . of a perception . . . not." The totalities of causes <note>original: "sāmagrī"</note> do not remain distinct if they are brought into conformity <note>original: "anusāra"</note> with a single perception. The fact that the qualities are immediate or indirect does not create a contradiction; this is shown to be consistent in the *Little Grains of Logic* <note>original: "Nyāyakaṇikā"</note>. Furthermore, the way objects are acted upon by a mind-stuff that is permanent (not momentary) is shown to be consistent in both the *Little Grains of Logic*³ and the *Examination of the Truth of Brahman* <note>original: "Brahmatattvasamīkṣā"</note>. Thus, the entire argument is made clear.

# 33. By the cultivation of friendliness towards happiness and compassion towards pain and joy towards merit and indifference towards demerit [the practitioner of yoga should attain] the undisturbed calm of the mind-stuff.

Of these <gloss>1</gloss> [four virtues] he should cultivate friendliness towards all living beings that have reached the experience of happiness; compassion towards those in pain; joy towards those whose character is meritorious <note>original: "dharma," referring to virtuous or righteous behavior</note>; indifference towards those whose character is demeritorious <note>original: "adharma," referring to unrighteous or wicked behavior</note>. And then the mind-stuff becomes calm; and when calm it becomes single-in-intent and reaches the stable state.

Because one whose central-organ <note>The "inner instrument" or "manas," which processes thoughts and feelings.</note> is unpurified and full of such [feelings] as jealousy cannot successfully effect concentration <note>original: "sampatti"</note> and the means of concentration, he proceeds to set forth the means of [securing] undisturbed calm of the mind, which are hostile to such [feelings] as jealousy. ### 34. Or [he gains stability] by expulsion and retention of breath.

Expulsion is the ejection of the air from the lungs through the nostrils by a special kind of effort. Retention is the restraint of the breath.—Or by these two he should attain to a stability of the <term>central organ<note>original: "manas"; the internal faculty that processes sensory information and thoughts.</note></term>.

He now states these means of obtaining stability.

### 34. Or [he gains stability] by expulsion and retention of breath.

The word "Or" signifies that there is a choice with regard to other means now to be stated, but not with regard to the cultivation of friendliness and of the other feelings; because the alternatives now mentioned are in addition to that cultivation. He explains the expulsion by referring to the breath within the body. By a special kind of effort, described in books of <term>Yoga<note>The philosophical and practical system of discipline aiming at spiritual liberation.</note></term>, the internal air is gradually emitted through the nostrils. He explains retention by saying "Retention is restraint of the breath." It is the restraint of that portion of the internal air that is emitted as breath; it is the keeping of it outside; it is, on the other hand, not allowing it to enter suddenly. By these two, the expulsion and retention of breath, his body becomes light and his central organ gains the stable state. In this <term>aphorism<note>original: "sūtra"; a concise rule or statement of principle.</note></term> we have to supply <note>original: "ākṛṣ," meaning to draw in or pull from elsewhere</note> the word ‘stability’ from the phrase ‘comes into a relation of stability’ found in the next aphorism; and this is to be connected with the words ‘should attain’ as is understood from the context <note>original: "artha"</note>.

38. **Or [the mind-stuff reaches the stable state] by having as the supporting-object a perception in dream or in sleep.** For example, consider a person who, in a dream, adores an image of the **Exalted Maheçvara** <note>original: "Maheśvara"; the "Great Lord," a title for the deity Shiva</note>. This image resides within a secluded forest and appears as if carved from the orb of the moon. Its limbs are as soft as lotus stems; it is made of precious moonstone gems and adorned with garlands of incredibly fragrant jasmine and **Mālatī** flowers <note>a specific variety of fragrant jasmine used in devotional offerings</note>; it captivates the heart. 

When the practitioner awakens from such a dream with a mind filled with undisturbed calm, they reflect upon that same image which supported their perception during the dream. While their <term>central-organ<note>original: "manas"; the internal faculty that processes sensory input and thought</note></term> maintains the exact form of that beautiful object, their mind reaches a state of stability in that very condition. 

Regarding sleep, in this context it is to be understood as having the quality of **sattva** <note>the quality of light, purity, and balance</note>. This is the kind of sleep where, upon waking, the person has the clear memory: "I slept well." In this specific state of sleep, the central-organ has become single-in-intent <note>focused on a single point or essence</note>. <page-num>77</page-num>
<header>77] Mastery of the mind [—I. 41</header>

...tell us that the nature of the **ultimate reality** <note>original: "Brahma"</note> is similar to a state of deep sleep. Moreover, since a perception that is severed from the object being perceived cannot be grasped by the senses, the practitioner must also bring the intended object of perception into the range of their mental focus.

### **39. Alternatively, the mind reaches a stable state by meditating on any object of one's choosing.**

The **practitioner** <note>original: "yogin"</note> should meditate upon whatever object they desire. Having achieved stability with that specific object, the **mind** <note>original: "citta"; often translated as mind-stuff, referring to the entire field of mental activity</note> will eventually be able to reach a stable state with other objects as well.

**39. Alternatively, the mind reaches a stable state by meditating on any object of one's choosing.** Why say more? Whatever object is desired, let the practitioner meditate on just that, regardless of which particular deity it might be.

---

### **40. The practitioner's mastery extends from the smallest particle to the greatest magnitude.**

When the mind enters into a subtle object, it achieves a stable state that reaches down to the **smallest particle** <note>original: "paramāṇu"; the fundamental building block of matter in ancient Indian physics</note>. When it enters into a large object, it reaches a stable state that extends to the greatest possible size. This freedom from any obstruction, while moving between these two extremes, is what we call complete mastery. Therefore, a practitioner’s mind that is fully filled with this mastery no longer requires the repeated purification typically achieved through basic practice.

But how is the **state of becoming one's true self** <term>identification with the self<note>original: "ātmībhāva"</note></term> to be understood as a stable state? In reply, the author says: **40. The practitioner's mastery extends from the smallest particle to the greatest magnitude.** He explains this by referring to the mind "entering into a subtle thing." Summarizing the points made above, he defines the word "mastery" using the phrase "both of these kinds" of limits. Finally, he describes the secondary benefits of this mastery by saying, "Therefore... of mastery."

---

Now, once the mind has reached this stability, what is the nature of **total absorption** <term>balanced-state<note>original: "samāpatti"; a state where the mind becomes one with the object of meditation</note></term> in its **essential form** <term>essential nature<note>original: "svarūpa"</note></term> **or** <note>original: "vā"</note> when it is directed toward an external object? This is explained in the next **aphorism** <term>aphorism<note>original: "sūtra"</note></term>:

### **41. The mind from which, just as with a precious gem, all fluctuations have dwindled away, is—with reference either to...**

<page-num>[78</page-num>
<header>I. 41—] Book I. Concentration or Total Absorption</header>

...to the knower, to the process of knowing, or to the object to be known; in a state of resting upon one of these three and being "tinged" or colored by one of these three, the mind thus enters the **balanced state** <note>original: "samāpatti"; a state of total mental absorption where the mind takes on the qualities of its object of focus</note>.

The meaning of the phrase "from which fluctuations have dwindled away" refers to the **mind-stuff** <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>original: "citta"</note> in which all distracting thoughts have come to rest. The author uses the example of a **precious gem** <note>original: "maṇi"</note>.¹ Just as a crystal is colored by the various hues of the different objects next to which it lies, and appears to take on the **form** <term>form</term> <note>original: "rūpa"</note> of the **supporting object** <term>supporting object</term> <note>original: "upāśraya"; the basis or background upon which something rests</note>, so the mind-stuff is influenced by focusing on the object to be known. It enters into a state of balance with that object and appears to take on the very nature of the object as it is in itself. 

When influenced by a **subtle** <term>subtle</term> <note>original: "sūkṣma"; referring to the underlying energetic or atomic essence of matter</note> element, the mind enters into a state of balance with that subtle element and seems to become the subtle element itself. Likewise, when influenced by focusing on a **coarse** element, it enters into a state of balance with that coarse form and seems to take on a coarse form. Similarly, when influenced by specific things in the world, it enters into a state of balance with those things and seems to take the form of the world. 

A similar situation is found regarding the **processes of knowing**, which is to say, the organs of the senses. Influenced by focusing on the act of perception, the mind enters into a state of balance with the process of knowing and appears to take the form of that process as it is in itself. Similarly, influenced by focusing on the **Self** as the knower, it enters into a state of balance with the Self and appears to take the form of the Self as the knower. Finally, influenced by focusing on a **liberated Self**, it enters into a state of balance with that liberated soul and appears to take the form of the liberated Self. 

Thus it is that the mind, which is like a precious gem, enters a state of resting upon one of these—the knower, the process of knowing, or the object to be known (that is, the Self, a sense-organ, or an element). While in this state of being "tinged" by one of these, and while resting upon one of these...

**Sūtra 41. [The mind-stuff]... as from a precious gem... the balanced-state.**

He explains this by using the words "dwindled away." The mind-stuff from which fluctuations—such as **sources of valid ideas** <term>valid ideas</term> <note>original: "pramāṇa"</note>—have dwindled away when they are driven by **energy** <note>original: "rajas"; the quality of passion and activity</note> or **inertia** <note>original: "tamas"; the quality of darkness and stability</note>, as a result of consistent practice and **passionlessness** <note>detachment or "vairāgya"</note>. 

The explanation of this is "of which the presented-ideas have come to rest." In this manner, it is stated that the **purity** <note>original: "sattva"; the quality of light, clarity, and goodness</note> of the mind-stuff, which is naturally clear, is no longer overpowered by energy and inertia. He makes the example clear by saying, "Just as." 

"The thing next to which it lies" is the **limiting condition** <note>original: "upādhi"; an external adjunct that colors something else</note>, such as a red hibiscus flower. "Influenced by" means changed into its likeness. The mind appears as if marked by the form of the red or blue or other color which is peculiar to the thing next to which it lies. He applies this illustration to the subject by saying, "so... the object-to-be-known." It is influenced by—that is, it penetrates into—the **object-to-be-known** <term>object-to-be-known</term> <note>original: "grahya"</note> to which it refers. 

In this way, he distinguishes the **object-to-be-known** from the **knower** <note>original: "grahītṛ"</note> and from the **process-of-knowing** <note>original: "grahaṇa"</note>. The mind-stuff covers over its own peculiar form as an **inner organ** <term>inner organ</term> <note>original: "antaḥkaraṇa"</note> and comes into a state of balance with the object-to-be-known; or it might be said that it seems to change into an objective state of being known. As a result of this, it appears as having the form of the object-to-be-known as it is in itself. 

**Influence** <note>original: "uparāga"; literally 'coloring' or 'tinting'</note> comes only from an object-to-be-known. The particular things of the world are evidently those with an **animate nature** (for instance, cows) and those with an **inanimate nature** (for instance, water-jars). In accordance with this, it has been shown that there are two concentrations:
1. That accompanied by **deliberation** <note>focusing upon coarse, physical objects</note>
2. That accompanied by **reflection** <note>focusing upon subtle, energetic essences</note>

When he says, "An analogous situation... also with reference to the **processes-of-knowing**, [that is] in the organs of sense," he means that sense-organs are processes of knowing because intended objects are known through them. He makes the same clear by saying "referring to a process of knowing." Since the process of knowing is itself that to which the mind refers, the mind is influenced—that is, permeated—by this. It covers over its own peculiar form as an inner organ and seems to be changed into a process of knowing, as if it were an **outer organ** <note>The sense organs themselves</note>.¹

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the Yoga Sūtras, moving from the definition of "deliberative" concentration to the "super-deliberative" state (nirvitarka). ### Book I. Concentration or Samādhi

When, however, the memory is purified from the conventional associations <note>original: "saṃketa"; the learned connection between a word and its meaning</note> of words, and when concentrated insight is free from logical relationships—whether they come from reasoning or from things heard—the object of focus remains exactly as it is in its true self and nothing more. It is specifically defined by that very form which it possesses in itself. This state is called the **super-deliberative balanced-state** <note>original: "nirvitarka samāpatti"; a stage of meditation where the practitioner perceives an object directly without the "noise" of language or theory</note>.

This is a form of higher perception. It is the root from which reasoning and verbal knowledge grow; indeed, reasoning and verbal knowledge derive their existence from it. Furthermore, this direct vision <note>original: "darśana"</note> is not accompanied by any abstract idea of logic or of what has been heard. Therefore, the practitioner’s <note>original: "yogin"</note> knowledge, derived from this super-deliberative concentration, is not muddied by any other source of ideas. The author illustrates the distinguishing characteristic of this super-deliberative concentration with the next aphorism.

**43. When the memory is completely purified, that balanced state—which seems as if it were empty of its own nature and shines forth only as the object itself—is called super-deliberative.**

This insight is shaped solely by the object’s true nature <note>original: "svarūpa"</note>. It occurs when the memory is cleansed of logical relationships—ideas born of reasoning or hearing—and from the common usage of words. After the mind seemingly discards its own identity as a "process of knowing," it becomes the very object intended <note>original: "padārtha"</note> and nothing more. It is, in a sense, transformed into the thing itself which is being known. This is the super-deliberative balanced-state, and it has just been explained.

For in this balanced state, the visible world—whether it be a living thing like a cow or an object like a water-jar—is understood as follows: 
1. It is the formation of a single act of understanding <note>original: "buddhi"</note>. 
2. Its essence is the object itself. 
3. Its essence is a unique arrangement of atoms.

And this particular kind of arrangement <note>original: "saṃsthāna"; the specific structural configuration of the object</note> is an apparent quality <note>original: "dharma"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the super-deliberative (nirvitarka) state, specifically addressing the philosophical reality of the "whole" (the composite object) versus its "parts" (atoms or subtle elements). It argues against the Buddhist or nihilist view that only parts are real, asserting that the "whole" is a valid object of perception and meditation.</meta>

<page-num>83</page-num>

### The coarse object and nothing more — [i. 43]

The "whole" is common to the subtle elements <note>original: "tanmātras"; the foundational potentials of sound, touch, color, taste, and smell</note> which compose it, and its existence as a whole is inferred from its visible, physical effects <note>The atom carries within itself the miniature of its effects.</note>. It is self-dependent and presents itself by changing into its phenomenal form <note>original: "sva-vyañjaka-añjana"; the process by which an object manifests its own characteristics</note> through the operation of the conditions that make it manifest <note>This expression also occurs elsewhere in the text on pages 37, 112, 207, and 282.</note>. This form disappears when another apparent form arises in the consciousness. 

This same apparent form is called a **whole** <note>original: "avayavin"; the philosophical concept of a composite entity that is more than the sum of its parts</note>. It is this whole that is singular, and can be great or very small, tangible, the site where actions occur, and impermanent <note>The relation of whole and part is a major topic in Indian logic, discussed in the "Aphorisms on Logic" (Nyāya-sūtra) and Udayana’s "Discrimination of the Truth of the Soul" (Atma-Tattva-Viveka).</note>. It is by means of these "wholes" that the business of life is carried on. 

But for someone to whom such a particular conglomeration is not perceptibly real—because they believe that a subtle cause is imperceptible due to an indefinite first impression <note>original: "avikalpa"; a raw sensory perception before the mind applies labels or categories. This word is omitted in several manuscripts, including those from Bikāner and those edited by Gaṅgādhara Shāstri.</note>—for such a person, there is no "whole." Following the statement that an erroneous idea is not based upon the true form of the object, nearly everything would be reduced to a mistake. And then, what would a "complete idea" even be, seeing that there would be no real objects to which it could refer? 

For whatever is perceived, all of it is influenced by its nature of being a "whole-having-parts." Therefore, a whole does exist, which changes by taking on different sizes and similar qualities. This "whole" is the object of the **super-deliberative balanced-state** <note>original: "nirvitarka-samāpatti"; a stage of deep focus where the mind reflects the object directly without linguistic or logical interference</note>.

In order to show the connection of the aphorism <note>original: "sūtra"</note>, the author explains first the super-deliberative concentration by saying: "When, however..." 

Purification, in this context, means removal. For certainly, logical inference and verbal communication begin to function only when triggered by memories of the conventional use of words. This conventional usage is essentially a false attribution where we confuse the word, the intended object, and the mental idea—for example, the word "cow," the animal itself, and the thought of a cow. 

As a result of this confusion, two types of predicate-relations arise in the form of an idea, coming either from inference or from hearing someone speak. When the mind is triggered by one of these, concentrated insight is still "deliberative" because it is still processing the coarse object through language and logic. 

But when the mind—in so far as it is absorbed in the intended object and nothing more, and is zealous for that object alone—reaches a state of inseparable fusion through practice, then the memory of conventional word-usages fades away.

be either different from the subtle elements or not different [from them]. 1. If it be different from them, how can it be the [common] substrate of them and how can it be the form (<term>ākāra: the internal structure or shape that gives a thing its appearance</term>) [which gives oneness]? For a water-jar is a different thing from a piece-of-cloth and cannot be the substrate [of the properties of the piece-of-cloth] nor can it be that which gives the form [of oneness] to this piece-of-cloth. 2. The point is this: any such thing as a water-jar is not absolutely different from the atoms, neither is it absolutely identical [with them]. In case it were different, as a horse and a cow are different, the relation [between them] of substance to its properties could not be consistently explained. In case it were identical, [so that the atoms were] like the substance, then this [substance] could not be consistently explained. Consequently it is in some respects different and in some respects identical. And so it must be, if all is to be consistently explained.

[And] it is proven by inference to any one who takes the opposite view. And in so far as it is identical with its cause, we may consistently say that it has the form of its cause.

### Subtile object permanent and impermanent [-i. 43

[...is no existence in coarse form.] For existence is subsumed <term>vyāpta: a logical relationship where one property necessarily accompanies another, like smoke accompanying fire</term> under the absence of contradictory qualities.^1 And connection with contradictory qualities—which is contradictory to existence—is found to exist in a "thing-having-parts." This excludes the possibility of its existence, since in such a case something contrary to the requirement [the absence of contradictory qualities] has been found. And so [to revert to the original point] there is in the "whole" a connection with contradictory qualities; for example, belonging to that place and not belonging to that place, being covered and not being covered, being red and not red, moving and not moving. [Accordingly, wholes in gross physical form do not exist.]' 

In reply to this, the author says: «But one to whom.» The intention [of what was first asserted] is this: [The whole in gross form is now said to be given in experience and to be an action realizing a purpose.] The existence which is given as the middle-term <term>hetu: the logical reason or premise used to prove a point</term> must either be given by experience and be such as even a ploughman^2 with dusty feet <note>A traditional metaphor for an ordinary, uneducated person relying on common sense.</note> can understand, or it must be something other than what is given by experience. 

Of these two, the latter cannot be a "middle-term" since it is not found in experience [that is, it must itself be established as existing]. But water-jars and such things have an existence given in experience, namely, their activity in realizing a purpose <note>i.e., we know a jar exists because it successfully holds water.</note>. [This practical form] is not distinct from its gross [physical] form. This [form given by experience and realizing a purpose] is the middle-term [the proof of existence], and by removing the existence of "coarseness" [as the opponent tries to do], this proof would destroy itself. 

In reply to this, [the Buddhist opponent] says, 'Existence is not [a permanent] coarseness, but is simply the negation of non-existence. And coarseness is merely the negation of non-coarseness. Moreover, these negations differ according to the variations of the things being negated. So even when there is no physical "coarseness," there is no destruction of existence.' 

[The reply to this would be:] By reason of variations in these negations, we may admit that there is a variation in the objects of the determination <term>avasāya: a definitive mental judgment or conclusion</term>. But would you, Sir, be good enough to say what the object is of the "source-of-the-valid-idea" which is not a first faint impression <term>vikalpa: a conceptual construction or mental fancy not based on reality</term>, and which is the necessary condition <term>pūrvaka: that which comes before</term> for these judgments? For if you say that the atoms of color which arise continuously—whose minute "that-ness" is unknown—[are the object], the reply is: Very well. These are intermingled^3 with the atoms of odor and taste and touch and are [therefore] not continuous. Therefore, if the mind be unaware of the...

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of the reality of "wholes" (unified objects like jars or trees) against the Buddhist argument that only atoms exist. The previous page established that if we cannot trust our perception of a unified object, then all knowledge becomes impossible.</meta>

<page-num>88</page-num>
<header>I. 43-] Book I. Concentration or Samādhi [88</header>

If there were intermediate spaces [between atoms], then this "indefinite first impression" <note>This refers to *nirvikalpaka pratyakṣa*, the raw, non-conceptualized initial moment of perception.</note>—which is based on atoms yet feels like the single, dense idea of a forest—would be false, just as a forest is made of individual trees with spaces between them. Consequently, the "indefinite first impressions" arising from this would not even indirectly relate to a perceptible object. 

If that were the case, how could one successfully prove that there are no "wholes" <term>avayavin: a unified object composed of parts</term> which are defined by these impressions? Therefore, if one wishes to maintain the validity of "definite later impressions" <note>This refers to *savikalpaka pratyakṣa*, our conceptualized and language-based understanding of what we see.</note>, one must admit the existence of that very coarseness <term>sthūla: the gross, physical density of an object</term> that we experience. This is necessary even if one does not agree with what is determined by conceptualized perception. To put it simply: if existence itself were to deny this kind of perception, it would be denying its own reality. To claim that atoms are extremely subtle and only become objects of experience through the medium of other atoms is a self-destructive argument. With this in mind, the author says:

> «To one for whom this particular conglomeration is not [perceptibly] real»

This refers to someone who believes that the subtle atoms should be the true objects of our conceptualized perceptions. To such a person, the author replies:

> «since a subtle cause is imperceptible through an indefinite first impression.»

If there is no "whole" object, then everything is reduced to an error. According to the definition of error <note>See Yoga Sutra I. 8</note>—that "an erroneous idea is not based on the actual form of the thing being perceived"—then everything based on physical coarseness and the existence that contains that coarseness would be a mistake. 

An objector might argue that even so, knowledge is not mistaken when it comes to one's own self, because the self does not appear as a "whole" made of parts. To this, the author replies:

> «Nearly.»

The objector might ask, "What if that is true?" In response, the author says:

> «And then.»

If our basic idea of existence is an error, then any idea caused by that existence—such as the claim that "there are no wholes made of parts"—would also be an error. This is because its object, which it tries to define, is certainly not a coarse physical thing <note>original: *sthūlam*</note> and is not concerned with clear, conceptualized impressions. Therefore, this object essentially does not exist. This is the core of the argument. If one asks why there is no object, the author replies with the word:

> «whatever.»

Any apparent contradictions must be resolved using the logical explanation <note>original: *upapatti*</note> provided earlier, which is based on the idea of "identity in difference" and the many ways that matter transforms. Once this is understood, the entire system becomes satisfactory.

### 44. By this same [balanced state] the reflective and the super-reflective [balanced states] are explained as having subtle objects.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of perception and meditation. The previous page (88) argued against the Buddhist idea that only atoms exist, establishing instead that we must accept the reality of "wholes" (like a jar or a tree) for our knowledge to be valid. Page 89 now transitions into the specific types of meditative focus (samādhi) used to understand these objects, moving from coarse physical objects to subtle elemental forces.</meta>

<page-num>89</page-num>
-> The subtle object and nothing more —i. 44 <-
-> 12 [H.O.S. 17] <-

Of these two types of focus, we call the **reflective** (<term>savicāra: a meditative state where the mind still uses subtle logic or categories</term>) "balanced-state" that which focuses on subtle elements. These elements have visible forms that have already appeared and are defined by our experience of their place, time, and cause. In this state, a subtle element—which can be understood through a single focused idea and is defined by its current, active forms (<term>udita: the "uprisen" or currently manifest state</term>)—acts as the foundation for the yogi's concentrated insight. 

However, there is another state called the **super-reflective** (<term>nirvicāra: a higher state of focus that moves beyond logical categories</term>). This state refers to subtle elements in every possible way, regardless of whether their qualities are quiet and hidden (<term>çānta: quiescent or past</term>), active and present (<term>udita: uprisen</term>), or yet to be defined (<term>avyapadeçya: indeterminable or future</term>). This state reflects the very essence of all forms. Because the subtle element is of this nature, it becomes the very thing the concentrated insight rests upon, and it even shapes the insight itself. Furthermore, when the insight becomes "emptied of itself," as it were, and becomes nothing more than the intended object, it is called super-reflective. 

Of these four states, the **deliberative** and the **super-deliberative** deal with "something great" <note>original: "mahad-vastu". This refers to coarse, physical objects.</note>; while the **reflective** and the **super-reflective** focus on a subtle object. Thus, by explaining the super-deliberative state, we have also explained how we can move past the mental categories and logical relations <note>original: "predicate-relations"</note> of both kinds <note>These two kinds refer to the transition into the highest forms of focus where the mind no longer labels what it sees.</note>.

### 44. **By this same balanced-state, the reflective and the super-reflective states are explained as having subtle objects.**

The phrase "those whose apparent forms have been manifested" refers to things like water-jars—objects that have taken a clear, physical shape. 
*   **Place** refers to, for example, whether an object is above, below, or to the side. 
*   **Time** refers to the present moment. 
*   **Cause** refers to the way an object is made. For example, an "atom of earth" is produced by five fine elements, with the fine element of "odor" being the most dominant. 
*   Likewise, an **atom of water** is produced from four fine elements, with the fine element of "taste" being dominant. 
*   An **atom of fire** comes from three fine elements (excluding odor and taste), with the fine element of "color" being dominant. 
*   Finally, an **atom of wind** is produced from the two fine elements starting with "sound" <note>The text mentions "beginning with odour," but in the traditional sequence of elements (Tanmātras), wind usually involves touch and sound.</note>, of which the...

### i. 44—] Book I. Concentration or Samādhi

The fine element of touch is the most prominent feature here. In the same way, the atom of air is formed from the fine element of sound alone. <note>This refers to the Sāṃkhya-Yoga theory of "tanmātras," the subtle potentials from which gross matter like air or earth is derived.</note> This is the underlying cause for all subtle elements. These subtle elements are experienced only when they are situated in a specific place, a specific time, and through a specific cause. An idea (<term>buddhi: the higher intellect or faculty of discernment</term>) that is capable of being specialized does not arise unless it is defined by such a specific experience. 

An objector might ask, "What is the similarity between the balanced-state with deliberation <note>savarka: focusing on coarse objects</note> and that with reflection <note>savicāra: focusing on subtle objects</note>?" In reply to this, the author says, "In this case also." For the atom of earth—which consists of a combination of the five fine elements <note>sound, touch, color, taste, and smell</note>—may be grasped by a single focused idea. Similarly, the atom of water and the other atoms, which possess essences of four, three, two, or even one fine element, may also be grasped by a single focused idea.

"Uprisen" <note>udita</note> refers to a form that is currently manifest and apparent; the element is defined by that current state. And finally, regarding this manifest form, it is noted that there is an overlap of word-based meanings and logical inferences shaped by our memory of how words are conventionally used. When we perceive something coarse, we do not see the individual atoms. We only understand them through verbal communication and logical inference. Therefore, it makes sense that this "reflective" balanced-state is considered "confused" or "intermingled" with language and logic.

He describes the super-reflective <note>nirvicāra: the higher state where logic and words fall away</note> balanced-state with the words, "But that which." The phrase "in all ways" means in every possible form of manifestation, such as blue or yellow. The grammatical ending <note>original suffix: "-tas"</note> in the word <term>sarvatas</term> <note>meaning "from all sides" or "in all ways"</note> is used here to represent all possible grammatical cases. In other words, it means "by all means"—including every experience of place, time, and cause. 

By this statement, it is shown that atoms, in their true nature, are not limited by time. Nor are they limited by time through the manifest forms that originate from them. This is what the author describes using the word "quiescent." "Quiescent" <note>śānta</note> refers to forms that are past. "Uprisen" <note>udita</note> refers to those that are present. "Indeterminable" <note>avyapadeśya</note> refers to future forms that have not yet appeared. The atoms themselves are not defined by these three states. 

If they are not defined by these manifest forms, is it correct to say atoms are unrelated to them? In reply, he says they "correspond to all apparent-forms." Through what kind of relationship do these atoms correspond to these forms? He explains they "are the essence of all apparent-forms." In other words, the manifest forms are different from the atoms in some ways, but in their core essence, they are the same. 

But why does this specific balanced-state focus on this kind of object? He replies, "Since... of this character." Put simply, once the mind has a direct realization of the "that-ness" <note>tattva: the ultimate reality or essence</note> of a perceptible object, it no longer concerns itself with things that lack that essential reality. Having defined the object of this state, he explains the state itself by saying, "Moreover the insight." Bringing these four states together, he...

# The limit of subtle objects
<meta>[—i. 45</meta>

The text describes the object as being useful to distinguish what things are in themselves by saying "Of these." He sums up with the word "Thus." The phrase "Of both kinds" refers to both the "super-deliberative" <note>nirvitarka: concentration without logical reasoning</note> and the "super-reflective" <note>nirvicāra: concentration without reflection on subtle qualities</note> forms of meditation.

### 45. The subtle object likewise terminates in unresolvable primary matter (*aliṅga*).

In the case of an atom of earth, the "fine element" <note>tanmātra: the potential or subtle essence of a physical quality</note> of smell—which is the cause of the earth atom—is the subtle object of the reflective and super-reflective meditative states. In the case of a water atom, the subtle element of taste is the object; for a fire atom, the subtle element of color; for a wind atom, the subtle element of touch; and for an air atom, the subtle element of sound. 

The "personality-substance" <note>asmitā: the sense of "I-am-ness" or ego-intellect</note> which is the cause of these elements is also the subtle object of this state of meditative balance. The "resolvable primary matter" <term>liṅgamātra: the "marked" or differentiated state of nature, also called the Great Principle or Buddhi</term>, which is the cause of this personality-substance, is also a subtle object. Finally, "unresolvable primary matter" <note>aliṅga: the "unmarked" or undifferentiated state of nature, known as Prakṛti</note>, which is the cause of the resolvable matter, is also the subtle object. 

Beyond this unresolvable primary matter, there is nothing more subtle. If someone objects that the Self <note>Puruṣa: the pure consciousness or soul</note> is subtle, the reply is that this is true. However, the subtlety of the Self in relation to the "resolvable primary matter" <note>the thinking-substance</note> is not the same as the relationship between the unresolvable and resolvable matter. This is because the Self is not the **material cause** <term>anvayin: the substance that actually turns into something else, like clay turning into a pot</term> of the thinking-substance, but rather the **instrumental cause** <term>hetu: the presence or purpose that triggers a process without becoming part of the physical result</term>.

Accordingly, it is explained that subtlety reaches its absolute limit in the primary substance of nature.

Does the meditative balance, which has a "thing-to-be-known" as its object, end only with the subtle elements? No. As stated: **45. The subtle object likewise terminates in unresolvable primary matter** (*aliṅga*). 

The state of the subtle element of smell, as it relates to the physical earth atom, is the subtle object of the meditative balance. One should make the same connection for the other elements. The "resolvable primary matter" <term>liṅga-mātra</term> is the Great Principle—that is, the "thinking-substance" <term>buddhi</term>. It is called "resolvable" because it eventually goes to "dissolution" <term>laya</term> back into the primary substance. The "unresolvable primary matter" is the original primary substance of the universe. It is called "unresolvable" because it does not dissolve into anything else. This is the core meaning. The author is stating that the scale of subtlety ends there.

<summary>This page explains Sūtra 1.45, tracing the hierarchy of meditative objects from physical atoms back to the "unmanifest" source of all matter (Prakṛti), while distinguishing the soul (Puruṣa) as being outside this material chain of cause and effect.</summary>
<keywords>subtle objects, primary matter, aliṅga, liṅgamātra, buddhi, Puruṣa, material cause, instrumental cause, Samādhi, Yoga Sūtras</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 45 regarding the limits of subtlety in nature and begins the explanation of Verse 46, which defines the "seeded" state of concentration. It maintains continuity from page 91’s discussion on the hierarchy of material causes.</meta>

->i. 45—] Book I. Concentration or Samādhi [92<-

...within the undifferentiated primal nature <note>original: *aliṅga*; the "unmarked" state of matter</note> as expressed in the words: "And beyond the undifferentiated primal nature, there is nothing more subtle." 

An objection might be raised: "Is the Self <term>Puruṣa: pure consciousness or the true soul</term> not also subtle, rather than the primal nature alone?" 

The author admits this is true. In other words, in so far as a thing acts as a "material cause" <note>the physical substance from which something is made</note>, the highest degree of subtlety belongs to the primal nature, but not to the Self. In this context, because the purpose of the Self acts as the "instrumental cause" <note>the reason or motive for creation</note> for the Great Principle <term>Mahat: the first stage of cosmic evolution, or universal intelligence</term>, the ego-substance, and other states, the Self is also considered a "cause," much like the primal nature. 

Asking how this specific type of subtlety is understood regarding the undifferentiated state, he asks "however" and provides the answer: "but it is not the same as that of the resolvable matter." <note>original: *liṅga*; matter that has taken a specific form</note> It is true that the Self is a cause, but it is not a *material* cause. The Self does not change or "mutate" into the Great Principle or other states the way primal nature does. He concludes by saying: "Accordingly, it is explained that subtlety reaches its utmost degree in the primary substance."

## **46. These same [balanced-states] are the seeded concentration.**

These four "balanced-states" <term>samāpattis: states of meditative absorption</term> are described as having "seeds" because they rely on external, perceptible objects as their foundation. Therefore, this concentration is called "seeded" <note>original: *sabīja*; meditation that still has an object of focus</note>. 

Of these four:
*   The **deliberative** and **super-deliberative** states focus on coarse or physical objects.
*   The **reflective** and **super-reflective** states focus on subtle or abstract objects.

In this way, the four kinds of concentration have been listed in order.

Regarding these four states where the object is something to be known, he states that a "conscious" form of concentration may occur. **46. These same [balanced-states] are the seeded concentration.** The word *indeed* <note>original: *eva*</note> is technically out of place in the sentence and should be read as following the word "seeded." This implies that these four states are strictly limited to being "seeded" because they focus on an object of knowledge. 

However, the "seeded" state itself is not limited only to objects of knowledge. It also persists when the meditation focuses on the "knower" (the subject) or the "process of knowing" (the perception), because it is not yet cancelled out by the distinction between things with descriptive relations and things without them. Thus, there are four balanced-states regarding the *thing-to-be-known*, and four regarding the *knower* and the *act of knowing*: making eight¹ of these concentrations in total. The rest of the commentary is self-explanatory.

---

<note>¹ The Bīkāner Manuscript and the Bombay Sanskrit Series text read "are established" [original: *siddhā*] in place of "these" [original: *te*].</note>

->Internal undisturbed calm [—i. 47<-

**47. When there is the clearness of the super-reflective [balanced-state, the yogin gains] internal undisturbed calm.**

When the purity <term>Sattva: the quality of light, harmony, and intelligence</term> of the mind-stuff <term>Citta: the thinking-substance</term>—whose nature is light—is freed from the covering of impurities, it develops a transparent and steady flow that is no longer disturbed by passion <term>Rajas: the quality of activity and restlessness</term> or inertia <term>Tamas: the quality of darkness and dullness</term>. This state is what is called "clearness" <term>Vaiśāradya: the skill or purity of meditative insight</term>. When this clarity arises in the super-reflective balanced-state <term>Nirvicāra-samāpatti: a state of absorption beyond discursive thought</term>, the practitioner achieves "internal undisturbed calm." This is a state of spiritual serenity <note>original: *adhyātma-prasāda*</note> characterized by a vivid <note>original: *sphuṭa*</note> flash of insight. This insight does not need to move step-by-step through logical processes; instead, it perceives the object exactly as it truly is, all at once. Regarding this, it has been said:^1^

> "Just as a man who has climbed a mountain peak looks down upon those on the plain below <note>original: *bhūmiṣṭha*</note>, so the man of insight, having ascended to the serenity of wisdom and being himself free from suffering, looks upon all living beings caught in their pain."

Of the four types of meditative balance that focus on an object of knowledge, the highest excellence belongs to the super-reflective state. The author describes this in the aphorism: **47. When there is the clearness of the super-reflective [balanced-state, the yogin gains] internal undisturbed calm.** He explains the term <term>clearness</term> using the discussion on "impurity." Impurity refers to the buildup of passion and inertia, a defilement that acts as a veil over the mind. Clearness is the state of being free from this veil. The phrase "the essence of which is light" means that the mind is naturally luminous. For this reason, the purity of the mind-stuff is no longer overwhelmed. 

An objection is raised: "This may be true. But if this meditative state focuses on an external object to be known, how can this 'undisturbed calm' focus on itself?" To this, the author replies that it "has as its intended-object the thing as it really is." In other words, the calm does not take the "self" as its object of observation, but rather the self serves as the foundation <note>original: *ādhāra*; the substrate or support</note>^2^ for this state. The phrase "does not pass successively through the serial order" means the perception is simultaneous rather than linear. On this point, he quotes the "Verse of the Supreme Sage" <note>original: *pāramārṣīṃ gāthām*</note>. Because the yogin is elevated above others by the perfection of his perception,^3^ he understands that all creatures are "in their pain," trapped by the three types of suffering <note>The three sufferings are: those caused by oneself, by other beings, or by nature/divine forces</note>.

---

^1^ Compare the *Mahabharata* (books 12.17.20 and 151.11) and the *Dhammapada* (verse 28). There is a striking similarity to Francis Bacon’s *Essay on Truth*: "No pleasure is comparable to the standing upon the vantage-ground of truth (a hill not to be commanded and where the air is always clear and serene) and to see the errors and wanderings and mists and tempests, in the world below."

^2^ This is clarified in the *Secret of the Patanjala System* <note>original: *Pātañjala Rahasyam*</note>: "A doubt arises whether a cause-and-effect relationship can exist between things in different locations; this addresses that concern."

^3^ Compare to page 62, note 2, and Sūtra ii. 15.

# Book I. Concentration or <term>Samādhi: a state of deep meditative absorption</term>
<meta>Header-left: i. 48—]</meta>

### 48. In this [calm] the insight is truth-bearing.

In one whose mind-stuff <term>Citta: the mental substance consisting of intellect, ego, and sensory mind</term> is concentrated, the insight <gloss>1</gloss> which arises in this [calm] receives the technical name of <term>Truth-bearing: *ṛtambharā*, meaning insight that carries only the truth, entirely free from error</term>. And this is a [term] whose meaning is intelligible of itself: [this insight] bears truth <gloss>2</gloss> and nothing else; in it there is not even a trace of misconception. And in this sense it has been said, “By the <term>Sacred Word: *Śruti*, or the revealed knowledge of the Vedas</term> [and] by inference and by eagerness for practice in contemplation, in three ways he promotes his insight and gains the highest yoga.” With regard to this same point he gives the consensus of <term>Yogins: practitioners of yoga</term> by telling of the term current among yogins which itself expresses the intended-object. **48. In this [calm] the insight is truth-bearing.** The Comment is easy. By the expression "Sacred Word" is meant the hearing <note>original: *śravaṇa*</note> prescribed by the <term>Vedas: the oldest scriptures of Hinduism</term>; by the expression "inference" is meant consideration <note>original: *manana*</note>. Contemplation is reflection. Practice in this is following it up one time after another. Eagerness for this is close attention [to it]. So in this way <term>Absorption: *nididhyāsana*, or profound and repeated meditation</term> is described.

**But this [insight]—**

### 49. Has an object other than the insight resulting from things heard or from inferences inasmuch as its intended-object is a particular.

<term>A thing heard</term> is knowledge derived from verbal-communication <note>original: *āgama*</note>. This deals with generic objects. For a <term>Particular: the unique, specific essence of an individual thing</term> cannot be connoted by a verbal-communication. Why [not]? Because a word does not have its conventional-usage established by the particular. Similarly, inference deals with <term>Generic objects: general categories or universal concepts</term> only. [For instance, compare i. 7], we say, where there is getting [to a place], there is motion; and where there is no getting [to a place], there is no motion. And by an inference we get a conclusion in generic [terms only]. Therefore no particular can be the object of verbal-communication or of inference. And of this subtile and hidden and remote <gloss>3</gloss> thing there is no knowledge by ordinary perception. Furthermore we cannot assert that this particular has no validity and does not exist. Therefore this particular as object, whether it belong to a subtile element or to the Self, is apper-

# Book I. Concentration or Samādhi
## Normative insight [—i. 49]

...perceptible by the concentrated insight only. Consequently, this insight has an object other than the objects of insight resulting from things heard <note>original: śruta</note> or from inference <note>original: anumāna</note>, inasmuch as its intended object is a particular <note>the unique, individual essence of a thing</note>.

The objection is made: “This may be true. But the super-reflective state <term>Balanced-state: *Samāpatti*, where the mind becomes like a transparent jewel, taking the form of the object</term>—which is produced by the perfection of impressions whose objects <gloss>1</gloss> refer to that which is known by verbal communication <note>original: āgama</note> or by inference—can refer <note>original: *gocarayet*, meaning to "range over" or perceive</note> only to the objects of verbal communication and inference. For surely a subliminal impression <term>Saṃskāra: a latent mental impression or habit-pattern</term> derived from the experience of one object is not able to produce knowledge with regard to another. For that would be an unwarranted assumption. Therefore, if the super-reflective state is truth-bearing, verbal communications and inferences must also be assumed to be truth-bearing.” 

In reply to this, the <term>Sūtra: a concise thread of knowledge or aphorism</term> says:

### 49. It has an object other than the insight resulting from things heard or from inferences, inasmuch as its intended-object is a particular.

For the <term>Sattva: the quality of purity, light, and intelligence</term> of the thinking-substance <note>the *Citta*</note> is naturally bright; although it has the power of seeing all intended objects, it becomes obscured by <term>Tamas: the quality of darkness, inertia, and heaviness</term>. Only when it is set free to manifest by <term>Rajas: the quality of energy, movement, and passion</term> does it then know the object. But when, through practice and passionlessness, the defilement of *rajas* and *tamas* is cast off and it shines forth spotlessly clear, then it passes beyond the limits of all measures <note>original: *māna*</note> and all things measurable <note>original: *meya*</note> and possesses endless brightness. What then, pray, can there be that is not within its scope? 

He explains the aphorism in these words: “A thing heard is knowledge derived from verbal communication. This deals with generic objects <note>general categories or universals</note>.” Why? “For a particular cannot be connoted by a verbal communication.” For what reason? Because a word does not have its conventional usage established by a particular instance, since the word is an infinite category and since it would have a "too-wide-pervasion" <note>original: *vyabhicāra*; a logical fallacy where a definition applies to too many things</note>. For we do not perceive the relation of a word and the thing it expresses in connection with every single particular instance of that word. And furthermore, the sense of a sentence cannot capture such a specific particular. 

Even in the case of an inference, which depends for its origin upon the knowledge of the relation between the "syllogistic mark" <note>original: *liṅga*, like smoke</note> and the "subject of the proposition" <note>original: *liṅgin*, like fire</note>, the same procedure holds good, as he says: “Similarly inference.” In the expression “where there is no getting to a place,” the words “where” and “there” should, by logical conversion, be made to indicate the "pervaded" and the "pervader" <note>the logical relationship where one thing necessarily accompanies another</note>. Therefore, here by an inference we get a conclusion only in generic terms. 

He sums up with the word “Therefore.” It might be admitted that then we have ordinary perception irrespective of a knowledge of the relation between the word and the thing expressed, and that this perception does not deal with generic objects only. In reply to this he says, “And of this... no.” It may not be admitted that ordinary perception depends upon a knowledge of the relation of word and thing; but it must be admitted that it depends upon...

the senses. And with this [higher insight] the senses have no pre-established harmony. This is the meaning. It is objected that if the individual is not within the scope of verbal-communications and inferences and perceptions, then it does not exist. For there is no source-of-valid-ideas for [it]. In reply to this he says «Furthermore . . . not.» For a source-of-valid-ideas is not [necessarily] a pervader nor a cause of the object-of-knowledge <note>original: *prameya*</note> to the extent that, if that [source-of-valid-ideas] should cease, the [object-of-knowledge] would cease to be. For surely, when the moon is a slender crescent <note>original: *kalāvant*</note>, those who accept sources-of-valid-ideas do not doubt the real existence of the deer¹ <note>Ancient Indian tradition often identifies the "man in the moon" as a deer or a hare</note> which is situated in the other part [of the moon's surface not then visible]. «Therefore,» for this reason it «is apperceptible by the concentrated insight only.» And here the atoms and the selves <note>the fundamental spiritual essences or souls</note> which are subjected to [this] discussion are endowed with a particularity peculiar to themselves, because, being substances, they are distinct from each other. Whatever things, being substances, are distinct from each other, these are endowed with a particularity peculiar to themselves, like a cripple or a man with a shaven head. According to this inference, and to the verbal-communication which is devoted to teaching what the truth-bearing insight is, [the peculiar individuality of this insight has been defined]. Although the individual is described, still in the absence of such a description doubt might arise, because it has been obtained by a line-of-reasoning ; yet in so far as it is not far² or remote, this pure-being <term>Sattva: the quality of light, clarity, and intelligence in the mind</term> is brought, with some difficulty, within the scope of verbal-communication or of inference. But they do not [make evident the existence of the particular] by as direct an experience as words of connexion, for instance, through their application of gender and number, [bring] the meaning of the word 'and' [within the scope of verbal-communication or of inference]. Therefore it is established that [this insight] has an object other than the insights resulting from things heard or from inferences.

When the practitioner of yoga <note>original: *yogin*</note> has gained concentrated insight, the subliminal-impression <term>Saṃskāra: a latent mental habit or "groove" left by an experience</term> made by the insight is reproduced again and again.

### 50. The subliminal-impression produced by this [super-reflective balanced-state] is hostile to other subliminal-impressions.

The subliminal-impression arising from concentrated insight inhibits the latent-impression from the emergent subliminal-impression <note>the habitual thoughts that arise when one is not in deep meditation</note>. After emergent subliminal-impressions have been repressed,

'Let this be granted. Let the [concentration] conscious [of an object] have a reality as its object by the practice of the aforesaid means. But this concentrated insight may be obstructed by beginningless emergent subliminal-impressions in so far as it is closely enveloped [by them], like minute flashes [of light] from a lamp in the eddy of a whirling wind.' To remove this doubt he introduces the next sutra <note>An aphorism or concise rule in Sanskrit literature</note> with the words «concentrated insight.» He recites the sutra 50. **The subliminal-impression produced by this [super-reflective balanced-state] is hostile to other subliminal-impressions.** The word <this> refers to the super-reflective balanced-state. The word <other> describes the emergence <note>The state of mind when one is not in meditation, but interacting with the world</note>. It is the nature of thoughts to incline¹ to intended-objects as they really are. This instability continues unsteady only so long as it does not reach the reality [literally, that-ness]. After reaching that and because it has taken a stable position there, [this] idea from the subliminal-impression does most certainly inhibit the series of ideas from subliminal-impressions which refer to what is not reality, even although [this series] is beginningless and rolls on as the wheel² of the series of [fluctuations and] subliminal-impressions. And in this sense outsiders³ <note>Philosophers from schools other than the Yoga/Samkhya tradition, likely Buddhists</note> also say, “There is no inhibition of the unviolated essence of a thing-as-it-really-is by contradictions even although these latter be from time without beginning. For it is the nature of the mind to incline to things as they are.” The objector would say, ‘This may be true. We may admit that, as a result of concentrated insight, there is a restriction of a subliminal-impression produced during the emergent state. <header>i. 50—] Book I. Concentration or Samādhi [98</header>

this,» which he removes with the words «these ... do not.» For the work of the mind-stuff <note>original: *citta*; the field of mental activity</note> is of two kinds: the enjoyment of <term>sensory perceptions</term> <note>original: *çabdādi*, literally "sound and the rest"</note> and discriminative discernment <note>The ability to distinguish between the eternal Self and the temporary material world</note>. With regard to these two kinds of work, the mind-stuff, when it carries the latent-impressions of past actions <note>original: *karma*</note> stemming from the five hindrances, proceeds toward the enjoyment of sensory things. But for the mind whose latent-impressions of past actions have been uprooted by the deep mental habits arising from spiritual insight, and whose task is nearly ended, the only work that remains is discriminative discernment.

Accordingly, the mental habits gained from concentration are not the reasons why the mind-stuff continues to seek enjoyment. On the contrary, they are hostile to that goal. They cause the mind-stuff to cease its worldly work; they make it incapable of seeking enjoyment. This is the meaning. Why? «For the movement of the mind-stuff terminates at the time of discernment.» Since, in order to enjoy, the mind-stuff moves only until it experiences the final realization. But when this realization has come to pass, the hindrances cease and the mind no longer has the task of seeking enjoyment. Consequently, the complete quietness of the task of enjoyment is the very purpose for which the impressions from insight exist. It is this that has been stated here.

---

->What further does he gain ?<-

**51. When this subliminal-impression also is restricted, since all is restricted, the yogin gains seedless concentration.**

This <term>seedless concentration</term> <note>original: *nirbija-samādhi*; a state of meditation where no "seeds" of future thoughts or rebirth remain</note> is counter not only to ordinary thoughts but is opposed even to the mental habits made during deep insight. Why? Because the mental habit produced by the act of "restriction" <note>the deliberate stopping of mental activity</note> inhibits even the habits produced by concentration. We can infer that these "restriction-habits" exist because of the experience of the lapse of time during which there is <term>stability</term> <note>original: *sthiti*</note> of that restriction. 

Together with the mental habits which arise out of both active and restricted concentration and which lead toward <term>Isolation</term> <note>original: *kaivalya*; the ultimate liberation of the soul</note>, the mind-stuff resolves itself back into its own permanent <term>primary-matter</term> <note>original: *prakriti*; the fundamental substance of the universe</note>. Therefore, these final meditative habits are counter to the mind’s usual tasks and do not cause it to remain active. Consequently, its task ended, the mind-stuff ceases to function along with those habits that led it to liberation. When it ceases, the Self abides in himself and is therefore called pure and liberated.

<summary>This page concludes the first book by explaining how even the "good" habits of meditation eventually stop, allowing the mind to dissolve and the soul to reach ultimate, seedless liberation.</summary>
