<page-num>99</page-num>
# The Attainment of Absolute Freedom [-i. 51]

He asks, "What further?" What does he also gain? Since the mind-stuff <note>original: *citta*; the collective term for the heart and mind</note> contains subliminal-impressions <note>original: *samskāra*; the latent habits or "grooves" in the mind formed by past experiences</note> produced during spiritual insight, it still has a task to fulfill, just as before, as long as it is capable of generating a flow of that insight. Therefore, to finally complete the task, something else is still required. This is the meaning. He provides the answer in the 51st aphorism (*sūtra*).

**When this [final meditative habit] is also restricted, and since every other mental activity is restricted, the practitioner gains seedless concentration.**

The higher state of detachment <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: *para-vairāgya*; a state of total desirelessness</note>, which is characterized by an undisturbed calm of perception, increases the strength of these restrictive habits. This process restricts not only the insight itself but even those subliminal-impressions <note>habits of mind</note> created by that insight. This is the meaning of the word "even." Since the entire stream of mental habits is restricted as it rises into consciousness, and because there is no remaining cause for activity, no further effect can be produced. This state is known as "seedless concentration" <note>original: *nirbīja-samādhi*; a state of meditation where no "seeds" of future worldly action or rebirth remain</note>.

He explains the aphorism with the phrase, "This [seedless concentration]." "This" refers to the seedless concentration arising from the highest detachment. This state is the opposite of even the highest focused insight. Through its own nature as a cause, <gloss>2</gloss> it becomes not only a counter-force to focused insight but also a direct contradiction to the lingering habits formed by that insight.

> It might be objected that, "A specific understanding (*vijñāna*) produced by detachment would—since an understanding is a real thing—only inhibit insight and nothing more. But how can it inhibit a subliminal-impression <note>a latent habit</note>, which is a different kind of thing than a conscious thought? For it is evident that a person, even when awake, retains a memory of an object seen in their dream. Therefore, latent habits are not truly inhibited."

With this objection in mind, he asks, "Why?" He gives the answer with the words "produced by restriction." "Restriction" is the process by which insight is stilled. It is the highest state of detachment. Because it is produced from this state, it is called a "subliminal-impression of restriction." Only through this habit of restriction—when it has been cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with earnest attention—and not by a mere conscious thought, are the habits of insight inhibited. This is the meaning. The objector continues:

> "This may be so. But what is the evidence <note>original: *pramāṇa*; source of valid knowledge</note> for the existence of these 'habits of restriction'? One would have to either perceive it directly or infer it from its effect, which is memory. Yet, when all the mind's fluctuations are restricted, the practitioner has neither perception nor memory. Since he has destroyed all mental activity whatsoever, it should be impossible for him to produce a memory of it."

In reply to this, he says, "in restriction." The stability of this restriction is the state of the mind-stuff when it is fully stilled. The existence of these latent habits of restriction is proved by the experience of the lapse of time—such as periods of forty-eight minutes (*muhūrta*), or a half-watch <note>about 90 minutes</note>, or a whole watch <note>about 3 hours</note>, or a full day and night, and so forth. What he means to say is this: according to the degree of perfection in one's detachment and practice, the perfection of this stillness is experienced by the practitioner. And the moments of higher detachment, in so far as they are...

<gloss>2</gloss> As explained in aphorism i. 18.

<page-num>100</page-num>
<header>i. 51] Book I. Concentration or Samādhi [100</header>

Because these moments of mental stillness are not related to each other in a fixed sequence, and because they last for varying periods of time, they are not initially capable of producing the full perfection of mental restriction. Therefore, the point is that we must admit there is a permanent accumulation of subliminal-impressions <note>original: *samskāra*; the latent habits or "grooves" left in the mind by experience</note> produced by the gathering of various moments of passionlessness. 

An objector might say, "The habits formed by meditative insight may perish, but why should the habits of mental restriction perish with them? And if they do not perish, then the mind-stuff would still have a task to perform." 

In reply to this, the author says: «out of the emergent.» 

The analysis of the Sanskrit compound <term>*tasya*</term> <note>meaning "of this"</note> refers to both the "emergence" (the active state of mind) and the "concentration of emergence" which restricts this active state. The subliminal-impressions arising out of these two are the habits conducive to Isolation <note>original: *Kaivalya*; the state of absolute freedom where consciousness is no longer entangled with matter</note>. These are the same as those produced by the restriction of the mind. 

The habits of active insight are eventually resolved back into the mind-stuff. Thus, the mind-stuff contains the latent habits of that insight. But the habit of restriction remains (<term>*āste*</term> <note>original: "it stays" or "it sits"</note>) as something just newly arisen in the mind-stuff. Although this habit of stillness is present, the **mind-stuff** has no further task to fulfill. 

This is because the mind-stuff only has a task to perform when it is bringing about the two purposes of the Self <note>original: *Purusha*; the pure, eternal consciousness</note>: 
1. The experience of sounds and other perceptible things. 
2. The ability to discern the difference between the Self and matter. 

These are the only two purposes of the Self. But when nothing is left but the habits of total mental restriction—and since the Self is no longer reflected (<term>*pratisaṁ-vedin*</term> <note>meaning the Self as the "knower" of the reflections in the mind</note>) in the thinking-substance—this state no longer serves the purposes of the Self. 

On the other hand, in the case of "discarnate" beings or those whose bodies are "resolved-into-primary-matter" <note>beings who have reached high states but are still bound to nature</note>, the mind-stuff still has a task to fulfill. This is because their minds are not only moving toward restriction but are also still pervaded (<term>*vāsita*</term> <note>literally "scented" or "perfumed"</note>) with spiritual hindrances. With this in mind, the author says «Consequently.» The rest of the argument is easy to follow.

The formal announcement (<term>*uddeça*</term>) and the definition (<term>*nirdeça*</term>) of **Yoga**, the characteristics of the mental fluctuations that exist for the sake of this Yoga, the means of practicing Yoga, and its various subdivisions—all of these have been sketched in this First Book.

# BOOK SECOND
## MEANS OF ATTAINMENT
<note>original: *Sādhana Pāda*; This section focuses on the practical disciplines and tools a practitioner uses to make spiritual progress.</note>

It has been stated what yoga is for a person whose mind is already concentrated. This sūtra <note>a concise aphorism or rule</note> introduces the problem of how even a person whose mind-stuff is distracted <note>original: *vyutthāna*; literally "emergent" or "rising up" into worldly activity</note> may be joined (*yukta*) in the discipline of yoga.

**1. Self-castigation and study and devotion to the Lord are the Yoga of action.**
<note>original: *Içvara* (Lord/Supreme Teacher); This sūtra defines *Kriya Yoga*, the yoga of outward action.</note>

Yoga is not perfected in someone who does not practice self-discipline <note>original: *tapas*; often translated as "self-castigation," it refers to the "heat" generated by spiritual austerities and the willing endurance of opposites like heat and cold</note>. Impurity—which is patterned with subconscious impressions <note>original: *vāsanā*; the latent tendencies or "habit-patterns" of the mind</note> from time without beginning, arising from the hindrances and from the law of cause and effect (*karma*), and into which the net of worldly objects has found entrance—is not reduced except by <self-castigation.> This is the use$^1$ of self-discipline. And this kind of discipline, because it does not disturb the calm of the mind-stuff, is judged by great sages to be worthy of the practitioner's earnest attention. <Recitation> is the repetition$^2$ of purifying mantras such as the Mystic Syllable <note>original: *praṇava*; the sacred sound 'Om'</note> or the study of scriptures concerning Liberation. <Devotion to the Lord> is the offering$^3$ up of all actions to the Supreme Teacher or the renunciation of the fruit of all these actions.

If it be objected that the First Book described yoga along with its means, its divisions, and its results, and that no reason remains why a Second Book should be begun, the author replies with the words "has been stated." For in the First Book, practice and detachment were described as the means to yoga. And since these two do not instantly come into being for one whose mind is still distracted, they stand in need of the means taught in the Second Book in order to purify the inner essence <note>original: *sattva*; the quality of the mind that is clear, light, and harmonious</note>. For by these means, the practitioner thoroughly purifies the *sattva* and performs the protective ordinances and daily duties...

---

$^1$ Similarly discussed in Book I, section 41.
$^2$ See Book II, section 44 and compare the *Linga Purana*, Book VIII, section 39.
$^3$ Contrast this with Book I, section 23 and see also the *Linga Purana*, Book VIII, section 40.

<summary>This page introduces the Second Book of the Yoga Sutras, establishing "Kriya Yoga" (Action Yoga) as the necessary starting point for practitioners whose minds are still caught in worldly distractions. It defines the three parts of this practice: self-discipline (tapas), sacred study (svādhyāya), and surrender to the Divine (içvara-praṇidhāna).</summary>

# BOOK II. MEANS OF ATTAINMENT
## Section on Practice
<note>original: *Sādhana Pāda*; This book focuses on the practical disciplines—the "means"—that a student uses to reach the state of yoga.</note>

The practitioner cultivates practice and passionlessness. The state of being concentrated is the state of being undistracted. How could even a man whose mind-stuff is emergent <note>original: *vyutthāna*; a mind that is still "rising up" into worldly thoughts rather than resting in meditation</note> become a yogin by being concentrated (*yukta*) through the means which are about to be taught? This is the central question. From among those observances which are to be described, the author of the sūtras <note>Patañjali</note> first teaches what the yoga of action is, having selected those most helpful for the beginner.

**1. Self-castigation, study, and devotion to the Lord are the Yoga of action.**
<note>original: *Kriya-yoga*; *Içvara* (Lord/Supreme Teacher)</note>

Action which is itself yoga is the "yoga of action," since it is a means of achieving yoga. Therefore, in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* <note>one of the eighteen major ancient Hindu texts</note>, in the dialogue between Khāṇḍikya and Keçidhvaja, starting with the passage: <margin>1</margin>
> "At first the yogin who is just beginning to apply himself is called a novice <note>original: *yoga-yuj*</note>," self-castigation and recitation and the like are set forth.

With the words "in him who is not self-castigated," the author shows by a negative example that self-discipline is a necessary means. By the words "from time without beginning," he shows that self-castigation has a subsidiary function which serves as a tool <margin>2</margin> for attaining yoga. The mind is colored by subconscious impressions <note>original: *vāsanā*; the deep habit-patterns of the mind</note> from time without beginning, arising from spiritual hindrances and from the law of cause and effect (*karma*). Therefore, impurity—which is an excess of passion <note>original: *rajas*</note> and inertia <note>original: *tamas*</note>—has woven itself into the mind like a net of worldly objects. This impurity is not thoroughly reduced without self-castigation <note>original: *tapas*; also translated as "austerity" or "heat," referring to the spiritual fire that purifies the practitioner</note>. "Reduction" means the thorough thinning out of that which was closely woven.

The objection is raised: "Even if we have recourse to self-castigation, if it causes a disorder of the bodily humours <note>original: *doṣa*; the biological energies—wind, bile, and phlegm—which must remain balanced for health in Indian medicine</note>, it would be hostile to yoga. How then can it be a means to attain it?" In reply to this, he says, "And this <margin>3</margin> kind." Self-castigation should be performed only so long as it does not bring on a disorder <margin>4</margin> of the humours. This is the meaning.

"Such as the Mystic Syllable" <note>the sacred sound OM</note>, that is, study such as the Hymn to the Cosmic Man <margin>5</margin> <note>original: *Puruṣa Sūkta*; Rig Veda 10.90</note> or the Prayer to the Howler <note>original: *Rudramaṇḍala*</note> or a *Brāhmaṇa* <note>a prose manual on ritual</note> or similar texts from the Vedas, or the *Brahma-pārāyaṇa* <margin>6</margin> from the Purāṇas.

Devotion to the Lord <note>original: *Içvara*</note>, that is, the Supreme Teacher, the Exalted One. Regarding Him, this <margin>7</margin> has been said:
> "Whatever I do, whether auspicious or inauspicious, whether intentionally or unintentionally, all that is surrendered unto Thee. Moved by Thee, I do it all."

Renunciation of the fruit <note>the results or rewards</note> of all these actions means performing them without attachment to the outcome. And regarding this, it has been said: <margin>8</margin>
> "Your concern is with actions only and never with their fruits. Do not let the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction."

<margin>3</margin> As opposed, for instance, to the more extreme forms mentioned in *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* ii. 11.
<margin>4</margin> Compare Book I, aphorism 30.

# PURPOSES OF THE YOGA OF ACTION
## Section II.2

Now, the purpose of this yoga of action is:

**2. To foster concentration and to thin out the hindrances.**

When a practitioner gives earnest attention to the yoga of action, it fosters a state of deep concentration and thins out the <term>hindrances</term> <note>original: *kleśas*; the five mental afflictions like ignorance and ego that cause suffering</note> to an extreme degree. Once these hindrances are extremely thinned, the fire of <term>Highest Discernment</term> <note>original: *prasaṁkhyāna*; also translated as "Elevation"</note> will render them unable to grow, much like seeds that have been burned by fire and can no longer sprout. 

Furthermore, the subtle insight—which is the ability to distinguish between the mind's highest purity <note>original: *sattva*</note> and the true Self—remains untouched by these hindrances because they have been so weakened. Having finished its work, this insight will be ready for <term>resolution</term> <note>original: *pratiprasava*; literally "inverse-propagation," where effects return to their original cause</note>. 

To explain the purpose of this practice, the author introduces the second verse with the words: "For the..."

**2. To foster concentration and to thin out the hindrances.** <note>The scholar Deussen provided an excellent translation of this concept as "Interiorization" (original German: *Verinnerlichung*).</note>

One might object: "If the yoga of action alone can thin out the hindrances, then we do not need the fire of Highest Discernment." 

To this, the author replies with the phrase "extremely thinned." The yoga of action only serves to weaken the hindrances; it does not "sterilize" them or make them completely incapable of ever returning. Only Highest Discernment can achieve that total sterilization. The phrase "like burned seeds" is used to show that the burned seeds of winter rice and these weakened hindrances are similar—neither can produce a "crop" or further effects.

Another objector might say: "This may be true. But if Highest Discernment alone can stop the hindrances from growing, then why do we need to thin them out first through yoga of action?"

In response, the author discusses the "thinning" of these obstacles. If the hindrances are not thinned out first, the ability to distinguish between the mind's purity and the true Self will be overwhelmed by powerful enemies. In such a state, this insight cannot even begin to arise, let alone destroy the obstacles. However, when the hindrances are made thin and weak, this discernment—aided by a lack of worldly passion and regular practice—finally emerges. 

Once this discernment (the sense of difference between the mind's purity and the Self) has finally arisen, it remains untouched and un-overwhelmed by the hindrances. This is what is called "subtle insight," and it is called "subtle" because its focus is beyond what the physical senses can perceive. This insight "will be ready for resolution"—meaning it is ready to dissolve back into its source. Why? Because its job is done. In other words, when the cause (the mind's activities) has finished producing its effects (the <term>qualities of nature</term> <note>original: *guṇas*</note>), its task is complete.

---
<note>1. Compare this concept of resolution in sections ii. 2, ii. 10, ii. 27, iii. 50, and iv. 34 of the original text.</note>

<summary>This page explains that the Yoga of Action is used to weaken mental obstacles (hindrances) so that the fire of meditative discernment can eventually destroy them completely, like burning seeds to prevent them from growing. It distinguishes between merely thinning out these obstacles and the final stage where the mind's work is finished and it returns to its source.</summary>

->**Section II. 3— Book II. Means of Attainment**<-

Now what are these <note>original: *te*; many manuscripts omit this word</note> hindrances and how many are they?

### 3. Undifferentiated-consciousness and the feeling-of-personality and passion and aversion and the will-to-live are the five <note>original: *pañca*; many manuscripts omit this word</note> hindrances.

This means that the so-called hindrances are five misconceptions <note>referencing Book I, aphorism 8</note>. These, when flowing out, make the <term>governing power</term> <note>original: *adhikāra*; the inherent tendency of nature to produce experiences</note> of the <term>qualities of nature</term> <note>original: *guṇa*; the three fundamental threads—purity, activity, and inertia—that make up the physical and mental world</note> more rigid; make a mutation more stable; swell the stream of effects and causes; and, becoming interdependent upon one another for aid, bring forth the fruition of <term>action</term> <note>original: *karma*</note>.

He raises a question by saying "Now" and replies to it by the <term>aphorism</term> <note>original: *sūtra*</note> upon "Undifferentiated-consciousness." 

**3. Undifferentiated-consciousness <note>original: *avidyā*</note> and the feeling-of-personality and passion and aversion and the will-to-live are the five hindrances.** 

He explains the word "hindrances" by the words "five misconceptions." Undifferentiated-consciousness, to begin with, is nothing but misconception. The feeling-of-personality and the others also have undifferentiated-consciousness as their material cause, and since they cannot exist without it, they too are misconceptions. And hence when undifferentiated-consciousness is destroyed, there would follow the destruction of them also. 

He mentions the reason why they should be destroyed, in that they are the cause of the round-of-rebirths <note>the cycle of reincarnation or *saṃsāra*</note>. This he states in the word "These." When flowing out <note>that is, moving continuously forth; compare with ii. 4 and iii. 13</note>, they "make the governing power of the qualities more rigid," that is, more powerful; and in consequence "make a mutation more stable." For in successive forms—as the unmanifested primary matter, as the "Great" thinking-substance, and as the personality-substance—they swell, that is, they intensify, the stream of cause and effect. 

He shows for what purpose they do all this in the words "one another." The three fruits of <term>action</term> <note>original: *karma*</note>, distinguished elsewhere <note>ii. 13</note> as being birth, length of life, and the quality of experience, have their <term>purpose</term> <note>original: *artha*</note> in the True Self. That purpose those hindrances bring to pass—that is, they accomplish it. Do they accomplish this singly? He says, "No." But they act "upon one another for aid," meaning the hindrances are aided by the actions, and the actions are aided by the hindrances.

### 4. Undifferentiated-consciousness <note>original: *avidyā*</note> is the field for the others, whether they be dormant or attenuated or intercepted or sustained.

Of these five, undifferentiated-consciousness is the field or the "propagative soil." The others are the feeling-of-personality and the rest...

It establishes that ignorance (avidyā) is the fundamental "soil" from which all other mental afflictions grow.</summary>

<header>Varieties of undifferentiated-consciousness [—Book II, Aphorism 4]</header>

[The five hindrances exist] in four kinds of forms: the dormant, the attenuated, the intercepted, and the sustained.

1.  Of these four, what is the **dormant** state? It is the tendency of the hindrances—which remain merely as potential in the mind—toward the condition of a "seed." The awakening of that dormant hindrance is the coming face-to-face with a particular object which makes that hindrance manifest. However, for one who has reached **Elevation** <note>original: *prasaṁkhyāna*; a state of high discernment or meditative realization</note>, and whose hindrances have become **burned seeds**, there is no such awakening. This remains true even when he is brought face-to-face with the object that would usually manifest them. For out of what can a burned seed germinate? For this reason, the **fortunate** <note>original: *kuçala*; referring to a person skilled in spiritual practice</note> man whose hindrances have dwindled away is said to be in his **last body** <note>original: *caramadeha*; the final incarnation before achieving liberation</note><sup>1</sup>. In him only, the "burned state" of the seeds—the fifth stage of the hindrances—is found, and not in other persons. So, although the hindrances still exist in a sense, the **vitality** <note>original: *sāmarthya*; the inherent power or capacity</note> of the seed is said to be already burned. Accordingly, even when the object is present, there is no awakening of these hindrances. Thus, both the dormant state and the failure of the "burned seed" to sprout have been described.

2.  **Attenuation** is now described. The hindrances, when **overpowered** <note>original: *upahata*</note> by the cultivation of their opposites<sup>2</sup>, become attenuated or weakened.

3.  When this is the case, other hindrances **intercept** the attenuated ones repeatedly, and move forth actively again in this or that **unattenuated form** <note>original: *ātmanā*</note>. In that case<sup>3</sup> they are called intercepted. How is this? Since, for instance, when one is in love, no anger is felt; this is because when one is in love, anger does not actively move forth. Furthermore, love felt toward one person is by no means absent toward other objects. When **Chāitra** <note>a traditional Sanskrit placeholder name, similar to "John Doe"</note> is known to be in love with one woman, it is not assumed that he is out of love for all other women. Rather, his love finds its active fluctuation fixed in this one direction, while in other directions the fluctuation is yet to come. For this third state—interception—is for the moment both dormant, attenuated, and blocked.

4.  That fluctuation which is fixed upon an object is **sustained** <note>original: *udāra*; also translated as "active" or "aroused"</note>. No one of all...

<sup>3</sup> When they form a succession of **attenuated** <note>original: *tanu*</note> and **not attenuated** <note>original: *atanu*</note> states.

It highlights that through spiritual "Elevation," these obstacles become like "burned seeds" that can never sprout again.</summary>

If this is so <note>original: *tarhi*</note>, what is this hindrance that is intercepted [or] dormant [or] attenuated or sustained? The answer is now given <note>original: *ucyate*</note>. It is exactly true [that all hindrances are forms of undifferentiated-consciousness]. But only when these [hindrances] are particularized, do they become intercepted and so on. He shows that hindrances are to be rejected in that they have their root in undifferentiated-consciousness.

**4. Undifferentiated-consciousness <note>original: *avidyā*; the fundamental spiritual ignorance or lack of awareness</note> is the field for the others whether they be dormant or attenuated or intercepted or sustained.**

When he asks «1. Of these [four], what is the dormant state?» his intention is to say that there is no proof for the real existence of hindrances, if they are not performing their peculiar purposeful activity. He tells the answer in the words «in the mind.» The hindrances may not indeed perform their purposeful activity, but in the case of the discarnate <note>original: *videha*; beings existing without physical bodies</note> and of those [whose bodies] are resolved into primary matter <note>original: *prakṛti*; the primordial substance of the universe</note>, they assume the form of seed and exist merely potentially, as curds exist in milk. For other than discriminative insight <note>original: *vivekakhyāti*; the ability to distinguish between the true self and the material world</note> there is nothing to cause the sterility of these [hindrances]. Hence the discarnate and those [whose bodies] are resolved into primary matter, who have not obtained discriminate discernment, have their hindrances dormant, until such time as [these hindrances] reach the time of their limitation. But when they reach that, since the hindrances revert once more, they come face-to-face with the various objects [of sense]. Thus these [hindrances] are those of which the basis is merely potential. <header>ii. 4-] *Elevation is the destroyer of hindrances* [110</header>

"Where then?" He says, "The hindrances are to be destroyed by meditation." The hindrances, which have been weakened by the <term>yoga of action<note>kriyā-yoga: practical discipline involving austerity, self-study, and devotion to God</note></term>, are to be destroyed by <term>Elevation<note>prasankhyāna: the highest state of meditative discernment or "higher prospection"</note></term>, and are to be brought to the state of being "burnt seeds" <note>A metaphor for mental impressions that have been so thoroughly roasted by wisdom that they can no longer "sprout" into future suffering or rebirth</note> by the <term>perfect knowledge of distinctions<note>saṁyag-jñāna</note></term>. Just as the coarse stains on a cloth are first shaken off and then the fine stains are removed by a more refined effort and specific means, so the gross mental fluctuations are first weakened by the yoga of action and then the fine fluctuations are destroyed by Elevation. — 11.

Now, what is the destruction of the fluctuations of the hindrances while they are yet to come? He says:

### 11. Their fluctuations are to be escaped by meditation.

Just as the fluctuations of the hindrances, which are gross, are weakened by the yoga of action, so also these fluctuations of the hindrances—once they have been weakened—are to be escaped by the power of <term>Elevation<note>prasankhyāna</note></term>, until they are made subtle and so reach the state of burnt seeds. Just as coarse stains on clothes are first shaken off, and then the fine stains are removed by a subsequent, more careful effort, so gross fluctuations of hindrances require but a small effort for their weakening, but the weakened fluctuations must be escaped by an extraordinary effort. — 11.

Having described the hindrances, he mentions the hindrances as the root of the <term>karmic storehouse<note>karmic residuum or karmāśaya: the latent pool of past actions waiting to bear fruit</note></term>. He says:

### 12. The karmic storehouse has its root in hindrances and is experienced in a present or in a future birth.

The collection of <term>merit<note>dharma</note></term> and of <term>demerit<note>adharma</note></term>, which has its origin in greed, in delusion, and in anger, is the karmic storehouse. And it is felt in a present birth or in a future birth. Within this, the karmic storehouse which is felt in a present birth is exemplified by the cases of <term>Nandiçvara<note>A devotee of Shiva who attained a divine body in his human lifetime through intense devotion</note></term> or <term>Nahusa<note>A king who was turned into a serpent during his life due to his pride and the curse of a sage</note></term>. Of these, that which has its origin in the intense practice of the yoga of action, or in the power of a sacred spell, or in the power of austerity, or that which is produced by the grace of the <term>Exalted One<note>The Lord or Ishvara</note></term>, or that which results from the service of those who are devoted to the Exalted One, is the karmic storehouse experienced in a present birth. 

The storehouse of demerit is experienced in a present birth in the case of those who repeatedly injure the terrified, the ill, the helpless, or those who have trusted them, or in the case of those who are repeatedly given to great crimes. For example, the karmic residue of the youth Nandiçvara passed from the human form and was transformed into the divine form. So also Nahusa passed from the divine form and was transformed into the form of a beast. Of these, the karmic storehouse which is to be experienced in a future birth is that which bears no fruit in the present lifetime.

«If this is so, what.» He rebuts it by showing that although they are of the same kind in so far as they are hindrances, they are particular because of the different previously described states. This he does in the words «The answer-is-now-given. It is true.» The objector says,¹ ‘This may be true. The hindrances may result from <term>undifferentiated-consciousness<note>avidyā: a fundamental spiritual ignorance or lack of awareness of the true self</note></term>; still why should they cease when undifferentiated-consciousness ceases? For surely no one would suppose that a piece of cloth ceases to be, when the weaver ceases to be.’ In reply to this he says «all these . . . without exception.» The distinctions² are only apparently distinctions, that is to say, they do not exist separately from this [undifferentiated-consciousness]. He asks a question in the words «Why is this?» He gives the reply in the words «all [hindrances].» This same point is made clear by the word «whatever.» «Is given a form» [that is] is falsely attributed. The rest is easy.

‘In the case of those who have been resolved into <term>entities<note>prakṛtilayas: souls who have merged back into the primal matter of the universe but have not yet achieved final liberation</note></term>, the hindrances are dormant; for <term>yogins<note>practitioners of yoga</note></term>, attenuated; and in case of those attached to objects, hindrances are intercepted or sustained.’ This is the summarizing-stanza.³

### Four errors of undifferentiated-consciousness [-ii. 5

It has been said, “Because of its first abode, and because of its origin, and because of its sustenance, and because of its exudations, and because of its death, and because it needs constant cleaning, the learned recognize that the body is impure.” Here the recognition of the pure in the impure is evident. If we say, ‘This girl, beautiful as the sickle of the new moon, her limbs formed of honey and nectar, her eyes large as the petals of the blue lotus, seeming to refresh the living world with her coquettish glances, so that we think that she has issued forth from the moon,’—then what could be the connection of this body with that <term>by what?<note>original: kena</note></term> [to which it is compared]? Just so <note>Compare the tale in Henry Warren's *Buddhism in Translations*, p. 297.</note> it is that there is a misconceived idea of the pure in the impure. In this way, by showing the recognition of the pure in the impure, one sees that there is the misconceived idea of merit where there is only demerit and of the useful where there is only the useless.—3. Similarly <term>Patañjali<note>The traditional author of the Yoga Sutras.</note></term> will describe <note>See ii. 15.</note> the recognition of pleasure in pain in the words, “By reason of the pains of mutations and of anguish and of subliminal-impressions and by reason of the opposition of fluctuations of the <term>aspects of nature<note>original: guṇa; the three fundamental qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas) that make up the physical and mental world.</note></term>—to the discriminating all is nothing but pain.” <term>Undifferentiated-consciousness<note>original: avidya; a fundamental spiritual ignorance.</note></term> is the recognition that there is pleasure in this pain.—4. Likewise the recognition of a self in the not-self, either in external aids <note>The commentator Bālarāma says: ‘Such as sons or cattle or servants or beds or seats, which are not the self.’</note> whether animate or inanimate, or in the body as the seat of outer experience, or in the central-organ <note>Likely referring to the mind or *manas*.</note> which aids the Self,—this is the recognition of a self in the not-self. In this sense it has been said of this, “He who counts any existing thing, whether phenomenalized or unphenomenalized [primary matter], as himself; or who rejoices in the success of <term>of these things<note>original: tasya</note></term>, deeming it his own success, or who grieves at the ill-success of these things, deeming it his own ill-success,—<term>these individuals<note>original: sa</note></term> are all unenlightened.” It is this four-fold undifferentiated-consciousness which becomes the root of that <term>unbroken-series<note>original: santāna; a continuous flow or stream.</note></term> of hindrances and of <term>latent-impressions of karma<note>The accumulated psychological imprints of past actions that shape future character and experience.</note></term> together with its fruition. <page-num>112</page-num>
<header>Book II. <term>Means of Attainment<note>Sādhana: the practice or discipline required to achieve spiritual liberation.</note></term></header>
<meta>Reference: ii. 5—]</meta>

...precisely as in the case of a foe (*a-mitra*) or of a trackless forest (*a-goṣpada*), is to be conceived as a really existing object. Just as a foe is not a "negative friend" or something that simply fails to be a friend, but is rather the opposite of a friend—a rival—so too a <term>trackless forest<note>original: a-goṣpada; literally a place where no cow has stepped. In Sanskrit grammar, the prefix 'a-' can imply the opposite rather than just a negation.</note></term> <note>1</note> is not merely a place not visited by cows, nor is it merely a patch of land the size of a cow’s footprint. On the contrary, it is a distinct and definite place, something entirely different from those two. Precisely so, <term>undifferentiated-consciousness<note>original: avidyā; fundamental spiritual ignorance or misconception.</note></term> is not a valid source of ideas, nor is it simply the absence of such a source; it is a specific kind of thinking that is the reverse of true knowledge.

**5. The recognition of the permanent, of the pure, of pleasure, and of a self in what is impermanent, impure, pain, and not-self is undifferentiated-consciousness.**

1. The word "effect" is a qualification which serves to indicate impermanence. Some people, indeed, believing the physical elements to be permanent and longing to reach their form, even offer devotion to them. Thus, believing the moon, the sun, the stars, and the heavenly regions to be permanent, they offer devotion to the "Paths"—specifically the <term>Way of the Fathers and the Way of the Gods<note>These refer to the two paths the soul may take after death in Vedic cosmology.</note></term>—which begin with the ritual Smoke. Similarly, believing the celestial beings, that is, the gods, to be deathless, they drink <term>soma<note>A ritual drink used in ancient Vedic sacrifices, believed to grant immortality or divine inspiration.</note></term> in order to reach their divine condition. For it is written in the <term>Rig Veda<note>original: RV; the oldest of the four Vedas, the primary scriptures of Hinduism.</note></term> [viii. 48. 3], "We have drunk the soma; we have become deathless." It is this recognition of the permanent in what is actually impermanent that constitutes undifferentiated-consciousness.

2. Likewise, mistaking the impure and highly repulsive body for something pure—at this point in the explanation, the author recites a verse from the sage <term>Vyāsa<note>2</note><note>The legendary compiler of the Vedas and author of the Great Epic, the Mahabharata.</note></term> to illustrate the body's repulsiveness. The words are "Because of its [first] abode." The "abode" refers to the mother's womb, which is polluted by substances like urine; the "seed" is the mother's blood and the father's semen. The "sustenance" is the transformation of food and drink into bodily fluids that hold the frame together. "Exudation" refers to sweat. Finally, death defiles the body of even a learned man, as a ritual bath is required after touching a corpse.

An objector might argue, "If the body is naturally impure, there is no use in cleansing it with earth and water." To this, the author replies, "because it needs [constant] cleaning." Although the body is naturally impure, purification must be applied to it, just as women produce fragrance by applying ointments...

...to the body. He completes the half-finished statement by saying "Here . . . in the impure." The meaning is that it is impure on the grounds stated before. He describes the recognition of purity [in the impure] by using the words "the new." "Coquettish" refers to behavior that is playful as the result of an erotic mood. What possible connection could the highly repulsive body have—through even the most remote <note>original: mandatama</note> similarity—with something as beautiful as the sickle of the new moon? — "In this way," refers to showing the false recognition of purity in the impure body of a woman. Similarly, in the case of a thing that is ultimately useless, such as money—because of the vast amount of pain required for getting it and keeping it—it is explained that there is [a discovery of] the idea of the "useful" in what is actually "useless." An objector might argue: "There is also another kind of ignorance that involves losing one's sense of direction, or the optical illusion where a whirled firebrand is seen as a solid circle of flame. Therefore, ignorance must have an infinite number of parts. Why then say it is only four-fold?" In reply to this, he says, "the root . . . of that." There may of course be other types of ignorance, but the specific spiritual ignorance which acts as the seed for the cycle of rebirth has only these four parts.

An objector says: "The word for ignorance (*a-vidyā*) might be a <term>negative compound<note>original: nañ-samāsa; a grammatical construction in Sanskrit where the prefix 'a-' or 'an-' negates the following word.</note></term>.³ In which case, there are three possibilities:
1. The first part (the 'not-') might be the most important <note>original: pradhāna</note>, as in the word 'fly-less' (meaning the absence of flies).
2. The second part might be the most important, as in 'not-a-king's-official' (meaning a person who is specifically an official, just not the king's).
3. The compound might refer to a third thing entirely, as in 'a flyless place' (a location defined by the absence of flies).

Given this, if we suppose the first case—where the 'not-' is most important—then <term>ignorance<note>original: avidyā</note></term> would be understood as a <term>prohibitive negation<note>original: prasajjya-pratiṣedha; a simple 'not-X' that negates an assertion but doesn't point to a new object.</note></term>.⁴ And this kind of mere absence could not be the actual cause of things like the <term>afflictions<note>original: kleshas; the psychological roots of suffering.</note></term>. ### Book II. Means of Attainment or <term>Spiritual Practice<note>original: Sādhana</note></term>

Suppose **2.** that the final member of the compound is to be the determinative factor; then it is "undifferentiated-consciousness" that is to be particularized by the negation of something. And this kind of undifferentiated-consciousness would be destructive of such things as the <term>hindrances<note>original: kleśas; the five afflictions including ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life.</note></term> and not the seed of them [because it would simply be a consciousness of the absence of something]. For it cannot be that the <term>subordinate member<note>original: guṇa</note></term> to the <term>determinative member<note>original: pradhāna</note></term> of the compound should break down that which it determines. Therefore, in order to make sure that it does not break down the determinative, something irregular—that is, the absence of something—must be supposed, on the other hand, to be found in the subordinate member of the compound.

Accordingly, in order that undifferentiated-consciousness as such should not be broken down, another meaning must be given to the negative, or another negative must be supplied. Or if we suppose, on the other hand, **3.** that another thing be the determinative to the compound, we should have to say that [undifferentiated-consciousness] is a <term>state-of-mind<note>original: buddhi; the higher intellect or discerning faculty.</note></term> in which <term>knowledge<note>original: vidyā</note></term> does not exist. And that could not be the seed of such things as the hindrances merely in so far as it is the absence of knowledge. For then a similar state of things would also have to be admitted in the case of that form of undifferentiated-consciousness which is attained in the state of restriction when preceded by <term>discriminative discernment<note>The highest state of clarity where the self is distinguished from the material world.</note></term>, [since here too there is an absence of knowledge].

Accordingly, in all these three ways, it has been shown that undifferentiated-consciousness is not the root of such things as the hindrances. In reply to this, the author says, "And this . . . has." A "really existing object" is the state of existence of a real object—that is, really existing objectivity. So in this way, it is evident that undifferentiated-consciousness is neither:

1.  A <term>negation where an affirmative is expected<note>original: prasajya-pratiṣedha; a technical term in Sanskrit grammar for a simple 'not X' negation.</note></term>;
2.  Nor again nothing but a defective kind of knowledge;
3.  Nor even is it a state-of-mind characterized as being the absence of knowledge;
4.  But **undifferentiated-consciousness** is described as being **misconceived thinking**, the opposite of <term>knowledge<note>original: vidyā</note></term>.

For the relation of word and thing is determined by conforming to the usage of the world. And because, according to the usage of the world, even a compound whose final member is determinative—and which is a negative compound and which <term>suppresses<note>original: upamardaka</note></term> the thing to be described by the last word of the compound—is now and then found in a sense contrary to this final member and suggested by this final member, there is therefore in this case also an <term>expressive meaning<note>original: vṛtti</note></term> in the sense of being contrary to this knowledge.

The author analyses the example: "Just as a <term>foe<note>original: a-mitra; literally 'non-friend'.</note></term> is not." A foe is not a "negative friend," nor again does a foe "amount to a friend." Supply¹ at this point in the text: "Some other thing, but the approach of this, a rival."

"So too a trackless forest" is not a "negative cow's² footprint," nor again is it merely a quantity of land which has a cow's foot as its measure; but, on...

on the contrary, nothing less than a spacious place, the opposite [in extent] of a cow's foot and other than the two negative <term>non-cow-footprints<note>original: a-gospada</note></term> [that is, 1. a place without any footprints of the cow, and 2. an object that is simply not a cow's footprint; these together would form the first type of negative cow's footprint; and 3. a stretch of land so entirely covered by a cow's footprint that the individual mark is lost, which would form the second negative cow's footprint]. ## 6. When the power of seeing and the power by which one sees have the appearance (*iva*) of being a single-self, [this is] the <term>feeling-of-personality<note>original: asmitā</note></term>.

The Self is the power of seeing; the <term>thinking-substance<note>original: buddhi; the highest mental faculty that reflects the light of consciousness.</note></term> is the power by which one sees. The <term>hindrance<note>original: kleśa</note></term> called the feeling-of-personality is a change by which these two appear to become a single essence (*svarūpa*). When there is any kind of failure to distinguish him who has the power of the enjoyer <note>The pure consciousness or Self.</note> from that which has the power of being enjoyed <note>The objective mind and world.</note>, which are as distinct as possible and as unconfused as possible, enjoyment is ready at hand. But when each has recovered its own essence, there is <term>Isolation<note>original: Kaivalya; the state of ultimate spiritual liberation and independence.</note></term>.—How is it that [at that time there could be anything] that could be called enjoyment? In this sense it has been said,¹ "He who should fail to see that the Self is other than the thinking-substance, distinct in nature and in character and in consciousness and in other respects, would make the mistake of putting his own thinking-substance in the place of that [Self]."

Having said that <term>undifferentiated-consciousness<note>original: avidyā; spiritual ignorance.</note></term> is the cause, he says that the feeling-of-personality is the effect, which [in its turn] is <term>supreme<note>original: variṣṭhā</note></term> over passion and the other [hindrances]. 

**6. When the power of seeing and the power by which one sees have the appearance of being a single-self, [this is] the feeling-of-personality.** 

The seeing and that by which one sees are precisely the two powers of the two, the self and the not-self. That <term>undifferentiated-consciousness<note>original: avidyā</note></term> which is characterized as being the perception of a self in what is the not-self, and which has the appearance of being a single intended-object, but which, in the strict sense, is not a single self,—this [<term>ignorance<note>original: avidyā</note></term>] is the feeling-of-personality. Instead of saying "of seeing and of that by which one sees," he uses the words <power of> in order to indicate the relation between them, that is, the capacity to be an enjoyer and to be objects to be enjoyed.—He elaborates the <term>aphorism<note>original: sūtra</note></term> by saying "The Self."—It might be asked, "Why, since"

<page-num>117</page-num>
<header>ii. 7-] Book II. Means of Attainment or <term>Sādhana<note>The practice or means of achieving spiritual goals.</note></term> [117</header>

at hand, the passion is for the pleasure and not for the means of attaining it. But in so far as there is no passion for the means, when these means are in experience, the passion is said to ensue upon a recollection. Thus, in the sense that the passion is for the pleasure, [the author] says «passion is for the pleasure.» The word «pleasure» means the *feeling* of pleasure. The word «dwells» means it has this as its object. This <term>passion<note>original: rāga</note></term> is the fourth <term>hindrance<note>original: kleśa; the mental states that cause suffering and bind one to the cycle of rebirth.</note></term>.

## 8. <term>Aversion<note>original: dveṣa</note></term> is that which dwells^1 upon pain.

That hate [or] indignation [or] rage, on the part of one acquainted with pain, ensuing upon a recollection of pain, for either the pain or for the means of attaining it, is aversion.

When one feels the discrimination, such states as aversion cease. So the <term>feeling-of-personality<note>original: asmitā; egoism.</note></term> brought to pass by <term>undifferentiated-consciousness<note>original: avidyā; spiritual ignorance or lack of awareness.</note></term> is the <term>root<note>original: nidāna</note></term> of such states as aversion. Accordingly, directly after the feeling-of-personality he gives the distinguishing-characteristic of aversion and of the rest [of the hindrances]. 8. Aversion is that which dwells upon pain. He explains this in the words «acquainted with pain.» For hate for a recollected pain ensues «upon a recollection of pain.» But while a pain is in experience there is no need of recollection. Since, however, the means for attaining pain are either remembered or perceived, the aversion must ensue upon a recollection of pain. And even when the means for attaining pain are at hand, the aversion is for the pain and not for the means of attaining it. But in so far as there is no aversion for the means, when these means are in experience, the aversion is said to ensue upon a recollection. Thus, in the sense that the aversion is for the pain, [the author] says «aversion is for the pain.» The word «pain» means the *feeling* of pain. The word «dwells» means it has this as its object. This [aversion] is the fifth hindrance.

## 9. <term>Abhiniveça<note>The instinctive will to live and the fear of death.</note></term> is the thirst for life that sweeps on by its own force [and] which is found in the wise just as much [as in the fool].^2

In all living beings there is this self-benediction 'Would that I might not cease to be! Would that I might live !' and it is constant. This self-benediction, of course, does not belong to one who has not experienced the nature of death. By this experience of a previous birth the experience of death is inferred. And this [hindrance] is seen to be «sweeping on by its own force.» Even in the case of a worm just born, this fear of death, which is a <term>state of mind<note>original: pratyaya</note></term> in the form of an anticipation of extermination, arises as he is about to die and is not to be accounted for by perception or inference or verbal testimony. Therefore it is inferred that the affliction resulting from the experience of the pain of death in a previous birth is [now] present. Just as this [thirst for life] is found in the extremely unskilled, so also it is found in the wise, who have [already] grasped the [reasons] for beginning and end. Because the <term>subliminal-impressions<note>original: vāsanā; latent memories or tendencies from past lives.</note></term> of the pain of death are similar in the unskilled and in the wise.

## 9. **The will-to-live sweeping on [by the force of] its own nature exists in this form even in the wise.** 

He discusses the meaning of the term **will-to-live** <note>original: abhiniveśa</note> in the words **all living beings.** **This craving for one's self** is the longing for one's self expressed in the words **May I not cease to live,** that is, 'May I not become non-existent,' [and also expressed] in the words **May I live** <gloss>original: *bhūyāsam*; may I exist</gloss> [that is] 'May I be alive' <gloss>original: *jīvyāsam*</gloss>. The longing for one's self is not possible unless the living creature have had residing in himself an experience of death. It is he only that has this craving for himself, [that is] the will-to-live, the fear of death. In the course of the discussion <gloss>original: *prasangatas*</gloss> he refers by the words, **And from [the existence] of this** to a heterodox-person <note>original: *nāstika*; one who denies the authority of the Vedas or the existence of an afterlife.</note> who denies that there is another birth. From the fact that the present body is being held together, it follows that there is an experience of a previous birth. In other words, a birth is a conjunction <gloss>1</gloss> [of the soul] with a body and sense-organs and feelings which are different from those of any previous [conjunction] and are characterized by the [definite location] in the collection. This [birth] is experienced [or] attained. And it is this [experience or attainment] that is made clear. How is this? In reply he says **And this is that well-known will-to-live.** Breaking off the sentence in the middle he tells of its hindering character in the word **hindrance.** This [will-to-live] is called a hindrance because it hinders, [that is] pains, living-creatures with unkindly actions and the like. He finishes what he had begun to say by the words **sweeping on by its own nature.** It has a disposition to sweep on by virtue of its own nature in the form of subconscious-impressions. But this disposition is not accidental. Even in the case of a worm just born [that is] full of pain and low in intelligence [this disposition] is not accidental. He tells the reason for this in the words **as a result of perception.** This fear of death, being inconceivable, that is, not acquired in this present <gloss>original: *pratyudita*</gloss> birth as a result of perception or inference or verbal-communication, it must be inferred that the pangs of death have been experienced in a previous birth. This is the point at issue. For even a child just born trembles at the sight of a murderous thing. And from this peculiar quivering [the child] infers the nearness <gloss>original: *pratyāsatti*</gloss> to himself of the experience of death and is found to be afraid of it. Thus we see that fear results from pain or from whatever leads to pain. Moreover in this birth he has not experienced or inferred or heard of death. So we gather that he has known only in a previous [birth] the pains [of death] or that which leads to the pain. And from this a memory of himself as he was in that condition persists. This moreover does not occur unless there be subliminal-impressions. Furthermore this subliminal-impression [cannot occur] without experience and the experience does not belong to this life. The only remaining alternative is that this [subconscious impression] <note>original: *saṃskāra*; a mental imprint or memory-trace</note> comes from a previous birth. Thus, there was a connection with a past life. The word "so" (*tathā*) requires a matching "just as." Therefore, by providing the phrase "just as" from the context of the sentence, the author shows, with the words "just as . . . this," what the meaning of the sentence is.

"In the unspeakably stupid" means those with the most sluggish intelligence. He explains the nature of this understanding by saying "some understanding of the prior and of the final limits [of human lives]." The "limit" is the end. Now, the prior limit of man is the round-of-rebirths <note>original: *saṃsāra*; the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth</note>; the latter limit is Isolation <note>original: *kaivalya*; the state of absolute spiritual freedom and liberation</note>. A person who has understood this through listening to teachings or through logical inference is called "one who has understanding of the prior and of the final limits." 

This well-known fear exists and has become established in both the worm and the wise man. It might be objected that while a fear of death is believable for the unwise, it should not exist in the wise man, since it would have been destroyed by his knowledge. Or, if the fear of death has not been destroyed, it would be present forever. With this in view, he asks, "Why is this?" The answer is, "Because . . . it is alike." He is not referring here to the wise man who has achieved conscious concentration <note>original: *samādhi*</note>, but rather to the scholar who discriminates based on what they have heard and what they have inferred. This is the crucial point.

**10. These [hindrances], [when they have become] subtle, are to be escaped by the inverse-propagation.** <note>original: *pratiprasava*; the process of a mental effect returning to its original cause, or "re-absorption."</note>

These five hindrances, when they have become like "burned seeds" <note>An image used to describe mental patterns that have been neutralized so they can no longer "sprout" into actions</note>, come to rest along with the mind. This happens after the mind, which has governed the actions of the yogin, is resolved back into primary matter <note>original: *prakṛti*; the fundamental substance of the universe</note>. 

Thus the hindrances have been described. We have also seen the four states of those hindrances that must be escaped: the dormant, the weakened, the interrupted, and the active. But why is the fifth state—the "subtle" state—not mentioned by the author of the sūtras, given that it is in the state of a "burned seed"? To this he replies: 

**10. These [hindrances], [when they have become] subtle, are to be escaped by the inverse-propagation.** 

The states that can be escaped through a person's own efforts have already been described; however, the "subtle" state is not within the scope of a man’s ordinary exertions to escape <note>original: *hāna*; the act of removal or cessation</note>. It may, however, be escaped by "inverse-propagation"—that is, by reducing the "mind-stuff" <note>original: *citta*</note> (which is an effect characterized by the "feeling-of-personality" <note>original: *asmitā*; egoism</note>) back into the state of its own cause, the "thinking-substance" <note>original: *mahat*; the first product of primary matter, the cosmic intellect</note>. He explains the sūtra using the word "These." The meaning is easy to understand.

# Book II. Means of Attainment or Spiritual Practice <note>original: *Sādhana*</note>

But regarding the permanent obstacles consigned to the condition of seeds—

**11. The active patterns <note>original: *vṛttis*; the "fluctuations" or movements of the mind</note> of these should be overcome by means of meditation.**

Those active patterns of the obstacles which are coarse, after having been weakened by the yoga of action <note>consisting of self-discipline, study, and devotion</note>, should be overcome by the highest discernment <note>original: *prasaṁkhyāna*; elevated contemplation</note> until they are made subtle and rendered like burned seeds <note>seeds that have been roasted so they can no longer sprout into new thoughts or actions</note>. And just as a spot of coarse matter upon pieces of cloth is first shaken off and afterwards the fine stain is removed with effort and by some appropriate means, so coarse patterns are those whose resistance to being overcome is very slight, but the subtle patterns are those whose resistance <note>original: *pratipakṣa*</note> is very great.

"Now when the obstacles have been weakened by the yoga of action, by directing his exertions towards what does a man accomplish the rejection [of these obstacles]?" In reply to this, the author says: "But of permanent obstacles consigned to the condition of seeds." By these words, he distinguishes them from those that have been made barren <note>original: *vandhya*; sterilized or unproductive</note>. He recites the core teaching: **11. The active patterns of these should be overcome by means of meditation.** He discusses this teaching using the phrase "of the obstacles." Now, when weakened by the yoga of action, these may also be eradicated—both the obstacles themselves and their effects—by returning them to the condition of their own causes. This is the process of reverse resolution <note>original: *pratiprasava*; often translated as "inverse propagation," where effects are folded back into their origins until they disappear</note>. Thus, the coarse patterns have been explained. When a person’s effort is still within the scope of highest discernment, the author states what the limit is with the word "until." He clarifies the expression "made subtle" by saying "burned." On this same point, he gives a comparison: "And just as... upon pieces of cloth." With an effort, such as by washing it, and by some means, such as an alkaline <note>original: *kṣāra*; a caustic cleaning agent</note> mixture. The likeness between the comparison and the thing to which it is compared lies merely in the fact that there is a coarse and a subtle stage, but not in the fact that they are both removable by the same kind of effort. For this removal is impossible in the case of obstacles which must be overcome by the process of reverse resolution. Those whose resistance is very slight, as described, are those that have simple causes of destruction. Those whose resistance is very great are those that have profound causes of destruction. And next below <margin>Coarse stains are removed by shaking; minute stains by washing; more minute by alkaline solution. Obstacles which persist are weakened by the yoga of action; the weakened are reduced to burned seeds by highest discernment; the burned seed is destroyed by reverse resolution.</margin> the process of reverse resolution as a means of attaining destruction—

That in which all Selves <note>individual souls or centers of consciousness</note> in the round-of-rebirths are latent (<term>āçerate</term>—meaning to lie dormant or rest) is<gloss>1</gloss> a <term>latent-deposit</term> (<term>āçaya</term>). The latent-deposits of karma are merit <note>good moral weight</note> and demerit <note>negative moral weight</note>. 

Merit, which is the cause of heaven and similar states, occurs when—as a result of some desire—there is an inclination for a work which is desirable. Similarly, there is demerit in such cases as when, from avarice, another is robbed of his money. Likewise, there is nothing but demerit in such cases as when, from infatuation <note>delusion or clouded judgment</note>, the idea of merit directs itself to killing or something of the kind which is actually demerit. 

But there is no merit which comes from infatuation. Merit does, however, come from anger, as for instance, the case of Dhruva<gloss>2</gloss> <note>A mythological prince who, out of anger at being rejected by his father, performed such intense penance that he was elevated to become the Pole Star</note> from anger at the slight [put upon him] by his father Uttānapāda. Demerit, however, due to anger and resulting in the murder of Brahmans, is well enough known to everyone. He describes the double character of this [latent-deposit] by saying "And this may be felt in a birth seen." <page-num>123</page-num>
<header>Three-fold fruition of karma [-ii. 13</header>

Just as grains of rice, when they are still encased within their husks, are capable of sprouting as seeds if they have not been burned, but neither the separated husks nor a burned seed can sprout; in the same way, the latent-deposits of karma <note>the subconscious residues of past actions</note>, when encased within the "hindrances" <note>the *kleshas*, such as ignorance and attachment</note>, are capable of producing fruition <note>the ripening of consequences</note>. However, neither the hindrances once they have been separated, nor the "seed" of karma once it has been burned by the fire of Elevation (<term>prasaṁkhyāna</term>) <note>original: *prasaṁkhyāna*; the highest state of meditative discernment or "higher prospection"</note>, is capable of producing results. 

And this fruition is of three kinds: **birth**, **length-of-life**, and the **kind-of-experience** <note>the specific joys or sorrows one encounters</note>. 

In regard to these three results, there is a discussion to be had: 
1. Is one single action the cause of one single birth? 
2. Or does one single action provide the impulse for more than one birth? 
3. Or do many actions combined project many different births? 
4. Or do many actions combined project one single birth?

Now, it is not true (1) that one action is the cause of one birth. Why so? Because the remaining karma—accumulated from time-without-beginning and being innumerable—along with the karma of the present, would have no set order for their results. If they had to wait for their turn one by one, it would lead to a sense of hopelessness or discouragement for everyone, as the debt would never be cleared. This theory is therefore rejected. 

Neither is it true (2) that one action is the cause of more than one birth. Why? Because if there are many actions waiting to bear fruit, but only one action at a time were to cause multiple births, there would simply be no time left for the remaining karmas to ever reach their own fruition. This is also rejected. 

Neither is it true (3) that many actions cause many births. Why? Since it is physically impossible for a person to undergo more than one birth simultaneously, one would have to suppose these births occur one after another. This, however, would lead back to the same problem of "lack of time" mentioned in the previous case.

The conclusion is then (4): the diverse accumulation of latent-deposits of karma—whether of merit <note>virtuous deeds</note> or demerit <note>non-virtuous deeds</note>—made between the start of a life and its end, exists in a hierarchy of subordinate parts and one dominant part. This entire "bundle" is made manifest at the moment of death, having grown compact into one single impulse (<term>ekapraghaṭṭakena</term>) <note>original: *ekapraghaṭṭakena*; a simultaneous gathering or collision of karmic forces</note>. After death occurs, this bundle takes on a rigid form and causes only a single birth. Furthermore, that birth receives its specific lifespan from that same bundle of karma. And finally, within that same lifespan, the person attains their specific kind-of-experience from that same karmic source. This latent-deposit of karma, since it is the—

<header>ii. 13—] Book II. Means of Attainment or Practice</header>

...the source of the birth, the length of life, and the specific kind of experience, is said to have a three-fold ripening. Consequently, this latent deposit of action <note>original: *karma*; the accumulated residues of past deeds</note> is said to have its limit in a single existence. On the other hand, a latent deposit of action which is to be felt within this current "seen" birth is said—since it causes only a specific kind of enjoyment <note>pleasurable or painful experience</note>—to originate a single kind of ripening, rather than an entire single existence. 

Or, when it is the source of both the length of life and the kind of experience, it is said to originate two results, as seen for instance in the case of <term>Nandīshvara</term> <note>a youth who, through intense devotion, was transformed into a divine being in the same lifetime</note> or of <term>Nahusha</term> <note>a king who was transformed into a serpent due to a curse</note>. 

But this mind-stuff <note>original: *citta*</note> is like a fish-net. It is spread out in different shapes on all sides and has, from time without beginning, a fixed form <note>original: *sammūrchita*; solidified or manifested</note> made of subconscious impressions. These impressions are like knots in the net, caused by the experience of the results of actions which spring from the "hindrances" <note>the *kleshas*, such as ignorance and ego</note>. Therefore, these subconscious impressions are said to be built up over more than one existence. 

It is this particular "latent deposit of action," however, which is said to be limited to one existence. Those deep-seated impressions which produce memory ¹ are called subconscious traces <note>original: *vāsanā*</note>, and these are said to exist from a time without beginning. 

But that latent deposit of action which is limited to a single existence has both a ripening that is limited in time and a ripening which is without a time limit. Of these two orders, the time-limitation <note>original: *niyama*</note>—in so far as it is limited to one existence—belongs only to the ripening which is to be felt in the current "seen" life and which is restricted in time. Whereas the ripening which is not to be felt in this current life, and which has no time limit, does not follow that same rule of being limited to a single birth. 

Why so? Because that ripening which is not felt in this "seen" life and which is without a time limit has three kinds of outcomes ² <note>original: *gati*; paths or ways of proceeding</note>: 
1. It may be annihilated <note>original: *nāsha*</note> when its potential for result is finished and it becomes unfruitful. 
2. It may be "cast away" or absorbed <note>original: *āvāpa-gamana*</note> into a more dominant action. 
3. It may continue for a long time, held in check by a dominant action which is currently producing a limited ripening. 

Of these three, the first—the annihilation of action that is finished and becomes unfruitful—is like the annihilation occurring in this present...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Yoga Sūtra II.13, addressing a potential objection: if our past actions (karma) are infinite, how can we ever achieve liberation? The text explains that just as a seed cannot sprout without soil and water, these past actions cannot "ripen" into new lives once the "root" of spiritual ignorance and affliction has been destroyed by higher discernment.</meta>

<page-num>[126</page-num>
# Book II. Means of Attainment or Spiritual Practice <note>original: *Sādhana*</note>
<meta>ii. 13-]</meta>

...therefore the <term>storehouse of past actions <note>original: *latent-deposit of karma*</note></term> having [its limit in] a single existence [must] be acknowledged.

[The objector says,] ‘Let this be granted. Since the <term>storehouse of past actions <note>original: *latent-deposit of karma*</note></term> is based upon <term>lack of wisdom <note>original: *avidyā*</note></term>, there may result, after the production of <term>wisdom <note>original: *vidyā*</note></term>, a destruction of <term>lack of wisdom</term>, and so there might not be any subsequent <term>storehouse of actions</term>. Still, the <term>storehouses of actions</term> done previously and accumulated by the succession from time without beginning of innumerable births, being unsettled in their period of development, it would be impossible by realizing the effects to cause [these actions] to dwindle in so far as they might be experienced. Because of this, it would be impossible to cut off the <term>cycle of rebirth <note>original: *round-of-rebirths*</note></term>.’ To this he replies with the <term>verse <note>original: *sūtra*</note></term> 13: 

**So long as the root exists, there will be ripening <note>original: *fruition*</note> from it [that is] birth, length of life, and the type of experience.** 

What he means to say is this: The result of the <term>storehouse of actions <note>original: *latent-deposit of karma*</note></term> is pleasure and pain; and, in so far as both birth and length of life have the same purpose [as the actions] and are the necessary consequence of it, [these two] are also propagated [by the actions]. Moreover, pleasure and pain are attached to passion and aversion. And the latter are the necessary conditions [for pleasure and pain], since pleasure and pain are not possible in the absence of these [that is, passion and aversion]. Furthermore, it is impossible to say that wherein a man is pleased or disgusted is not to him, as the case may be, either a pleasure or a pain. 

So this soil of the self, sprinkled with the water of the <term>afflictions <note>original: *hindrances* or *kleśas*</note></term>, becomes a field propagating the fruits of <term>action <note>original: *karma*</note></term>. Thus it is true that the <term>afflictions</term> co-operate with the <term>storehouse of actions</term> for producing also the after-effects of the fruits. So when the <term>afflictions</term> are quite cut off, [the stored actions] are deprived of this [aid] also. Therefore, although the <term>stored actions</term> are endless and their period of ripening is unsettled, still, when in their condition as seeds they are burned by <term>Higher Discernment <note>original: *Elevation* or *prasāṁkhyāna*</note></term>, they cannot be in a position to bear fruit. 

The sense expressed is made clear by the Comment in the words, «While . . . exist.» With regard to this same point he gives a simile: «Just as . . . the chaff.» Although seeds have their chaff, their condition as a seed [the ability to sprout] is burned away by <term>heat <note>original: *sveda*</note></term> and in other ways. He applies the simile to the point-to-be-illustrated by saying, «similarly.» 

If it be objected that the <term>afflictions <note>original: *hindrances*</note></term> cannot be removed because no [really] existing things are removed, he replies in the words, «nor seed in the condition of having been burned by <term>Higher Discernment <note>original: *Elevation*</note></term>.» He shows the threefold character of the <term>ripening <note>original: *fruition*</note></term> in the words, «And this.» <term>Ripening</term> is that which is brought to completion or brought to perfection by <term>actions <note>original: *karmas*</note></term>. 

The first point-under-discussion [1. and 2.] deems the unity of <term>action <note>original: *karma*</note></term> to be fixed and considers whether births are one or more than one. The second [3. and 4.], however, deems the manifoldness to be fixed and considers whether births are one or more than one. Thus there are four alternatives...
