<meta>This page continues the commentary on Yoga Sūtra II.13, which discusses how our past actions (karma) lead to future results. Having established that actions only "ripen" if the "root" of spiritual affliction is present, the author now uses a process of elimination to determine exactly how actions translate into lifetimes.</meta>

<page-num>127</page-num>

# Limits of time for the ripening of actions
<meta>ii. 13</meta>

This leads to a set of four alternative propositions <note>original: *vikalpa*</note>. Of these, he refutes the first by stating, "Now, it is not true (1) that a single action is the cause of a single birth." He asks, "Why is that?" He provides the answer by saying, "because of time-without-beginning." 

If we assume that each individual action from our infinite past lives resulted in exactly one future birth, the sheer number of actions would be overwhelming. Even after subtracting the actions that are exhausted in each life, the remaining, unspent actions accumulated since time-without-beginning would be so vast that the world would fall into deep discouragement <note>The text suggests that if liberation were mathematically impossible due to the sheer volume of karma, no one would bother trying to be virtuous.</note>. And such a conclusion is prohibited by the teachings. 

What he means to say is this: Since the process of exhausting past actions is <term>sporadic <note>original: *virala*; literally "broken by intervals" or "thinly spread"</note></term>, and since new actions are produced in such abundance, the <term>unconscious impressions <note>original: *latent-deposits* or *karmāśaya*</note></term> press against one another. They spring up incessantly, in breathless haste, toward their own <term>ripening <note>original: *fruition*</note></term>. For this reason, even a very clever person could not determine the order in which these results will occur. Thus, everyone would be struck by hopelessness regarding the pursuit of meritorious acts.

He rejects the second alternative with the words, "Neither (2) is a single action the cause of more than one birth." He asks, "Why is this?" He answers by saying, "of more than one birth." If a single action <term>deposited <note>original: *āhita*</note></term> in the mind were the cause of a result that spanned multiple lifetimes, there would simply be no time left for the remaining thousands of actions to manifest. That, too, is a prohibited conclusion. If actions were thus rendered fruitless because they never got a "turn" to manifest, people would likely stop performing them. Furthermore, if there is already discouragement at the idea of one action being uprooted in a single life because there is no <term>fixed <note>original: *niyata*</note></term> order of results, there would be even more despair if one action required multiple lives to clear. In that case, one would infer that there would be no time in the future for current actions to ever ripen, leading again to hopelessness.

He refutes the third alternative with the words, "Neither (3) is a group of actions the cause of multiple births." He gives the reason for this in the word "this." Since it is impossible for those who are not <term>yogis <note>original: *yogins*; advanced practitioners believed to possess the power to manifest multiple bodies at once</term></note> to experience more than this one present birth at a single time, births must occur one after another. If a thousand actions could simultaneously generate a thousand births, then—because a thousand actions would have been exhausted at once— there would be time for the remaining actions to ripen in a <term>fixed <note>original: *niyata*</note></term> order. However, for ordinary people, such simultaneous births do not happen.

Having thus rejected the first three propositions, he accepts the only remaining possibility (4) through a process of elimination: that a collection of many actions is the cause of a single birth. As he says, "The result is . . . birth." 

The compound phrase "between-birth-and-the-end-of-life" refers to the interval between those two points—both the birth and the death. This accumulation of actions is diverse because it produces results varied by pleasures and pains. An action is "dominant" if it produces its result with absolute intensity and immediacy, whereas it is "subordinate" if its result is delayed. The "ending-of-life" refers to death. To be "made manifest" by death means being brought into the state where the action is ready to produce its effects. 

By one single impulse...

<page-num>128</page-num>
## Book II. Means of Attainment or Spiritual Practice

...means simultaneously. Becoming tightly packed or gathered together <note>original: *saṁ-mūrchita*</note> into a single mass in order to produce a specific result—namely, the next reincarnation—this store of actions produces only one birth and not several. This birth may be human or some other state of being. The phrase "and this birth receives its lifespan from that same store of actions" means that the duration of that life is determined by various periods of time. Furthermore, the phrase "and again in that same lifespan, from that same store of actions, it attains its particular experience" means that the soul directly experiences pleasure and pain. Thus, because this <term>latent deposit of action <note>original: *karmāśaya*; the accumulated "residue" of past deeds that waits to ripen</note></term> is the source of the birth, the lifespan, and the specific experiences, it is said to have a threefold <term>ripening <note>original: *fruition* or *vipāka*</note></term>. 

The author sums up the main argument by saying: "Consequently, this latent deposit of action is said to be limited to a single existence." To have a "single existence" <note>original: *āikabhavika*</note> means to be bound to one life. This grammatical compound follows the rules of the ancient grammarian <term>Pāṇini <note>A foundational Sanskrit grammarian (c. 4th century BCE) whose rules govern the structure of the language</note></term> starting with the rule regarding temporal antecedents. The grammatical suffix used here indicates possession. Thus, the meaning is "that which results in one existence." In other versions of the text, the term used is slightly different, but the meaning remains that the result of the actions is confined to a single birth. 

Having established the main point—that actions clustering for one life have three results (birth, span, and experience)—he now distinguishes between these and actions that are felt in the "seen birth" (the current life) and pertain to this world. By using the word "seen," he refers to figures like **Nandīçvara**, whose lifespan as a human was cut short at eight years <note>According to legend, Nandīçvara was a boy destined for a short life who, through intense devotion to Shiva, was granted immortality and became a divine attendant.</note>. In that case, a specific type of merit was created through a powerful and intense spiritual method. This merit had two results: it determined the length of his life and his experiences. 

Conversely, in the case of **Nahuṣa**, his lifespan had already been determined by actions that led him to the throne of Indra (the king of gods). However, due to a specific demerit—striking the sage **Agastya** with his heel—he suffered a specific type of painful experience <note>Nahuṣa was temporarily transformed into a serpent as punishment for his arrogance toward the sage.</note>. 

An objector might ask: "Do the subconscious impressions <note>original: *vāsanā*</note> left by spiritual afflictions, like the store of actions, also limit themselves to a single existence? If the subconscious memories of past experiences only point toward a specific type of experience, then a human reborn in the body of a beast would not know how to behave according to its new species." <note>The objector is asking: if we only carry over the "results" of actions into one life, how do we retain the instincts (like eating or mating) appropriate to a specific animal body if we haven't been that animal for a long time?</note> In response, he says "the actions stemming from the spiritual afflictions." Being "of a fixed form" means gathered together into one mass. He describes the subconscious impression in this way to distinguish it from...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Yoga Sūtra II.13. Now, the text moves to the exceptions: actions that do not necessarily result in a single, immediate birth, but may be canceled out or delayed across multiple lifetimes.</meta>

<page-num>129</page-num>
<header>Fruitions not limited in time [—ii. 13</header>
<sig>17 [H.O.S. 17]</sig>

The author distinguishes between right-action (<term>dharma <note>Action that is in accord with cosmic order or virtue</note></term>) and wrong-action (<term>adharma <note>Action that goes against moral law; vice</note></term>) by using the phrase "subliminal-impressions which." In order to state certain exceptions to the general proposition—which is that the <term>latent-deposit of action <note>original: *karmāśaya*; the stored potential of past deeds</note></term> has its limit in a single existence—he prepares the ground by saying, "But that . . . which." By the word "But," he shows that there is a distinction from the subconscious impressions. 

The time-limit of being restricted to a "single existence" belongs only to the <term>fruition <note>original: *vipāka*; the ripening or result of one's deeds</note></term> which is to be experienced in the birth of this "seen" life <note>The current lifetime one is currently inhabiting</note> and which has a set duration. In contrast, the fruition which is not to be felt in this "seen" life does not have that same limit in time.

Of what kind, then, is fruition which is not limited in time? He asks the reason in the words, "Why so?" He provides the reason in the words, "Because that." First, he gives one outcome (<term>gati <note>Literally a "path" or "way" things go</note></term>) in the words, "is finished;" the second, in the words "dominant;" the third, in the words "has a limit in time." 

Of these three, he analyzes the first by saying, "Of these three . . . is finished." Other than the actions (<term>karmas</term>) of the mendicant (<term>saṁnyāsin <note>A person who has renounced worldly life for spiritual liberation</note></term>), which are neither bright nor dark <note>The actions of an enlightened person are considered "colorless" because they do not produce new karmic results</note>, there are only three types of actions: the dark (bad), the bright-dark (mixed), and the bright (good). 

Now, in this world, a latent-deposit of "bright" action—obtained through self-discipline, the recitation of sacred texts, and other spiritual means—once it arises in the mind, acts as the annihilator of "dark" action which has not yet produced its fruit. And because there is no fundamental distinction between purely dark and "dark-bright" (mixed) actions, we must suppose that this bright deposit also annihilates the "many-colored" actions—that is, the mixed ones—because of the dark elements contained within them. 

With reference to this, the Exalted <term>Vyāsa <note>The traditional commentator who clarified the meaning of the Yoga Sūtras</note></term> cites the Sacred Word <note>Likely referring to the Vedas or ancient Shruti literature</note> when he says: "With regard to which this." Verily indeed, actions should be known to be "by twos and twos," <note>original: *dve dve*</note> meaning the dark and the bright. It is a single mass made of merit that destroys these. Such is the construction of the sentence. By repeating the word "twos," he indicates that there is a very great number of such actions. 

In reply to the question, "Belonging to whom?" he says, "belonging to a sinful [man]." In other words, belonging to a person who has done wrong. What is it that destroys? To this he replies, "A single mass made of merit." This is because a collection includes all the individual units (<term>samūhin</term>) that make it up. Thus, the bright latent-deposit of action is described as the third outcome. 

What he means to say is this: This bright latent-deposit of action, which is obtained by methods that do not harm others, is of such a kind that although it is a single mass of merit, it can destroy the dark and mixed latent-deposits of action, even when they are numerous and absolutely opposed to it.

The word "then" (<term>tat</term>) means "therefore." The word "Wish thou" <note>original: *kāmayasva*</note> is in the middle voice <note>A grammatical form in Sanskrit</note> because it is <term>Vedic <note>Refers to the archaic, ritualistic language of the Vedas</note></term>. The rest is easy to understand. And so we see here (<term>atra</term>) that the power in the arising of "bright" action is so indescribably great that it alone makes the others cease to be. However, one could not say that the dark actions cease simply because of the pain caused by performing recitations and other right actions. For a wrong-action (<term>adharma</term>) is not opposed by pain in general, but only by that particular kind of merit which is...

<header>ii. 13—] Book II. Means of Attainment or Sādhana <note>The Sanskrit word *Sādhana* refers to the practice or means of achieving spiritual goals.</note></header>

the effect of itself [that is, the wrong-action]. Now the pain resulting from recitations and other [right actions] is not their effect. [And if this pain resulting from recitations and other right actions] is supposed to be the effect of this [wrong-action], then it is needless to make [special] prescriptions of recitations and other right actions, because then these [recitations and right actions] could be produced (<term>utpatti <note>The arising or coming into existence of a result</note></term>) merely by the help of those [wrong-actions]. And if [this wrong-action] should not produce (<term>anutpatti <note>The failure of a result to arise</note></term>) [the pain which results from recitations and other right actions], then the Cooking Pot [Hell] <note>A reference to *Kumbhīpāka*, a specific hell in Indian cosmology where the wicked are said to be cooked like food in a pot.</note> and other [pains] are [specially] prescribed,—[because the wrong-action must result in something—and] because, if [Hells and other pains] be not [specially] prescribed, these [Hells] would never be produced at all.¹

Thus all is four-square.—He analyses 2. the second outcome in the word «*dominant.*» In the dominant karma, as for instance in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* <note>A significant Vedic ritual sacrifice involving the Soma plant, intended to secure a place in heaven.</note> and similar [sacrifices], that which is accessory (<term>aṅga <note>A limb or subordinate part of a larger ritual</note></term>) [karma] to this, namely the killing of the animal, is cast away [into the dominant karma]. For there are two effects of killing and of the other [acts]: 1. since it is prescribed [by the tradition] in so far as it is accessory to the dominant [karma], it assists; 2. since killing is forbidden by the rule "Let no living being be killed", it is needless. We see then that [killing], because it is performed as accessory to the dominant [karma] and not as being the dominant, ought not immediately [<term>drāg <note>Instantly or without delay</note></term>] and independently of the dominant [karma] to generate its own fruition, a useless result, but that it remains rendering assistance to the dominant [karma], the fruition of which has already commenced. And while rendering assistance to the dominant karma it remains, with reference to its own effect, as seed only, and is cast away into the dominant karma. «With reference to which it has been said» by *Pañcaçikha* <note>An ancient legendary sage of the Sāṃkhya-Yoga school.</note>. The slight admixture of the invisible-influence (<term>apūrva <note>The 'unseen' potential energy created by a ritual that stays with the soul until the result is ready to manifest</note></term>), which is the dominant [karma] resulting from the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other [sacrifices], with the invisible-influence resulting from the killing of the animal and similar [acts] and producing what is not desired (<term>anartha <note>An undesirable or harmful consequence</note></term>),—[this admixture] may be removed. For, by doing a certain amount of penance it may be removed. Or should a man heedlessly not have gone through the penance, [the slight admixture of guilt] comes to fruition at the time of the fruition of the dominant karma. In spite of all this, whatever undesired result be generated by this [accessory invisible-influence] may be overlooked. For the fortunate (<term>kuçala <note>Those who are spiritually expert, wise, or virtuous</note></term>), plunging deep into the great pool of the nectar of pleasure brought near by the gathering together of merit, overlook a slight spark of [pain].

¹ Since however Hells are produced without any special prescription (<term>vidhāna <note>A formal rule or injunction</note></term>), it follows as a general rule that the consequences of wrong-actions require no special prescription. ### **14. These [fruitions] have joy or extreme anguish as results in accordance with the quality of their causes whether merit or demerit.**

⟨These⟩ [that is] birth and length-of-life and kind-of-experience. Those with merit <note>original: *punya*; virtuous or "right" actions</note> as cause have pleasure as result; those with demerit <note>original: *apunya*; non-virtuous or "wrong" actions</note> as cause have pain as result. And just as the nature of this pain is counteractive <note>meaning something to be resisted or overcome</note>, so for the <term>yogin <note>A practitioner of yoga who has attained a high level of spiritual discernment</note></term>, even at the moment of pleasure in an object, there is nothing but counteractive pain. <note>This refers to the Buddhist and Yogic idea that even worldly pleasure is a form of suffering because it is fleeting and leads to attachment.</note>

He explains the aphorism <note>original: *sūtra*</note> in the words, "«<These> [that is] birth and length-of-life and kind-of-experience.»" Although birth and length-of-life do result in joy or extreme anguish (since they must happen before these feelings can occur), the kind-of-experience follows the rise in consciousness of joy and extreme anguish. In fact, its very essence is the direct experience <note>original: *anubhava*</note> of them. Still, insofar as being "directly experienced" is the same as a "kind-of-experience" <note>original: *bhoga*</note>, we may suppose that joy and extreme anguish are results of experience only because they are the *objects* of that experience.

It is objected: "The birth, length-of-life, and experiences that result from extreme anguish are clearly things to be rejected <note>original: *heya*</note>, since they are felt to be oppressive. But why should those results which come from merit <note>virtue</note> be renounced? They have pleasure as their result since they are felt to be agreeable <note>original: *anukūla*</note>. This agreeableness, which everyone can feel, cannot be denied by even a thousand verbal arguments or logical inferences. Moreover, neither joy nor extreme anguish can exist without the other. For while joy is being received, extreme anguish—since it cannot be entirely driven off—may also fall to one’s lot, because the two have separate causes and separate forms." 

In reply to this he says, "«And just as . . . this.»" Although ordinary individuals do not perceive the oppressiveness of objects at the time they are feeling pleasure, <term>yogins <note>practitioners of Yoga who have attained high levels of discernment</note></term> are conscious of this underlying counteractiveness.

### 15. Because of the pains of change <note>mutations</note>, anxiety, and deep-seated habits <note>subliminal impressions</note>, and by reason of the inner conflict of the fluctuations of the three qualities of nature <note>original: *guṇa*</note>—to the person of discernment, all is nothing but pain.

1. For everyone, this experience of pleasure is permeated with passion and is dependent upon living and non-living instruments. In this case, we have a latent-deposit of <term>karma <note>the storehouse of past actions that determines future consequences</note></term> arising from passion. Likewise, a person also hates the instruments of pain and becomes infatuated by the instruments of confusion. Thus, there is also a latent-deposit made by aversion and by infatuation. And in this sense it has been said, “Enjoyment is impossible unless one has killed <note>or harmed</note> some living creature.” Therefore, there is also a latent-deposit of karma, caused by harm, belonging to the body. <header>Inevitability of pain [-ii. 15</header>

is pleasure in an object of sense ¹." That which is the subsidence <note>the settling or satisfaction</note> of the organs because of their satiation with enjoyments is pleasure; after there has been a craving, the failure to subside is pain. And by the application of the organs to enjoyments one cannot make one's self free from thirst for enjoyment. Why is this? Since passions increase because-of <note>original: *anu*</note> application to enjoyments, and the skill of the organs also increases. Therefore application to the enjoyment of pleasure is not a way of approach <note>a method</note> to freedom from thirst for objects. Surely one aiming at pleasure and permeated by objects is sunk in the deep bog of pain, like the man who, while in fear of the scorpion's poison ² is bitten by the poisonous snake. This is the so-called painfulness of mutation <note>original: *pariṇāma-duḥkha*; the suffering caused by the fact that everything changes</note>; it is counteractive; even in a condition of pleasure it hinders the practitioner of yoga <note>original: *yogin*</note> himself.

2. Now what is the painfulness of anxiousness <note>original: *tāpa-duḥkha*; the suffering caused by distress or heat</note>? Every one has the experience of anxiousness; it is permeated by aversion and is dependent upon animate and inanimate instruments. Here we have a latent-deposit of karma <note>the stored psychological traces of past actions</note> arising from aversion. And a man yearning for the instruments of pleasure, throbs in the body and in the organs of speech and in the central-organ <note>original: *manas*; the coordinating faculty of the mind</note>. Since it then aids or <note>original: *ca*</note> thwarts others by aiding them or by injuring them, it amasses right-actions and wrong-actions. This latent-deposit of karma is the result of greed and of infatuation. For this reason it is called the painfulness of anxiousness.

3. But what is the painfulness of subliminal-impressions <note>original: *saṃskāra-duḥkha*; the suffering caused by deep-seated mental patterns</note>? There is a latent-deposit of subliminal-impressions of pleasure arising from the experience of pleasure; and there is a latent-deposit of subliminal-impressions of pain arising from the experience of pain. Thus analogously <note>original: *evam*</note>, while the fruition from the karmas is under experience, there is on the other hand an accumulation of a latent-deposit of karma. Thus this stream of pain from time-without-beginning, spreading wider and wider, agitates even the practitioner of yoga <note>original: *yogin*</note> because its essence is counteractive. Why is this? It is because a wise man is like an eyeball. Just

<header>Book II. Means of Attainment or Sādhana</header>

Just as a fine thread of wool falling upon the eyeball causes pain through its touch, but does not do so when it falls upon other parts of the body, so these subtle pains <note>arising from subliminal impressions</note> hinder only the practitioner of yoga <note>original: *yogin*</note>, who is as sensitive as an eyeball, but not any other perceiver. 

But for the other person <note>one who is not a yogin</note>—who repeatedly casts off the pain brought upon him by his own past actions <term>karma</term> only to receive that pain back again and again, and who is, as it were, permeated through and through from all sides by a restless mind-stuff that has been complicated since time-without-beginning by its own subconscious impressions—the situation is different. Under the influence of spiritual ignorance <term>*avidyā*</term>, this person identifies himself with the "I-substance" <note>the ego</note> and the "mine-substance" <note>possessiveness</note> regarding the very things that ought to be rejected. Upon him, as he is born again and again, the three-fold anguishes <note>internal suffering, external suffering from others, and suffering from natural forces</note> sweep down from both internal and external causes. 

This being the case, the practitioner of yoga, having seen himself and the whole multitude of creatures being swept away by this beginningless stream of pain, seeks refuge in perfect insight <term>*samyag-darçana*</term>, which is the cause of the dwindling of all pain. 

**<And because the fluctuations of the fundamental qualities of nature (<term>*guṇa*</term>) are in opposition to one another, the person of spiritual discrimination sees that all is nothing but pain.>** 

The qualities <term>*guṇa*</term> of the thinking-substance—taking the forms of brightness <note>Sattva</note>, activity <note>Rajas</note>, and inertia <note>Tamas</note>—become interdependent by assisting one another. They give rise to a presented idea that is either tranquil, cruel, or infatuated, depending on which of these three qualities is dominant. “And because the changes <term>*vṛtta*</term> of these qualities are unstable, the mind-stuff is in a state of rapid transformation.” Thus we have been told. <note>This teaching is attributed to the ancient philosopher Pañcaçikha</note> 

“The outer forms and the inner fluctuations oppose each other when they are developed to a high degree; however, the generic forms of these qualities cooperate with those that are highly developed.” Thus, since these qualities produce ideas of pleasure, pain, and delusion by relying upon one another, every quality <term>*sarve*</term> possesses the nature of all the others. The distinction between them is simply due to one being in a dominant state while the others are subordinate. Therefore, to the person of spiritual discrimination—

<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>Medical analogues to the Four Noble Truths [—ii. 15</header>

...terminating all is nothing but pain.> So the seed out of which this huge aggregate of pain grows forth is spiritual ignorance <term>*avidyā*</term> <note>original: "undifferentiated-consciousness (*avidyā*)"</note>. And the reason for the cessation <term>*abhāva*</term> <note>original: "failure-of-growth (*abhāva*)"</note> of this ignorance is focused-insight. 

Just as a system of medicine has four divisions—namely, **Disease**, the **Cause of Disease**, **Health**, and the **Remedy**—so this system of spiritual liberation also has four divisions: the **Round-of-Rebirth** <note>the cycle of reincarnation known as *saṃsāra*</note>, the **Cause of the Round-of-Rebirth**, **Release**, and the **Way to Release**. 

Of these four:
1. The **Round-of-Rebirth**, with its mass of pains, is that which is to be escaped <term>*heya*</term>. 
2. The conjunction of the primary-cause <note>nature or *prakṛti*</note> and of the Self <note>the pure consciousness or *puruṣa*</note> is the **cause** of this which is to be escaped. 
3. The final destruction of this correlation is the **escape** <term>*hāna*</term> <note>the state of liberation or *kaivalya*</note>. 
4. The means of escape is **focused-insight**. 

In the state of focused-insight, he who escapes—as he is in his true essence—can neither be accepted nor rejected <term>*heya*</term> <note>meaning the pure Self is beyond the categories of "getting" or "getting rid of" something</note>. For if there were a rejection <term>*hāna*</term>, that would involve the doctrine of the total extermination of the self. And <insert>as noted in some manuscripts</insert> if there were an acceptance, that would involve the doctrine that the self is a produced effect with a cause <note>which would imply the self is not eternal</note>. By denying both rejection and acceptance, we arrive at the doctrine that the Seer, as he is in himself, is eternal. This is the goal of focused-insight.

In order to account for this, the author introduces the next aphorism <term>*sūtra*</term> after first asking the question, "How can this be accounted for?" The aphorism begins with the word **15. . . . mutation** and ends with the word **discriminating**. 

The compound word in the aphorism is analyzed as follows: mutation, anxiety, and subliminal-impressions—these themselves are the pains. He describes how even the pleasure found in the objects of the senses is actually painful, insofar as all changes are eventually painful, by saying: "For every enlightened one, this is so." 

Pleasure is surely impossible unless it be permeated by passion. One cannot say they find no happiness in a thing while simultaneously taking pleasure in it. Moreover, since pleasure leads to action, and action causes a latent-deposit of merit and demerit <term>karma</term>, there is also a latent-deposit of action produced by passion; a thing which does not exist cannot produce an effect. Under these circumstances <term>*tadā*</term>, a person experiencing pleasure and feeling attachment to it also feels aversion toward any instruments of pain—though that aversion may be in a dormant or intercepted state. Furthermore, being unable to prevent these causes of pain, the person becomes infatuated <note>blinded by delusion</note>. 

Thus, there is also a latent-deposit of action <term>karma</term> created by aversion and by infatuation. There is nothing contradictory in saying that infatuation—another name for misconception—is the cause of further deposits of "infatuation-action." If it be asked,

In reply to this he says, **"it has been said, 'Spiritual ignorance (<term>avidyā</term> <note>original: "undifferentiated-consciousness (*avidyā*)"</note>) is pleasure in an object-of-sense'"** by [us when] showing [ii. 5] that spiritual ignorance is characterized by four kinds of misconceived ideas. There is of course, merely at the first impression (<term>āpātatas</term>), an experience which any one can feel of pleasure which follows even after eating food mixed with sweet poison; but after a lapse of time there is no pleasure. And as such it has been shown by The Exalted [the Lord <note>original: *Īçvara*</note> in the *Gītā* <note>The *Bhagavad Gītā*, a central Hindu scripture.</note> xviii. 38], "After there has been contact of the sense-organs with objects, that pleasure which is at the beginning like nectar and in the course of time like poison is known to be full of **passion-energy** (<term>rajas</term> <note>one of the three fundamental qualities of nature, associated with activity, movement, and suffering.</note>)." 

He raises a doubt by saying, **"which ... with enjoyments."** The objector says, "We do not accede to the statement that pleasure is the joy in objects. On the contrary, when men are not satiated and when their minds are afflicted with yearnings for one object after another, it is the very thirst itself that is the great pain. And this [thirst] does not subside unless enjoyment follow. Furthermore the full subsidence of this [thirst] is not permeated with passion and similar [states of mind]. Thus it cannot be said that this subsidence has the painfulness of mutation <note>The idea that all things are constantly changing and therefore cause suffering.</note>." 

This is the point. — **"Because of their satiation"** means: Because the thirst [for enjoyment] has dwindled, there is a subsidence of the organs; in other words, there is no activity [of the organs] with regard to objects-of-sense. He makes this same clear by a negative instance in the words **"arising from a craving."** He rebuts an objection with the words **"And ... by the organs ... not."** The word **"because of (<term>anu</term>)"** is used in the sense of cause. It is true that the dwindling of thirst [for objects] is the flawless¹ pleasure. But application to enjoyment is not the cause of this [dwindling of thirst]; but it is the cause of the thirst which is just the opposite of this [dwindling of thirst]. Just as they say,² "Lust by the enjoyment of

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Yoga Sūtra II.15, shifting from the psychological reasons for suffering to the structural nature of reality. It explains how opposing mental states conflict and why, ultimately, the discerning person sees the entire cycle of existence as suffering. It introduces the "four-fold" structure of the Yoga system, comparing it to a medical diagnosis.</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>ii. 15-] Book II. Means of Attainment or Spiritual Practice <note>Sādhana</note></header>

'How can we make known the qualities of tranquillity, cruelty, and infatuation, which are opposed to each other?' In reply to this, the author says: «"The primary forms, when developed to a high degree, and the inner fluctuations, when developed to a high degree, oppose each other."» These «forms» are the eight states<gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: bhāva</note> beginning with virtue or right-action. The «fluctuations» are feelings such as pleasure and pain. So, in this case, vice or wrong-action—when it is in such a condition of high development—is opposed by right-action when that right-action is in the process of bearing fruit. Similarly, knowledge is in opposition to ignorance, passionlessness to passion, and power to weakness, just as pleasure is opposed by pain. 

However, the general forms <note>original: generic forms</note> which are not actively manifesting do not oppose those which are highly developed; instead, they co-operate with those that are actively moving forth.

The objector asks: 'We understand this. Yet how can pleasure found in worldly objects have an intrinsic quality of pain?' In reply to this, the author says: «Thus since these.» This is because the underlying material cause of both pleasure and pain is the same. Because their essence is that same material cause, there is also no difference in their material effects <note>original: upādeya</note>. 

'So then, is this identity between pleasure and pain absolute? If so, the distinction between the two within the thinking-substance would be impossible.' In reply to this, he says: «in a subordinate or in a dominant position.» In relation to the general essence <note>original: ātman</note>, one element is subordinate; in relation to the element that is highly developed, the other is dominant. So, both from an external view and by their very nature <note>original: svabhāvatas</note>, ->to the discriminating person, all is nothing but pain.<- 

Consequently, men of insight should seek to escape <note>original: heya</note> pain. Yet it cannot be escaped unless its root cause <note>original: nidāna</note> is also escaped. Moreover, it cannot be escaped unless its cause is thoroughly understood. So, he shows what this radical cause is in the words: «So . . . of this.» This refers to the seed from which the total sum of pain grows or arises. 

He shows the reason for destroying this growth in the words «And . . . in this.» Now he shows that this system—which has begun its work for the sake of showing favor <note>See Book i. 1</note> to all beings—is similar to another system of the same kind by saying: «Just as.» This refers to a system described as having four divisions, meaning it consists of four compactly arranged parts <note>This likely refers to the medical model of disease, cause, health, and remedy</note>.

It is objected: 'Why is there not a contradiction when you previously said that pain is to be escaped, but now you describe the entire round-of-rebirth as something to be escaped?' In reply to this, he says: «Of these four divisions, the round-of-rebirth exists with its mass of pains.» That which causes the soul to undergo the round-of-rebirth is spiritual ignorance <note>original: avidyā</note>; this constitutes the specific activity that causes the cycle of rebirths. He describes this in the words: «of the primary cause and of the Self.» 

He explains what liberation is in the words: «of the correlation» <note>referring to the ending of the link between nature and the spirit</note>. He tells what the means of liberation are in the words: «the means of escape.» There are some practitioners<gloss>3</gloss> who regard liberation as the total extermination of the one-who-escapes <note>original: hātṛ</note>—the seeker's own self.

<header>The Self may escape pain [—ii. 16</header>

In this sense they say, “Like the blowing-out (<term>nirvāṇa</term>) <note>The literal meaning of nirvāṇa is the extinguishing of a flame.</note> of a lamp is the deliverance of this anguished<gloss>¹</gloss> (<term>tāpin</term>) [mind].” Others<gloss>²</gloss> again teach that, as a result of the extermination of the hindrances with their subconscious impressions, purified mental-states (<term>vijñāna</term>) <note>Pure consciousness or specialized awareness.</note> are produced; and that this itself is liberation. In reply to these he says, “In this [focused-insight].” In this case he first finds fault with the escape by saying, “For if there be an escape . . . for him.” Since no rational man ever exerts himself to exterminate himself. It is objected, ‘We see some persons, all of whose pleasures are uprooted by intense disease and who drag about their bodies, as it were, laden with pain, striving to exterminate themselves.’ True, he says in reply, there are a few such. But not of this kind are men living in [the ordinary] round-of-rebirth. [For] their lot is to enjoy diverse and strange and celestial delights. Even those [others], however, are evidently desirous of liberation. Accordingly we should not concede that liberation is the extermination of him who escapes—as he is in himself—since that would involve what is not one of the aims of man. The objector says, ‘Very well then, let us say that he who escapes—as he is in himself—is something that may be accepted.’ In reply to this he says, “And if there be an acceptance . . . the doctrine [that he has] a cause.” For if there be an acceptance [of him], then, because he would be impermanent in so far as he is an effect, he might also fall even from [his] state of liberation. For liberation is deathlessness. And [we could] not [say] that an uninterrupted succession of purified mental-states is deathless. Because the uninterrupted series, over and above the members-of-the-series (<term>saṁtānin</term>), not being anything [perceptibly] real, does not exist; and because the members-in-the-series are not permanent. Therefore we should strive to have such a theory as [would teach that the Self as he is in himself is] eternal. For this being so, liberation (<term>apavarga</term>) might be [one of] the aims of men. So he says, “And by denying both.” Consequently, liberation is nothing but [the Seer] abiding in himself [i. 3]. Precisely this is the right point of view.

->This same system is set forth in its four divisions.<-

### 16. That which is to be escaped is pain yet to come.

Pain past, that is, transferred beyond experience, cannot properly be called (*<term>pakṣe vartate</term>*) <note>original: "occurs in the subject" or "is predicated of"</note> a thing to be escaped. And present pain in its own moment [of existence] has attained experience; so it cannot at the next moment be so changed that it can be escaped. Consequently only that pain which is yet to come is that which hinders the <term>yogin</term> only, who is like an eye-ball,<gloss>³</gloss> <note>The yogi is compared to an eye-ball because of his extreme sensitivity to the slightest "dust" of suffering, while others are less sensitive.</note> but [this does] not [hinder] any other perceiver. Only this pain becomes so changed that it may be escaped.

<page-num>140</page-num>
<header>ii. 16—] Book II. Means of Attainment or <term>Sādhana</term> <note>The practice or means used to achieve a spiritual goal.</note> [140</header>

«This same system is set forth in its four divisions.» <note>This refers to the "Fourfold Arrangement" (Chaturvyuha), a philosophical framework similar to a medical diagnosis: 1. The illness (suffering), 2. The cause of the illness, 3. The state of health (liberation), and 4. The treatment (yoga practice).</note> **16. That which is to be escaped is pain yet to come.** The words «yet to come» exclude the past and the present. He makes this consistent by saying «pain past.» <note>Pain that has already occurred is gone; pain currently being felt is already in process. Only future pain can be truly prevented or "escaped" through practice.</note> If it be objected that present pain now in experience is not to be transferred beyond experience, he replies «And present.» Easy.

Therefore the cause of this same thing that is described as something to be escaped is once more specified.

**17. The correlation of the Seer and the object-of-sight is the cause of that which is to be escaped.**

The Seer is the Self <note>The Purusha, or pure consciousness.</note> conscious by reflection of the thinking-substance. <note>The mind-stuff or "citta" which reflects the light of consciousness.</note> Objects-of-sight are all external-aspects (*<term>dharma</term>*) <note>The qualities, properties, or phenomena of the material world.</note> which have struck upon the <term>sattva</term> <note>The highest, most transparent quality of the mind-substance, capable of reflecting consciousness.</note> of the thinking-substance. So this same object-of-sight giving its aid, like a magnet,¹ <note>original: "Compare i. 4; ii. 18; iv. 17." The analogy means that just as a magnet moves iron simply by being near it without "doing" anything, the world affects the soul through proximity.</note> by the mere fact of being near, becomes, by reason of its being an object-of-sight, the property of the Self, its proprietor, whose nature is seeing. It becomes changed into an object upon which experience operates,—in so far it has the nature of another. Having acquired [this new] being, although self-dependent, [it becomes] by serving one-not-itself,² <note>original: "Compare iv. 24"</note> dependent on one-not-itself. The correlation of these two, the power of seeing and the power by which one sees, is from time-without-beginning and is effected for [two] purposes. [This correlation is] the cause of that which is to be escaped, in other words, the cause of pain. And in this sense it has also been said, “By avoidance of the cause of correlation with this [thinking-substance] the antidote for pain would be absolute.” Why [would this be so]? Because we know the antidote to prevent the cause of pain. For example, we know that the liability-to-scratches inheres in the sole of the foot, the power to scratch inheres in the thorn, the prevention [of scratching] is either by not stepping with the foot upon the thorn or by stepping [upon it when the sole of the foot] is covered by a foot-protector. Whoever understands these three [scratch and cause and prevention] has begun the antidote therefor and is not exposed to the pain from scratches.

<summary>This page introduces the core logic of the Yoga system: identifying future suffering as the problem and the entanglement between the pure observer (the Self) and the observed world (the mind and objects) as its cause. It uses the analogy of a thorn and a foot-protector to explain how understanding the cause of pain leads to its prevention.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the "Fourfold Arrangement" of Yoga, specifically moving from the definition of future pain (Sutra 16) to the root cause of that pain: the entanglement of consciousness with matter (Sutra 17).</meta>

<page-num>141]</page-num>
<header>Cause of pain [—ii. 17</header>

Why is this? It is because of the Self’s power to perceive the three-fold nature of experience. To continue the argument <note>original: *atrāpi*</note>, the quality of light and purity <note><term>sattva</term>: the refined, transparent quality of the mind</note>, which is the thing being affected, comes under the ownership of the quality of activity <note><term>rajas</term>: the energy of motion and passion</note>, which acts as the "afflictor." Why is this? Because the mind-substance stands in a passive relationship to the active force of that energy. This act of affliction affects the mind-substance as a passive object, but it does not affect the unchanging and inactive Soul <note><term>kṣetrajña</term>: literally "the Knower of the Field," the pure conscious Self</note>. [Why is the Soul inactive?] Because its only role is to have objects presented to it. However, if the mind-substance is undergoing affliction, the Self appears to conform itself to the shape of that mind-substance, and thus it seems to be afflicted right along with it.

That which is to be escaped <note>Referring to future suffering, as defined in the previous sutra</note> has been described. Its cause <note>original: *nidāṇa* - a medical term for diagnosis/cause</note> is now described:

**17. The connection between the Seer and the object-of-sight is the cause of that which is to be escaped.**

The author explains who the "Seer" is with the words: "The Seer... conscious by reflection of the thinking-substance." The pure power of intelligence <note><term>citi</term></note> belonging to the Self <note>original: *Pums* - the individual Spirit</note>, although it remains detached and independent, becomes conscious by being reflected in the mind-stuff. This occurs because the mind-stuff acts as a mirror, catching the "shadow" <note>original: *chāyā*</note> or reflection of that intelligence. 

It is objected that "even if this is true, the Self could only perceive the mind-stuff itself; it could not see the various external things, such as sound and other sensations <note>original: *çabdādi* - literally "sound and the rest"</note>, which are entirely separate from it." To this he replies: "Objects-of-sight... the refined mind-substance." When the mind-stuff flows through the channels of the senses, it transforms into the shapes of various external objects. Since the mind-stuff itself is the primary object that the Self perceives, these external forms also become objects of sight. 

It might be further objected: "Insofar as the mind-stuff takes on the form of these things, it may indeed possess their shape. But if we assume the Self has a relationship with the mind-stuff, the Self would have to be subject to change. Yet if there is no relationship at all, how can external things—even if present in the mind—be seen? Surely an object that has no connection to a Seer cannot be called 'seen.'" To this he replies: "This same object-of-sight." 

All this was explained in detail in Book One [i. 7], where we showed that the refined mind-substance, although it does not possess natural consciousness <note><term>cāitanya</term></note> because it is material, is so perfectly clear that it contains the reflected image <note>original: *bimba*</note> of pure intelligence. It thus appears to reach a state of balance with that intelligence and experiences various things. Consequently, the Seer, experiencing the pleasures and other sensations offered by the mind-substance as it transforms into various shapes, becomes the "owner" or proprietor. The mind-substance, performing these transformations, becomes his "property." Thus, this mind-substance, containing the forms of all things, becomes the object-of-sight; and acting like a magnet attracting metal, it becomes the property of the Self, whose very nature is the act of seeing and who acts as the proprietor.

<summary>This page explains Sutra 2.17, identifying the root of suffering as the "union" or correlation between pure consciousness (the Seer) and the mind (the object). It uses the metaphor of a mirror and a magnet to show how the inactive Soul mistakenly identifies with the changing experiences of the mind.</summary>

<page-num>142</page-num>
<header>ii. 17— Book II. Means of Attainment or *Sādhana*</header>

Why [is this]? He says, "the experience." Because [the quality of purity <note>original: *sattva*</note> in the thinking-substance] is changed into an object upon which experience operates. The "experience" is the enjoyment on the part of the Self; the "operation" is the activity; the "object" is the condition of being enjoyed; because it is "changed into" this, it becomes the property [of the Self].—The objection is made, ‘How can the purity <note>original: *sattva*</note> of the thinking-substance, which is luminous in itself, be the object of an experience?’ In reply to this he says, "in so far as it has the nature of another." For if the pure quality <note>original: *sattva*</note> of the thinking-substance were really like the pure consciousness <note>original: *caitanya*</note>, it would be luminous in itself. But it has acquired [this new] being, it is property <note>original: *sva*</note>, it is other than pure consciousness <note>original: *caitanya*</note>, and inert in nature. Therefore it is the object of the experience on the part of this [consciousness].

It is objected, ‘One thing is dependent upon another thing, when in some way or other it exerts itself for the sake of the other. Whereas the purity <note>original: *sattva*</note> of the thinking-substance does not in any way exert itself for the Self which is detached [from it]. And how can [the thinking-substance] be dependent on this consciousness <note>original: *caitanya*</note>? And this being so, it cannot be an object upon which [the Self] operates.’ In reply to this he says, "although self-dependent." "By serving the purpose of one-not-itself," by serving the purpose of the Self, it becomes "dependent on one-not-itself," dependent upon the Self.

The objector says, ‘This relation between the power of seeing and the power by which one sees must be either natural or accidental. If it be natural, since the two terms of the relation are permanent, the relation is one that cannot be exterminated; and this being so, the cycle of rebirth <note>original: *saṃsāra*</note> would be permanent. But if it be accidental, then in so far as mental hindrances <note>original: *kleśa*</note> and actions <note>original: *karma*</note> and its subconscious impressions <note>original: *vāsanā*</note> are fluctuations of the internal organ, the former exist only so long as the internal organ exists, and if at the same time (and <note>original: *ca*</note>) the internal organ is to have these as its cause, there would be the fault of mutual interdependence; and [you could not] explain this fault away by bringing in a series without beginning,] because it is impossible that there should be anything from time-without-beginning at the beginning of the creation, for then the cycle of rebirth would not be produced at all. On which point it has been said, “Even in the opinion of those who think that the Self is not an agent, how can the primary qualities <note>original: *guṇa*</note> bring about the very first activity? For then the results of action <note>original: *karma*</note> do not yet exist. Neither is there then an erroneous idea nor passion nor hatred nor similar [hindrances]. For all these are fluctuations of the central organ and the central organ has not been produced at that time.”’

This doubt he removes by the words, "The correlation of these two, the power of seeing and the power by which one sees, is from time-without-beginning and is effected for [two] purposes." It is true that the relation is not natural, but accidental. But it is not to be supposed that it has a beginning. For in so far as it is the result of a cause <note>original: *nimitta*</note> which is from time-without-beginning, it itself is also from time-without-beginning. Furthermore the uninterrupted succession of hindrances and actions and the subconscious impressions of these is from time-without-beginning.

<summary>This page addresses philosophical objections regarding how the pure Self can "experience" the mind and why their connection—though accidental—has no beginning in time, thus allowing for the cycle of rebirth to exist without a specific starting point.</summary>

<page-num>143</page-num>
<header>Return to the state of equipoise [-ii. 17</header>

And although at the time of each reversal of creation <note>the periodic dissolution of the universe</note> this succession has been reduced to the state of <term>equipoise</term> <note>original: sāmya; a state of perfect balance between the three qualities of nature</note> in the primary cause, still at the beginning of a creation it becomes again as before, just as some kinds of <term>sprouting plants</term> <note>original: udbhijja</note>, reduced at the end of the rains to a state of earth, assume again their proper form when the rains return. More than once this has been made known previously. In so far as it brings it to growth, undifferentiated-consciousness <note>the fundamental layer of the mind</note> is the cause of the correlation; in so far as it is the reason for its stability, the purpose of the Self is the cause. For this conjunction is stable by virtue of this purpose of the Self <note>the Soul’s need for experience and eventual liberation</note>. It is this that is stated in the words, "effected for two purposes." "And in this sense it has also been said" by <term>Pañcaçikha</term> <note>an ancient sage of the Samkhya school of philosophy</note>. "By conjunction with this" means by conjunction with the thinking-substance <note>the mind</note>. This same is the cause of pain. By the avoidance of this conjunction, this antidote for pain would be absolute. So what is implied is (<term>in effect</term> <note>original: arthāt</note>) that pain results from a failure to avoid it. In connection with this same point he states an extremely well-known simile in the words, "For example." "A foot-protector" is a sandal. An objector says, ‘Let this be granted. But if it be said that correlation with the <term>qualities of nature</term> <note>original: guṇa</note> is the cause of the castigation <note>the "burning" or suffering of experience</note>, then we must say that the <term>qualities</term> <note>original: guṇa</note> are the <term>afflictors</term> <note>original: tāpaka; those who cause the "burning"</note>. And since the action of castigating does not remain within the agent—as is the case in an intransitive act like simply "being"—we must expect some other thing to be castigated <note>the one who suffers</note>. And the Self is not the passive object of this act as being something to be castigated, for in so far as he is immutable <note>unchanging</note>, it is not fitting that he should be such as to reap the consequences which come from actions. Therefore we come to the result that the act of castigating, which is concomitant with the thing castigated, ceases when the thing castigated also ceases, just as there is an absence of smoke when fire is lacking.’ So he says, "And to resume the argument . . . . the castigator." It is the <term>qualities of nature</term> <note>original: guṇa</note> only that are in the relation of the "afflicted" and the "afflictor." Of these three, <term>purity</term> <note>original: sattva; the quality of light and goodness</note>, because it is soft like the sole of the foot, is the object to be castigated <note>the thing that feels the pain</note>. Whereas <term>passion</term> <note>original: rajas; the quality of energy and movement</note>, inasmuch as it is keen, is the castigator <note>the source of the pain</note>. This is the point. He asks, "Why so?" That is to say, why is <term>purity</term> <note>original: sattva</note> alone, and not the Self, the object to be castigated? He gives the answer in the words, "the <term>purity-quality</term> <note>original: sattva</note> as a passive object." ‘Is not then the Self castigated at all? If so, let it be the inanimate <term>purity-quality</term> <note>original: sattva</note> that receives the castigation. What does it matter to us?’ In reply to this he says, "Since it has objects shown to it. But if the <term>purity-quality</term> <note>original: sattva</note> be under castigation, the Self, it appears, conforming itself to the form of this purity-quality is itself castigated along with the purity-quality." The cause of its being castigated along with it is that objects are shown to it and this has been explained previously [i. 4].

<header>ii. 18—] Book II. Means of Attainment or Spiritual Practice <note>original: Sādhana</note> [144</header>

The author explains the nature of the object-of-sight itself.

**18. With a disposition to brightness and to activity and to inertia, and with the elements and the organs as its essence, and with its purpose the experience and the liberation [of the Self],—[this is] the object-of-sight.**

The <term>quality of purity</term> <note>original: sattva; the element of light and clarity</note> has the disposition to brightness; the <term>quality of passion</term> <note>original: rajas; the element of energy and movement</note> has the disposition to activity; the <term>quality of darkness</term> <note>original: tamas; the element of heaviness and stability</note> has the disposition to inertia. These <term>three qualities of nature</term> <note>original: guṇa</note>—with their [three] separate parts influencing each other,—with <term>external properties</term> <note>original: dharma</note> in conjunction or in separation,—with <term>physical forms</term> <note>original: mūrti</note> brought about by their interdependence upon one another,—with separate powers that, although serving each other, remain distinct,—with <term>corresponding patterns</term> <note>original: anupātin</note> according to various different or similar powers,—with their presence revealed when they become dominant,—with their existence included in the dominant quality even when they are subordinate (as inferred from their <term>functional-activity</term> <note>original: vyāpāra</note>),—with their faculties used effectively for the purposes of the Self,—with their aid given, like that of a magnet, simply by being nearby,—following a change in any one of themselves without any outside cause—these <term>qualities of nature</term> <note>original: guṇa</note> are what is meant by the word <term>primary cause</term> <note>original: pradhāna; the fundamental root of the material world</note>. 

And this is called <the object-of-sight.> This same object-of-sight transforms into the physical elements and the senses—into elements such as earth and others in <term>coarse</term> <note>tangible, physical matter</note> and in <term>subtle</term> <note>fine or energetic matter</note> forms. It transforms likewise into organs such as the <term>organ-of-hearing</term> <note>original: çrotra</note>. 

However, it does not act without a driving force. On the contrary, it acts only by responding to an impelling force. For the object-of-sight exists specifically for the sake of the experience and the liberation of the Self <note>the Soul</note>. Of these two, "experience" is the perception of things as desirable or undesirable, so long as this perception does not distinguish [the Self from the <term>thinking-substance</term> <note>the mind</note>]. "Liberation" is the realization of the—

For the Self, as we know, has the experience of the results of these processes.

Bondage belongs to the thinking substance alone and consists of the failure to achieve the goals of the Self. Release is the completion of the Self’s purpose. In this way, the <term>processes of knowing</term> <note>original: vṛtti</note>, the processes of memory, the <term>logical inclusion of particulars</term> <note>original: ūha</note>, the <term>removal of doubts</term> <note>original: apoha</note>, real knowledge, and the will to live—all of which exist in the thinking substance—are assumed to exist in the Self. For the Self, as we know, experiences the results of these activities.

The author explains the "object of sight" by referring to the <term>aphorism</term> <note>original: sūtra</note> starting with the word "brightness" and ending with "object of sight." <term>Brightness</term> <note>original: prakāśa</note> is a portion of the <term>quality of goodness</term> <note>original: sattva</note>; it is influenced by dejection, which is a quality of <term>inertia</term> <note>original: tamas</note>, or by pain, which is a quality of <term>passion</term> <note>original: rajas</note>. Similarly, this must be understood for the quality of passion and the rest. This is what is meant by the phrase “with the [three] separate parts influencing each other.” It refers to the <term>external properties</term> <note>original: dharma</note> being in conjunction with, or in separation from, the Self. <page-num>146</page-num>
## ii. 18—] Book II. Means of Attainment or <term>Sādhana</term> <note>The practice or disciplined path toward spiritual liberation.</note> [146]

"...red and white and black and which brings forth many offspring like herself; while another male goat deserts her after having enjoyed her." <note>This is a traditional metaphor for Nature (Prakriti) and its three qualities—red for energy, white for clarity, and black for inertia. The "male goat" represents the soul: one soul is entangled in nature, while another, having understood it, becomes free.</note>—Limitations-in-extent, such as the element of earth, are those which have been brought about by basing them upon interdependence of one upon another. 

The objector says, ‘This may be true. When a quiescent <note>peaceful or calm</note> idea is to be produced by **clarity** <note>original: *sattva*</note>, since **energy** <note>original: *rajas*</note> and **inertia** <note>original: *tamas*</note> also, in so far as they are accessory to clarity, are the causes of this idea, there is a power in them. If this be so (*iti*), and whenever energy or inertia might be the principal influence, then a peaceful idea might always arise, rather than a cruel or a dull and infatuated one, just as in the case when clarity was dominant.’ 

In reply to this he says, «with separate powers, although in subservience to each other, still unconfused.» Let it be granted, when a peaceful idea is to be produced, that energy and inertia are in a supporting role, still their individual powers are not mixed together. For the fact that their powers are not commingled may be inferred from the fact that there is no commingling of their effects. Whereas effects of the peaceful, cruel, and infatuated forms are seen to move actively forth in so far as their specific form is unmixed. Thus it is established that the powers remain unconfused. 

The objector says, ‘Suppose this be granted. If the powers are unconfused, then the **qualities** <note>original: *guṇa*</note> cannot be supposed to work harmoniously together. Evidently things whose powers are different never have effects that are produced by a harmonious working together. Threads, for instance, and lumps of earth and dry grasses do not work harmoniously together to produce a water-jar.’ 

In reply to this he says, «with conformations according to various disparate <note>dissimilar</note> and comparate <note>similar</note> powers.» Although the power of serving as a material cause is found in a thing which is similar to its effect, and not elsewhere, and although the power of serving as a co-operative cause may be found in dissimilar things, still when it is a water-jar that is to be generated, it is not in the power of dry grasses to serve even as co-operative causes; and this being so, these grasses do not work harmoniously with threads. This is the point. 

—[He analyses the compound word.] Those are referred to whose character it is to conform to certain kinds of powers with regard to possible dissimilar and similar things.—«At the time when they become dominant.» When a supernormal <note>divine or celestial</note> body is to be generated, the **clarity** <note>original: *sattva*</note> is dominant and the energy and inertia are accessory. Similarly when a human body is to be generated, the **energy** <note>original: *rajas*</note> is dominant and the clarity and inertia are accessory. Likewise when an animal body is to be generated, the **inertia** <note>original: *tamas*</note> is dominant and the clarity and energy are accessory. Thus these qualities have their presence manifested at the time when they become dominant. In other words, they contribute to the effect in proportion as they become reintensified. And the word «dominant» is to be taken as the abstract form of dominance¹ <note>original: *bhāvapradhāna*</note>.

¹ He wishes to exclude the other meaning of **Primary Source** <note>original: *pradhāna*</note>, that is, the root-matter of the universe. Just as [in the phrase of Pāṇini’s <term>sūtra</term><note>A concise rule or aphorism in Sanskrit literature; here referring to the foundational rules of grammar by the scholar Pāṇini.</note> i. 4. 22,] “The dual and singular are used in case of two and one”, [the words two and one are] in this case to be understood as twoness and oneness; in other cases [such as of measurable numbers], they are to be understood as two and as one.—An objector says, ‘At that time [of dominance], it is possible to say that the dominant exists in so far as it is in its intense form. But is there any source-of-valid-ideas [to prove] the real existence of its accessories which are not in the intense form?’ In reply to this he says, «although subordinate.» Although not intensified, still, because they have no discrimination [to recognize that they are themselves inanimate], and [yet] because they do work harmoniously together,—from the mere fact of their functional-activity in so far as there is co-operation, —their existence is inferred as being included in the primary cause <note>original: *pradhāna*</note>. The objector says, ‘We may grant that the aspects <note>original: *guṇa*; the three fundamental threads or qualities of nature: clarity, energy, and inertia.</note> have faculties and work harmoniously together, but why do they perform this [co-operation]? For surely just because one says there is a faculty, one generates no [actual] effect on the ground that there may not be any cessation in the production of effects.’ In reply to this he says, «employed as effective for the purposes of the Self.» After this [purpose has been effected], when all the purposes of the Self have been ended, the aspects [afterwards] cease and produce no effects. This is what he means to say. If it be asked, ‘How can a thing which does not aid the Self, use impelling force as being a purpose of the Self,’ he replies «aid given merely by being near.» <note>This refers to the philosophical concept that Nature acts for the Soul's benefit simply by being in its proximity, much like a magnet moves iron without "doing" anything.</note> It is objected that ‘the impeller of the aspects is a cause characterized only as being merit and demerit; but can [these aspects be made to produce effects] when impelled by the purpose of the Self?’ In reply to this objection he says, «without any external cause.»—[He explains the phrase.] «The rest» [of the aspects], even «without any external-cause <note>original: *pratyaya*</note>» [or] efficient-cause <note>original: *nimitta*</note> such as merit, «following the fluctuation of any one of them,» either of clarity <note>original: *sattva*</note> or of energy <note>original: *rajas*</note> or of inertia <note>original: *tamas*</note>, as dominant and as being active towards the production of its own effect. In which sense he will say later [iv. 3], “The efficient-cause gives no impulse, but [the mutation] follows when the barrier to the evolving-causes is cut, just as in the case of the peasant.” <note>A famous analogy: just as a farmer opens a gate to let water flow into a field naturally, the spiritual process removes obstacles to allow nature to evolve for the Self.</note>—The construction of the sentence is, these aspects <note>original: *guṇa*</note> are denoted by the word primary-cause <note>original: *pradhāna*</note>. According to its derivation [the word *pradhāna*] is that by which the universe is produced <note>original: *pradhīyate*</note> or put forth.¹ This is said to be the object-of-sight. —Having mentioned the nature of the aspects <note>original: *guṇa*</note> he describes the effect of this disposition in the words, «this same.» In order to establish the doctrine of the pre-existent effect <note>original: *satkāryavāda*; the theory that the effect already exists within its cause before it is manifested.</note>, he says that a thing enters into mutation as a form of that thing, whichever it may be, that is its essence. <header>ii. 18-] Book II. Means of Attainment or Spiritual Practice [148</header>

Regarding <term>liberation</term><note>original: *apavarga*; the final release from the cycle of rebirth.</note>, which is part of the <term>sūtra</term><note>An aphorism or concise rule.</note>, the commentator provides an introduction by stating "not without an impelling force." He clarifies the word <term>experience</term><note>original: *bhoga*; the enjoyment or suffering of the fruits of past actions.</note> by specifying "of these [two]." For pleasure and pain belong to the thinking-substance <note>original: *buddhi-tattva*; the intellectual faculty or mind-stuff.</note> because it is composed of the three <term>aspects</term><note>original: *guṇa*; the three fundamental qualities of nature: clarity (sattva), energy (rajas), and inertia (tamas).</note>. This thinking-substance undergoes change because its nature is defined by these three aspects. Experience is said to occur when there is a definite perception of things as they relate to these qualities.¹ Accordingly, he says, "so long as they are undivided." We have pointed this out several times already.

He further explains the word <term>liberation</term> by saying it is "of the enjoyer" <note>the Self or *Puruṣa*.</note>. Liberation is literally that by which one is "wrenched off" or set free. He emphasizes that there is no other motivating purpose for the material world by saying "in addition to these two" <note>referring to experience and liberation.</note>. "And in this sense it has been said" by the ancient sage Pañcaśikha: "But he who..."

An objection is raised: "If experience and liberation are real events produced by the thinking-substance, how can they be attributed to the Self, which is neither their cause nor the place where they happen?" In response, he says, "These two." The idea that the Self is the "enjoyer" has been explained and will be further discussed later [iii. 34]. But in the strictest sense, as the text says, "Bondage belongs to the thinking-substance alone, and it consists of the failure to achieve the goals of the Self." The word "thus" refers to the way experience and liberation are described as being connected to the Self. In this same way, the processes of knowing and other mental activities should be understood as being attributed to the Self.

<margin>Dasgupta, Y.P. 194.</margin>
Among these, the "process-of-knowing" is thinking of an intended object exactly as it is; the "process-of-retention" is the memory of that object; "comprehension-of-particulars" <note>original: *ūha*</note> is the act of grasping the specific details belonging to a thing; "removal-of-faults" <note>original: *apoha*</note> is the dismissal of wrongly attributed details through stable reasoning <note>original: *yukti*</note>. It is through these two alone—comprehension and removal—that a given thing is determined, resulting in real knowledge. Finally, the "will-to-live" is the act of rejecting or accepting something, following this determination of reality.

# 19. The divisions of the aspects (guṇas) are: the particularized, the unparticularized, the resoluble only [into primary matter], and the irresoluble primary matter.

Of these four stages, the elements of ether, air, fire, water, and earth are the "particularized" forms of the "unparticularized" fine...

### Successive developments of the aspects

<margin>[—ii. 19</margin>

...elements (<term>tanmātra</term><note>The "fine" or "subtle" elements that serve as the blueprint for the physical world.</note>) such as sound, touch, color, taste, and smell. Similarly, the organs of the **thinking-substance** <note>original: *buddhi*; the higher intellect.</note> are the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose, along with the organs of action: the voice, hands, feet, and the organs of excretion and generation. To these we add the eleventh: the **central-organ** <note>original: *manas*; the mind that processes sensory input.</note> which can focus on all kinds of objects. These sixteen are the *particularized* forms of the *unparticularized* **personality-substance** <note>original: *asmitā*; the "I-sense" or ego-structure.</note> which is characterized by the feeling of individual personality. This represents the sixteen-fold mutation of the **aspects** (<term>guṇa</term><note>The three fundamental qualities—clarity, activity, and inertia—that make up all material and mental reality.</note>).

The *unparticularized* forms are six in total: the fine element of sound, the fine element of touch, the fine element of color, the fine element of taste, and the fine element of smell. As we understand them, these five unparticularized forms possess one, two, three, four, or five distinguishing characteristics respectively. The sixth unparticularized form is that which we can only describe as the **feeling-of-personality** <note>The ego-sense before it differentiates into specific senses or physical elements.</note>. 

These six are the unparticularized forms of the **Great thinking-substance** (<term>mahat-tattva</term><note>The "Great Principle"; the first and highest evolution of nature, representing pure cosmic intelligence.</note>), of whose being we can only say that "it exists." Prior to these unparticularized forms is the **Great Substance** itself, which is described as "resoluble" <note>original: *liṅga*; meaning it has a "mark" or characteristic and can be dissolved back into its cause.</note>. Remaining within this **Great Being** (<term>ātman</term><note>Used here to refer to the essential nature of the cosmic intellect, not the individual soul.</note>), which is the state of mere existence, these six unparticularized forms reach the limit of their development. 

When the process of creation is reversed, these forms return to that same Great Being of mere existence. From there, they revert further back to that which has neither existence nor non-existence—a state where both existence and non-existence as we know them have been set aside. This is the **unphenomenalized and unresoluble primary-cause** <note>original: *aliṅga* or *Prakṛti*; the primordial state of nature before anything is manifest.</note>. This Great Being (the state of mere existence) is the first mutation of the aspects. That ultimate state, which has neither existence nor non-existence, is the mutation of the aspects known as the *unresoluble* primary cause. 

Therefore, the purpose of the **Self** <note>original: *Puruṣa*; the pure consciousness for whom nature exists.</note> is not the reason for the existence of this unresoluble state. Since the Self’s purpose (experience and liberation) is not yet active at the very beginning when nature is in its unresoluble state, the Self's purpose is not the *cause* of that primary state. <note>This implies that Nature in its highest, unmanifested form exists independently of the soul's need for experience; see also i. 45.</note>

<summary>This page outlines the hierarchy of material evolution in Yoga philosophy, tracing the path from the unmanifest primary cause (Prakṛti) down to the sixteen physical elements and organs that make up our daily experience.</summary>
