# Book II. The Path to Practice (*Sādhana*)
### [-ii. 28]

...as the author will state later <note>original reference: iv. 3</note>, “The external cause does not drive the process, but rather the transformation follows once the obstacles to nature’s creative causes are removed—just as a farmer removes a barrier to let water flow into his fields.” Thus, we speak of a "cause of attainment" only in relation to the final result: spiritual discernment <term>discriminative discernment: the rare and essential ability to distinguish between the eternal Self and the changing material world</term>.

**7. The cause of disjunction.** In any situation where something acts as a secondary aid to this spiritual discernment, that same thing serves as a cause of separation or "disjunction" <note>separating the soul from its entanglement with matter</note>.

**8. The cause of transformation.** He describes this by using the example of **"the goldsmith and the gold."** When we focus on the specific forms—the bracelets, earrings, or anklets—we see difference. When we focus on the gold itself, which is present in all these forms, we see no difference. The goldsmith, in making a bracelet, acts as the cause that transforms the gold into a new shape. However, while he changes the gold into an earring, the gold itself remains identical. 

Although fire was used as an example of **modification** <note>see cause 5 on the previous page</note> in the case of cooking, it is not considered a cause of "transformation" in the same sense. In cooking, the difference between the substance—the raw grains—and the property—the cooked lump of rice—is not the main point; the substance of the rice simply persists through the change. Therefore, fire is a cause of modification rather than transformation. This ensures there is no overlap in our definitions. Furthermore, one should not think that the transformation of a substance is merely a change in how its parts are arranged; if that were true, the example of the "goldsmith" would not be appropriate.

Having explained how transformation works in the outer world, he illustrates the inner cause using this example: **"Similarly, if a single woman..."** 

Here, "Ignorance" <term>avidyā: a fundamental lack of spiritual awareness or "undifferentiated consciousness"</term> manifests as a thought like, ‘This woman is to be loved.’ Depending on the viewer, the very same idea of this woman changes:
*   In the case of a man named Chāitra <note>a traditional placeholder name, like "John Doe"</note>, his complete infatuation makes him dejected if he cannot have her. He says to himself, ‘Alas! That jewel of a woman belongs to that lucky man Māitra, and not to me, who is devoid of luck!’ 
*   Conversely, the hatred felt by a rival wife becomes the cause of pain associated with the idea of this woman. 
*   The passion felt by her husband, Māitra, is the cause of the pleasure found in the idea of her. 
*   Finally, for the wise person who recognizes reality—seeing that the body is merely a collection of skin, flesh, fat, bone, and marrow, and is impure in its origin and nature—this same woman becomes the cause for a detached attitude, also known as "passionlessness."

**9. The cause of sustentation.** This is the cause that maintains the body and its senses. In the case of the physical body, it is the organs that sustain it. The five vital breaths, starting with the "life-force" <term>Prāṇa: the primary vital energy or breath</term>, are the functions...

It highlights that the goal of these causes is to lead the practitioner toward spiritual discernment and the separation of the Self from material suffering.</summary>

# Eight aids to yoga [-ii. 29]

...of the organs in general. For if they were not, the body would fall. Similarly in the case of the parts of the body, the flesh and the other parts, there is the reciprocal relation of sustained and sustainer. Likewise the great elements, that is, the earth and the other elements; and these elements are in the reciprocal relation of sustained and sustainer in the case of bodies dwelling in the worlds of human beings or of Varuṇa <note>The Vedic deity of the celestial ocean and cosmic order</note> or of the Sun or of the Wind <note>original: *gandhavaha*, literally "the carrier of fragrance"</note> or of the Moon. 

Thus in the case of earth, which has the qualities <term>guṇa: the fundamental sensory attributes—here specifically smell, taste, color, touch, and sound</term> of odor and taste and color and touch and sound, there are five great elements standing in the reciprocal relation of sustained and sustainer; in the case of water there are four; in the case of fire three; in the case of wind two. <note>In this philosophical system, each denser element contains the qualities of the subtler elements above it.</note> 

Furthermore animal and human and divine bodies stand in a relation of sustained and sustainer. Some one asks, "How can this reciprocal relation of sustained and sustainer be so, if the bodies are not in the relation of holder and held?" He replies, "since human [bodies] . . . depend upon each other." For the human body is sustained by the use of the bodies of tame animals and of birds and of wild animals and of plants. Similarly bodies like the tigers' are sustained by the use of the human bodies and those of tame and wild animals and of others. And again in the same way the body of the tame animal and of the bird and of the wild animal is sustained by the use of plants and similar things. 

Likewise the divine body is sustained by the use of sacrifices—of goats and deer and the flesh of grouse and ghee and baked-rice-cakes¹ and branches of mango <note>original: *sahakāra*</note> and handfuls of sacred grass <note>original: *prastara*, likely Darbha grass used as a ritual seat or offering surface</note>—offered by human beings. In the same way the deity also sustains human beings and the rest by granting boons and showers. Thus the dependence is reciprocal. This is the meaning.—The rest is easy.

In this aphorism <note>original: *sūtra*</note> the aids to yoga are determined.

**29. Abstentions and observances and postures and regulations-of-the-breath and withdrawal-of-the-senses and fixed attention and contemplation and concentration are the eight aids.**

The following up of these must be performed in succession. And what they are we shall describe.

Now with the intent of excluding either a larger or a smaller number he determines what are the aids to yoga by saying "In this aphorism the aids to yoga are determined." The aphorism begins with the word **29. Abstentions** and ends with the word **aids**. Practice and passionlessness and belief and energy and the rest <note>Referring back to the requirements for spiritual growth mentioned in Book I, aphorism 20</note>, both by reason of their own selves and in so far as they are indispensable, are also properly to be included among these same.

<page-num>178</page-num>
<header>ii. 30—] Book II. Means of Attainment or <term>Sādhana: the disciplined practice toward a spiritual goal</term></header>

Of these [eight aids]—

**30. Abstinence from injury, abstinence from falsehood, abstinence from theft, abstinence from incontinence, and abstinence from the acceptance of gifts are the [five] abstentions.** <note>original: *yama*. These represent the universal ethical restraints required of a practitioner.</note>

Of these [five], abstinence from injury <note>original: *ahiṃsā*</note> means the absence of malice towards all living creatures in every way and at all times. All other abstentions and observances are rooted in this principle. Insofar as their aim is the perfection of non-injury, they are taught in order to refine it. And in this sense it has been said, “Surely this same seeker <note>original: *brahman*; here referring to one following the path of sacred knowledge</note> in proportion as he desires to take upon himself many courses of action, in this same proportion, by refraining from heedlessly giving injury, fulfills the abstention of non-injury in order to give it the full character of its spotlessness.” 

Abstinence from falsehood <note>original: *satya*</note> means speech and mind that correspond to the object intended; it is speech and mind corresponding to what has been seen, inferred, or heard. If speech is spoken so that one’s own knowledge may pass to someone else, it should not be deceitful, mistaken, or lacking in information; then it truly constitutes abstinence from falsehood. It should be used for the service of all, not for the ruin of creatures. And even when used thus, should it result only in the ruin of creatures, it would not be abstinence from falsehood; it would be nothing less than wrong. Insofar as there would be a false kind of merit and a mere resemblance of merit, it would become the worst of evils. Therefore, let the practitioner <note>original: *yogin*</note> consider first what is good for all creatures and then speak with truthfulness.

Theft is the unauthorized <note>original: *açāstrapūrvaka*; literally, "not preceded by the sacred scriptures"</note> appropriation of things of value from another. While abstinence from theft <note>original: *asteya*</note>, when free from coveting, is the refusal to do this.

Continence <note>original: *brahmacharya*</note> is the control of the hidden organ of generation.

Abstinence from the acceptance of gifts <note>original: *aparigraha*</note> is the abstinence from appropriating objects, because one sees the disadvantages in acquiring, [preserving, or losing them].

<header>Five abstentions [-ii. 30</header>

...ing them or keeping them or losing them or in being attached to them or in harming them. These then are the abstentions.

Having announced the aids [to <term>yoga: the practice of mental concentration and spiritual discipline</term>] of which the first are the abstentions and the observances, he introduces a <term>sūtra: a concise aphorism or rule</term> which specifies the abstentions by saying «of these [eight].» The <term>sūtra</term> begins with the words **30. Abstinence from injury** and ends with the word **abstentions.** He describes the aid to <term>yoga</term> [called] abstinence from injury by saying, «in every way.» He praises such abstinence-from-injury with the words, «And the other.» «Rooted in it» would mean that, even if these are performed without observing abstinence from injury, they are as if they had not been performed, since they are quite fruitless. This is the meaning. The following up of them has nothing as its aim but the perfection of this [abstinence-from-killing]. 'If abstinence-from-killing has the others rooted in it, how can it be that they aim at the perfection of the abstinence-from-injury?' To this he replies, «in order to teach it.» «Perfection» [in other words] the rise into consciousness of a thought. An objector asks, 'This may be true. But if the others exist for the sake of knowing abstinence from injury, what need of them, since this thought comes from the other source?' In reply he says, «its spotlessness.» If the others were not followed up, abstinence-from-injury would be defiled by falsehood and other [vices]. With reference to this same point he tells of a concurrent opinion of <term>āgamika: those who follow the sacred tradition</term> in the words, «And in this sense it has been said.» Easy.—He gives the distinguishing characteristic of abstinence-from-falsehood in the words, «speech and mind such as correspond to the object-intended.» The word such (<term>yathā: just as</term>) raises an expectation which is fulfilled by the words «corresponding to what is seen.» He brings this into connexion with the correlated word «corresponding-to (<term>tathā: in that way</term>)» in the expression «speech and mind corresponding to.» [This should be,] whenever there is a desire to say [something]. [If spoken] otherwise [than as seen], it is not abstinence-from-falsehood. This is stated with an explanation in the words «to some other person.» In order that knowledge thereof may pass to some one else, speech is spoken [or] uttered to produce knowledge similar to one's own knowledge. If it is not deceitful [or] the cause of deceit, [it is abstinence-from-falsehood]. 

Just as when Droṇa the Master [from the Great Epic of the Bharatas, Book vii. chapter 190] asked Yudhiṣṭhira [the king] with regard to the death of his own son Açvatthāman, 'Venerable sir (<term>āyuṣman: O long-lived one</term>), thou who art rich in truth, has Açvatthāman been slain?' And he having in mind the elephant who had the corresponding name said, 'It is true, Açvatthāman is slain.' This is an answer which does not make Yudhiṣṭhira's own knowledge pass to [the other person]. For his own knowledge derived from the sense-organ¹ had as its object the slaying of the elephant and this [knowledge] was not passed [to Droṇa]. But quite another knowledge, that of the slaying of the latter's son, was formed [in Droṇa's mind].—«Or mistaken» means due to a mistake, either

at the time when one desires to say something, or at the time of determining what the object-to-be-perceived is.—"Barren of information as regards information," as for instance an outlandish tongue <note>original: "mleccha," referring to non-Sanskrit languages or those outside the Vedic culture</note> is barren of information to <term>Aryans: the noble or cultured members of society</term>; or it might be purposeless, as for instance speech the utterance of which is not meant to be uttered. For in this [latter case], although one’s own knowledge does pass to the other person, still it is exactly the opposite of making [knowledge] pass [to another], because it was not purposed.¹ An <term>abstinence-from-falsehood: truthfulness or satya</term> even when it has these distinguishing characteristics, if it results in injury to another, would be a false kind of <term>abstinence-from-falsehood</term>, but would not be <term>abstinence-from-falsehood</term>, as he says in the words, "If it." For example, one who practises austerities in <term>abstinence-from-falsehood</term>, when asked by robbers which way the rich merchant had gone, told the way the rich merchant had gone. <note>This refers to the story of the ascetic Kaushika, who told the truth to bandits and was blamed for the merchant's death; in Yoga, truth must be coupled with non-injury.</note> "It should be used," that is, uttered. The rest is easy.—Since an [explanatory] negative idea depends on that of the positive he explains the distinguishing characteristic of <term>theft</term> by saying, "Theft is the unauthorized." Here the generic idea is characterized by a qualification. This is the meaning. Since verbal and bodily operations are preceded by mental operations, it is the operation of mind, because it is dominant, that is mentioned in the words, "free from coveting." He tells what <term>continence: brahmacarya, or self-restraint in sexual matters</term> is in the word "hidden." For even if his organ of generation is held in control, still if he become attached at the sight of a woman or upon [hearing] her talk or upon touching her limbs which are the seats of <term>Kandarpa: another name for Kamadeva, the god of desire and love</term>, he has no continence. So to exclude this case he says, "the hidden organ." Other organs also that are very ardent for this [woman] are to be watched.—He tells what <term>abstinence-from-acceptance-of-gifts: non-possessiveness or aparigraha</term> is by saying, "objects." He mentions the disadvantage due to attachment to these [objects] in the words [ii. 15], “Since passions increase because of application to enjoyments, and the skill of the organs also increases.” The disadvantage which is characteristic of <term>injury</term> is also expressed by the words,² “Enjoyment is impossible unless one has harmed some living creatures.” Although obtained without effort, objects if unauthorized have disadvantages when one acquires them, since the acquisition of such things is censured. And even authorized objects, when acquired, are evidently disadvantageous, in that they must be kept and so on. Therefore <term>abstinence-from-acceptance-of-gifts</term> is the refusal to appropriate them.

## Book II. Means of Attainment or Sādhana
### ii. 32—

...recital of books that treat of release or the repetition of the syllable of adoration (<term>praṇava: the sacred sound 'Om'</term>). — Devotion to the <term>Içvara: the Supreme Lord or Teacher</term>¹ is the offering up of all actions to the Supreme Teacher. “He who rests in himself, for whom the network of **perverse-considerations** (<term>vitarka: negative or distracting thoughts</term>) has been destroyed, whether resting upon a bed or on a seat, or wandering upon a road, would behold the destruction of the seed of the round-of-rebirths, would be permanently released, would participate in deathless delights.” With regard to which this has been said, [i. 29], “Thereafter comes the right knowledge of him who thinks in an inverse way, and the removal of obstacles.”

He expounds **cleanliness** and the other **observances**. The <term>sūtra: aphorism</term> begins with the word 32. **Cleanliness** and ends with the word **observances**. He explains [the sūtra] by saying «**cleanliness**.» The words «or the like» are meant to include cow-dung and such things <note>In ancient Indian ritual traditions, products of the cow were considered spiritually purifying agents for physical space</note>. Pure sacrificial food is the barley [mixed with] cow’s urine and the rest [eaten at the <term>Crāvaṇī festival: a ritual performed during the full moon of the month of Shravana</term>].² There is a consumption and other [requirements] with regard to this [food]. «The other requirements» are meant to cover regulation of the dimensions and of the number of these morsels. Instead of saying ‘produced by the consumption and other requirements with regard to pure sacrificial food’ he says «and by the consumption and other [requirements] with regard to pure sacrificial food.» For in the effect the cause is supposed figuratively to exist. — «The **stains** of the mind-stuff» such as arrogance and pride and jealousy; the removal of this is cleanliness of the central-organ <note>The 'central-organ' refers to the mind (manas) or the internal faculty of thought</note>. — «**Contentment**» is the desire to take no more than is necessary for the general maintenance of life, because it follows the renunciation of what had been before one’s own property. This is its distinction [from **abstinence-from-acceptance-of-gifts**]. — «**Stock-stillness**» is the absence of any indication of one’s intention even by signs; «**formal stillness**» is merely refraining from speech. — In the phrase «for whom the network of **perverse-considerations** has been destroyed» the words «**perverse-considerations**» will be [later ii. 33] described. And doubts and misconceptions should be added [as parts of the network]. To this extent his intention is said to be pure. — These **abstentions** and **observances** are also described in the <term>Viṣṇu Purāṇa: an ancient scripture dedicated to the god Vishnu</term> [vi. 7. 36-37].³ “Wishing to reduce the mind to its proper state he should resort to **abstinence** from **incontinence** and from injury and from falsehood and from theft and from **acceptance-of-gifts**. A man whose self is curbed should practise study and **cleanliness** and **contentment** and **self-castigation**. He should also make his mind incline towards the higher <term>Brahman: the ultimate reality or absolute</term>. These abstentions together with...

# Inhibition of abstentions and observances [ii. 34

the observances are declared to be five each. They give a special result when they are approached with a desire [for some special thing], and in the case of persons free from all desires they yield final release.”

As for these abstentions and observances,

**33. If there be inhibition by perverse-considerations (<term>vitarka: negative or distracting thoughts that run contrary to yoga</term>), there should be cultivation of the opposites.**

Whenever [in the mind] of this seeker <note>The original uses "brahman," referring here to a spiritual practitioner or one striving for holy knowledge</note> [practising the abstentions and observances] injuries and similar [faults] arise as perverse-considerations, such as for instance, ‘I will kill him who hurts me; I will also lie; I will also appropriate his money; and I will commit adultery with his wife; and I will also make myself master of his property.’ Thus inhibited by the blazing fever of perverse-considerations, let him cultivate the opposites of these. Let him ponder, ‘Baked upon the pitiless coals of the round-of-rebirths <note>The cycle of birth, death, and rebirth known as Saṃsāra</note>, I take my refuge in the rules (<term>dharma: the natural law or righteous path</term>) for yoga by giving protection <note>1 This phrase occurs in the Laws of Manu, book viii, verse 303.</note> to every living creature. I myself after ridding myself of perverse-considerations am betaking myself to them once more, like a dog. As a dog returns to his vomit, even so I betake myself to that of which I had rid myself.’ Other similar [inhibitions of perverse-considerations] should be applied in the other aphorisms also [upon the aids to yoga].

Since “good things <note>2 The original includes a Sanskrit quote from the play Çakuntala: "Oh, the fulfillment of desired objects is full of obstacles"; and a Greek quote from Plato's Republic: "Fine things are difficult."</note> are full of difficulties,” he introduces a sūtra <note>An aphorism or concise rule</note> whose object is to give advice which will prevent the possibility of exceptions to these [abstentions and observances]. So he says, “As for these abstentions and observances.” The sūtra, **33. If there be inhibition by perverse-considerations, there should be cultivation of the opposites.** In the Comment upon perverse-considerations there is nothing at all that seems obscure.

**34. Since perverse-considerations such as injuries, whether done or caused to be done or approved, whether ensuing upon greed or anger or infatuation, whether mild or moderate or vehement, find their unending consequences in pain and in lack of thinking, there should be the cultivation of their opposites.**

<summary>This page explains how to combat negative impulses (perverse-considerations) that hinder spiritual progress by consciously contemplating their opposites and recognizing the cyclical suffering they cause. It emphasizes that even approving of harm or acting out of mild greed carries lasting consequences of pain and ignorance.</summary>

# [ii. 34—] Book II. Means of Attainment or <term>Sādhana: the disciplined practice or means to achieve spiritual goals</term>

Of these considerations, first of all, injury—since it is done, caused to be done, or approved—is three-fold. Moreover, each of these is three-fold, depending on whether there is greed (such as desire for meat or skin), anger (as when a man thinks he has been ‘hurt by that man’), or infatuation (as when a man thinks that what he is doing ‘will be merit for me’). 

Again, since greed, anger, and infatuation are three-fold as being mild, moderate, or vehement, there are thus twenty-seven varieties of injuries. Yet again, since these are categorized as gentle, moderate, and extreme, they are three-fold as follows: gently mild, moderately mild, and keenly mild; similarly, gently moderate, moderately moderate, and keenly moderate; likewise, gently keen, moderately keen, and vehemently keen. <note>The text is using a mathematical grid to show how one negative impulse can manifest in 81 distinct intensities and types (3x3x3x3).</note> Thus, injury is of eighty-one varieties. 

It is, however, truly innumerable because of the varieties due to specifications (<term>niyama: restrictive rules</term>), options (<term>vikalpa: alternatives</term>), and aggregations (<term>samuccaya: combinations</term>), and due to the fact that the varieties of those-who-breath-the-breath-of-life <note>A poetic reference to all sentient beings</note> are themselves innumerable. 

In the same manner, this classification is to be applied to falsehood and to the other crimes. Now, since these perverse considerations have endless consequences in pain and in a lack of thinking, one should cultivate their opposites. In other words, there is a cultivation of those things the endless consequences of which are pain and a lack of thinking.

And to continue, he who commits an injury first of all reduces the strength of the victim, then causes him pain by falling upon him with a knife or something of the kind, and afterwards even deprives him of life. <note>This explains the three-fold karmic debt: loss of power, physical suffering, and loss of life.</note> When once he has taken away the victim’s strength, his own animate or inanimate aids <note>Original: "prāṇyaprāṇyupakaraṇāni" – referring to his tools, possessions, or helpers.</note> begin to have their strength dwindle away. As a result of causing pain, he himself experiences pain in hells and in the bodies of animals and of departed spirits and in other forms. As a result of uprooting the victim from life, he himself continues from moment to moment at the very point of departure from life. And even while wishing for death he...

With the intent to describe what the cultivation of the opposites is, he states the different natures and kinds and causes and properties and results of the contrary-considerations, as well as the objects for the meditation on the opposites in the aphorism which begins with the words **34. . . . perverse-considerations** and ends with the words **cultivation of their opposites.** He explains [the aphorism] with the words, "Of these . . . injury." So it is that these perverse-considerations also result in lack of thinking [as well as arise out of undifferentiated-consciousness]. For the cultivation of their opposites is precisely [the thought of] the endless consequences in pain and in lack of thinking. By virtue of this there is a revulsion from these. This same cultivation of the opposites he makes clear by the words, "of the victim." The victim is some tame animal. "Strength" is the energy which is the cause of the functional activity of the body. [This] he first reduces by tying him to a sacrificial post. For in this way the animal loses his spirit. The rest is very clear.

<header>ii. 35—] Book II. Means of Attainment or Spiritual Practice <note>original: *Sādhana*</note></header>

## 35. As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from injury, his presence begets a suspension of enmity.

[This] occurs on the part of all living creatures.¹

The abstentions and observances have been described, and the escape from the exceptions to these—the perverse considerations—as a result of the cultivation of the opposites has been described. Now he makes clear the signs indicative of thorough knowledge of perfection <note>original: *siddhi*</note> in these various abstentions and observances which results from practice in these [latter]. By a thorough knowledge of which signs [the <term>yogin</term> — a practitioner of yoga] accomplishes what is to be done in each particular case and acts with reference to what is yet to be done, as he says, «When . . . for this [<term>yogin</term>].» **35. As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from injury, his presence begets a suspension of enmity.** Even [enemies] whose hostility is everlasting² like horse and buffalo, mouse and cat, snake and mongoose, in the presence of the Exalted [<term>yogin</term>] who is grounded in abstinence from injury <note>original: *ahimsā*, the practice of non-violence</note>, conform themselves to his mind-stuff <note>original: *citta*, the mental or conscious field</note> and renounce altogether their hostility.

## 36. As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from falsehood, actions and consequences depend upon him.

If [the <term>yogin</term>] says to a man, ‘Be thou right-living <note>original: *dhārmika*, following the path of virtue</note>,’ the man becomes right-living. If he expresses the wish ‘Attain thou heaven,’ the man attains heaven. What he says <note>original: *vāk*, his speech or word</note> comes true. **36. As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from falsehood, actions and consequences have their residence [in him].** Actions mean right-living and wrong-living <note>original: *dharma* and *adharma*</note>; and consequences of these are such things as heaven and hell. Dependence upon the sense that these same depend upon him. Having dependence upon him is the abstract state of this [dependence]. Since such a thing happens in the case of the Exalted One's speech, [the Comment] says that actions depend upon him by saying «right-living.» He says that consequences depend upon him by saying «heaven.» «Comes true» signifies that it is not prevented <note>The yogi's word becomes an unfailing creative force</note>.

## 37. As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from theft, all jewels approach him.

From all directions jewels approach to be his.

**37. As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from theft, all jewels approach him.** Easily understood.

## 38. As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from incontinence, he acquires energy.

By the acquisition of which the <term>yogin</term> <note>a practitioner of yoga</note> increases [his] unhindered$^1$ qualities. And when he is perfected he is able to transfer [his] thinking to [his] pupils.

**38. As soon as he is grounded in abstinence from incontinence <note>original: *brahmacharya*, often translated as celibacy or containment of vital energy</note>, he acquires energy.** Energy [that is] power. By the acquisition of which he increases [or] accumulates qualities, such as minuteness <note>the mystical power to become as small as an atom</note>, which are unhindered [that is] which have not been blocked. And when perfected he is endowed with the eight perfections of which the first is called <term>Crossing</term>$^2$ <note>original: *tāra*</note> and also by other names such as <term>Reasoning</term> <note>original: *ūha*</note>. He is able to transfer his thinking which relates to the aids to <term>yoga</term> to his pupils [or] disciples.

## 39. As soon as he is established in abstinence-from-acceptance-of-gifts, a thorough illumination upon the conditions of birth—

—Becomes his. ‘Who was I? How was I? Or what [can] this birth be? Or how [can] this [birth] be? Or what shall we become? Or how shall we become?’ Such a desire to know his own condition in former and later and intermediate times becomes of itself fulfilled$^3$ for him. These when he is established in the abstentions are the perfections.

**39. As soon as he is established in abstinence-from-acceptance-of-gifts <note>original: *aparigraha*, the practice of non-possessiveness or non-greed</note>, a thorough illumination upon the conditions of birth.** Birth is [coming into] relation with a body and with sense-organs and the rest which are particularized as belonging to some class [of beings]. There is a thorough illumination, a direct perception of the conditions [of birth] [or] of what kinds [of birth]. That is to say, a thorough knowledge of a quiescent <note>past</note> or uprisen <note>present</note> or indeterminable <note>future</note> birth together with its form [of experience]. He desires to know the past in the words, «‘Who was I?’» He desires to know the different details as to origin and persistence of this same [birth] in the words, «‘How was I?’» He desires to know what the present birth itself is in the words, «‘Or what?’» Is the body made directly of elements, or is it nothing but an aggregation of elements, or is it other than these? Here also the words ‘Or how’ might be supplied.$^4$ Elsewhere this is the actual reading. He desires to know the future in the words, «‘Or what shall we become?’» Here again the words ‘Or how’ are [to be] supplied.$^4$ «Such ... for him.» The former [time] is past time;

The later state is the future; the intermediate state is the present. The existence of the self in these states is defined by its relationship with a physical body and other material things. There is a natural desire to know this, and from that desire comes knowledge, following the ancient maxim: "Whatever a person desires, that same thing they act upon."

We will now speak regarding the observances <note>original: *niyama*, the second limb of yoga consisting of five personal disciplines</note>.

### 40. As a result of cleanliness, there is disgust at one’s own body and a lack of desire for intercourse with others.

As soon as a practitioner feels a sense of disgust with their own body, they have truly begun the practice of <term>cleanliness</term> <note>original: *śauca*, which includes both external hygiene and internal purity</note>. Seeing the naturally offensive nature of the physical body,<note>¹ Compare this to the earlier discussion in Book II, Sutra 5.</note> the practitioner is no longer attached to it and becomes an <term>ascetic</term> <note>original: *yati*, a person who has restrained their worldly impulses</note>. Furthermore, there is no longer a desire for physical intercourse with others. Once the practitioner perceives the true, decaying nature of the body—and is eager to escape<note>² Referencing the *Linga Purana*, a traditional text of ancient Indian lore, book 8, verses 32-33.</note> even their own physical form despite washing it with earth, water, and other purifying substances—how could they seek intimacy with the bodies of others, which are entirely unhallowed?

**40. As a result of cleanliness, there is disgust at one’s own body and no intercourse with others.** By this <term>sūtra</term> <note>an aphorism or concise rule</note>, we are told the signs of reaching perfection in external cleanliness.

---

Furthermore, as other results:

### 41. Purity of the mind’s essence, gentleness, singleness of intent, subjugation of the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self arise.

The word "arise" completes the meaning of the sentence. As a result of internal cleanliness, there is a purification of the <term>sattva</term> <note>the quality of the mind that is clear, light, and luminous</note>; from that purity comes a gentle and pleasant disposition; from gentleness comes "singleness of intent" or total focus; from focus comes the mastery and subjugation of the senses; and from this mastery, the <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>original: *chitta-sattva*, the thinking substance of the individual</note> becomes fit and ready to actually see the true Self. Thus, the practitioner gains access to this ultimate vision as a result of being firmly established in cleanliness.

The author describes the signs of inner perfection by saying "Furthermore." **41. Purity of essence, gentleness, singleness of intent, subjugation of the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self.** When the defilements of...

<page-num>189</page-num>
<header>Results of observances [—ii. 43]</header>

The impurities of the <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>original: *citta*, the collective layers of consciousness</note> are washed away, and the mind-stuff appears undefiled. As a result of this freedom from defilement, there arises a gentleness and transparency of <term>lucidity</term> <note>original: *sattva*, the quality of light, harmony, and goodness</note>. From this transparent state, the mind gains a single-minded focus. Through the subdual of the <term>central-organ</term> <note>original: *manas*, the coordinating mind</note>, the practitioner gains control over the sense-organs which depend upon it. After this, the lucidity of the thinking-substance becomes fit to behold the true self.

### 42. As a result of contentment, one acquires superlative pleasure.

And in this sense it has been said,<note>¹ Quoted from the *Mahabharata* (Peace Parvan 174. 46) and the *Vayu* and *Linga Puranas*.</note> “The pleasure of love in this world and the supreme pleasure of heaven are not worth even a sixteenth part of the pleasure found when <term>craving</term> <note>original: *tr̥ṣṇā*, the unquenchable thirst for worldly experience</note> has dwindled away.”

**42. As a result of contentment, one acquires superlative pleasure.** "Superlative" refers to a state beyond which nothing more excellent exists. This was echoed by King Yayāti<note>² Referring to a famous legend in the *Vishnu Purana* and *Mahabharata* where the king traded his old age for his son Puru's youth, only to realize that desire is never satisfied by indulgence.</note> when he returned his borrowed youth to his son Puru: “The wise man, casting away that craving which is so hard for the strong-willed to abandon—and which does not age even as the body grows old—is filled completely with pleasure and nothing else.” He illustrates this same point with the verse beginning with the words, "What constitutes the pleasure of love..."

### 43. Mastery over the body and the senses is achieved as impurity dwindles through self-discipline.

<term>Self-discipline</term> <note>original: *tapas*, literally "heat," referring to spiritual austerities and ascetic practices</note>, as it reaches completion, destroys the stains caused by the veil of impurity. Once this covering of impurity is removed, the body attains perfections, such as <term>atomization</term> <note>original: *animan*, the yogic power to become as small as an atom; see Book III, Sutra 45</note>. Likewise, the senses reach perfection, such as the ability to hear or see at a great distance.

The author now explains what indicates the perfection of self-discipline: **43. Mastery over the body and the senses is achieved as impurity dwindles through self-discipline.** Whatever veil has the characteristics of impurity is made of the qualities of <term>inertia</term> <note>original: *tamas*, the quality of darkness and heaviness</note> and its effects. The "perfections of the body" like "atomization" also include powers like becoming infinitely large, or weightless, or the ability to reach any place instantly. This is straightforward.

<header>ii. 44—] Book II. Means of Attainment or <term>Practice</term> <note>original: Sādhana</note></header>

### 44. As a result of study there is communion with the chosen deity.

Divine beings, ancient sages, and those who have reached spiritual perfection come within the physical or mental vision of the practitioner who is dedicated to <term>sacred study</term> <note>original: *svādhyāya*, the recitation of mantras or the study of scriptures</note>; these beings then become helpful to the practitioner’s spiritual work.

The author now explains what indicates that one has mastered this study. **44. As a result of study there is communion with the chosen deity. The meaning is clear.**

---

### 45. Perfection of concentration as a result of devotion to the Lord.

A practitioner whose entire nature is surrendered <gloss>1</gloss> to <term>the Lord</term> <note>original: *Īśvara*, the supreme soul or divine teacher</note> achieves perfection in <term>concentration</term> <note>original: *samādhi*, the state of deep meditative absorption</note>. Through this concentration, the practitioner knows all things as they truly are <note>original: *avitatham*, without error or falsehood</note>, even those things existing in distant places, within other bodies, or in different periods of time. From that point on, the practitioner's inner insight perceives the world exactly <term>as it is</term> <note>original: *yathābhūtam*</note>.

**45. Perfection of concentration... resulting from devotion to the Lord.** One might argue that if devotion to the Lord alone is enough to perfect <term>objective concentration</term> <note>original: *samprajñāta samādhi*, concentration where the mind still holds onto a specific object or idea</note>, then there is no need for the other seven limbs of yoga. This is incorrect. These seven limbs, through their supporting influence—both in ways we can observe and through subtle spiritual effects—serve to perfect one's devotion to the Lord, and simultaneously perfect the state of objective concentration. 

Consider the analogy of curds used in a ritual <gloss>2</gloss>: the curds serve the requirements of the religious sacrifice while also fulfilling the personal nutritional needs of the people involved. In the same way, <term>focused attention</term> <note>original: *dhāraṇā*</note>, <term>meditation</term> <note>original: *dhyāna*</note>, and <term>absorption</term> <note>original: *samādhi*</note> are the <term>internal aids</term> <gloss>3</gloss> <note>original: *antaraṅga*, literally "inner-limbs"</note> to yoga. These three are considered "internal" or immediate because they share the same focus as the concentration itself. Devotion to the Lord, however, is a <term>mediate aid</term> because its primary object is the Lord, rather than the specific object chosen for meditative knowledge. Thus, the relationship between these practices is clear. Finally, the words "sees into" are used here to explain the literal root and meaning of the word "insight."

---

3. The commentator Balarama defines an <term>internal aid</term> as "whatever happens immediately before a result." In this context, while devotion to the Lord is a powerful cause, it is the final three limbs—focus, meditation, and absorption—that are the direct, immediate components of the meditative state.

<header>Varieties of postures [--ii. 46</header>

The abstentions and observances together with their perfections have been described. We have the following to say of the postures <note>original: *āsana*</note>¹ and the other [aids to yoga]. In this [sūtra <note>a concise rule or aphorism</note>, it is said]—

### 46. Stable-and-easy posture.

For example, the lotus-posture <note>original: *padmāsana*</note> and the hero-posture <note>original: *vīrāsana*</note> and the decent-posture <note>original: *bhadrāsana*</note> and the mystic-diagram <note>original: *svastikāsana*</note> and the staff-posture <note>original: *daṇḍāsana*</note> and [the posture] with the rest and the bedstead, the seated curlew and the seated elephant and the seated camel, the even arrangement, the stable-and-easy—also called, as-is-easiest—and others of the same kind.

He introduces the next sūtra with the words <<The abstentions and observances have been described. We have the following to say of the postures and the other [aids to yoga].>> In this [sūtra, it is said] **46. Stable-and-easy posture.**

Stable means motionless. That posture which is easy, which brings ease is the one intended by the sūtra. The word <term>āsana</term> <note>posture or seat</note> means either that whereon a man sits [that is, a seat] or the manner in which he sits [that is, a posture].

The lotus-posture is well known.²—A man settled down <gloss>sthitasya</gloss> rests one foot on the ground and the other is placed over the partially contracted knee, —this is hero-posture.—Bringing the soles of his feet near to each other close to the scrotum, he should make a hollow of his hands and place them over it in the shape of a tortoise,—this is the decent-posture.—Inserting the contracted left foot into the space between the right shin and thigh and inserting the contracted right foot into the space between the left shin and thigh,—that is the mystic diagram <note>the *svastika* posture, named after the ancient symbol of well-being</note>.—Sitting down with the great-toes placed together and with ankles placed together and stretching out upon the ground shins and thighs and feet placed together, let him practise the staff-posture.—Because there is a use of the <term>yogic table</term> <note>original: *yoga-paṭṭaka*, a support or strap used to hold the limbs in place during long meditation</note>³, this is [the posture] with the rest.—Lying down with the arms stretched around the knees is the bedstead.—The curlew and the other seats may be understood by actually seeing a curlew and the other animals seated. — The two feet are contracted and pressed against each other at the heels and at the tips of

### 47. By relaxation of effort or by a state of mental balance with reference to the Infinite—

—[A posture] results. With these words the sentence is completed. When efforts cease, the posture is completed, so that there is no agitation of the body. Or the mind-stuff <note>the collective conscious and subconscious mind</note> comes into a balanced state with reference to <term>Ananta</term>¹ <note>The Infinite One; the celestial serpent who supports the world</note> and produces the posture.

Having stated what the postures are, he tells what are the means of attaining them. **47. By relaxation of effort or by a state of mental balance with reference to the Infinite.** A natural effort sustaining the body is not the cause of this kind of posture which is to be taught as an aid to <term>yoga</term> <note>the discipline of joining the individual soul with the divine</note>. For if its causes were such, the preaching of it would be purposeless in that it could be naturally perfected. Therefore, this natural effort does not accomplish this kind of posture which is to be taught and is contrary [to it]. For in so far as this natural posture is the cause of an arbitrarily chosen posture, it is the destroyer of the specific kind of posture. Consequently, a man, practicing the specific posture as taught, should resort to an effort which consists in the relaxation of the natural effort. Otherwise, the posture taught cannot be accomplished.—"Or . . . with the **Infinite**," the Chief of Serpents, who upholds the globe of the earth upon his thousand very steadfast hoods,—[with him] the mind-stuff comes into a balanced state and produces the posture.

---

### 48. Thereafter he is unassailed by extremes.

As a result of mastering the postures, he is not overcome by the extremes, by cold and heat and by the other extremes <note>referring to dualities like pleasure and pain or hunger and thirst</note>.

He tells what is indicative of complete mastery of postures by saying **48. Thereafter he is unassailed by extremes.** The Comment explains itself by a mere reading. Posture is also described in the <term>Vishṇu Purāṇa</term> <note>an ancient scripture regarding the god Vishnu; vi. 7. 39</note>: “Having assumed a posture so as to possess the excellences of the decent-posture and the other [postures].”

<header>Varieties of restraint of breath —ii. 50</header>

**49. When there is this [stability of posture], the restraint of breath cutting off the flow of inspiration and expiration [follows].**

After the mastery <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: *jaye*</note> of posture [follows the restraint of the breath]. Inspiration is the sipping in of the outer wind; expiration is the expulsion of the abdominal wind. Restraint of the breath <note>original: *prāṇāyāma*</note> is the cutting off the flow of these two, the absence of both kinds.

After describing [postures], he shows that these precede restraint of the breath and tells the distinguishing characteristic of this [restraint of the breath].
**49. When there is this [stability of posture], the restraint of breath cutting off the flow of inspiration and expiration [follows].** In the case of emission <note>original: *recaka*</note> and inhalation <note>original: *pūraka*</note> and suspension <note>original: *kumbhaka*</note>, the words "the cutting off of the flow of inspiration and expiration" give the general characteristic of restraint of the breath. To explain: when in inhalation the outer wind sipped in is held inside, there is a break in the flow of inspiration and expiration; again when in emission the abdominal wind forced out is held outside, there is also a break in the flow of inspiration and expiration. Similarly in the case of suspension also. This same is said by the Comment in the words "After the subjugation of posture."

But this [restraint of breath] is,
**50. External or internal or suppressed in fluctuation and is regulated <gloss>2</gloss> in place and time and number and is protracted and subtile.**

It is external in case there is no flow [of breath] after expiration; it is internal in case there is no flow [of breath] after inspiration; it is the third [or] suppressed in fluctuation <note>original: *stambha-vṛtti*</note> in case there is no [flow] of either kind [neither of expiration nor inspiration], as the result of a single effort [to suppress both], just as water dropped upon a very-hot stone shrivels up wherever it falls, so both at once cease to be. And each of these three is regulated in space; [each] deals with a certain amount of space. [Each] is regulated in time; in other words, defined by a limitation to a certain number of moments. [Each] is regulated in number; the first rising up [of the vital current from the navel to the palate is measured] by so

...many inspirations and expirations. In the same manner, the second rising up of the checked [vital current] is measured by so many inspirations and expirations. Likewise the third. Similarly it is gentle [in method]; similarly it is moderate; similarly it is keen. Thus it is regulated by number. So then, practiced in these ways, [the breath] becomes protracted and subtile.

He introduces the <term>sūtra</term> <note>original: "sūtra"; a concise rule or aphorism in Sanskrit literature</note> which gives the characteristics of the three particular restraints of the breath by saying, "But this." He refers to exhalation (<term>recaka</term> <note>original: "recaka"</note>) when he says "In case . . . expiration." He refers to inhalation (<term>pūraka</term> <note>original: "pūraka"</note>) when he says "In case . . . inspiration." When by only one effort of retention there results an absence of both inspiration and expiration, and when there is not, as before, an effort to prolong a long stream of efforts of emission; but, on the other hand, just as water thrown upon a very-hot stone dries altogether and shrivels up wherever it falls, so this wind, whose nature it is to flow, when its action is restricted by a mighty effort of retention, becomes subtilized and remains in the body. [Suspension] does not inhale and so is not inhalation; does not emit and so is not emission. 

The words "deals with a certain amount of space" means as measured by a span <note>The space between the outstretched tips of the thumb and the forefinger</note>, by a <term>vitasti</term> <note>original: "vitasti"; the distance from the extended thumb to the tip of the little finger</note>, or by a hand. And it is inferred as being external [in so far as it causes] motion in a blade of grass or a piece of cotton in a windless spot. Similarly if internal, it begins at the sole of the foot and extends to the head. And it is inferred by [an internal] touch light as that of an ant [moving on the body]. 

A moment is one quarter of the time required for the act of winking. [The wind] is defined by the limitation of a certain number of these [moments]. An instant (<term>mātrā</term> <note>original: "mātrā"</note>) is the time limited by snapping thumb and forefinger after having three times rubbed one’s own knee-pan with the hand. The first rising up (<term>udghāta</term> <note>original: "udghāta"</note>) measured by thirty-six such instants is called slow. The same [<term>udghāta</term>] when doubled is moderate. The same tripled, called the third, is keen. This same restraint of the breath he describes as being regulated by number in the words "by number." The time for snapping thumb and forefinger as described is equal to the time defined by the action of inhalation and exhalation of a man in good health.¹ The rising up² which has been made the object of the action of the first rising-up is conquered [and] mastered [and] checked. repressed fluctuation also there is no flow of either. What then is [its] distinction
from this [fourth]?’ In reply he says, «the third.» The third does
not follow after any regard paid to [objects] and is completed by a single effort.

### 52. As a result of this the covering of the light dwindles away.

In the case of the <term>yogin</term> <note>a practitioner of yoga</note> who is practising restraints of breath <note>original: "prāṇāyāma"</note>, the <term>karma</term> <note>the accumulated effects of past actions</note> capable of covering discriminative thinking dwindles away. What this is they tell in the words, "Having covered the <term>sattva</term> <note>original: "sattva"; the quality of purity, light, and harmony within the mind</note> which is disposed to light with delusion <note>original: "indrajāla"; literally "Indra's net," a metaphor for magic or illusion</note> made of infatuation, [undifferentiated-consciousness] assigns the same [obscured form] to deeds which are not to be done." Therefore by practising restraint of breath his karma which covers the light, together with its bondage to the round-of-rebirth <note>original: "saṃsāra"</note>, becomes powerless. And from moment to moment it dwindles away. And in this sense it has been said "There is no self-castigation <note>original: "tapas"; spiritual discipline or heat</note> higher than restraint of breath; from it comes purity from defilement and the clear shining of thought."

<margin>He describes the subsidiary purpose [served by] restraint of breath. **52. As a result of this the covering of the light dwindles away.** The covering is that by which the purity <note>original: "sattva"</note> of the thinking-substance is covered, in other words, hindrances and evil. He explains [the aphorism] in the words "restraints of breath." Thinking <note>original: "jñāna"</note> is that by which anything is thought. It is the light of the purity of the thinking-substance. Discriminative thinking is the thinking of discrimination <note>the ability to distinguish the true self from the material world</note>. For this [hindrance], since it covers discriminative thinking, is called the coverer <note>original: "āvaraṇīya"</note> according [to the rules of the grammarian Pāṇini iii. 4. 68 which says that] "what is to be" <note>original: "bhavya"</note> and "what is to be sung" <note>original: "geya"</note> and "what is to be inclined" <note>original: "pravaṇīya"</note> and similar forms have been shown to be used as exceptional forms in the sense of an active agent, just as for instance the words "tending to anger" <note>original: "kopanīya"</note> and "tending to passion" <note>original: "rañjanīya"</note>. So here also the grammatical ending of the future passive participle is used to denote the agent <note>meaning the "covering" is an active force that hides the light</note>. The word "karma" connotes the merit which results from it and the hindrance which is the cause of it. On this same point he states that there is a concurrence of opinion with those who have the tradition <note>original: "āgamin"; those who follow sacred revealed texts</note> in the words "What this is they tell." Extreme infatuation is passion. Undifferentiated-consciousness <note>original: "avidyā"; spiritual ignorance</note> too, which is inseparable from it, is also to be understood by this word. A deed "not to be done" is wrong-living. An objector asks, 'If restraint of the breath causes evil to dwindle, what need is there of self-castigation?' In reply to this he says "becomes powerless." It does not dwindle away entirely. Therefore to make it dwindle away altogether self-castigation is needed. On this point also he states that there is a concurrence of opinion with those who have the tradition by saying "And in this</margin>

<page-num>197</page-num>
<header>Fixed attention and withdrawal of the senses [--ii. 54</header>

...sense it has been said. Manu <note>an ancient lawgiver and sage in Hindu tradition</note> also [vi. 72] says,
> “By restraints of breath one should burn up defects.”

And that restraint of breath is also an aid to yoga is also stated by the Vishnu Purāṇa <note>one of the eighteen major Hindu religious texts</note> [vi. 7. 40-1], 
> “But restraint of breath which masters by practice the wind called breath is to be recognized as being seeded and as seedless. When the two winds, breath (*<term>prāṇa</term>*) <note>the vital life-force or inhalation</note> and out-breath (*<term>apāna</term>*) <note>the downward-moving breath or exhalation</note> have overcome each other, that is two-fold. The third is the result of a subdual of these two.”

Furthermore,

### 53. For fixed attentions also the central organ becomes fit. 

Merely in consequence of practice in restraint of breath [the central organ becomes fit for fixed attentions] in accordance with the statement [i. 34], 
> “Or [he gains stability] by expulsion and retention of breath.”

Furthermore, **53. For fixed attentions also the central organ becomes fit.** For restraint of breath steadies the central organ <note>original: "manas"; the mind acting as a coordinating sense organ</note> and makes it fit for fixed attentions <note>original: "dhāraṇā"; the practice of holding the mind to a single point or object</note>.

Now what is the withdrawal of the senses?

### 54. The withdrawal of the senses is as it were the imitation of the mind-stuff itself on the part of the organs by disjoining themselves from their objects.

When there is no conjunction with their own objects <note>such as sights, sounds, or smells</note>, the organs in imitation of the mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the collective mental functions of intellect, ego, and memory</note>, as it is in itself, become, as it were, restricted. When the mind-stuff is restricted, like the mind-stuff they become restricted; and do not, like the subjugation of the senses <note>ordinary efforts to control desires</note>, require any further aid. 

Just as when the king-bee <note>While the text says "king-bee," modern readers would recognize this as the "queen-bee." This metaphor is also found in the Praçna Upanishad.</note> flies up, the bees fly up after him; and when he settles down, they settle down after him. So when the mind-stuff is restricted, the organs are restricted. This then is the withdrawal of the senses <note>original: "pratyāhāra"; the fifth stage of yoga where the senses are retracted from the world</note>. 

The <term>yogin</term> <note>a practitioner of yoga</note> being refined in this way by means of abstentions and other [aids], begins, for the sake [of attaining] constraint <note>original: "saṃyama"; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and absorption</note>, the withdrawal of the senses. This is what is called the imitation of the mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the collective functions of the mind including memory, ego, and intellect</note> by the senses. Because, as the mind-stuff settles down upon an entity <note>an object of focus or meditation</note>, the organs of this [mind-stuff] cannot be said to imitate the mind, since their object is always external,—therefore he says "in imitation . . . as it were." And the motive for this is shown in the same place [vi. 7. 44],

> "In the case of men who have become motionless, the result of that [withdrawal] is perfect mastery of the organs. A yogin with unmastered [organs] cannot accomplish yoga."

### 55. As a result of this [withdrawal] there is complete mastery of the organs.

There are some who think 1. that the mastery of the organs is a lack of desire for the various things sounds and so forth. Longing (*<term>vyasana</term>*) <note>often translated as "addiction" or "vice"</note> is attachment in the sense that it puts him a long way from (*vy-asyati*) a good <note>the author is providing a word-play or etymology: 'vy-asyati' means 'to throw away' or 'cast aside' one's own well-being</note>. 2. [Others think that] unforbidden experience is legitimate <note>the view that mastery is simply avoiding what is prohibited by scripture while enjoying the rest</note>. 3. Others, that there may be conjunction [of the organs] with the [various things] sounds and so forth as one desires <note>the view that mastery is the power to use the senses whenever one wishes without being compelled by them</note>. 4. Others think that there is a subjugation of the senses when there is no passion or aversion after the thinking of the various things is without pleasure or pain. 5. Jāigīṣavya <note>a legendary ancient sage and master of Yoga</note> thinks that it is refusal to perceive [the various things beginning with sound] as a result of the mind-stuff's singleness-of-intent. And as a result of this, when [the yogin's] mind-stuff is restricted, the organs are restricted, [and] there is not as in the case of the subjugation of the other organs, any further need of

<header>Complete mastery of the organs [-ii. 55</header>

means performed with effort. But this mastery which is this singleness-of-intent <note>the state of one-pointed concentration</note> is the complete [mastery].

The sutra is explanatory of this [mastery]. **55. As a result of this [withdrawal] there is complete mastery of the organs.** An objector asks, ‘Are there other and incomplete masteries in comparison with which this may be called complete?’ Undoubtedly, [he says in reply]. He shows what these are in the words «the various things beginning with sound.» <note>This refers to the five objects of the senses: sound, touch, sight, taste, and smell.</note> He elaborates the same by saying «desire.» Desire is passion, attachment. According to what derivation? It is that which rejects him [or] throws him away from a good. When there is none of this, there is absence of desire, in other words, mastery. 2. He describes yet another [incomplete] mastery in the words «unforbidden.» That devotion to things which is not forbidden by the Sacred Word <note>The Vedas or scriptural authorities</note> and other [authorities], and the absence of sense activity with regard to those things which are forbidden by these. Such is legitimate because it does not depart from the law. 3. He describes yet another [incomplete] mastery in the words «contact [of the senses] with the [various things] beginning with sound.» Contact of the organs with the [various things], sounds and so forth, as one desires. The meaning is that with regard to matters of enjoyment he is independent and not dependent on enjoyment. 4. He describes yet another [incomplete] mastery in the words, «no passion and no hatred.» Some say that it is a thinking without pleasure or pain, of the [various things], sounds and so forth, by a detached observer. 5. He describes that mastery which is approved by the author of the sūtras and is also approved by the Supreme Sage, as he says, «as a result of the mind-stuff’s singleness-of-intent.» <term>Jaigiṣavya</term> <note>A legendary ancient sage renowned for his total mastery of Yoga</note> says that when the mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the collective mental functions</note> together with the organs is single-in-intent, there is no sense-activity with regard to [various things] beginning with sound. The [commentator] says that this is the complete mastery in the words, «But . . . the complete.» The word «but» distinguishes it from other masteries. For the other masteries, in so far as they are in contact with the <term>poisonous snake</term>¹ (<term>āçīviṣa</term>) of <term>objects-of-sense</term> (<term>viṣaya</term>), do not escape the possibility of contact with the poison of the hindrances. For even a man who knows the lore of poisons and who is a perfect master of serpents does not take a serpent on his lap and quietly go to sleep. This mastery, on the other hand, from which all intermixture with objects has been removed, since [in it] there is no distrust, is called complete, as he says, «not as in the case of the subjugation of the other organs.» Although, in the case of consciousness of endeavour [ii. 15], when one organ is subdued there is still need of another effort to conquer the other organs, yet, when the mind-stuff is restricted, there is no such need of further exertion in order to restrict the other senses. This is the meaning.

<header>ON THE NECESSITY OF REVELATION</header>

# ON THE SUPERNATURAL
## FIRST PART

---

### ON THE NECESSITY OF REVELATION

<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas], *Summa Theologiae* Part I, Question 1, Article 1.</margin>
I. **Concerning the necessity of revelation regarding supernatural truths.** — Since the ultimate end <note>original: "finis ultimus"; the final goal or purpose of human life</note> of man is supernatural—that is, placed beyond every capacity of created nature—it was necessary for the truths required to attain this end, which entirely surpass human reason, to be manifested to man through divine revelation. This can be demonstrated by several reasons:

1. *From the nature of the object.* Supernatural truths, as they are in themselves, cannot be known by human reason alone because they belong to a higher order. Just as the sense of sight cannot perceive sounds, so natural reason cannot perceive those things which are above nature unless it is divinely enlightened.

2. *From the nature of the goal.* Since man is directed toward a supernatural goal, it is necessary that he knows the means leading to that goal. However, these means (such as <term>grace</term> <note>divine help for salvation</note>, the <term>sacraments</term>, and the <term>mysteries</term> <note>truths that cannot be fully understood by reason alone, such as the Trinity</note>) are supernatural; therefore, they had to be revealed.

<margin>First Vatican Council, session III, chapter 2. (Denzinger 1786).</margin>
II. **Concerning the necessity of revelation regarding natural truths.** — Here the question is whether revelation is necessary even for those truths which are accessible to human reason by themselves, such as the existence of God, the immortality of the soul, etc.

A distinction must be made between *absolute* and *moral* necessity.

1. *Absolute necessity* does not exist. For human reason, by its own natural powers, is able to arrive at the knowledge of God the Creator through the things that have been made.

2. *Moral necessity*, however, must be admitted. In the present condition of the human race <note>referring to the state of "fallen nature" after original sin</note>, it was necessary that religious and moral truths—which are not inherently inaccessible to reason—could be known by everyone with ease, with firm certainty, and with no mixture of error.

<margin>Vatican I, ibid.</margin>
> "It is to be attributed to this divine revelation that those things in divine matters which are not inherently inaccessible to human reason can, even in the present condition of the human race, be known by everyone with ease, with firm certainty, and with no mixture of error." <note>original: "Huic divinae revelationi tribuendum est..."</note>

<vocab>On the Supernatural, Revelation, Supernatural truths, Natural truths, Absolute necessity, Moral necessity, St. Thomas Aquinas, First Vatican Council, Denzinger</vocab>

# BOOK THIRD
## SUPERNORMAL POWERS

The five indirect aids <note>The five external limbs of Yoga described in Book 2: restraints, observances, posture, breath control, and withdrawal of the senses.</note> [to yoga] have been described. Fixed-attention <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "dhāraṇā"</note> is [now] to be described.

**1. Binding the mind-stuff to a place is fixed-attention.**
Binding of the mind-stuff, only in so far as it is a fluctuation <note>referring to the active thoughts or "waves" of the mind</note>, to the navel or to the heart-lotus or to the light within the head or to the tip of the nose or to the tip of the tongue or to other <gloss>2</gloss> places of the same kind or to an external object,—this is fixed-attention.

The First and Second Books described Concentration and the means thereto. In the Third Book the supernormal powers <note>the "siddhis" or extraordinary abilities gained through practice</note> are to be described which are reasons for propagation of belief and which are favourable to this [concentration and its means]. These supernormal powers are to be accomplished by <term>constraints</term> <note>original: "saṁyama"; the combined practice of fixed-attention, contemplation, and concentration</note>. And constraint is the combination of fixed-attention and of contemplation and of concentration. So inasmuch as these [three] are the means of accomplishing the supernormal powers, we have here a mention of these three, in order to make known the particular quality of each as being direct aids to yoga and as contrasted with the five which are indirect aids. And with regard to these [three], fixed-attention and contemplation and concentration are in the relation of cause to effect, and the serial order <gloss>3</gloss> [of causes and effects] is specified. Therefore this order is followed in the order of the statements. Accordingly, fixed-attention is the first to be characterized. So he says:

**1. Binding the mind-stuff to a place is fixed-attention.** He describes a place belonging to one’s self by the words «to the navel.» By the words «other places of the same kind» we must understand the palate and so forth. The binding is a relation. He describes an external place by the words «or to an external.» And with an external object the mind-stuff as such cannot have a relation. So it is said, «only in so far as it is a fluctuation,» in other words, only so far as it is a perception. On this point also there is a <term>Purāṇa</term> <note>a genre of ancient Indian literature consisting of history, lore, and philosophy</note>, <gloss>4</gloss>
> " Having mastered his breath by restraint of breath and his organs by with-

### Book III. Supernormal Powers <note>original: "Vibhūti"</note>

"...withdrawal of the senses, he should make a localization of the mind-stuff upon some auspicious support." <note>This refers to the transition from external sensory control to internal mental focus.</note> Auspicious supports are external, such as the Golden Womb <note>original: "Hiraṇyagarbha," the creator deity</note> and the King of Gods <note>original: "Vāsava," an epithet for Indra</note> and the Lord of Creatures <note>original: "Prajāpati"</note> and so forth. While performing this or while doing, as he wills, some other action wherein his mind does not wander, he should then deem this [fixed-attention] to be perfected."

**2. Focusedness of the presented idea upon that place is contemplation <note>original: "dhyāna"</note>.**
The focusedness of the presented idea upon the object to be contemplated³ in that place—in other words, the stream [of presented ideas] of like quality unaffected by any other presented idea.
He characterizes the contemplation which is to be effected by fixed-attention.
2. Focusedness of the presented idea upon that place is contemplation. Focusedness is singleness-of-intent. The Comment is easy. ### 5. As a result of mastering this constraint, there follows the shining forth of insight.

As a result of mastering this <term>constraint</term> there follows the shining forth of concentrated <term>insight <note>original: "prajñā"</note></term>.<gloss>1</gloss> Just in proportion as constraint enters the stable state, in that proportion the concentrated insight becomes clear.

### 6. Its application is by stages.

The application<gloss>2</gloss> of it, that is, the constraint is to that stage which is next the stage already mastered. For by overleaping the next stage without having first mastered the lower stage, the yogin does not gain constraint in the highest<gloss>3</gloss> stages. If he did not gain that constraint, how could he gain the shining forth of insight? Again, the constraint of one who by the grace of <term>the Lord <note>original: "Içvara"</note></term> has gained a higher stage does not apply to such things as the mind-stuff’s thinking<gloss>4</gloss> in other persons who are on the lower stages. Why is this? Since the purpose of this has been obtained from elsewhere. Yoga is itself the only spiritual guide which can show that this stage is next to that stage. How is this? Because it has been said to be thus,

> ->Yoga increases yoga’s store.<-

> ->In yoga rests for evermore.<-

<margin>1 Vishnu Purana 6. 7. 86-88 and Naradiya Purana 67. 63-65.</margin>
But when applied, in what cases can this <term>constraint <note>original: "saṃyama," the combined practice of the final three limbs of yoga</note></term> have these results? In reply he says, **6. Its application is by stages.** The author of the Comment particularizes the meaning of the word stage by saying, "of it." Its application is to that state as yet unmastered which is next to the stage already mastered. When the <term>reflective concentration <note>original: "vitarka-samādhi," focus on physical or "coarse" objects</note></term>, whose object is coarse, is mastered by constraint, the next application of constraint is to super-reflective concentration which has not yet been mastered. When this too is mastered, the application of the restraint is to <term>deliberative concentration <note>original: "vicāra-samādhi," focus on subtle elements or abstract qualities</note></term>. Similarly, when this is mastered, the application is to super-deliberative concentration. Hence in the <term>Purāṇa <note>ancient Indian scriptures containing mythology and philosophy</note></term>,^1 when the <term>balanced-state <note>original: "samāpatti," where the mind becomes one with its object</note></term> the object of which is coarse is perfected, then there is later introduced that concentration the object of which is subtle, in that the various weapons and ornaments are removed:

> "Then the wise man should ponder upon the serene form of the <term>Exalted One <note>here referring to the deity Vishnu</note></term>, without its conch-shell and mace and discus and <term>Çārṅga <note>original: "Shārnga," the celestial bow of Vishnu</note></term>, but having its string of beads. When the <term>fixed-attention <note>original: "dhāraṇā"</note></term> has become stable upon this form, then he should keep in mind the form without the ornaments, especially the diadem and the armlets. The wise man should make the god to have only one limb and should think ‘I am he’. Then after that he should devote himself to thought of ‘I’."

But why after having mastered a lower stage does he master a higher stage? And why is there not a reverse process? In reply to this he says, "without having first subjugated the lower stage, the <term>yogin <note>practitioner of yoga</note></term> does not." For a man proceeding to the Ganges from <term>Çilahrada <note>original: "Shilahrada," meaning "Stone-pool," an allegorical or local landmark on a journey</note></term> does not reach the Ganges unless he first get to the <term>Meghavana <note>original: "Meghavana," meaning "Cloud-forest"</note></term>. "Again of one who by the grace of the <term>Içvara <note>the Lord or Supreme Being</note></term> has gained a higher stage"—why does he say this? Because the purpose of this, the success in the higher stage which comes next, has been obtained from elsewhere, that is, from the devotion to the Içvara. For when an act has its action finished, then a <term>means-of-attaining <note>original: "sādhana"</note></term>, which does not produce anything in particular, falls outside the function of what can be called a means. The objector says, ‘This may be true. It is known in a general way (*āgamataḥ* <note>meaning: "according to tradition or scripture"</note>) what the different subordinated stages are. But how is there a knowledge of which comes after the other?’ In reply to this he says, "this stage." Yoga which has been previously mastered is the reason for proceeding to the thinking of the yoga which comes after. This passage is to be understood by supposing that a state is equivalent to a yoga which contains a state.

# iii. 7—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or <term>Vibhūti <note>The Sanskrit word for "manifestations" or "supernormal powers" achieved through advanced yoga</note></term> [208

But why is constraint applied in various places, and not the other five aids to yoga, although all without distinction are aids to yoga? In reply he says,

**7. The three are direct aids in comparison with the previous [five].**

These three means-of-attainment, inasmuch as their object is the same as [the object of the yoga] to be accomplished, are direct aids. But abstentions and the other [four] are not so. They are therefore indirect aids. These three means-of-attainment are direct aids only with reference to [yoga] conscious [of objects], but not to <term>seedless yoga <note>original: "nirbīja-samādhi"; a state of meditation without an object of focus</note></term>. For since [yoga] not conscious [of an object] is seedless [and has no object], it does not have the same object as these [three]. And since after these have been restricted for a long time, [unconscious yoga] arises subsequent to the higher passionlessness consisting in the undisturbed calm of perception, another name of which is the higher limit of conscious [yoga]. So he says, "The same three."

## 8. Even these [three] are indirect aids to seedless [concentration].

Even these, the three direct means-of-attainment, are indirect aids to seedless yoga. Why is this? Since this latter occurs even when these are absent.

**8. Even these [three] are indirect aids to seedless [concentration].** Hence that which determines the relation of direct aid to this is sameness of objects and not a mere sequence. For this [sequence] in so far as it might exist in the case of devotion to the <term>Lord <note>original: "Içvara"</note></term>, which is an indirect aid, would make the application [of direct aid] too wide (<term>inconsistent <note>original: "vyabhicāra," a logical term for when a definition applies to things it should not</note></term>). If this is established, even this over-wideness of the characterization which would include mere sequence could not apply to this [constraint]. Therefore it is still less probable that [this] constraint would be a direct aid to [concentration] not conscious [of an object]. To show that this is so it is said, "Since this latter occurs even when these are absent."
