<page-num>209</page-num>
<header>Alternation of emergence and restriction — [iii. 9]</header>

**The subliminal impression of restriction and the mutation of restriction are inseparably connected with the mind-stuff during its period of restriction.**

The <term>subliminal impressions <note>original: "saṃskāra"; the latent traces or mental "grooves" left by past experiences and thoughts</note></term> of emergence are <term>external aspects <note>original: "dharma"; the properties or qualities that manifest in the mind-stuff</note></term> of the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the collective mental field including the intellect and ego</note></term>. Since they do not consist of conscious thoughts, they are not suppressed even when conscious thoughts are restricted. The subliminal impressions of restriction are also external aspects of the mind-stuff. <When these two [states of mind-stuff] become visible or become invisible,> [that is when] the subliminal impressions of emergence are withdrawing and the subliminal impressions of restriction are being brought into place. This period of restriction is inseparably connected with the mind-stuff. Accordingly, the <term>mutation <note>original: "pariṇāma"; the process of change or transformation</note></term> of restriction is this periodical alteration of subliminal impressions within a single mind-stuff. In this state, the mind-stuff contains nothing but subliminal impressions, as has been explained in the section on the <term>concentration of restriction <note>referring to Book i. 18; a state of meditation where all conscious thought has ceased, leaving only latent impressions</note></term>.

<margin>¹ This does not refer to <term>concentration <note>original: "samādhi"</note></term> in general, but only to the concentrated <term>insight <note>original: "prajñā"</note></term> described in i. 47-48, which is without influence from objects and is an undisturbed succession of clarified <term>mental impressions <note>original: "saṃskāra"</note></term>. See also i. 18, p. 47⁶; ii. 27, p. 166³ (Calcutta edition); also i. 51 and the <term>aphorisms <note>original: "sūtras"</note></term> iii. 9-15.</margin>

With the intent to give information here about the three mutations which are to be used in the aphorism [iii. 16], "As a result of <term>constraint <note>original: "saṃyama"; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and absorption</note></term> upon the three mutations," the author asks, as an aside to the topic of "seedless" concentration: "Now, how does this happen?" In the case of "emergence" (the outgoing mind) and of <term>yoga conscious of objects <note>original: "saṃprajñāta-yoga"</note></term>, there is no need for this question because we can clearly experience a series of various mental changes. However, in the case of "restriction" (the quieted mind), the transformation is not consciously experienced. Furthermore, one cannot argue that because it is not experienced, it does not exist. Since the mind-stuff is composed of the three <term>fundamental aspects <note>original: "guṇa"; the three qualities of nature: sattva (purity/light), rajas (activity), and tamas (inertia)</note></term>, and since the changes of these aspects are never stable, it is impossible for mutation to cease even for a single moment. 

The answer to this question is found in aphorism 9... "emergence... mutation of restriction..." When compared with <term>concentration unconscious of any object <note>original: "asamprajñāta-samādhi"</note></term>, even "conscious concentration" is considered a form of emergence (an outgoing state). "Restriction" is that which suppresses these outgoing states. It is the undisturbed calm of perception and is also known as the "higher passionlessness." There is a process of these two states becoming visible or invisible—specifically, the subliminal impressions of the active mind becoming invisible while the subliminal impressions of the restricted mind become visible. The mind-stuff, which serves as the underlying substance during this period of restriction, is inseparably connected with this process.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of how the mind transforms during deep meditation. It specifically addresses why new mental "habits" of stillness are required to counteract the momentum of active thoughts, even after those thoughts have been stopped.</meta>

<page-num>210</page-num>
<header>iii. 9—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or Vibhūti [210</header>

...both of these states. For the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the collective mental field including intellect, ego, and consciousness</note></term> as a substance—whether it is in a conscious or unconscious state—does not fundamentally change, even as its <term>subliminal impressions <note>original: "saṃskāra"; the latent traces or mental "grooves" left by past experiences</note></term> become visible or invisible within it. 

An objector says, "Just as later obstacles based upon <term>undifferentiated consciousness <note>original: "avidyā"; a state of spiritual ignorance or misperceiving the world</note></term> cease to exist once that ignorance is gone (meaning there is no need for extra effort to stop them), shouldn't the impressions of 'active thinking' cease the moment the active thinking itself stops? Therefore, to stop those old impressions, we shouldn't need to create new impressions of 'restriction' or stillness." 

With this in view, the author mentions: "The subliminal impressions of emergence." In general, the disappearance of a cause does not automatically mean the disappearance of its effect. For example, even if a weaver stops existing, the cloth he made does not necessarily vanish. However, if the cause that actually *constitutes* the nature of the effect (like the threads of the cloth) disappears, then the effect disappears. Now, other mental obstacles have been described as being made *of* undifferentiated consciousness. So, when that ignorance ends, it is right that those obstacles end too. 

But subliminal impressions, whose very essence is "presented ideas," are not like that. For even if an idea has been <term>restricted <note>original: "nivṛtti"; the suppression or turning back of mental activity</note></term> for a long time, we still see a "connecting recollection" (a memory) surfacing later. Therefore, even if active ideas are repressed, one must still rely on an accumulation of new "impressions of restriction" to fully suppress the lingering momentum of those old active thoughts. This is the meaning. The rest is easy to understand.

### 10. This [mind-stuff] flows peacefully by reason of the subliminal impression.

Because of the "impression of restriction," the peaceful flow of the mind requires skill or "dexterity" in applying these impressions of stillness. When these impressions of stillness become weak, the impression that focuses on the external aspects of stillness is <term>overwhelmed <note>original: "abhibhava"; the process of one mental state being overpowered by another</note></term> by the lingering impressions of active <term>emergence <note>original: "vyutthāna"; the state of the mind when it is active and thoughts are arising</note></term>.

But if there were a total overwhelming of these active impressions in every respect, what would a transformation look like when backed by a powerful impression of restriction? In reply to this, the author says: **10. This [mind-stuff] flows peacefully by reason of the subliminal impression.** This "calm flowing" is a continuous stream of stillness, undefiled by any lingering habits of active thinking. Why is "dexterity" or skill in these impressions needed, rather than just ordinary impressions? In answer to this, he says: "When these..."

### 11. The$^1$ <term>mutation of concentration <note>original: "samādhi-pariṇāma"; the process where the mind's tendency to wander decreases and its ability to focus increases</note></term> is the dwindling of dispersiveness and the uprisal of singleness-of-intent belonging to the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the collective mental field including intellect, ego, and consciousness</note></term>.

Dispersiveness$^2$ is an external-aspect of the mind-stuff. Singleness-of-intent is an external-aspect of the mind-stuff. The dwindling of dispersiveness means that it disappears ; the uprisal of singleness-of-intent means that it becomes apparent. The mind-stuff is inseparably connected with both of these as the substance [in which they inhere]. This same mind-stuff being inseparably connected with these two external-aspects which belong to itself,—the passing away [of the distributiveness] and the coming forth [of the singleness-of-intent],—becomes concentrated. This is the mutation of concentration.

He shows what the state of the mind-stuff is in the mutation of concentration conscious [of objects]. 11. . . . dispersiveness . . . mutation of concentration. Dispersiveness is distractedness. Being existent$^3$ it does not <note>original: "san na"; being existent, it does not</note> cease to be. Dwindling is disappearing. Because a non-existent does not arise [in consciousness], an uprisal is a becoming apparent. The mind-stuff which is inseparably connected with the passing away of dispersiveness and the coming forth of singleness-of-intent, which are its external-aspects—the dispersiveness having the passing away and the singleness-of-intent having the coming forth—this mind-stuff is concentrating itself, that is, is becoming qualified as having a concentration which is to be attained in successive steps.

⟨Thus,⟩ by the already (iii. 9) described mutations of mind-stuff in external-aspect and in time-variation and in intensity. The mutation of external-aspect in elements and organs, the mutation of time-variation and the mutation of intensity are to be understood as having been described. Of these [three] the mutation of external-aspect takes place in the substance and is the becoming invisible of the external aspect of emergence and the becoming visible of the external aspect of <term>restriction <note>original: "nirodha"; the meditative state of suppressing mental fluctuations</note></term>. And the mutation of time-variation is the restriction having the three time-variations, [that is,] connected with the three <term>time-forms <note>original: "adhvan"; literally "paths," referring to the three periods of time (past, present, and future)</note></term>. This [restriction], one may say, puts aside the first time-form whose time-variation is yet to come, and passes into the present time-variation, without however passing out of its state as external-aspect. But in this [condition] it becomes manifest as being what it is. This is its second time-form. And it is not completely severed from past or from future time-variations.—Likewise <term>emergence <note>original: "vyutthāna"; the state of the mind when it is active and distracted, as opposed to restricted</note></term> has the three time-variations; it is connected with the three time-forms. Having put aside the present time-variation it passes over into the past time-variation, without however passing out of its state as external-aspect. This is its third time-form.

And it is not completely severed from the future and the present time-variations. This then is the external-aspects' mutation of intensity. 

In these cases the substance has a mutation in its external-aspects; the external-aspects have mutation in time-variations; and the time-variations also have mutation in intensities. <header>External-aspect, time-variation, intensity [-iii. 13</header>

brought forward by others "that since all three time-variations are [thus said to be] connected with everything that is in the mutation of time-variation, it must follow (<term>it logically results <note>original: "prāpnoti"; a term used in Indian logic to indicate an inevitable conclusion or a consequence of an argument</note></term>) that the time-forms are confounded." We meet this objection thus (<term>the removal of this difficulty <note>original: "tasya parihāra"; the standard opening for a rebuttal in Sanskrit philosophical commentary</note></term>). What is termed the common nature of things as external-aspects <note>the specific qualities or attributes of an object</note> cannot be brought into existence [at our pleasure]. The common nature [as external aspect] exists [independently] and therefore in regard to it the distinctions of time-variations must be maintained. Thus it must not be said that the common nature of this or that thing exists only in the present time. Because if this were so, the mind-stuff <note>original: "chitta"; the field of consciousness including the intellect, ego, and sensory mind</note> could never become subject to passion [for a certain object]. For anger [against some other object being by supposition now present in the mind-stuff], desire would not move actively forth.

Moreover it is not possible for the three time-variations <note>past, present, and future</note> to belong simultaneously to one and the same [individual] phenomenalized form. But what is possible is the presentation (<term>existence <note>original: "bhāva"; the state of being or the actual presence of a quality</note></term>) in successive times of its phenomenal <gloss>1</gloss> [form] by the operation of the conditions-which-phenomenalize (<term>manifesting agents <note>original: "vyañjaka"; factors like time, place, or internal causes that trigger a latent quality to appear</note></term>) it. Thus it has been said, <gloss>2</gloss> "The [outer] forms [when developed to] a high degree and the [inner] fluctuations [when developed to] a high degree oppose each other; but the generic forms co-operate with [these when developed to] a high degree." Hence [time-variations] are not confounded. 

To take an example. When we say absolutely (<term>exclusively <note>original: "eva"; an emphatic particle used here to narrow the scope of a statement</note></term>) that passion for a certain thing has shown itself, [we do not mean] that at that time [passion] for another object is non-existent; [but we mean that passion for another object] continues to be present [in the mind-stuff] though in a generic [unphenomenalized] form. Hence it [the passion] for that [other object] exists at that time (<term>it exists there at that time <note>original: "tadā tatra tasya bhāva"; a phrase asserting that a quality is present even if not currently active</note></term>). A similar [explanation can be given] in the case of time-variation [also]. The three time-forms do not belong to the substance but to the external-aspects. These [external-aspects] have a time-variation or do not have a time-variation. And as entering into various intensities are known by different names [which imply] an alteration of intensity but not of matter. Thus

Some persons have objected “that in the case of a thing which mutates in intensity [the substance of the thing] must logically be held to be (<term>logical consequence <note>original: "prasaṅga"; an inevitable conclusion or logical necessity in Indian philosophy</note></term>) absolutely permanent.” How is this? On the ground that it is functional activity<gloss>2</gloss> of the thing which determines the [special] time-form of the thing. Thus a thing is said to be a future thing when it is not exerting its own activity, and a present thing when it is thus active, and a past thing when it has ceased from activity. Hence, say these persons, it follows that substance and external-aspect and time-variation and intensity are all absolutely permanent.

But that [alleged] weakness, [we say], does not exist [in our position]; for we hold that although a substrate (<term>the possessor of qualities <note>original: "guṇin"</note></term>) is permanent, its aspects (<term>qualities <note>original: "guṇa"; the fundamental strands or attributes of nature</note></term>) suffer a variety of antagonisms. The following serves as an illustration:

1. The substance clay passes from its external-aspect in the form of a round lump of clay into another external-aspect. And thus as an external-aspect enters into mutation in the form of a water-jar.
2. The water-jar-form putting aside its future time-variation assumes its present time-variation; here is the mutation as time-variation.
3. The water-jar is every moment undergoing oldness and newness [in its parts] and thus passes through mutations of intensity.

<header>Substances and external-aspects contrasted [—iii. 13</header>
<meta>Handwritten numeral "7" at the top center of the page.</meta>

such as a cow or a water-jar as an external-aspect <note>The Sanskrit term is *dharma*, referring here to the perceptible properties or "form" that a substance takes.</note> of the substances earth and other elements. And the external-aspects have mutations of time-variation <note>This refers to *lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*, the change from being "future" to "present" to "past".</note> such as past and future and present. Again the cow or other [animal] changed into its present time-variation has mutations of intensity <note>This refers to *avasthā-pariṇāma*, the degrees of change within the present state, such as aging.</note>, such as childhood and boyhood and youth and old age. And the water-jar or other [thing] has its mutation of intensity, such as newness or oldness.—Similarly organs, which are substances, have external aspects, which are the seeing of blue or of other colours. The external aspect has the present and the other time-variations. The time-variation which has the seeing of a jewel or some other [thing] has a mutation of intensity, such as the clearness or lack of clearness [of the seeing]. 

This mutation, thus described, of elements and of organs, is to be understood as being based upon the distinction between the substance and its external-aspects and time-variations and intensities. But as referring to the lack of distinction between them, it is mentioned when he says «But in the strict sense.» The word «but» differentiates this from the view that they are distinct. The absolute reality of this [mutation] is asserted, but [the absolute reality] of the other [three-fold] mutation is not denied. Why? «For the external-aspect is nothing more than the substance itself.» 

An objector says, 'If the external-aspect is merely an evolved form of the substance, how then should the idea prevail in the world that there is no confusion in the case of these [three] mutations?' In reply to this he says, «in the form of an external-aspect.» The word «external-aspect» is here equivalent to external-aspect and to time-variation and to intensity. It is the substance that enters into evolved-forms through the medium of these. So the [evolved-form] is one and is also not confused with [another]. Because [the external-aspects] the medium of this [substance], although not distinct from the substance, are not confused with each other. 

An objector says, 'If the external-aspects are not distinct from the substance, and if the time-forms of the substance are distinct, then since the external-aspects are not different from the substance, the external-aspects would be like a substance.' To which he replies, «In such cases . . . of the . . . external-aspect.» The «state» means a particular arrangement-of-parts.<gloss>1</gloss> Just as a plate of gold<gloss>2</gloss> or of some other substance may receive a particular name and [be called] a necklace or a lucky-cross <note>original: "svastika", a Sanskrit term for a cross-shaped ornament or symbol of well-being.</note>, [so] there is an alteration only as [concerns the form of the ornaments], but the matter gold does not become something not gold, because there is no absolute distinction [between the substance and the external-aspect]. 

This is the intention of what he is about to say. He brings forward a Buddhist <note>The text here engages with the Buddhist philosophical position that denies a permanent underlying "self" or "substance," arguing instead that only the fleeting moments of change are real.</note>, who holds the doctrine of the absolute unity [of substance and external-aspect], by saying, «An opponent objects as follows.» 'For the necklace and other things thus coming into existence are external-aspects only and are real in the strict sense. ## iii. 13—Simultaneity of contrary qualities

...cause. **"A subtile form"** <note>original: *sūkṣma*; referring to a state of matter that is not currently manifest to the senses</note> [that is] one not capable of being seen. And hence there is no conscious perception of it.

Having thus substantiated the mutation of external-aspect <note>Sanskrit: *dharma-pariṇāma*; the change in the properties or qualities of a substance</note>, he substantiates the mutation of time-variation <note>Sanskrit: *lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*; the transition of a property through past, present, and future</note> also, in so far as they are inseparably connected with each other, by saying, **"in the mutation of time-variation."** The meaning is that each time-variation is inseparably connected with the two others. 

The objector says, ‘When one time-variation is in connection, other time-variations are not perceived. How then [are these] connected with the former?’ 

In reply he says, **"Take the case of a man."** For an absence of experience does not do away with that which is established by the <term>source of a valid idea</term> <note>Sanskrit: *pramāṇa*; a reliable means of knowledge such as perception or logic</note>. For the very fact that this [time-variation] has been made to rise [in consciousness], is the proof for the real existence of these [other time-variations], because a non-existent thing, such as **"a man’s horns,"** <note>A standard example in Indian logic used to describe something that is impossible and logically non-existent.</note> cannot be made to rise in consciousness. 

He sets up the objection uttered by another when he says, **"Here . . . in the mutation of time-variation."** ‘If when an external-aspect is present, it is at the same time past and future, then all the three time-forms would be confounded. And if the time-forms are to be in successive times, then it would follow that the production of the non-existent [becomes possible].’ 

He meets the objection with the words, **"We meet this objection thus."** For the existence of external-aspects in the present only is established by experience. From this it follows that [external-aspects are] in relation to earlier and to later time. [Why does it follow?] Because of course a non-existent does not come into being, nor is an existent annihilated, as he says, **"Because if this were so, the mind-stuff could never."** 

For the <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>Sanskrit: *citta*; the totality of the mind, including intellect, ego, and sensory mind</note> at a time following after anger, is experienced as having the external-aspect of passion. And if passion did not exist at the time of anger, in so far as [passion] was [at that time] future, how then could [passion] rise into consciousness? And if it should not rise in consciousness, how could it be experienced? 

[The objector continues,] ‘Even if this be granted, why would there not still be confusion of time-forms?’ The question is [contained in the phrase,] **"Moreover it is not possible."** ‘What cause is there for not confounding [the time-forms]?’ And (*ca*) is used in the sense of ‘but’. 

The answer is given in the words, **"the three."** The three time-variations cannot possibly exist simultaneously. In what? In one fluctuation of mind-stuff <note>Sanskrit: *vṛtti*; a single wave or state of consciousness</note>. But in successive times it is possible for each one of the time-variations to exist in its phenomenal [form] by the operation of the conditions which bring it into appearance. Since the discussion of the time-variations depends upon the things-which-have-time-variations, therefore the time-variations, in so far as they have the form of the things-which-have-time-variations, belong to [or have the same nature as] these <note>original: *tad-vattā*; the state of "having that" nature or quality</note>, that is, the things-which-have-time-variations.

He takes up the subject referred to in the illustration by saying, **"A similar [explanation] in the case of <term>time-variation</term>."** <note>Sanskrit: *lakṣaṇa*; the temporal status of a property, specifically whether it is past, present, or future.</note>

In reply to this he says, **"The three time-forms do not belong to the substance."** Because it is the external-aspects, which are distinct from it, that have the three time-forms. That it is the external-aspects which are connected with the three time-forms is made clear by the words, **"These [external-aspects]."** 

**"Have a time-variation"** means manifested [that is] present. **"Do not have a time-variation"** means unmanifested [that is] future or past. Of these [two], those-that-have-a-time-variation, when they attain to the various intensities, either to powerfulness or to weakness, are referred to as being different <note>original: *anyatvena*; reading as "by way of difference."</note> from other intensities, but not from other matter. 

The word **"intensity"** <note>Sanskrit: *avasthā*; the degree of strength, weakness, or maturity of a specific property at a specific time.</note> is here used in the sense of external-aspect and of time-variation and of intensity. Since the external-aspects and the rest are not absolutely identical with the substance, to the extent that the common nature of the external-aspect and of the other [mutations] should have the form of the substance. Nor is there absolute difference, to the extent that the common nature of external-aspects should be [as different as] horses and cows.

Just as the arrangement of parts, $^1$ which is defined <term>lakṣaṇa</term> <note>original: "lakṣaṇa"; a distinguishing characteristic or definition.</note> by being a transformation of earth and of other [gross elements], is itself merely an external property and has a beginning and an end (in that it eventually becomes invisible)—[so] «sound and the rest,» the subtle elements of sound, touch, color, taste, and smell, are not perishable when compared with the objects they produce, and they do not, like those objects, become invisible. He shows how this applies to evolving matter with the words, «so the resoluble.» «To it the term evolved-form <term>vikāra</term> <note>original: "vikāra"; a modification or transformation of a base substance.</note> is applied.» 

But the Power of Thought <term>citi-śakti</term> <note>original: "citi-śakti"; the power of pure consciousness or the Seer, which does not change.</note> is not subject to this kind of evolution of form. This is the main point.—Having thus used both evolved matter and the underlying cause of evolution (which are well known to philosophers) as illustrations, he now focuses only on evolved matter (which is familiar to the common person). He discusses the variety of conflicting qualities <term>guṇa</term> <note>original: "guṇa"; the three fundamental strands or qualities of nature: goodness, activity, and inertia.</note> which lead to different types of change—change in properties, change in time-status, and change in intensity—by saying, «The following serves as an illustration.» 

There is no requirement that the change in intensity must only belong to variations in time. For all three—the property, the time-variation, and the intensity—are covered by the word ‘intensity.’ Therefore, one kind of transformation is "intensity," which is common to all. Accordingly, he says, «Thus the substance only.» He provides the defining characteristic of the transformation that includes everything by saying, «in a permanent.» The term ‘external-aspect’ serves as a label for the property, the time-variation, and the intensity, because it is the foundation in which all of them exist.

### The three states of substance — iii. 14

...one or another [form] of the single [substance]. Of these [forms] that is called present, if it be that the **external-aspect** <term>dharma</term> <note>original: "dharma"; here referring to the property or characteristic that manifests from a substance.</note> is passing through [the state] of its peculiar functional-activity. This is different from the other external-aspects both the **quiescent** <term>śānta</term> <note>original: "śānta"; refers to the past state where the activity has ceased.</note> and the **indeterminable** <term>avyapadeśya</term> <note>original: "avyapadeśya"; refers to the future state which cannot yet be specifically described.</note> [states]. But when it has rejoined its general [or latent] form, then how could that external-aspect be distinguished from any other, since it is then of the very nature of the substance itself? 

There are, as every one knows, three of these external-aspects within the substance: the quiescent, the uprisen, and the indeterminable. 

*   Of these, the **quiescent** are those that have come to rest by finishing their functional-activity. 
*   The **uprisen** <term>udita</term> <note>original: "udita"; the present, active state.</note> are those in active function; and these [uprisen] are *immediately-contiguous* (*samanantara*) to the future time-variation. 

While the past come after the present. Why do not the present come after the past? Because there is no relation of antecedent and consequent [between them]. The relation of antecedent and consequent in the case of the future and the present <note>The Vārttika <note>A critical commentary on earlier texts.</note> says that this is **antecedent non-existence** <note>original: "prāgabhāva"; the state of a thing before it is produced.</note>.</note> is not the same as [this relation] in the case of the past <note>In this case there is **destruction of what previously existed** <note>original: "prāgdhvaṁsa"; the state of a thing after it has been destroyed.</note>.</note> [and of the present]. **14. Among these [mutations] a substance conforms itself to quiescent and uprisen and indeterminable external-aspects.** 

A **substance** <term>dharmin</term> <note>original: "dharmin"; the underlying "possessor" of properties.</note> is a thing that has **external-aspects** <term>dharma</term> <note>original: "dharma"; here meaning properties, qualities, or characteristics of the substance.</note>. "The substance" means a material object such as clay. "Only a power" [that is] the power of producing the dust and the lump of clay and the water-jar. This is the external-aspect,³ in so far as these are contained in this [substance] in an unphenomenalized <note>That is, a latent or hidden state.</note> state. This is the point.

In reply to this he says, "as limited by its pre-established-harmony." The power to produce the water-jar is defined as being pre-established-harmony for things which fetch water. Hence the power to fetch water and the other [purposeful] acts are also obtained by the water-jars and other things from their own cause only. ...regard to the substance]. This is the point.—There is another interpretation. One might be asked, ‘What are substances?’ The reply is, “Of the substance as limited by its **inherent potency** <term>yogyatā</term> <note>original: "pre-established-harmony"; this refers to the latent capacity or suitability of a substance to manifest specific qualities.</note>.” One might be asked, ‘What is an external-aspect?’ The reply is, “An external-aspect is only a power <note>original: "śakti"</note>.” The meaning is that an external-aspect is only an inherent potency belonging to these substances. Hence it is proven that the thing which has this external-aspect is the substance. Thus it becomes clear.

He describes the **source of the valid idea** <term>pramāṇa</term> <note>The means by which we gain accurate knowledge, such as direct observation or inference.</note> which proves the real existence of these external-aspects in the words: “And it... is inferred by the kind of effect which it generates.” This refers to the single substance in one or another form, such as dust, or a lump of clay, or a water-jar. This is the meaning. And it differs because there are evidently different effects. This is another way of putting it (<term>iti yāvat</term> <note>original: "iti yāvat"; a Sanskrit phrase meaning "this is to say" or "in other words."</note>). It is observed or **apperceived** <note>The conscious recognition of a perception.</note>. 

With regard to these external-aspects, he describes the difference between the lump of clay—which strikes upon the thinking substance of experience and is present—and the **quiescent** <term>śānta</term> <note>The "past" state, where the quality has already done its work and gone into rest.</note> state of the clay as dust, and the **indeterminable** <term>avyapadeśya</term> <note>The "future" state, where the quality is not yet active or defined.</note> state of the clay as a water-jar, by saying: “Of these forms, that is called present.” 

If there be no difference, then the dust and the water-jar would have their **functional activity** <term>arthakriyā</term> <note>The capacity of an object to perform its specific purpose, like a jar holding water.</note> co-extensive with that of the lump of clay. This is the point. But in the case of the **unphenomenalized** <note>A state where the object's qualities have not yet appeared to our senses.</note> lump of clay, the establishment of the difference, as stated above, is impossible. This he says in the words, “But when.” What then is this difference? By establishment of what difference will there be a differentiation? 

Having thus mentioned that there is this establishment of a difference between the external-aspects, he analyses this difference in the words, “There are, as every one knows.” The word “uprisen” <note>original: "udita"</note> means present. He now deduces the priority and the sequence of the **time-forms** <term>lakṣaṇa</term> in the words, “And these.” 

A question is raised in the words, “Why does not?”—‘For what reason does not the present come after the past?’ This is the meaning. The reason is, “There is no relation of **antecedent and consequent** <note>The logical order of cause and effect.</note> [between them].” By speaking of the object (that is, the absence of antecedence and consequence) he indicates that which contains as its object the non-apperception of this object. He shows what this same non-apperception is, in so far as its properties are opposite to those of apperception, in the words, “in the case of the future and the present.” 

He brings the discussion to a close with the word, “Consequently.” Consequently (<term>tat</term> <note>original: "tat"; here meaning "therefore."</note>) means for this reason. The future only is immediately contiguous as being antecedent to the present; but the past is not. The present is immediately contiguous to the past as being antecedent to it; but the indeterminable (future) is not. Therefore it is established that the **youngest** <note>In this philosophical sequence, the past is considered the "youngest" because it is the final stage in the flow of time from the unmanifest future to the manifest present and finally to the stored past.</note> of the time-forms is the past. 

An objector says, “This may be true. The uprisen and the past may be surmised...”

## 15. The order of the sequence (*krama*) is the reason for the order of the mutations.

If it be possible <note>Reading the Sanskrit word *prasakte*. However, other manuscripts (Kashmir and Gaṅgādhara Shāstri) read *prasakteḥ*, which would suggest the opposite: that this sequence is necessary *because* a single substance cannot undergo every mutation at once. This follows grammatical rules found in Pāṇini [i. 4. 31] and the Siddhānta Kaumudī.</note> that a single substance has only a single mutation <note>a change in state or form</note>, then the order of the sequence is the cause of the order of the mutation. One finds, for example, clay in the form of dust, clay in the form of a lump, clay in the form of a water-jar, clay in the form of potsherds [and] clay in the form of small bits. It is in this sense that there is a sequence.

1. Whenever one external-aspect is immediately-contiguous to another external-aspect, it is [then in] sequence with it. The lump of [clay] falls away and the water-jar comes into existence. It is in such cases that a sequence in the mutation of external-aspects occurs.

2. There is a sequence in the mutation of time-variations. By reason of there being a future [time-variation] of the water-jar, there is a sequence [to it in the] present [time-variation]. Likewise by reason of there being a present [time-variation] of the lump [of clay], there is a sequence [to it in the] <margin>Refer to note 47, n. 2</margin> past [time-variation].

<page-num>231</page-num>
<header>231] Continuity of successive mutations [—iii. 15</header>

There is an order of the mutations <note>original: *pariṇāma*, referring to the process of one state transforming into another</note>. Both ordinary men and men of trained minds search out with their own eyes, in clay which is one, a sequential succession of mutating form of dust and lump and water-jar and potsherds and small bits. And the immediate succession between the dust and the lump is one thing; and that between the lump and the water-jar is another; and that between the water-jar and the potsherds is another; and that between the potsherds and the small bits is another. Whatever is sequent with respect to the one is antecedent <note>coming before in the sequence</note> with respect to the other. This same difference of sequences, since it does not correspond to a single mutation, leads one to conclude that there are different mutations. Moreover the clay, although a single substance, undergoes a succession of mutations in sequences following the sequence of contact <term>samavadhāna<gloss>the conjunction or assembly of various necessary conditions and causes</gloss></term> with various co-operating causes which fall one after another into the sequence, and does not leave it [the succession of mutations] to chance. And as in the case of the order of the mutation of the **external-aspects** <note>original: *dharma*, the qualities or forms an object takes</note>, so the reason for the order of the mutation of **time-variations** <note>original: *lakṣaṇa*, the status of being past, present, or future</note> and for the order of the mutation of **intensities** <note>original: *avasthā*, the degree of newness or oldness of a state</note> is of the same kind as the order of the sequence. All this is made luminous in the words of the Comment, «a single substance.» On the assumption that there is an identity between the sequence and that which is in the sequence, it is said that this is its sequence, in the words, «There is none the less a sequence in the mutations of intensity.» 

For it is thus when rice-grains, carefully guarded in a granary by a miser, after very many years become reduced to atoms, in that the arrangement of the parts [of the grain] is likely to crumble even at a touch of the hand. Such a [condition] would not result so suddenly <term>akasmāt<gloss>literally "without a 'what'" or without a preceding cause; accidentally</gloss></term> in the case of brand-new rice-grains. Therefore in the sequence of successive moments this fact [that they are reduced to atoms] is seen to characterize those [grains] which have gotten into the sequence of very large and less large and large and minute and more minute and very minute. This same order in the sequence does depend upon the distinction between the substance and the external-aspects, as he says, «These same sequences.» Extended from the evolved-effect and up to resoluble [primary matter] <note>referring to the hierarchy of Prakṛti, from the grossest objects back to the most subtle fundamental nature</note> there is this contingent relation of substance and external-aspects. 

Even [coarse elements] such as earth are external-aspects as compared with subtile elements, as he says, «the external-aspect also.» Because unresoluble [primary matter] is, strictly speaking, the only substance, it is usual to attribute identity to it. «By virtue of <term>taddvāreṇa<gloss>through the door of that; by means of that relationship</gloss></term>» [that is] by virtue of having a common locus the substance would itself be an external-aspect. For this very reason there would be only one mutation, that of the substance, since external-aspects and time-variations and intensities have entered into the substance itself. If this is so, it is almost equivalent to saying that the substance is far-removed from being absolutely permanent.

While discussing the mutations of the external-aspects he also states the diversity in the kinds of external-aspects of the mind-stuff <note>original: *citta*, the field of consciousness including intellect, ego, and sensory mind</note> by saying «of the mind-stuff.» «Perceived» means direct perceptions; «unperceived» means indirect perceptions. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Yoga Sutra III.15, concluding the discussion on how change is inferred in the mind before moving to Sutra III.16, which describes how a practitioner can gain knowledge of the past and future through deep focus on these transitions.</meta>

<page-num>232</page-num>
<header>iii. 15—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or Vibhūti</header>

Those whose essence consists of presented-ideas—such as the sources of valid ideas and the passions—are easily recognized. However, by using the words «real things only», the author refers to the non-illuminating character of certain objective things. An objector might say, 'This may be so. But if these things are unperceived, they surely do not exist.' In reply to this, the author says «by inference.» These external aspects are described as things whose existence as real entities is brought within our reach through logical inference. The word inference (<term>anu-māna<gloss>literally "after-measurement"</gloss></term>) means the proof (<term>māna</term>) which comes after (<term>anu</term>) a perception; and, since it shares the same nature of proving what is not seen, verbal communication <note>original: *āgama*, referring to sacred teachings or testimony</note> is also included in this term. He brings together the seven unperceived external aspects of the mind in a memorial verse <note>a mnemonic verse used by students to memorize complex lists</note> by saying, «Restriction.»

1.  **The restriction** of fluctuations is the unconscious stage [i. 51] of the mind-stuff. We come to a knowledge of it through sacred teachings and by inference, recognizing it as a state in which only subliminal impressions <note>latent mental tendencies or "seeds" of past actions</note> remain.
2.  The word **«right-living»** is meant to include merit and demerit <note>the spiritual "bank account" of good and bad actions</note>. Elsewhere the reading is 'karma' <note>original: *karman*, meaning action and its consequences</note>. In this case also, the merit and demerit produced by this right-living would have to be understood. These are known either by sacred teachings or by inference based upon our experience of pleasure or of pain.
3.  But **«subliminal-impression»** is inferred from the existence of memory.
4.  Likewise, since the aspects (<term>guṇa<gloss>the three fundamental qualities of nature: brightness, activity, and inertia</gloss></term>) are three, the changes of the aspects of the mind-stuff are never stable; therefore, **«mutation»** from moment to moment is inferred.
5.  Similarly **«vitality»**, which is a kind of effort to sustain the breath. Since it is not directly known to the conscious mind, this external aspect is inferred from the acts of breathing out and breathing in.
6.  Likewise **«movement»** of the mind (<term>cetas</term>) is its activity, seen in how it connects with the various senses and parts of the body; this activity is also inferred from that very connection.
7.  Similarly **«power»**¹ is a subtle state of effects that are becoming more intense. It is an external aspect of the mind, and it is inferred only by experiencing its coarse, visible effects.

From here on, the discussion focuses on the "field of operation" for the constraint <note>original: *saṃyama*, the combined practice of fixed-attention, contemplation, and concentration</note> reached by the yogin who has mastered the means for attaining their desired goal.

# 16. As a result of constraint upon the three mutations [there follows] the knowledge of the past and of the future.

Yogins acquire knowledge of the past and of the future as a result of deep constraint upon the mutations of external aspects, time-variations, and intensities. Fixed-attention, contemplation, and concentration—three stages of meditation acting as one—has been called constraint [iii. 4]. By this constraint, the three mutations are directly experienced.

¹ Compare ii. 14, p. 211¹² (Calcutta edition).

# Doctrine of the word-prototype [-iii. 17

assigned] permeates the thinking-substance <note>original: "citta"</note> of the ordinary man with subconscious-impressions [which come from the syllable-sounds]. Thus as a result of common understanding <term>sampratipatti (the social agreement on what words mean)</term> [the word] is thought to be something real in itself. It is owing to our knowing what this [word] means in accordance with conventional-usage that we attempt to divide it [into sounds of syllables]. But conventional-usage is essentially [what has been handed down] by the memory [of man]. It is a kind of erroneous identification of the word and the thing signified. So that there is a confusion of the word with the intended-object, and of the intended-object with the word. Here we see how conventional usage is a kind of erroneous identification of each with the other based upon memory. Thus it is that these [three], the word ‘cow’ and the intended-object ‘cow’ and the presented-idea ‘cow’, get confused, because erroneously identified with one another.

But he who recognizes these three as quite distinct is the knower of all. Furthermore, every word has the power¹ to express a [complete] sentence <note>This is the concept of "sentence-power" or *vākya-śakti*</note>. Thus when we utter the word ‘tree’, we imply that it exists. For no intended-object of a word can lack existence. Similarly no action expressed [by a verb] is possible without the means-of-attaining [the action]. And so when we utter the word ‘cook-s’, certain relations which are later expressly mentioned² are supplied to specify the meaning [by excluding other relations]. Thus we mention the man Chāitra <note>Chaitra is a traditional placeholder name in Indian logic, much like "John Doe."</note> as the agent,³ rice as the object,⁴ and fire as the means⁵ of the action [expressed by the verb ‘cook’].

### Sounds and words [—iii. 17]

"...the lips and the palate." This vocal organ has its function only in [uttering the sounds of the] syllables as they are known to ordinary sense-perception, and not as expressive of meanings. He explains the object of the functional-activity of the organ of hearing in the words "the organ-of-hearing." The organ-of-hearing, however, has that only as its object which is mutated in the form of a particular [sound of a] syllable, which has as its essence a particular mutation of an emission-of-air (<term>udāna</term> <note>the upward-moving vital breath that drives speech</note>) subjected-to-contact (<term>abhighātin</term> <note>the physical striking of air against the throat or palate</note>) with [the various places-of-articulation] belonging to the vocal organ. But its object is not a word-expressing-a-meaning. This is what he wishes-to-say (<term>ity artha</term>). 

He distinguishes the word-expressing-a-meaning from the [sounds of the] syllables as known to ordinary sense-perception, by saying "the word [as significant sound]." But it is the mental-process that grasps the word as expressing-meaning by seizing the letter-sounds each in turn (<term>anu</term> <note>successively or one-after-another</note>) and binding them together [into one word]. Having grasped the letter-sounds (<term>nāda</term> <note>the audible vibration</note>) as [the sounds of] syllables (<term>varṇa</term> <note>the abstract linguistic unit or letter</note>) one by one as they are known in sense-perception, it binds them in turn—that is, afterwards—so that they are made to change into a unity and we can say **g-o-ḥ** <note>The Sanskrit word "Gauḥ" meaning "cow," used here as a standard linguistic example</note> [that is to say] one word. 

By this [mental-process] the word is grasped. Although each of the preceding mental-processes [by stages] brings each word, [so long as it] has the form of the [sounds of] syllables, into consciousness, still the word [expressing meaning] does not clearly lie [before us]. But at the last mental-act (<term>vijñāna</term> <note>the definitive cognitive realization</note>) it becomes clear. Thus it is said "a mental-process (<term>buddhi</term> <note>the intellect or faculty of judgment</note>) grasps the word [as significant sound] by seizing the letter-sounds each in turn and binding them together [into one word]." 

To [the <term>Mīmāṁsaka</term> <note>a member of the Mīmāmsā school of philosophy, which emphasizes the eternal nature of the Vedas and the inherent power of sounds</note>] who maintains that the [sounds of the] syllables in themselves express a meaning, in that a word cannot be discerned as one because the [sounds] are heterogeneous, he replies "the [sounds of the] syllables." Now these [sounds of the] syllables must either:
1. Each singly (<term>pratyeka</term>) arouse the idea (<term>dhī</term>) having a word expressing meaning as its content, like a row of pegs¹ upon which a bag-of-netted-cords is hung; or 
2. In combination (<term>saṁhata</term>) like the stones which when together hold the pot. 

Not, in any case, the first alternative, because from the single [sound of a syllable] the sense-perception of the thing does not rise in consciousness; or because if it did proceed from a single one, the second and the third need not have been uttered. For when an action is completed, a means-of-attaining [that action] which adds nothing new cannot be counted as (<term>nyāyātipāta</term> <note>a logical superfluity or an unnecessary step</note>) a means-of-attaining. 

Therefore the second [alternative] remains. For the stones in combination can hold up the pot, because they are there at the same time. But the [sounds of the] syllables cannot be simultaneous <note>because sounds vanish the moment they are spoken, they cannot physically "stand together" like stones</note>. Accordingly, since it cannot be that aid is reciprocally given and received, they cannot by being together arouse the idea of the meaning. These [sounds of syllables] not attaining themselves to a single special word and therefore not conveying [the meaning], become now audible (<term>āvis</term>) and now inaudible (<term>tiras</term>). <meta>This page continues the technical debate from page 238 regarding the "sphoṭa"—the theory that a word is a single, indivisible unit of meaning that "bursts forth" in the mind, rather than being just a collection of individual sounds. It addresses why a sequence of syllables cannot independently create the mental image of an object.</meta>

<page-num>239</page-num>
<header>239] The word-essence (sphota) [—iii. 17</header>

[Of these alternatives] none can [be admitted], because of the difficulties in the assumption. It must be assumed that this [mental purification] is the very same as that which follows <term>pūrva</term> <note>former or previous</note> sacrificial merit. However, this [word-type], which is a single unit, cannot be produced by the experiences of [the sounds of] syllables in sequences. Since we would have to assume [the existence] of many subsidiary mental traces (<term>saṃskāra</term>) each of the same kind [as the others]. It is this that is the difficulty. 

Furthermore, so long as we do not know that this mental purification serves as a cause to make the intended object known, it cannot be accepted as serving to produce this [meaning]. For a relationship which is not known to serve the purpose of presenting the intended object cannot be accepted as serving [that purpose]. 

And as for the subliminal impression which is inferred from the memory—which is its result—it is restricted [referencing section i. 11] to that specific object, namely, the experience which was its cause. It is therefore not in a position to arouse a subliminal impression which has something else as its object [namely, the presentation of the intended object of that experience]. For if this were so, anyone having experienced any one object would be able to know any [other] object. 

And it is not right to say that [the sounds of] syllables which arise in the mirror of such a memory—taking its origin in the sum-total (<term>piṇḍa</term>) of subliminal impressions produced by the experience of each syllable singly—can express meaning [just because the sounds of the syllables] are recognized as belonging together. For that would involve the conclusion that the idea of the intended object could be produced indiscriminately (<term>aviceṣeṇa</term>), whether the [sounds of the syllables] be experienced in a sequence, out of sequence, or in reversed sequence. And it cannot be that this knowledge from memory can bring before itself (<term>gocarayitum</term> <note>literally "to make into a field of perception"</note>) that specific succession of syllable sounds which was active in the previous experience. 

Hence, in so far as it is not possible from the [sounds of the] syllables alone to have the mental presentation of the intended object, it must be supposed that there is an experience¹ of the word as being a single unit which could give rise to [the presentation of the intended object²]. 

The same objection, moreover, does not apply with reference to the word itself. For the word is manifested (phenomenalized) by [sounds of] syllables only when they are single and differ according to the difference³ in the effort [of articulation]. And inasmuch as the words are alike in so far as they are produced through the action of the same places [of articulation, like the throat or teeth] by sounds which are the conditions that manifest the various words—each unlike the other—[the sounds] do make a word seem similar [to other words]. This word [*cow*, original: <term>go</term>] is similar to other words which have the ‘g’ sound, but in other respects it is dissimilar, since their dissimilarities are different in so far as the various other [syllables] are associated [with this syllable]. Because of [this] peculiarity of this [word], although it is one, and...

->iii. 17—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or <term>Vibhūti</term> <note>The third chapter of the Yoga Sutras, detailing the extraordinary abilities gained through advanced meditation.</note><-

altogether a unit (<term>anavayava</term> <note>original: "anavayava"; meaning partless or indivisible</note>), still the sounds-of-the-syllables make it appear as a collection (<term>sāvayava</term> <note>original: "sāvayava"; meaning having parts or composite</note>) and not as a unit. Just as a face, although it is one, with a definite colour and dimension and look, is made to appear, by [reflection in] a gem $^1$ or a sword-blade or a mirror, to be more than one and as having more than one colour and dimension and look. But this is not so in the strict sense. Whereas the [sounds of the] syllables are parts of the partless word and are formed of the similarities and peculiarities.

Therefore the mental-process (<term>buddhi</term> <note>the intellectual faculty of the mind</note>) of which this [word], in the case of a particular word, supports itself upon the word-prototype (<term>sphoṭa</term> <note>the theory that meaning "bursts forth" from a word as a whole rather than from a sum of its parts</note>) which is undivided and partless, although it seems to be divided and seems to have parts. Therefore a part, the letter ‘g’, of one particular word-prototype, the word ‘go’ <note>Sanskrit for "cow"</note> cannot cause that [namely, the partless prototype] of which it [the ‘g’] is part to come forth, because of the similarity of this word-prototype with that of words like *gaura* <note>Sanskrit for "white" or "fair"</note>. Therefore when made special-and-distinct by the letter ‘o’, it is able to cause that of which it is a part, [namely the word-prototype ‘go’,] to come forth.

Similarly the part which is the letter ‘o’ is also not able, because of its similarity with words like *çociḥ* <note>original: "çociḥ"; meaning light or flame</note>, to cause that of which it is a part, namely the word-prototype ‘go’, to come forth. So when made special-and-distinct by the letter ‘g’, it is able to cause [its own prototype] to come forth. And although [these two ‘g’ and ‘o’] do not naturally belong together, still through [their] subliminal-impressions <note>mental traces or residues of past experiences</note> they do belong together. And thus it is consistent to have the relation of qualified and qualifier between them. Nor can it be said that the two subliminal-impressions have each a different object, since the experiences whose objects were the two parts, and also the two subliminal-impressions which result from the experiences, have one word as their object. The word moreover is not distinctly (<term>avyakta</term> <note>original: "avyakta"; unmanifest or indistinct</note>) experienced when only part of it is experienced.

Whereas it is perceived distinctly by the idea which seizes the [sounds of the] syllables in turn and binds them together,—[the idea] which is produced by the subliminal-impressions which arise from the experience of the parts. This is the difference. And we find that the first indistinct experience does produce a distinct experience by arousing subliminal-impressions in a sequence [of degrees of distinctness], just as the presented-idea that the tree when seen from a distance is green $^2$ (<term>harita</term> <note>original: "harita"</note>), although indistinct, leads to the distinct presented-idea of the tree. But this kind [of an idea] is impossible in an experience wherein the [sounds of the] syllables should represent intended-objects. For surely one cannot say that the [sounds of the] syllables do each singly give rise to an indistinct presented-idea of the intended-object, and ultimately to a distinct idea. For distinctness and indistinctness are restricted to cases of perceptive thinking. But [in this case] the presentation of the intended-object is to be aroused by the—

Because by itself <note>original: tanmātrasya</note> it has no capacity. Thus it is the sentence that in all cases expresses the words; but the words do not. However, as forming parts of this [that is, the sentence], the words also have expressive power with respect to the sense of the sentence, just as with respect to the word the [sounds of the] syllables as constituting it have also expressive power. Thus then just as each single [sound of a] syllable embraces the power to express all intended-objects of words, so also each single word embraces the power to express the meaning of all sentences. This is what is expressed by the words «Furthermore, every word has the power to express a [complete] sentence. Thus when we utter the word ‘tree’, we imply that it exists.» The meaning is that the word ‘tree’ in conjunction with the implied word ‘is’ leads to the meaning of the sentence. Therefore as forming part of the sentence, the word ‘tree’ produces that meaning <note>original: tatra vartate</note>. But if it be asked why the word ‘is’ is implied, the reply is «No intended-object can lack existence.» For the means for defining the meanings of words is <term>popular-usage</term>¹ <note>original: loka</note>. And this <term>popular-usage</term> combines the meaning of the word as it is alone with the meaning ‘is’ and in all such cases makes the meaning of a sentence. This same [popular-usage] is the meaning of a word which cannot lack existence. Hence those² who know the functions of words have [this] agreement-of-usage <note>original: vyavahāra</note>, “Wherever there is no other verb, ‘is’ in the sense of being should be used.” —Having stated that a <term>nominal-base</term>³ <note>original: prātipadika; the core form of a noun before grammatical endings are added.</note> never lacks its action [expressed by a verb], he shows that any particular verb is never without a relation by saying «And so

This page moves into the linguistic problem of ambiguity, explaining why we must break down sentences into individual words and words into their grammatical parts to avoid confusion between identical-sounding terms.</meta>

# The unity of the word
### [-iii. 17]

...when we utter.>> For when we utter the word 'cooks', all the relationships which are naturally associated with that action are implied. For this reason, we make specific statements about the unique relationships of this verb, and the purpose of doing so is to exclude other possible relationships. Thus, the meaning of a sentence consists of nothing but the narrowing down or specializing of these relations.

Similarly, although a single word can be found to represent the entire meaning of a sentence, the sentence itself holds even more potential within its constituent words. So the author says, <<We observe.>> But this does not mean that words like "Reader," which appear complete in themselves, can convey their full meaning as long as they are not combined with verbs like "is." Even in the case of a word like "Reader," the meaning should be understood only in so far as it forms a part of a larger sentence. This is the essential point.

An objector might say, "This may be true. But if individual words already possess the expressive power of a full sentence, then there is no further need for the sentence itself, since its meaning can be gathered from the words alone."

In reply to this, he says, <<[And conversely] in this sentence.>> It has already been stated that if a speaker wishes to convey information, the meaning of their words is not fully understood from the words in isolation; they must be brought into combination with other words. Therefore, if we suppose the words to be separated from the sentence, a part of it—such as the relationship or the verb—must be explained by analyzing and listing these words, and by assigning specific roles to the word, its <term>base and suffix</term> <gloss>original: pratyaya; the grammatical parts added to a root word to determine its meaning</gloss>, and so on.

"But why is so much trouble taken to go through this detailed analysis of words?"

In reply to this, he says, <<Without such [an analysis].>> This analysis is necessary because nouns and verbs can look identical in certain cases. For example:
*   "A water-jar *is* <note>original: bhavati; here used as a verb</note> there" and "O *Lady* <note>original: bhavati; here used as a respectful feminine address</note>, give alms" or "While *Your Honor* <note>original: bhavati; here used as a formal masculine or neutral address</note> is standing." <note>1</note> <note>2</note>
*   Similarly: "Thou didst *go*" <note>original: açvas; a verb form</note> and "The *horse* <note>original: açvas; a noun</note> walks." <note>3</note>
*   Similarly: "*Goat's milk* <note>original: ajā-payas</note> drink thou" and "Thou didst *conquer* <note>original: ajāpayas</note> the foes."

Because there is a likeness in the form of the verb and the noun, it is often ambiguous whether these words should be analyzed as nouns or as verbs. When we do not account for the specific form of the word, and because a word's meaning cannot be known when it is withdrawn from the context of a sentence, how can it be properly understood as a noun or a verb? <note>4</note>

Therefore, words should be extracted from the sentence and analyzed. However, simply accounting for the form of a word does not, strictly speaking, create a true distinction between the words themselves, the objects they refer to, and the ideas they present. Having thus treated the different kinds of words through their <term>etymology</term> <gloss>the study of the origins and parts of words</gloss>, the author intends to show that, in reality, there is no confusion between words, the objects they represent, and the thoughts they trigger.

---

<note>2</note> Or possibly, "Something is standing upon Your Honor."
<note>3</note> The verb form could also mean "to swell," coming from the root *çvi* or *çvū*.
<note>4</note> This whole subject is discussed in much greater detail in another work by <term>Vācaspati Miśra</term> called <term>The Drop of Truth</term> <note>original: Tattvabindu</note> (Benares, 1893). This specific passage is found on page 15 of that text.

<page-num>246</page-num>
<header>Book III. Supernormal Powers or <term>Vibhūti</term> <note>Sanskrit: Vibhūti refers to the "manifestations" or "extraordinary powers" gained through advanced yoga practice.</note></header>
<meta>iii. 17-]</meta>

# Book III. Supernormal Powers or *<term>Vibhūti</term>*

The author discusses mental concepts which had become confused as a result of social convention <note>original: "conventional-usage"</note>, which erroneously identifies a word with the object it represents. He proceeds to say:

> «There is a distinction between these words, the actual objects they represent, and the mental concepts they evoke.»

> «To illustrate this distinction: when we say, ‘The palace whitens,’ the word <note>original: "çabdaḥ"</note> signifies an action <note>the process of a verb</note>.»

In this example, it is quite clear that the action of "becoming white"—which is a process still in progress and occurring through a series of steps—is different from the quality "white," which is an already completed state. Even in cases where both the word and the object are viewed as completed states, the word remains distinct from the object, as the author says:

> «‘The white palace’; here a relationship is meant.»

In this instance,^2 there is no specific grammatical ending used to show a relationship because the relationship is already implied <note>expressed by the nominative case according to the rules of the grammarian <term>Pāṇini</term> ii. 3. 1</note>. The author further distinguishes between the physical object and the word by saying:

> «in essence both an action <note>denoted by a verb</note> and a relation . . . the intended-object of which.»

The meaning is that the actual object referred to by both these words is, in its essence, both an action and a relationship. He then distinguishes the mental concept from the word by saying «and the mental concept.» The word «and» indicates that the phrase «the intended-object of which is this [the action and relation]» should also be applied here. The word «this» is to be understood <note>Sanskrit: <term>sambadhyate</term>, meaning "it is linked to"</note> as being subordinate to another word in a compound. It is described this way because the object’s essence is understood as both an action and a relation, as they are perceived to be the same.

An objector might ask, "Since words, objects, and mental concepts are usually all mixed up in our minds, how can there be any real distinction between them?" With this in mind, the author asks:

> «But why is this so?»

He answers by saying:

> «Because this process is identified with its result, the quality of being white.»

The mental concept that blurs these distinctions is limited by social convention, which mistakenly identifies the word with the thing. However, this blurred mental concept has no basis in actual fact. The term "conventional-usage" is used here to show that social habit is the root cause of our failure to distinguish between the act of "whitening" and the quality "white." He clarifies the reality of the situation by saying:

> «But the white object itself is that which...»

This refers to the intensity of the object, such as whether it is new or old. When we say things «correspond,» we mean they are being confused. Thus, by the practitioner’s <term>yogin</term> "constraint" <note>Samyama: a technical term for the combined practice of focused concentration and meditation</note> upon these distinctions, they can understand the cries of all living beings—including tame and wild animals, crawling creatures, and birds. They can even perceive the "unmanifested" speech among them, the objects they are referring to, and the mental concepts behind them. In this case, the same mental "constraint" used to understand human speech is applied to these animals as well, since the underlying principles of communication are comparable. Thus—

^2 Compare the phrase "the white horse" <note>Sanskrit: *çveto 'çvo*</note> in the philosophical text *The Drop of Truth* <note>Latin/Sanskrit title: *Tattva Bindu*</note>, page 16, line 12.

<header>Jāigīṣavya and Āvatya [—iii. 18</header>

It is established that the yogin has intuitive knowledge of these cries, the objects they refer to, and the mental concepts associated with them.

**18. As a result of direct perception of <term>subliminal impressions</term> <note>Sanskrit: saṃskāras. These are the deep-seated mental residues or "latent tendencies" left behind by every action and thought.</note>, there is intuitive knowledge of previous births.**

These <term>subliminal impressions</term> are of two distinct kinds: 

1. Those that cause memory and mental obstacles <note>referring to the *vāsanas*, or the subconscious traits that shape our personality</note>.
2. Those that result from past deeds, categorized as <term>right-living</term> <note>merit or dharma</note> and <term>wrong-living</term> <note>demerit or adharma</note>.

These impressions, formed in previous lives, are like the subtle changes in our mental state—mutation, movement, and life-force. They are usually unperceived aspects of the <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>Sanskrit: citta</note>. By practicing <term>Constraint</term> <note>Samyama; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and total absorption</note> upon these traces, a yogin gains direct perception of them. 

Furthermore, one cannot truly experience these traces without also perceiving the specific place, time, and cause of their origin. Therefore, by gaining intuitive knowledge of these mental impressions, the yogin discovers his previous incarnations. In the same way, by perceiving the subliminal impressions in others, he gains an awareness of the previous births of other beings.

On this subject, the following legend has been passed down:

> "The Exalted **Jāigīṣavya**, through the direct perception of his subliminal impressions, beheld the sequence of his own transformations throughout ten <term>great creative-periods</term> <note>Sanskrit: mahākalpas. In Hindu cosmology, these are vast cycles of time representing the birth and death of the universe.</note>. Through this, the knowledge born of discrimination became clear to him. 
> 
> Then, the Exalted **Āvatya**, who had manifested a physical body for this purpose, spoke to him: 'Across these ten great cycles, because the <term>purity</term> <note>Sanskrit: sattva</note> of your thinking-substance has remained unclouded by <term>passion</term> <note>rajas</note> or <term>darkness</term> <note>tamas</note>, you have witnessed the suffering caused by being born in hells or as animals. You have also been born repeatedly as a god or a human. Tell me: among all these lives, which have you found to be more prevalent—pleasure or pain?' 
> 
> Jāigīṣavya replied to the Exalted Āvatya: 'Across ten great cycles, because the <term>purity</term> of my thinking-substance is unclouded, I behold...'"

<page-num>248</page-num>
<header>Book III. Supernormal Powers or Vibhūti</header>

"...pain caused by birth in hells and in the bodies of beasts; coming into existence over and over again among gods and human beings—this I know. Whatever pleasure I have passed through, all this is nothing but pain." 

The Exalted Āvaṭya <note>A legendary sage or disciple mentioned in various yoga traditions</note> spoke thus: "Are Your Worship's mastery over the primary-cause <note>referring to *Prakṛti*, the fundamental substance of the universe</note> and the pleasure of ineffable bliss—are these also to be counted as pain?" 

The Exalted Jāigīṣavya <note>Considered one of the greatest masters of Yoga and Sāṃkhya philosophy</note> spoke: "This can be called the pleasure of ineffable bliss only in comparison with pleasure derived from the objects of the senses; but it is nothing but pain in comparison with <term>Isolation</term> <note>Sanskrit: *Kaivalya*; the state of ultimate spiritual liberation and independence from the material world</note>. Because this ineffable bliss is an external aspect of the <term>pure intelligence-stuff</term> <note>Sanskrit: *sattva*; the quality of light, clarity, and harmony</note> of the thinking-substance, and so it still possesses the <term>three aspects</term> <note>Sanskrit: *guṇas*; the three fundamental qualities—*sattva* (clarity), *rajas* (activity), and *tamas* (inertia)—that make up all material nature</note>. Because any mental concept that possesses these three aspects is counted as something to be eventually cast aside, the remaining thread of desire even in this high bliss is of the nature of pain. But by the removal of the anguish of the pain of desire, this pleasure of ineffable bliss is undisturbed calm, uninhibited, and favorable in the eyes of all."

### 18. **As a result of direct perception of <term>subliminal impressions</term> <note>Sanskrit: *saṃskāras*; the latent mental traces or "grooves" left in the mind by every action and experience</note> there is intuitive knowledge of previous births.**

For the subliminal impressions which are produced by knowledge are the causes of memory, whereas the subliminal impressions produced by undifferentiated consciousness <note>Sanskrit: *avidyā* or ignorance</note> are the causes of the hindrances <note>the *kleshas*, or mental afflictions like ego and attachment</note> which begin with undifferentiated consciousness. 

As to the causes of <term>fruition</term> <note>the "ripening" or result of one's past actions</note>: fruition consists of birth, the length of one's life, and the kind of experiences one enjoys. The causes of this fruition are the various kinds of right-living <note>merit or *dharma*</note> and wrong-living <note>demerit or *adharma*</note>. 

The subliminal impressions accumulated in previous births are brought to completion by their own specific causes. Just as a <term>curry</term> <note>original Sanskrit: *vyañjana*; used here as a metaphor for something prepared by blending many distinct ingredients</note> is <term>put together</term> <note>original Sanskrit: *saṃskṛta*; refined or prepared</note> by combining many different items, so it follows that the mind's state has been constructed. Change, movement, restraint, power, and vitality are external aspects of the <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>Sanskrit: *citta*</note>. Likewise, the unperceived subliminal impressions are external aspects of the mind-stuff. 

<term>Constraint</term> <note>Sanskrit: *saṃyama*; the technical term for the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and total absorption</note> upon these impressions, along with their attachments to specific places, times, and causes—whether these impressions were originally learned or inferred—is sufficient to bring about the direct perception of both kinds of subliminal impressions. 

And if it be asked how there can be direct perception of previous births, even if it is possible to perceive these impressions through constraint, the author replies: "Moreover, there is no [limitation] of place." "Cause" refers to the previous body, the sensory organs, and the rest. Direct perception of subliminal impressions, along with their accompanying factors <note>Bālarāma <insert>a commentator</insert> mentions as instances of "attachments": mother and father, birth, country, city, or time</note>, allows the yogin to see the past.
