...necessarily involves the direct perception of such things as births. This is the meaning. The <term>constraint</term> <note>Samyama; the combined practice of fixed attention, contemplation, and concentration</note> with respect to one's own subliminal impressions he extends by analogy to those of others also in the words "Precisely as in other cases also." With this in view, he introduces as an aid to faith the dialogue between Jāigīṣavya and Āvaṭya, who had passed through the experience, by saying "On this point this tale is handed down." A great creative-period is a great mundane cycle <note>A Kalpa, or a vast period of cosmic time</note>. By the words "who had assumed a [coarse] body" the perfection of a created body¹ is described. Spotless is brilliant; that from which the stains of <term>rajas</term> <note>the quality of passion, activity, and movement</note> and <term>tamas</term> <note>the quality of darkness, inertia, and delusion</note> have been removed. Mastery over the primary cause <note>Prakṛti, the fundamental matter of the universe</note> means power. By having this [power] and by creating movements in the primary cause, he gives to any one that kind of perfection of body or of organs which he wishes to confer upon him; and further, having created his own bodies and organs by thousands, he roves through air and sky and earth at will. Bliss (*santoṣa*) is the dwindling of desire and the external aspect of undisturbed calm belonging to the <term>sattva</term> <note>the quality of light, purity, and intelligence</note> of the thinking-substance.

**19. [As a result of constraint] upon a presented-idea [there arises intuitive] knowledge of the mind-stuff of another.**
As a result of constraint upon a presented-idea <note>Pratyaya; the content or object currently held in someone's mind</note>, in consequence of the direct perception of the presented-idea, there arises the [intuitive] knowledge of the mind-stuff of another.

**19. [As a result of constraint] upon a presented-idea [there arises intuitive] knowledge of the mind-stuff of another.**
"As a result of" direct perception of the presented-idea, [that is] of mind-stuff in general of another.

**20.² But [the intuitive knowledge of the presented-idea of another] does not have that [idea] together with that upon which it depends [as its object], since that upon which it depends is not-in-the-field [of consciousness].**
The yogin knows that the presented-idea is affected <note>e.g., he knows the person is feeling anger or affection</note>. But he does not know that it is affected in dependence upon [this or] that [object] <note>e.g., he does not necessarily see the person or thing the other is angry at</note>. When the presented-idea of another [person] is in dependence upon something, this [object] does not become something upon which the mind-stuff of the yogin depends. But it is the other's presented-idea only upon which the yogin's mind-stuff comes to depend.

<page-num>250</page-num>
<header>iii. 20-] Book III. Supernormal Powers or <term>Vibhūti</term> [250</header>

<note>Vibhūti: Supernormal powers or spiritual manifestations</note>

Just as the direct perception of <term>subliminal impressions</term> <note>Samskaras; the latent traces of past actions and experiences</note> implies the direct perception of previous births and the circumstances attached to them, so the direct perception of another’s <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>Chitta; the total field of mental consciousness</note> might seem to imply the direct perception of the specific object upon which that mind is currently focused. Regarding this conclusion <note>original Sanskrit: prāpta</note>, the author says:

**20. But [the intuitive knowledge of the thoughts of another] does not include the object of those thoughts, since that object is not within the yogi's field [of consciousness].**

That <term>constraint</term> <note>Samyama; the unified practice of fixed attention, contemplation, and concentration</note> described in the previous section has as its object the subliminal impressions and their associations ¹; but this specific power has as its object the other person’s mind-stuff alone and nothing more. This is what the author intends to say.

**21. As a result of constraint upon the [outer] form of the body, when its power to be perceived is suspended, then—as a consequence of the disconnection between the light [of the observer] and the eye [of the observer]—there follows the invisibility [of the yogi’s body].**

As a result of constraint upon the form of the body, the <term>yogi</term> <note>A practitioner of Yoga</note> inhibits that imperceptible power by which the coarse, external body is normally known. When its power to be known is stopped, and as a result of the disconnection between the light (belonging to the observer) and the organ of the eye, the invisibility of the yogi is achieved. In this same way, it should be understood that the ability to become imperceptible to sound and other sensory objects has also been described.

21. . . . body . . . invisibility.

A body has its essence in the five coarse elements <note>Earth, water, fire, air, and ether</note>. Because it has form, it falls under the domain of the eye. For by having form, the body and its color become the object of the process of seeing by the eye. Thus, when the yogi performs a special kind of constraint upon this external form, the power of being perceived—which belongs to the color and is the source of seeing a body with form—is suspended. Therefore, when this power to be known is stopped, the yogi becomes indiscernible. In other words, the body of the yogi no longer becomes an object for the observer's eye to process. The meaning is that once this is done, the suspension of perception is the result.

"In this way": When, as a result of constraint upon sound, touch, taste, or smell in relation to the body, the power of these four sensory objects to be known is suspended, and when there is no connection between the light <note>referring to the sensory medium of the observer</note> and the observer's organs of hearing, touch, taste, or smell—then the yogi becomes imperceptible to those organs. This, with the necessary changes having been made <note>original Latin: mutatis mutandis</note>, is the meaning of the <term>sūtra</term> <note>An aphorism or concise rule of spiritual philosophy</note>.

---

¹ These <insert>the adjuncts or associations</insert> Bālarāma has defined in his note (5) on p. 230⁵ (Calcutta edition).

<page-num>251</page-num>
<header>Fast and slow development of karma [—iii. 22</header>

**22. Advancing and not-advancing is karma;** as a result of constraint upon this [two-fold karma] or from the signs of death [there arises an intuitive] knowledge of the latter end. 

<term>Karma</term> <note>The law of cause and effect where past actions determine future circumstances</note> having its <term>fruition</term> <note>The "ripening" or realization of consequences</note> in length-of-life is of two kinds: the **advancing** <note>Sopakrama; karma that is actively manifesting its results</note> and the **not-advancing** <note>Nirupakrama; karma that is dormant or maturing slowly</note>. 

Of the two: 
1. Just as a wet cloth spread out dries in a shorter time, so is **advancing karma**; 
2. And just as the same cloth rolled into a ball becomes dry a long time after, so is **not-advancing karma**. 

Furthermore:
1. **Advancing karma** is also like fire set in dry grass, which spreads on all sides with the breeze and burns in the briefest time. 
2. And just as the same fire, put bit by bit into a pile of grass, burns a long time after, so is **not-advancing karma**. 

This is the karma having its limit in a single existence and causing the specific length of one's life, divided into these two kinds. As a result of <term>constraint</term> <note>Samyama; the technical practice of unified focus, meditation, and absorption</note> upon this, there is intuitive knowledge of the **latter end** <note>The moment of death or the departure of the soul from the body</note>.

—<Or from the **signs of death** there arises an intuitive knowledge of the latter end.> 

A **sign of death** <note>Ariṣṭa; portents or omens signaling that death is near</note> is of three kinds: 
1. That pertaining to **self**, 
2. That pertaining to **other creatures**, 
3. And that pertaining to **divine beings**. 

Of these three:
1. A **sign of death pertaining to one's self** would occur when one with stopped ears does not hear the sound of the <term>vital spirits</term> <note>The internal resonance or life-force sounds within the body</note> within one's own body; or when one with closed eyes does not see the inner light. 
2. Likewise, a **sign pertaining to other creatures** would occur when one sees the **Men of Yama** <note>The messengers or agents of the God of Death</note>, or when one unexpectedly sees the **Fathers** <note>Pitrs; the spirits of deceased ancestors</note> who have departed. 
3. Similarly, a **sign pertaining to divine beings** would occur when one sees heaven or the **Siddhas** <note>Perfected or semi-divine beings with supernatural powers</note> unexpectedly, or when the natural order of everything appears reversed. 

By these signs, the practitioner also perceives that the end of life is near at hand.

**22. Advancing . . . or . . .** 

And karma having its fruition in length-of-life is of two kinds: the advancing and the not-advancing. Now that karma—which is limited to a single existence and which is the source of one's birth, the length of one's life, and the quality of one's experiences—reaches its fruition in the span of that life. 

1. And this karma is ready to provide that experience without the delay of even a very— <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page</note>

short time. It has afforded much of its intended enjoyment and only a little of its fruit remains. Its active manifestation continues only because it is impossible for it to have its total ripening suddenly in one body; therefore it delays. This is **advancing [karma]**. The "advance" is the active manifestation; the <term>karma</term> <note>The law of cause and effect where past actions determine future circumstances</note> is connected with this active manifestation. 

2. The same karma, when it affords little fruit and requires time for this, and when, engaged in providing fruit, its manifestation is intermittent and slow, is **not-advancing**. This same point is made clear in two similes with the words "Of these 1. just as." On the same point, for greater clearness, the author gives another simile in the words "2. Or just as fire."

The ultimate-end is the great <term>cosmic dissolution</term> <note>original: 'mahapralaya'; the end of a world cycle</note>. As compared with this, death is the "latter end." As a result of <term>meditative constraint</term> <note>original: 'samyama'; the technical practice of unified focus, meditation, and absorption</note> upon the right-living and wrong-living <note>virtue and vice</note> in that karma, there follows intuitive knowledge of the latter end <note>the time of death</note>. And as a result of this the <term>yogin</term> <note>A practitioner of yoga</note>, knowing his own karma which is advancing, and having created many bodies for himself, experiences suddenly the fruit of his karma and dies when he wills. 

Incidentally, the author says "Or [the intuitive knowledge of the latter end] is the result of the **signs-of-death**." Signs-of-death <note>original: 'ariṣṭa'</note> are things which terrify, such as an enemy <note>original: 'ari'</note>. These indications of death are of three kinds. 

"Or when everything is reversed"—that is, even when there is no magic or trickery involved, the person deems villages and cities to be heaven, and thinks the world of mere human beings to be a world of divine beings <note>This refers to the cognitive distortions or hallucinations that may precede death</note>.

### **23. [As a result of constraint] upon friendliness and other [sentiments there arises] powers [of friendliness].**

**Friendliness**¹ and **compassion** and **joy** are the three sentiments. As to these three, by feeling friendliness for living beings who are in a state of happiness, the practitioner discovers the **power of friendliness**; by feeling compassion for those in pain, he discovers the **power of compassion**; by feeling joy for those who are disposed to merit <note>virtue</note>, he discovers the **power of joy**. As a result of these sentiments, there arises the <term>meditative constraint</term> which is concentration, and from it there arise powers of unfailing energy. 

**Indifference**, however, for those disposed to evil is not one of these practiced sentiments. And therefore, there is no concentration upon it. For this reason, since it is impossible to perform meditative constraint upon it, there is no "power" resulting from indifference <note>Indifference is a neutral state of withdrawal rather than an active cultivation of energy</note>.

### **23. [As a result of constraint] upon friendliness and other [sentiments there arises] powers [of friendliness].**

By meditative constraint upon friendliness and other sentiments, he gains powers of friendliness and other powers. Of these three, as a result of the sentiment—

--- Page 299 ---
<meta>Continuity check: This page completes the discussion on predicting death from Sutra 22 and begins the explanation of the "Social" or "Ethical" powers derived from the four sublime states—friendliness, compassion, and joy—in Sutra 23.</meta>

Through the cultivation of friendliness there arises in the practitioner that kind of power by which he makes everybody happy. As a result of this, he is kindly to all. Similarly, through the power resulting from compassion, he delivers living beings from pain and from the causes of pain. Likewise, through the power of joy, he imparts a detached attitude to everybody. He states what will be of assistance in the following sections, namely, that these sentiments cause concentration, as he says: "As a result of the sentiments there arises the constraint which is concentration." Although <term>constraint</term> <note>original: 'samyama'; the unified practice of focus, meditation, and absorption</note> consists of three parts—fixed-attention, contemplation, and concentration—and not concentration alone, concentration is used here as a figure of speech for constraint, since constraint follows as an effect after concentration, and concentration is the most dominant of the three. Some manuscripts read ‘The sentiments are concentration.’ In this case, we must suppose that the sentiments and concentration, as being parts of the whole which is constraint, serve as the causes of that constraint. "Energy" refers to exertion. By its means, a person who has the powers of friendliness and so forth towards those in happiness and so forth, becomes unfailing in his exertion when tasks are to be performed for others. Indifference is the detached attitude <note>original: 'upekṣā'; equanimity or neutrality</note>. In this case of indifference, there is no sentiment <note>meaning no active emotional projection</note>, nor is there anything that might arise out of it as is the case with those who are experiencing happiness.

### **24. As a result of constraint upon powers, there arise powers like those of an elephant.**

As a result of <term>meditative constraint</term> upon the power of an elephant, one gains the power of an elephant. As a result of constraint upon the power of <term>Vāinateya</term> <note>The son of Vinata, also known as the <term>Garuḍa</term> bird, the divine king of birds</note>, one gains the power of <term>Vāinateya</term>. As a result of constraint upon the power of the wind, one gains the power of the wind. And so forth in the same way.

**24.** [As a result of constraint] upon powers [there arise] powers like those of an elephant. He gains the power of whatever thing upon which he exercises his meditative constraint.

### **25. As a result of casting the light of a sense-activity, there arises the intuitive knowledge of the subtile and the concealed and the obscure.**

The <term>yogin</term> <note>A practitioner of yoga</note>, by casting the light of that sense-activity of the central organ which is called "luminous" <note>referring to Sutra i. 36, the sorrowless, luminous state of mind</note> upon an object—whether it be subtile<gloss>1</gloss>, concealed, or obscure—gains direct access to that object.

25. . . . Sense-activity . . . intuitive knowledge. By casting his mind with meditative constraint upon a subtile, concealed, or obscure intended-object, he has access to that intended-object.

## 26. As a result of constraint upon the sun [there arises the intuitive] knowledge of the cosmic-spaces <note>original: 'bhuvana'</note>.

The enumeration of these cosmic-spaces: there are seven worlds. Among them: 

1. Starting from the Bottomless Hell <note>original: 'Avīci'; the lowest level of existence</note> and extending up to the summit of the central mountain <note>original: 'Meru'</note> is the Earth-world <note>original: 'bhū-loka'</note>. 
2. Beginning from the summit of the central mountain and going as far as the Pole-star <note>original: 'dhruva'</note> is the world of Intermediate Space, which is made diverse by planets, constellations, and stars. 

Beyond that is the five-fold Heaven-world <note>original: 'svar-loka'</note>: 

3. The world of Great Indra <note>original: 'Mahendra'</note>, the third world.
4. The Great world <note>original: 'Mahar'</note> of the Lord of Creatures <note>original: 'Prajāpati'</note>, the fourth world. 
5. The three-fold world of Brahma, consisting of the World of Generation <note>original: 'Jana'</note>.
6. The World of Austerity <note>original: 'Tapas'</note>.
7. The World of Truth <note>original: 'Satya'</note>. <note>These seven layers represent the totality of the manifest universe in ancient Indian thought.</note>

> “The world-of-Brahma in its three stages,
> Below it the world-of-Prajāpati, the Great [world],
> And [below it] Mahendra’s [world]: [these five] are called
> Heaven <note>original: 'svar'</note>.
> In the sky [of Intermediate-Space] are the stars; on earth,
> the creatures.”

Thus says the Summary-Stanza. Rising in a series above the Bottomless Hell, there are six regions <note>original: 'bhūmi'</note> of the Great-Hell <note>original: 'mahā-naraka'</note>, supported respectively by solid matter, water, fire, wind, air, and darkness. Their names are: The Great Black, the Frying Pan, the Howling, the Great Howling, the Thread of Time, and the Blind Darkness <note>original: 'Mahākāla, Ambarīṣa, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Kālasūtra, and Andhatāmisra'</note>. In these realms, living creatures are born to experience the misery incurred as the result of their own actions <note>original: 'karma'</note>, having been allotted a long and grievous length of life. 

Next are the seven lower-worlds <note>original: 'pātāla'</note>, named Great-surface, Moisture-surface, Without-surface, Well-situated, Distinct-surface, Surface-below-surface, and the Bottomless <note>original: 'Mahātala, Rasātala, Atala, Sutala, Vitala, Talātala, and Pātāla'</note>.

And as the eighth, there is this earth with its seven lands <note>original: 'dvīpa'; often translated as islands or continents</note>, and in the midst of it, the golden King of Mountains, Sumeru. Its peaks on the four sides are made of gems of silver, of lapis...

In the third world of Brahma, in the <term>Satya-world</term> <note>the World of Truth</note>, there are four groups of gods: the <term>Acyutas</term> <note>the Unfallen</note>, the <term>Çuddhanivāsas</term> <note>those of the Pure Abodes</note>, the <term>Satyābhas</term> <note>the Truth-Shining</note>, and the <term>Saṁjñāsaṁjñins</term> <note>those with and without perception</note>. By them no laying down foundations for a dwelling is made; they are grounded in themselves and placed one above the other; they have the mastery over the primary cause <note>original: 'pradhāna'; the fundamental root of nature</note> and live as long as there are creations. 

Of these four, the <term>Acyutas</term> delight in deliberative contemplation; the <term>Çuddhanivāsas</term> delight in reflective contemplation; the <term>Satyābhas</term> delight in contemplation where there is nothing but joy; and the <term>Saṁjñāsaṁjñins</term> delight in contemplation where there is the feeling of personality and nothing more. These also remain in the three worlds. <note>Specifically within the "World-Egg" or the physical universe; they are not yet fully released from the cycle of existence.</note> These seven worlds are all without exceptions worlds of the Brahman. But the discarnate and those whose bodies are resolved into primary matter exist in the state of release and are not placed in the worlds. By performing constraint <note>original: 'saṃyama'; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and absorption</note> upon the <term>door of the sun</term> <note>This refers to the spiritual gateway to the higher realms, often described in ancient texts like the Māitrī, Muṇḍaka, and Chāndogya Upaniṣads</note> the yogin should directly perceive all this. Then also upon other objects than upon the sun. Thus to this extent he should practise, until all this is seen.

### 26. As a result of constraint upon the sun [there arises the intuitive] knowledge of the cosmic-spaces (*bhuvana*).

Up to the pole-star from the summit of <term>Meru</term> <note>the sacred mountain at the center of the world</note> in this world. Thus in this way from here up to the end of the <term>Summary-Stanza</term> <note>original: 'saṁgraha-çloka'</note> the seven worlds <note>For further reading, see historical studies on the "Abode of the Blest."</note> are briefly described. He describes them in detail in the words «Among them . . . above <term>Avīci</term>» <note>the lowest and "waveless" hell</note>. The word «solid-matter» means earth. The word «region» means a place but not a hell. These great hells must be understood to be accompanied by several lesser hells. These same are brought together under other names in the words, «<term>Mahākāla</term>» <note>Great Time</note>. As the sun moves forward, day and night revolve about <term>Sumeru</term>, as it were fast bound to him. The meaning is that night is in that part of it which the sun leaves; and day is in that part which the sun shines upon. He gives the extent of the whole <term>Land of the Rose-Apple</term> <note>original: 'Jambudvīpa'; the continent inhabited by humans</note>.

He now tells who they are that dwell there in the words «Here, in the lower-world.» He describes the arrangement of Sumeru in the words, «Sumeru is»—Thus having described the Earth-world specifically, he describes specifically the world of Intermediate Space with the words «The planets.» The «impulsion» is the functional activity.—He shows the Heaven-world in the words «They who dwell [in the world of] <term>Mahendra</term> <note>the Great Indra, king of the gods</note>.»

3. «Groups of gods» are kinds of gods. He also describes the perfection of the form of the six groups of gods by saying «All [these] fulfill their desires.» All objects yield to them even at nothing more than a desire. «Goodly to behold» [that is] to be worshipped. They delight in love [that is] are fond of sexual pleasure. Their bodies are not caused by parents, [but] quite without cause; without union of parents, they obtain a supernal body from atoms thoroughly purified¹ by peculiar merit. 

4. He describes the <term>Mahar-world</term> <note>the "Great" world, the fourth of the seven upper worlds</note> in the words, «In the Great.» These have the mastery over the great elements. Whatever they like the great elements confer upon them. And the great elements remain in this or that arrangement as they desire. «Their food is contemplation» means that they are sated with contemplation merely and are nourished [thereby]. 

5. He describes the <term>Jana-world</term> <note>the "World of People," the fifth world</note> with the words «In the first.» In accordance with the order of the worlds as described «they have the mastery over the elements and the organs.» Earth and the other elements, and the organ-of-hearing and the other organs are employed just as they choose to employ them.

So say those who have the tradition. «Twice as long as the previous.» The <term>Great Radiant Ones</term> <note>original: 'Mahābhāsvaras'</note> have double as long a life as the <term>Luminous Ones</term> <note>original: 'Ābhāsvaras'</note>; and the <term>Great Radiant Ones of Truth</term> <note>original: 'Satyamahābhāsvaras'</note> have double as long a life as these latter. «Upwards.» Upwards in the <term>World of Truth</term> <note>original: 'Satya-loka'; the highest of the seven heavens</note> there is no impediment to their thinking. But from the <term>Deepest Hell</term> <note>original: 'Avīci'</note> right up to the <term>World of Penance</term> <note>original: 'Tapas-loka'</note> they discern all subtle and concealed or other things. This is the meaning.

7. He describes the third world of Brahma in the words «In the third.» They are so described by whom the laying down of a dwelling or house has not been made. Just because they have nothing to hold them, they are grounded in themselves. They are such as are grounded in their own bodies. They have the mastery over the primary cause; at their wish the <term>purity</term> <note>original: 'sattva'</note>, <term>activity</term> <note>original: 'rajas'</note>, and <term>inertia</term> <note>original: 'tamas'; these three qualities represent the fundamental forces of nature</note> come into activity. «They live as long as the creation,» as it is handed down in the Sacred Word <note>Note: This refers to the traditional scriptures. Contrast with the Vāyu Purāṇa, book 101, verse 85</note>, “All these having perfected their souls, together <note>Note: Compare the Bhagavad Gītā, chapter 8, verse 16</note> with Brahma enter, when the <term>dissolution of the universe</term> <note>original: 'pratisaṁcara'</note> is reached at the end of the highest [world], into the highest state.”

Having thus stated the common qualities of these four groups of gods, he describes their special qualities by taking them up in detail with the words, «Of these [four].» The gods called <term>The Unfallen</term> <note>original: 'Acyuta'</note> take delight in contemplation upon coarse objects. With this they are satisfied. The gods called <term>The Pure Abodes</term> <note>original: 'Çuddhanivāsa'</note> take delight in contemplation upon subtle objects. With this they are satisfied. The gods called <term>The Luminous Truths</term> <note>original: 'Satyābhas'</note> take delight in contemplation upon the sense organs <note>Note: Compare Vācaspati’s commentary on section 1.41: "as if it had become an external organ; thus it is accompanied by joy"</note> as objects. With this they are satisfied. The gods called <term>Those with and without Perception</term> <note>original: 'Saṁjñāsaṁjñins'</note> take delight in contemplation upon the feeling of personality and nothing more. With this they are satisfied. All these have recourse to <term>conscious concentration</term> <note>absorption directed toward an object</note>.

And if it be asked why there is no mention here, among [these] worlds, of those who have given themselves to concentration not conscious [of an object], those namely who are discarnate and those [whose bodies] are resolved into primary matter, the reply is «But the <term>bodiless ones</term> <note>original: 'videha'; those who have reached a state of existence without physical form</note> and those [whose bodies] are <term>resolved into nature</term> <note>original: 'prakṛtilaya'; those whose awareness has merged back into the root cause of the material world</note>.» For those whose thinking-substance is in fluctuation, and to whom objects are shown, carry on worldly affairs and remain in the world. But the bodiless and those resolved into nature, although they have a task to perform, do not so remain. This is the meaning.—All this, with the exception of the World of Truth and as far [down] as the Deepest Hell, is directly perceptible to the <term>yogi</term> <note>a practitioner of yoga who has attained supernormal vision</note>.

«Upon the door of the sun» means upon the tube called the <term>Central Channel</term> <note>original: 'Suṣumṇā'; the primary psychic passage in the subtle body</note>. And inasmuch as, even with such an extent [of meditation], direct perception of [all] this does not occur, he says «Then.» Then also upon other [objects], that is, also upon objects other than the Central Channel taught by the professor of yoga, until all this world is seen. For the <term>luminous purity</term> <note>original: 'sattva'</note> of the thinking-substance is by its own nature capable of illumining the whole [world]. But when covered by the defilement...

# Book III. Supernormal Powers or <term>Vibhūti</term> <note>original: 'Vibhūti'; refers to the extraordinary powers or 'perfections' gained through advanced yoga practice</note>

of <term>inertia</term> <note>original: 'tamas'</note> it illumines only that portion which is laid bare by <term>activity</term> <note>original: 'rajas'</note>. It illumines the cosmic space laid bare by the <term>constraint</term> <note>original: 'saṃyama'; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and absorption</note> upon the door of the sun. But this does not apply similarly in other cases also. Since constraint upon this cosmic space has power to lay only so much bare. Thus all is cleared up.

**27. [As a result of constraint] upon the moon [there arises the intuitive] knowledge of the arrangement of the stars.**

By performing constraint upon the moon he would discern the arrangement of the stars.

**28. [As a result of constraint] upon the pole-star [there arises the intuitive] knowledge of their movements.**

Then by performing constraint upon the pole-star he would know the movements of the stars. By constraint upon heavenly cars, [for example, the chariot of the sun], he would discern them.

**29. [As a result of constraint] upon the wheel of the navel [there arises the intuitive] knowledge of the arrangement of the body.**

By performing constraint upon the <term>wheel</term> <note>original: 'cakra'</note> <gloss>1</gloss> of the navel he would discern the arrangement of the body. The <term>humours</term> <note>original: 'doṣa'</note> are three: <term>wind</term> <note>original: 'vāta'</note>, <term>bile</term> <note>original: 'pitta'</note>, and <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: 'kapha'</note>. The <term>corporeal elements</term> <note>original: 'dhātu'</note> <gloss>2</gloss> are seven: skin and blood and flesh and sinew and bone and marrow and semen. Here (*eṣa*) the mention is such that the preceding element is in each case exterior to that next preceding.

**30. [As a result of constraint] upon the well of the throat [there follows] the cessation of hunger and of thirst.**

Below the tongue there is a cord; below that is the throat; below that the well. As a result of concentration upon that, hunger and thirst do not torment.

<header>261] Specimens of applied power [—iii. 33</header>

### 31. Through meditative <term>constraint</term> <note>original: 'saṃyama'; the unified practice of concentration, meditation, and absorption</note> upon the tortoise-shaped vessel, there follows the stillness of the <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>original: 'citta'; the foundational layers of consciousness</note>.

Beneath the hollow of the throat, within the chest, there is a subtle channel shaped like a tortoise. By performing <term>constraint</term> upon this vessel, the <term>yogin</term> <note>a dedicated practitioner of yoga</note> achieves a state of absolute motionlessness, similar to that of a serpent or a lizard.¹

Whenever the <term>yogin</term> desires to know one thing or another, they should perform <term>constraint</term> upon that specific object. Thus, the practice of <term>constraint</term> which leads to the cessation of hunger and thirst, and which leads to physical stillness, is taught by the words of the <term>Sutra</term> <note>the aphorisms of Patanjali</note> and is explained by the Commentary with an explanation that is simply a matter of reading the text. Therefore, it is not further explained here.

### 32. Through <term>constraint</term> upon the radiance in the head, there follows the vision of the <term>Siddhas</term> <note>original: 'Siddhas'; perfected beings or semi-divine masters who roam the celestial realms</note>.

Within an aperture in the skull, there is a resplendent, brilliant light.² As a result of focusing <term>constraint</term> upon this radiance, the practitioner attains the sight of the <term>Siddhas</term> who move through the spaces between the sky³ and the earth.

**32. Through <term>constraint</term> upon the radiance in the head, there follows the vision of the Siddhas.**

The phrase "in the head" refers to the subtle energy channel (*nāḍī*) known as the <term>Susumna</term> <note>original: 'Suṣumṇā'; the central channel of the subtle body</note>—the author means one should perform <term>constraint</term> upon that.

### 33. Or, through the power of spiritual <term>vividness</term> <note>original: 'prātibha'; spontaneous, intuitive illumination or 'flash' of knowledge</note>, the yogin discerns all.

This so-called "vividness" is the <term>deliverer</term> <note>original: 'tāraka'; literally 'the one who helps cross over'</note>.⁴ This is the preliminary form of the intuitive knowledge derived from discrimination. It is like the light at dawn which precedes the rising of the sun. In this alternative way, the <term>yogin</term> knows everything⁵ at the moment this vivid, intuitive knowledge arises.

**33. Or, through the power of spiritual vividness (*prātibha*), the yogin discerns all.**

Vivid light is a form of spontaneous <term>reasoning</term> <note>original: 'ūha'; the faculty of mental discovery</note>. This develops into full spiritual vividness. For in the case of one who practices a <term>constraint</term> which leads to the Elevation <note>The text likely refers to the 'Elevation of Peace', original: 'praśam-'; the manuscript appears to break off here</note>.

### 34. [As a result of meditative constraint] upon the heart [there arises] a consciousness of the mind-stuff.

In this citadel of the Absolute <note>original: 'Brahma'; refers here to the body as a temple. **34. [As a result of constraint] upon the heart [there arises] a consciousness of the mind-stuff.**

The word "heart" is explained in the words, "in the citadel of the Absolute." Because it is great <note>original: 'br̥hat'</note> the self is the Absolute. His "citadel" is his retreat. For with reference to this [citadel] he knows this—that it is his property. The cave is a den. That same lotus with its head turned downward is the dwelling of the central-organ <note>the 'manas' or coordinating mind</note>. He gives the reason for this consciousness of the <term>mind-stuff</term> by saying "a discernment of that." By <term>constraint</term> upon this, he discerns the <term>mind-stuff</term> with its own peculiar fluctuations.

### 35. Experience is a presented-idea which fails to distinguish the *sattva* and the Self, which are absolutely uncommingled [in the presented-idea]. ### 35. [Experience comes from the failure to distinguish between the Self and the pure quality of the mind, which are absolutely unmingled. By meditative constraint upon that which exists for its own sake (the Self), distinct from that which exists for another (the mind), there arises knowledge of the Self.]

. . . <term>pure quality</term> . . . [intuitive] knowledge. When, by reason of its being altogether overwhelmed by the <term>active quality</term> <note>original: 'rajas'; the quality of passion and movement</note> and the <term>dark quality</term> <note>original: 'tamas'; the quality of inertia and ignorance</note>, even the <term>thinking-substance</term>, bright in form and exceedingly clear though it is, can in its mutation as a <term>discriminative discernment</term> <note>the ability to tell the difference between the material mind and the spiritual Self</note>, be absolutely distinguished from intelligence, how much more so then the <term>active</term> and <term>dark</term> qualities, which are inert <note>original: 'jaḍa'; unconscious or material</note> by nature! With this in mind the author of the Sūtras <note>Patañjali</note> uses the words, 〈the <term>pure quality</term> and the Self.〉 Taking up this same point the author of the Comment <note>Vyāsa</note> also says «The <term>pure quality</term> of the <term>thinking-substance</term>, with its disposition to brightness.» Not merely one whose disposition is to brightness, but one which has entered into a mutation in the form of <term>discriminative discernment</term>. Inasmuch as it is altogether undefiled [by objects] and bright, it is absolutely similar to intelligence <note>original: 'cāitanya'; the pure awareness of the Self</note>. So there is a commingling, as he implies in the words «equal.» «Dependent upon the <term>pure quality</term>» means a relation without which it cannot exist. The <term>active</term> and <term>dark</term> qualities which are equally dependent upon the <term>pure quality</term> are so-called [in the Comment]. Mastered means overwhelmed. He states that there is no commingling in the words «Therefore . . . even.» The word *ca* is here in the sense of ‘even’. [Contrary in quality] not merely to the <term>active</term> and <term>dark</term> qualities [but even to the <term>pure quality</term>]. This is the meaning. The word «mutable» indicates the quality contrary to the Self who is immutable. A presented idea which fails to distinguish, because the <term>thinking-substance</term>, which is serene and cruel and infatuated, takes the image of the intelligence <note>original: 'cāitanya'</note>. And so the serene and other forms are falsely attributed to the intelligence, just as the trembling of the clear water which reflects the moon is falsely attributed to the moon <note>A classic Indian philosophical metaphor: the moon (Self) is still, but it appears to move when reflected in moving water (the mind)</note>. He gives the reason for the experience in the words «Because the Self has objects shown to it.» This has been explained more than once.^2 If it be objected that the <term>pure quality</term> of the <term>thinking-substance</term> might be different from...

...the Self, but that experience could not be different from the Self, he replies «This [same].» This [same] presented-idea of experience is a presented-idea of a kind of experience belonging to the <term>pure quality</term> <note>original: 'sattva'; the highest, most transparent aspect of the mind-stuff</note>. Hence as something for the sake of another, experience is an object-for-sight. For the <term>pure quality</term> is for the sake of another in that it is a combination of parts <note>In this school of thought, anything composed of various qualities is seen as a "tool" or "object" intended for use by a higher, singular consciousness</note>. And because experience is an external-aspect of this <term>pure quality</term>, it would also be for the sake of another. Furthermore, that other for whose sake it is, would be the experiencer. His is the experience. — Or [another explanation]. For <term>experience</term> <note>original: 'bhoga'</note> is <term>passing-through</term> <note>original: 'anubhava'</note> pleasure or pain which are felt to be coactive or counteractive. And this [experience] cannot be coactive or counteractive to itself. Because a fluctuation cannot be opposed to itself. Therefore experience must be for the sake of something that is to be made coactive or counteractive. This experiencer is the self. Experience is an object-for-sight to him. 

«But . . . that presented-idea, which is distinguished from this» which is for the sake of another. These words [from the Comment] are explained by supplying the other words in the ablative case 'for the sake of another'. An objector says, 'This may be true. But if the insight has the Self for its object, then whew! Sir! the Self becomes the object-for-insight by the insight! There would surely be other insights, one after the other, and we should fall into an <term>infinite regress</term>!' <note>A logical trap where a process must repeat forever because there is no final stopping point; here, if the mind observes the Self, something else must observe that observation, and so on</note> In reply to this he says «The Self is not . . . . by that presented-idea of the Self.» 

The connexion-of-ideas is this. The <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: 'citi'</note> illumines that which is <term>inert</term> <note>original: 'jaḍa'; that which lacks its own light or consciousness, like the mind or physical matter</note>, and that which is inert does not [illumine] the intellect. The idea presented to the Self has as its essence that which is not intelligent. How can this [presented-idea] illumine a being whose essence is intelligence? On the other hand, how can [the Self], whose essence is intelligence and whose brightness does not depend upon another, be properly said to illumine that which is inert? When he says «whose essence is the <term>pure quality</term> of the thinking-substance» he describes the inertness in so far as there is identity with the non-intelligent form. 

[We say that the <term>pure quality</term> of the thinking-substance] depends upon the Self to the extent that it depends on the image of the Self as entered into the <term>pure quality</term> of the thinking-substance, in the same sense that a person depends upon [his] face reflected in a mirror [if he wish to see himself]. [And the <term>pure quality</term> is said to depend upon the Self.] But not [as the objector said], because the <term>pure quality</term> of the thinking-substance illumines the Self. It is the <term>pure quality</term> of the thinking-substance which reflects the Self united with this presented-idea, and which depends upon the <term>Intelligence</term> <note>original: 'caitanya'</note> which has been <term>mirrored</term> <note>original: 'chāyāpanna'; literally 'fallen into the shadow' or reflected</note> in it [as the intelligence] of the Self. Thus it exists for the sake of the Self. On this same point he quotes the Sacred Word by saying «For in this sense it has been said» by the <term>Lord</term> <note>original: 'Içvara'; the Supreme Being or Source of wisdom</note> «"the Discerner."» The meaning is that [He is discerned] by no one.

<summary>This page argues that while the mind (sattva) reflects the Self, the Self remains the ultimate subject and observer. Using a mirror metaphor, the text explains that the mind is an inert object that only appears conscious because it reflects the true Self, thus avoiding the logical trap of infinite regress.</summary>

<header>Hyperaesthetic sensations [—iii. 37</header>

## 36. As a result of this [constraint upon that which exists for its own sake], there arise vividness and the organ-of-[supernal]-hearing¹ and the organ-of-[supernal]-feeling and the organ-of-[supernal]-sight and the organ-of-[supernal]-taste and the organ-of-[supernal]-smell.

As a result of vividness, there arises an [intuitive] knowledge of the subtile or concealed or remote, whether past or future. As a result of the organ-of-[supernal]-hearing, one hears supernal <note>meaning divine or heavenly</note> sounds ; as a result of the organ-of-[supernal]-feeling, one has access to supernal touch ; as a result of the organ-of-[supernal]-sight, one has the consciousness ² of supernal colour ; as a result of the organ-of-[supernal]-taste, one has a consciousness of supernal flavour ; as a result of the organ-of-[supernal]-smell,³ one has an [intuitive] knowledge ⁴ of supernal fragrance. These unceasingly arise.

This restraint, moreover, upon that which exists for its own sake <note>the Self</note> continues until the primary cause has fulfilled its peculiar <term>task</term> <note>original: 'kārya'</note>, the [intuitive] knowledge of the Self. He describes all the supernormal powers which [the yogin] receives before that [intuitive knowledge comes]. **36. As a result of this . . . there arise . . .** So then it has been asserted that the central-organ and the organ of hearing and of feeling and of sight and of taste and of smell, which have been helped by the external-aspects which arise from yoga, are in each single case in direct causal relation with the supernal sounds and so forth and with the [intuitive] knowledge of <term>vividness</term> <note>original: 'prātibha'; referring to a flash of intuitive genius</note>. The five organs, of hearing and so on, which apperceive supernal sounds and so forth have technical names such as the organ-of-[supernal]-hearing and the rest. The Comment is easy.

## 37. In concentration these [supernal activities] are obstacles ; in the emergent state they are perfections <note>original: 'siddhi'; supernatural powers</note>.

These, the vividness and so forth, arising in the yogin whose mind-stuff is concentrated, are obstacles, in that they go counter to the sight which belongs to this [concentrated mind-stuff].

<header>iii. 37—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or Manifestations</header>

[But] arising [in the yogin] whose mind-stuff is emergent <note>meaning the mind is active and directed toward the external world rather than absorbed in deep meditation</note>, they are perfections.

Occasionally a man, after beginning constraint <note>the combined practice of fixed attention, contemplation, and concentration</note> upon the self as the object of his focus, acquires those perfections which are subsidiary to this, and thinks because of the power <note>original: 'prabhāva'</note> of these [perfections] that he has effected his purpose, and so might cease the constraint. So [the author] says, 

**37. In concentration these [supernal activities] are obstacles; in the emergent state they are perfections (<term>siddhi</term>).** 

For a man whose mind-stuff is emergent <note>functioning in the ordinary state of consciousness</note> thinks highly of these perfections, just as a man born in misery considers even a bit of wealth a pile of wealth. But a yogin whose mind-stuff is concentrated must avoid these [perfections] even when brought near to him. One who longs for the final goal of life, the absolute assuagement of the three-fold anguish <note>the traditional Indian classification of suffering: internal (physical/mental), external (other beings), and divine (natural forces)</note>, how could he have any affection for those perfections which go counter to [the attainment] of that [goal]? This is the meaning both of the Aphorism and of the Comment.

### 38. As a result of slackening the causes of bondage and as a result of the consciousness of the procedure [of the mind-stuff], the mind-stuff penetrates into the body of another.

By virtue of the latent-deposit of <term>karma</term> <note>the storehouse of past actions and their potential effects</note> in the body, the central-organ <note>the mind or 'manas'</note> which is changeable and unstable becomes established. This is bondage. By virtue of concentration there is a slackening of this <term>karma</term> which is the cause of bondage. And the consciousness of the procedure <note>the pathway or movement</note> [of the mind-stuff] comes only from concentration. As a result of the dwindling of the bondage of <term>karma</term>, and as a result of the consciousness of the procedure of his mind-stuff, the yogin by withdrawing mind-stuff from his own body deposits it in other bodies. The organs <note>the senses and vital forces</note> also fly after [see ii. 54] the mind-stuff thus deposited. Just <note>Compare the Prashna Upanishad, chapter 2, verse 4.</note> as, for instance, when the king-bee flies up, the bees fly up after him, so the organs follow after the mind-stuff in its penetration into the body of another.

After thus stating that power, in the form of [intuitive] knowledge extending as far as the sight of the Self, is the result of constraint, he gives, as another result of constraint, power in the form of action. **38. . . . The causes of bondage . . . penetration.** When he says «By virtue of concentration» this means under 1. the power of the constraint whose object is the causes of bondage. The word «concentration» is used [instead of ‘constraint,’] because it is predominant [in constraint].—A procedure is that by which something proceeds into...

<header>Externalizing of mind-stuff [—iii. 39</header>

...another thing. It means the <term>channels</term> <note>original: 'nāḍī'; subtle conduits within the body for energy and consciousness</note>—that is, the paths for the coming and going of the mind-stuff. As a result of 2. performing constraint <note>the combined practice of fixed attention, contemplation, and concentration</note> upon this passage, there is a conscious awareness of it. And as a result of this [as well as of 1. the constraint upon the causes of bondage], since the causes that bind the soul to the body are loosened, the mind-stuff is not held back by this <term>yoga practitioner</term> <note>original: 'yogin'</note>. Although the mind-stuff is not restricted as it soars into the upward path, it cannot pass out from his body or enter into another's body without an unobstructed path. Therefore, the passage for this must also be known. Furthermore, the sensory and motor organs follow the mind-stuff and settle down in their respective places in the other person's body.

**39. By mastering the <term>upward breath</term>, one avoids contact with water, mud, thorns, and similar objects, and gains the power of rising upward [at death].**
<note>original: 'Udāna'; the specific vital force governing the upper body and throat</note>

The movement of the entire complex of organs, which is distinguished by the different <term>vital forces</term> <note>original: 'prāṇa'</note>, constitutes vitality or life. <gloss>1</gloss> Its activity is five-fold. The <term>in-breath</term> <note>original: 'Prāṇa'</note> has its course through the mouth and nose, and its movement extends as far as the heart. The <term>equalizing breath</term> <note>original: 'Samāna'</note>, so named because it distributes nutrients and energy equally, has its movement starting from the navel. The <term>downward breath</term> <note>original: 'Apāna'</note>, which leads away or down, moves as far as the soles of the feet. The <term>upward breath</term> <note>original: 'Udāna'</note>, which leads upward, moves as far as the head. The <term>pervasive breath</term> <note>original: 'Vyāna'</note> spreads throughout the entire body. Among these, the <term>in-breath</term> is the primary force. By mastering the <term>upward breath</term>, one does not sink into water or mud, and is not pricked by thorns or similar objects; and at the time of death, there is an upward ascent of the soul. This upward flight is attained through mastery of the <term>upward breath</term>.

39. <term>Upward breath</term> . . . and . . . the upward flight. The active movement of the whole complex of organs is life. The words "distinguished by having the different vital forces" refer to that movement of which the various breaths are the defining parts. The organs have two kinds of movements: an inner and an outer. The outer is distinguished by the <term>sensory perception</term> <note>original: 'ālocana'</note> of colors and similar sensations. The inner movement is life itself. For this is a special kind of effort that leads to the different activities of the <term>vital winds</term> <note>original: 'māruta'</note> which the body contains. This effort is common to all the organs. As they say <gloss>2</gloss> "The movements common to the internal organs are the five <term>vital winds</term> <note>original: 'vāyu'</note>—the vital breaths and so on." This is because these winds are the identifying characteristics of life.

(Book III. 15). It is also mentioned in the list in verse 18.

<page-num>268</page-num>
<header>iii. 39—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or Vibhūti [268</header>

The action [or] function of this effort is of five kinds:

1. **<term>In-breath</term>** <note>original: 'Prāṇa'</note> extends from the tip of the nose to the heart.
2. **<term>Equalizing breath</term>** <note>original: 'Samāna'</note> is one which evenly distributes as required in different places the various juices which are mutations of food eaten and drunk. And its locality extends from the heart and to the navel.
3. **<term>Downward breath</term>** <note>original: 'Apāna'</note> is that which leads to the carrying off of urine, faeces, foetus, &c. And its activity <note>original: 'vṛtti'</note> is from the navel and to the sole of the foot.
4. **<term>Upward breath</term>** <note>original: 'Udāna'</note> is so-called because it leads up [that is] leads upwards such things as secretions. And its activity is from the tip of the nose and to the head.
5. **<term>Pervasive breath</term>** <note>original: 'Vyāna'</note> is one that pervades [the whole body].

Of these thus described, the **In-breath** is predominant, since the Sacred Word <note>original: 'Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.3'</note> declares that when that goes forth all goes forth: “Following the *Prāṇa* when it goes forth, all the vital-forces (*prāṇa*) go forth.”

Having thus explained the differences between the vital-forces <note>original: 'prāṇa'</note> with respect to activity and locality, he leads up to the meaning of the <term>aphorism</term> <note>original: 'sūtra'</note> with the words «As a result of subjugating the *Udāna*.» When constraint <note>meditative focus</note> has been performed upon the **Upward breath**, [then] as a result of its subjugation, [the practitioner] is not held back by water or similar objects. And at the time of death, his upward flight is by the <term>path of the gods</term> <note>original: 'devayāna'; the spiritual path toward liberation, described in the Upaniṣads as beginning with the flame or light</note> which commences with the flame. As a result of this [constraint] he attains by mastery to this upward flight. These supernormal powers that result from constraint upon the vital-forces beginning with the In-breath, if there be success in it, should be understood according to the differences in the mastery of activities and of localities [in the body].

### 40. As a result of subjugating the <term>equalizing breath</term> <note>original: 'Samāna'</note> [there arises] a radiance.

The <term>yoga practitioner</term> <note>original: 'yogin'</note> who has subjugated the **Equalizing breath** by causing a pulsation of the flames <note>the inner digestive fires</note>, becomes radiant. <note>original: 'prabhā bhāskarasya'; literally "the splendor of the sun"</note>

40. . . . the *Samāna* . . . a radiance. There is «a pulsation,» a flaming forth of the flame in the body.

<header>Supernormal audition [—iii. 41</header>

The processes of hearing <note>original: 'çravaṇa'</note> that are in the same place have the same quality of hearing <note>original: 'eka-çrutitvam'</note>.¹ And this fact—that the ether is the location of sounds—is declared to be the first characteristic mark of the ether. And the second is that it is not covered or obstructed ² by anything more extensive. Thus, because a thing which is incorporeal or formless <note>original: 'amūrta'</note> is evidently not covered by anything, it is also recognized that ether is all-pervasive. From the perception of sounds, it is inferred that the organ of hearing exists. For in the case of a deaf man and of a man not deaf, the one perceives sound and the other does not. Hence, it is the organ of hearing only which is the field of operation for sound. — For the yoga practitioner <note>original: 'yogin'</note> who has performed meditative constraint upon the relation between the organ of hearing and the ether, the divine <note>supernal</note> ³ ear begins.

It has already been stated [iii. 36, p. 246¹⁻³ Calc. ed.] that as a result of meditative constraint upon that which exists for its own sake <note>this would be the 'mukhya' or primary Self</note>, there remains a secondary perfection, the divine organ of hearing and other organs. Now the divine organ of hearing and other organs result from the constraint which has the divine organ of hearing and other organs as its sole purpose. **41. . . . Organ-of-hearing . . . organ-of-hearing.** He says that the object of the constraint is the relation between the organ of hearing and the ether, in the relation of the contained to the container, in the words «For all.» All organs of hearing, although made of the personality-substance <note>the 'ego-material' or ahaṃkāra</note>, have the ether <note>original text says 'air', but refers to the subtle element</note> which is contained in the hollow space of the auditory canal as its physical basis. The organ of hearing has its seat <note>original: 'āyatana'</note> there. For if we assist or injure this auditory canal, we find that the organ of hearing has been assisted or injured. Ether is also the physical basis for sounds, which are causes co-operating with the organ of hearing. When a sound is to be heard as coming from an earthen or other substance, the organ of hearing, which is in the hollow of the auditory canal, presupposes that there is a special sound residing in the ether ⁴ <note>original: 'nabhas'</note> which is its own [that is, the organ’s] substance. That this is so is clear <note>original: 'dṛṣṭam'</note> from analogy. Thus when, for instance, one wishes to have an external sensory perception <note>original: 'ālocana'</note> of smell, which is contained in this case in earth, by means of the organ of smell—which is a co-operating non-material cause for those things which have smell and taste as their specific qualities—we find similarly that the sense of smell...

requires such a special kind of smell in so far as it is contained in the earthen thing which contains it]. And it has already been said that the organs of smell and of taste and of touch and of sight and of hearing, although made of the personality-substance <note>original: 'ahaṃkāra'; the sense of "I-maker" that forms the individual ego</note>, do have the elements as their locus. For if we assist or injure the elements, we find that we have assisted or injured the organ-of-smell or some other of the organs. This same organ-of-hearing, which is made of the personality-substance, moreover resembles a piece of iron in that it is attracted by a magnet-like sound, in the mouth, produced by the mouth of the speaker, and, by a succession of its own functions (*vṛtti* <note>the fluctuations or mental modifications of the mind-stuff</note>), has the external sense of the word which has come to the mouth of the speaker. Hence there are sense-presentations of sounds functioning at different points of space. [And this sense-presentation], common to all living-beings, cannot in the absence of inhibition, be counted as an invalid-source-of-ideas. And in this sense there is an utterance by Pañcaçikha <note>an ancient teacher of the Sāṅkhya school of philosophy</note>, “All those whose-processes-of-hearing (*çravaṇa*) are in the same place have the same kind-of-hearing.” Those persons whose processes-of-hearing are in the same place are those persons, like Chāitra <note>a traditional placeholder name in Sanskrit logic, similar to "John Doe"</note>, whose organs-of-hearing are of that kind. The meaning is that the processes-of-hearing of all are in the air (*ākāśa* <note>more accurately translated as 'ether' or 'space', the subtlest of the five elements</note>). The air, moreover, the locus of the organs-of-hearing, because it is produced from the fine-element (*tanmātra* <note>the subtle essence of an element before it becomes gross matter</note>), whose [specific] quality is sound, has sound as its specific quality.¹ By which sound as a co-operating [non-material] cause it grasps the sounds from earthen and other substances. Therefore there is for all one species of hearing (*çruti*) with regard to sound. This is the meaning. Thus then it has been shown that air is the locus of the organ-of-hearing and that it has sounds as its [specific] quality.—And this fact that there is one kind of hearing (*ekaçrutitvam*) is the [first] characteristic mark of air. For this one kind of hearing is that condition which phenomenalizes sound <note>makes sound perceptible as a phenomenon</note>. This very thing which is its substrate (*āçraya*) is the thing expressed by the word air. For in the absence of such a hearing there is no [individual] phenomenal sound [belonging to earthen and other substances]. Moreover such a hearing cannot be a quality (*guṇa*) of the various [coarse substances] such as earth, because, if it be such, these cannot be both the thing-to-be-phenomenalized and the conditions-which-phenomenalize. —And the [second] characteristic mark of air is that it is not covered [by anything more extensive]. If there were no air, the things not-limited-in-extent would be pressed together and could not be separated even by needles. And so as a result everything would be covered by everything. And it cannot be said that the not being covered [by anything] is merely because things-not-limited-in-extent are not present. For this negation implies a positive entity [for example, a thing-limited-in-extent]. And if this positive entity do not exist, there can be no negation of it. Nor can it be said that the

<page-num>271</page-num>
<header>Levitation [—iii. 42</header>

The **Power of Consciousness** <term>original: *citiçakti*; the pure, unchanging awareness that underlies the mind</term> could be the substrate for this¹ [free space not covered by anything]. For being immutable, it cannot have [spatial] properties that precisely determine location. And again, it cannot be said that **space** <note>original: *diç*; directional space</note> and **time** are **substances** <note>original: *dravya*</note> over and above earth and the other [four coarse elements: water, fire, air, and ether]. Consequently, that particular transformation [which provides space and is not covered by anything more extensive] belongs to the **ether** <note>original: *ākāça*; the most subtle element, often translated here as "air"</note> only. 

Thus all is cleared up.—When it is proved that the fact that nothing covers it is a characteristic mark of the ether,—so that wherever there is anything that has nothing covering it, there always the ether is,—then [all-] pervasiveness is also proved, as the teacher says, "Thus, because a thing is not limited in its physical extent."

He gives the basis for valid knowledge to prove the real existence of the **organ of hearing** by saying, "From the perception of sounds." For [every] action must be carried out by an instrument, just as the action of chopping is carried out by an axe or something similar. So in this case also, the act of perceiving sound must be accomplished by an instrument. And that which is the instrument is the organ of hearing. 

Now if it be asked why the eye or some other organ may not be the instrument of this [act], he replies, "In the case of a deaf man and of a man not deaf." This is determined by positive and negative logic <note>referring to the method of 'agreement and difference'; hearing occurs when the organ is present and fails when it is damaged</note>. And this is only an abbreviated statement. For we must apply the same logic to the other senses: as a result of **constraint** <term>original: *saṃyama*; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and total absorption on a single object</term> upon the relation between the **organ of touch** and the **wind** <note>original: *vātā*</note>, between the **organ of sight** and **radiance**, between the **organ of taste** and **water**, and between the **organ of smell** and **earth**, supernatural touch and other [divine sensations] would also arise.

### 42. Either as the result of constraint upon the relation between the body and the ether (*ākāça*), or (*ca*) as the result of the balanced-state of lightness, such as that of the cotton-fibre, there follows the passing through air.

Wherever there is a body there is **ether** <note>original: *ākāça*</note>, because it [the ether] provides the space for the body to exist. The relation [of the body] with this [ether] is one of pervading or occupying space. By performing **constraint** <note>meditative focus</note> upon this relation, the **yogi** <note>a practitioner of yoga</note> masters the relationship with the ether. 

And by gaining the **balanced-state** <term>original: *samāpatti*; a deep meditative absorption where the mind becomes like a clear jewel, taking on the qualities of the object of focus</term> of lightness, such as that of a cotton-fibre—even down to the lightness of the atoms of a cotton-fibre—the yogi becomes light himself. 

And by reason of this lightness, he can walk with both feet upon water. Next after this, however, he walks upon nothing more than a spider’s thread, and then upon sunbeams. Thereafter, he travels through the air at his own will.

### iii. 42—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or Vibhūti [272]

42. . . . body . . . . passing through. By performing **meditative constraint** <term>original: *saṃyama*; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and total absorption</term> upon the relationship between the body and the air, or upon something light such as a cotton-fibre, [the practitioner] gains the **balanced-state** <term>original: *samāpatti*; a state where the mind, like a clear jewel, takes on the properties of the object it contemplates</term>—that is, the state of the mind which rests in the object and in which it is "tinged" [as described in Book i. 41] by it. He describes the sequence of these perfections <note>The "perfections" or *siddhis* are the supernatural abilities resulting from yoga</note> by the words, "upon water." <note>This refers to the ability to walk on water or spider-webs without sinking.</note>

**43. An outwardly un-adjusted fluctuation is the Great Discarnate; as a result of this, the covering of the brightness is thinned away.**

The movement or "fluctuation" assumed by the **mind** <term>original: *manas*; here called the "central-organ"</term> outside the body is the **fixed-attention** <term>original: *dhāraṇā*</term> called **Discarnate** <term>original: *videhā*; meaning "without a body"</term>. If it is only an "outer" fluctuation of the mind while the mind still abides within the physical body, it is called **adjusted** <term>original: *kalpita*; also translated as "contrived" or "imagined"</term>. But if it is an outer movement of the mind where the mind itself is externalized—in that the movement disregards the body entirely—it is called **un-adjusted**. 

Practitioners <note>original: *yogins*</note>, by using the "adjusted" state as a means, accomplish the **un-adjusted Great Discarnate** state, through which they are able to enter the bodies of others. Furthermore, as a result of this fixed-attention, the "covering" of the **purity** <term>original: *sattva*; the quality of light and intelligence in the mind</term> of the thinking-substance begins to dwindle away. This purity is essentially brightness, but it is obscured by the three-fold results <note>The three-fold fruits of karma: birth, lifespan, and the quality of experience (pleasure/pain)</note> of mental obstacles <term>original: *kleśas*</term> and past actions <term>original: *karma*</term>, the roots of which are **passion** <term>original: *rajas*</term> and **inertia** <term>original: *tamas*</term>.

The author describes yet another constraint which leads to the penetration of another’s body and which leads to the fading of mental obstacles, past actions, and their consequences. 

43. An outwardly . . . . dwindling. 

He describes the **Discarnate** state in the words "The fluctuation assumed." In order to show how to reach the "Great Discarnate" state (the un-adjusted one), he first describes the basic discarnate state in the words "If it is." The words "only a fluctuation" mean thinking only in an imaginary or mental way. He then describes the Great Discarnate in the words "But if it is." He shows that the adjusted and the un-adjusted states have the relationship of a means to an end by saying "among these two." 

Is it that one merely enters another’s body as a result of this? Not so, he says in the words "And as a result of this." "As a result of this fixed attention" means when the Great Discarnate activity of the mind has been perfected. This activity has its three-fold fruition, arising from the obstacles and from past actions, in the form of birth, the length of one's life, and the kind of—

### **44. As a result of constraint upon the coarse (<term>sthūla</term>) and the essential-attribute (<term>svarūpa</term>) and the subtile (<term>sūkṣma</term>) and the inherence (<term>anvaya</term>) and the purposiveness (<term>arthavattva</term>), there is a subjugation of the elements.**

In this [system] i. the [five elements] beginning with earth [which in essence are a generic form and a particular] have [as particulars] sounds and other perceptible things; [these] particulars, together with their properties (**quality** <term>dharma</term>), shape and the rest [which are to be described], are technically called **coarse**. This is the first form of the elements.—ii. The second form is its generic-form. For example, limitation-in-extent (**form** <term>mūrti</term>) is the [generic-form] of earth; liquidity, of water; heat, of fire; wind [is] mobile, for air goes everywhere. This second form is technically called **essential-attribute**. This generic-form has sounds and other [concrete perceptible things] as its particulars. And in this sense it has been <note>original: "pūrvācārya-saṁvādaṁ āha"; The commentator Vijñāna Bhikṣu notes that this is stated as an agreement with earlier teachers.</note> said, “All these [perceptible things] that are inseparably connected with one **predicable genus** <note>original: "genus praedicabile"; a Latin logical term referring to a category or class that can be asserted about a subject</note> are distinguished only by their properties.” In this system a **substance** <term>dravya</term> is an **aggregate** <term>samudāya</term> of the generic-form and of the particular. For a **collection** <term>samūha</term> is of two kinds: 
1. that in which [the names of] its different component parts have disappeared, as for instance, a body, a tree, a herd, a forest <note>Compare the *Tattva Bindu*, a philosophical text on language and meaning.</note>; 
2. and that collection in which the different component parts are specified [each] by a term, as for instance ‘of both kinds, gods-and-human-beings.’ <note>Compare the *Satapatha Brahmana*, an ancient ritual text: "The gods and human beings are two kinds."</note> One part of the collection is gods and the second part is human beings. The having of experience and of release as their purpose is inherent in the **qualities** <term>guṇa; the three fundamental forces of nature: sattva (light/purity), rajas (movement/passion), and tamas (heaviness/inertia)</term>. And the aspects are [inseparably connected] with the elements and the products of the elements. Thus all has a purpose. By constraint upon these five elements of the present time in their five forms, the sight of the essential-attribute of this or that form and the subjugation of it come about. [The practitioner] by mastering the five essential-attributes of the elements, masters the elements, [and] as a result of their subjugation, the evolving-causes of the [coarse] elements follow the commands of his will just as the cows follow their own calves.

the term <term>collection</term> can be imposed. By the words «of both <term>kinds</term>» which
describe a thing as having two parts, the idea of the <term>collection</term> is expressed,
since a sentence cannot but express the object-intended by the sentence.
This is the point. Once more he describes a difference in qualities by saying
«Furthermore.» Both the identity and the distinction are emphasized. He
describes the emphasis laid upon the difference in the words, «‘a grove of

is prescribed <note>Referencing the rules of Pāṇini, the ancient Sanskrit grammarian, specifically section ii. 3. 50.</note> to express a distinction, as for instance, ‘a cow belonging to
the <term>Gargas</term><note>A famous clan or family of sages often used as an example in grammatical texts.</note>.’ He describes the emphasis laid upon the identity in the words <note>According to Pāṇini viii. 4. 5, a specific phonetic rule changes the 'n' sound to 'ṇ' in certain compound words.</note>

analysed thus,] the <term>mango-trees</term> which themselves make up the grove.
Inasmuch as he wishes to emphasize the identity between the <term>collection</term> and
its parts, [the words] refer to the same subject. This is the meaning. He states
another kind of <term>collection</term> by saying «Again [the <term>collection</term>] is two-fold.»
A <term>collection</term> of which the parts exist separately, is one the parts of which
have an independent existence, apart, with intervals between ; for when the
word ‘herd’ or ‘grove’ is spoken, the trees and the cows which are the
parts of these [<term>collections</term>] are thought to] have intervals between them.
A tree, a cow, or an atom is a <term>collection</term> of which the parts do not exist
separately, since neither the <term>generic-form</term><note>original: "sāmānya." The general characteristic shared by a class.</note> and the <term>particular</term><note>original: "viśeṣa." The specific, individual quality.</note>, which are the
parts of these, have intervals between them, nor do the <term>dewlap</term><note>The fold of skin hanging from the neck of a cow, a standard example in Indian logic to define the essence of "cowness."</note> and the
other [<term>characteristic parts</term>] of the cow have intervals between them. From
among these same <term>collections</term> he selects that <term>collection</term> which constitutes

# Supernormal Powers
## Book III. Vibhūti
### —iii. 44

part a particular, wherein these parts cannot separately exist and yet have no intervals between them. And just as the atom is a <term>subtle</term><note>original: "sūkṣma"</note> form, so all the <term>fine elements</term><note>original: "tanmātra." These are the potential or "quantum" states of matter—sound, touch, color, flavor, and odor—before they become gross physical objects.</note> are a subtle form. He brings this to a close in the words "This is."

—«iv. Now the fourth form of the elements. The aspects with dispositions to discernment and to activity and to inertia and conforming to the nature of [their] effects» means those whose disposition it is to be inseparably connected with <note>original: "anu-gantum"</note>, that is, to conform to <note>original: "anu-pat"</note> the nature of [their] effects. Hence they are described by the term <term>inherence</term><note>original: "anv-aya." This refers to the way the three qualities (gunas)—clarity, activity, and inertia—are present in every physical object.</note>.

—«v. Now the fifth form of these [elements] is purposiveness.» He elaborates the word <term>purposiveness</term> by saying "experience." An objector asks ‘Even if it be granted that the aspects have a purpose, how can you still say that their effects are purposive?’ In reply to this he says «the aspects.» Products of the elements are such things as cows or water-jars.

Having thus described the object of the <term>constraint</term><note>original: "samyama." The combined practice of concentration, meditation, and pure absorption.</note>, he describes the constraint itself and its results in the words «upon these.» «The evolving-causes of the [coarse] elements» are the elements themselves.

**45. As a result of this, <term>atomization</term><note>original: "aṇiman"</note> and the other [perfections] come about; [there is] perfection of body; and there is no obstruction by the properties of these [elements].**

As to these <note>See Vācaspati in the <term>Moonlight of Sāṁkhya Truth</term> (Sāṁkhya Tattva Kaumudī) on Verse 23.</note> [eight perfections]: 

1. **Atomization** occurs in case [the <term>yogin</term>] becomes atomic; 
2. **Levitation** occurs in case [the <term>yogin</term>] becomes light; 
3. **Magnification** <term>mahiman</term> occurs in case [the <term>yogin</term>] becomes magnified; 
4. **Extension** <term>prāpti</term> occurs in case [the <term>yogin</term>] touches the moon with a mere finger’s tip; 
5. **Efficacy**, the non-obstruction of desire, occurs in case [the <term>yogin</term>] dives into the earth underground [and] emerges again, as if in water; 
6. **Mastery** <term>vaśitva</term> occurs in case [the <term>yogin</term>] masters elements and products of elements and is not mastered by others; 
7. **Sovereignty** occurs in case [the <term>yogin</term>] is sovereign over the production, absorption, and arrangement of these [elements and products]; 
8. **The capacity of determining things according to desire** <note>original: "yatra-kāmāvasāyitva"</note> is the capacity to will actual facts so that the elements which are the evolving-causes remain as he wills. 

And although having power, he does not cause reversal of things. Why not? Because at the will of another [the <term>Lord</term><note>original: "Īśvara"</note>], who determines things according to desire, and who from the beginning is perfected, the elements have been so willed. These are the eight powers.
