## Eight magic powers
### —iii. 45

Perfection of the body is described later. Its external aspects are no longer obstructed. Earth, with its inherent limit in extent [its essential attribute], does not restrict the actions of the body and the organs of the <term>yogin</term><note>A practitioner of Yoga who has attained high levels of spiritual and mental discipline.</note>. For he can penetrate even solid rock. Water, liquid as it is, does not wet him. Fire, hot as it is, does not burn him. Wind, with its power of movement, does not budge him. And even in the air, whose nature is that nothing is hidden or covered by it, his body can remain hidden. Nay more, not even the <term>Siddhas</term><note>Semi-divine "perfected beings" who possess supernatural powers.</note> may behold him.

When the elements follow the commands of his will, what perfection is attained by the <term>yogin</term>? In reply he says: **45. As a result of this [mastery], the power of atomization and the other powers appear, along with bodily perfection and the non-obstruction of its functions.** From the mastery resulting from <term>constraint</term><note>samyama: a technical term for the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and meditative absorption on a single object.</note> upon the **a. coarse elements**, four perfections follow, as he says "As to these":

1. <term>Atomization</term><note>original: "aṇiman"</note>: though great, he becomes small.
2. <term>Levitation</term><note>original: "laghiman"</note>: though great, he becomes light and stays in the air like the tuft of a reed.
3. <term>Magnification</term><note>original: "mahiman"</note>: though small, he becomes in dimension an elephant or a mountain or a town.
4. <term>Extension</term><note>original: "prāpti"</note>: all things become close at hand for the <term>yogin</term>. For instance, even while standing on the earth, he can touch the moon with the tip of his finger.

He describes the perfection resulting from the subjugation by constraint of **b. the essential attribute** in the words "5. <term>efficacy</term><note>original: "prākāmya"</note>, the non-obstruction of desire." His own form is not obstructed by the limitations in extent and other essential attributes of the elements. He dives underground and emerges again as if in water.

**c. He now gives the perfection resulting from constraint of a subtle object by saying "6. mastery."** The elements are earth and the other coarse elements. The products of the elements are such things as cows and water-jars. He becomes master of them, independent with regard to them, and not mastered by them. Since there is a mastery of the atoms of earth and of the other coarse elements, and of the subtle elements which are the causes of these elements and products, there follows a mastery of the effects of these. Therefore those particular elements or products of elements, when put into a certain state, remain in that state.

**d. He now gives the perfection which results from subjugation by constraint upon inherence (<term>anvaya</term><note>The way the three fundamental qualities of nature (gunas) are present in all physical things.</note>) as its object by saying "7. sovereignty."** Having subjugated the radical cause of these elements and products of elements, he becomes sovereign both over their growth or production, and over their decay or destruction, and over their arrangement or proper arrangement.

**e. He now describes the perfection which is the result of constraint upon purposiveness by saying "8. Fulfilment of whatever is desired is the volition which becomes effective."** Whenever a <term>yogin</term> who has been successful with regard to the purposiveness of the aspects wishes anything to serve a particular purpose, that thing serves him for that purpose. ...he wills that it have the effect of nectar and makes them live. An objector says, "This may be so. But why does he not also exchange the nature of things, just as he reverses their powers? Why could he not make the moon into the sun, or make the new moon <term>Kuhu</term><note>A technical term for the new moon day when the moon is completely invisible.</note> into the new moon <term>Sinivali</term><note>The day of the new moon when a tiny crescent is still visible.</note>?" 

The reply is: **"And although having the power, he does not."** For assuredly, these yogis whose desires are fulfilled do not venture to transgress the order of the Exalted Highest Lord <term>Ishvara</term><note>The Supreme Being or God in Yoga philosophy.</note>. However, the powers (<term>shakti</term>) of things are not limited in their nature, insofar as they differ in species, place, time, and intensity. So it is proper that these powers should follow the commands of this <term>yogi</term>. These are the eight powers of sovereignty (<term>aishvarya</term>).

With regard to the words **"and there is no obstruction by the properties of these [elements],"** by the very mention that "atomization" and the other perfections come about, it is clear that there is no obstruction by the physical properties of these elements. But this is mentioned again to make known the rewards resulting from the constraints upon all the objects mentioned in this <term>sutra</term>. And the same holds good with reference to perfections of the body. The rest is easy to understand.

## 46. Beauty and grace and power and the compactness of the thunderbolt—this is perfection of body.

The perfect body is handsome, alluring, unexcelled in power, and as compact as a thunderbolt <note>original: "vajra"; symbolizes something that is indestructible and diamond-hard.</note>.

He describes the perfection of the body. **46. Beauty... perfection...** A compactness as of the thunderbolt. Of such a kind that the arrangement of the body's parts is firm and solid.

## 47. As a result of constraint upon the process-of-knowing, the essential-attribute, the feeling-of-personality, the inherence, and the purposiveness, there follows the subjugation of the organs.

The "object-to-be-known" consists of sounds and other perceptible objects whose essence includes both the generic form and the specific detail. 

1. **The process-of-knowing** is the activity or "fluctuation" of the senses with reference to these objects. This process does not merely perceive their general form. For if the specific object were not seen by the sense organ, how could it be determined by the mind (the central organ)? 
2. But **the essential-attribute**¹...

### Five subjugations of the organs — Book III, Sutra 47

[The sense organ] is a collection, inherent in different parts which cannot exist separately. It is a collection of the generic form [for example, the general capacity to hear] and of the particular [for example, specific sounds and so forth]. This collection belongs to the <term>Sattva</term><note>original: "sattva"; the quality of light, purity, and intelligence within nature.</note> of the <term>thinking-substance</term><note>original: "buddhi"; the higher intellect or discriminative faculty.</note> whose essence is brightness. The organ is itself such a substance. 

3. The third form of these [organs] is the <term>personality-substance</term><note>original: "asmitā-tattva"; the fundamental principle of "I-am-ness" or ego-awareness.</note> with the feeling-of-personality as its distinguishing characteristic. The individual senses are specific variations of this generic ego-form. 

4. The fourth form is the <term>aspects of nature</term><note>original: "guṇa"; the three fundamental qualities—Sattva (balance), Rajas (activity), and Tamas (inertia)—that make up all physical and mental reality.</note> whose essence is determination^1 and whose disposition is toward brightness, activity, and inertia. The organs, along with the personality-substance, are a mutation of these three aspects. 

5. The fifth form, which is inseparably connected with these aspects, is the <term>purposiveness</term><note>original: "arthavattva"; the inherent purpose of nature to provide experience and eventual liberation for the soul.</note> of the Self. 

<note>This passage describes a ladder of meditation: one moves from the physical act of hearing or seeing, up through the ego, to the basic qualities of nature, and finally to the very purpose of existence.</note>

Constraint is performed upon each of these five forms of the organs, one after another. As a result of mastering each of these five stages of sensory function, the <term>yogin</term><note>original: "yogin"; a dedicated practitioner of yoga.</note> achieves total subjugation of the organs.

---

After the practitioner has mastered the elements, the method for mastering the senses is described:

**47. Mastery over the organs comes from performing constraint upon the process of knowing, the essential attribute, the feeling of personality, the inherence, and the purposiveness.**

As a result of focused <term>constraint</term><note>original: "samyama"; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and total absorption on a single object.</note> upon these five—the process of knowing, the essential attribute, the feeling of personality, the inherence, and the purposiveness—mastery is achieved. 

The "process of knowing" is an <term>act of perception</term><note>original: "grahīti".</note>. To be described, this process requires an object to be known. Therefore, the author describes the object-to-be-known as "that whose essence is both the generic form and the particular." Having described the object, he describes the process of knowing with the words "with reference to these." 

The mental fluctuation involved is essentially the same as an <term>external sense process</term><note>original: "ālocana"; the first moment of sensory awareness before the mind labels the object.</note>, which is an act of the mind changing into the form of an object. In response to those who claim that the senses only perceive the "general" or "generic" form of things, he says: "And this has not [only the generic for its object]." It is called a process of knowing because something specific is known. This process does not^3 have the generic form alone as its object. The <term>central organ</term><note>original: "manas"; the mind or "internal sense" that coordinates the five external senses.</note>, which depends upon the external organs, acts upon external particulars. If it were otherwise—if the senses did not grasp specific details—we would have to admit that there are, for example, no blind or dumb persons. If the organ did not have a particular object to grasp, then...

---

^1 In accordance with the *Verses on Samkhya* (*Sāṃkhya-kārikā*) xxiii, it is clear that this term denotes the three aspects (*guṇas*) insofar as they function as the thinking-substance (*buddhi*).

^2 Compare Book II, sutra 23; also *Verses on Samkhya* xv and the *Samkhya Aphorisms* (*Sāṃkhya-sūtra*) i. 129.

^3 Reading "it does not have the generic alone as its object" (*na sāmānyamātragocaram*).

It also clarifies that our senses perceive specific, individual objects rather than just abstract generalities.</summary>

that particular would not be externally-sensed by that [organ]. How then could particulars be determined by the <term>central-organ</term><note>original: "manas"; the internal sense or mind that coordinates sensory data.</note>? Therefore the perception of the organs has for its object both the generic-form and the particular. This then is the process-of-knowing which is the first form of the organs. 2. He describes the second form in the words «But the essential-attribute.» For the <term>personality-substance</term><note>original: "asmitā"; the fundamental ego-sense or "I-am-ness."</note> out of a portion of its own <term>sattva</term><note>The quality of purity, light, and harmony.</note> generated the organs. Hence that generic-form of the organs which belongs to all of them, and those particular features which are limited to some such object as colour,—both of these two kinds also have brightness as their essence. 3. Thus since it is common to all the organs, it is the generic-form of the organs. This is the meaning. 4. He speaks of «The fourth form» because the <term>aspects</term><note>original: "guṇa"; the three primary qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—that constitute all nature.</note> have a double form, one whose essence is a determination, and another whose essence is to be the object of the determination. Of these [two forms], with reference to the fact that its essence is an object of determination [and] that it is an object of knowledge, the five fine elements and the elements and the products of the elements form themselves; but with reference to the fact that its essence is a determination and that it has the form of a process-of-knowing, the organs together with the personality-substance [form themselves]. This is the meaning. The rest is easy.

### 48. As a result of this [there follows] speed [great as that] of the central-organ, action of the instruments of [knowledge] disjunct [from the body], and the subjugation of the primary-cause.

Speed of the mind means that the body acquires motion comparable [to that] of the mind. Action of the <term>instruments</term><gloss>1</gloss><note>original: "indriya"; the sensory and motor organs.</note> of knowledge disjunct [from the body] is the acquisition by the discarnate organs of the <term>fluctuation</term><note>original: "vṛtti"; the activity or modification of the mind or senses.</note> required for the place and time and object desired. Subjugation of the <term>primary-cause</term><note>original: "pradhāna"; the unmanifested, root state of all matter and nature.</note> is the mastery over all evolving causes and evolved effects. These three perfections are called <term>Honey-Faced</term><note>original: "madhupratīka"; a stage of high spiritual attainment where the practitioner experiences "honey-like" bliss or clarity.</note>. And they are acquired as the result of the subjugation in five forms of instruments [of perception].

He describes the perfections which result from the subjugation, in five kinds, of the organs. **48. As a result of this . . . . and the subjugation.** The fact that the organs are instruments [of perception] even for the discarnate is described as being the action of the instruments [of perception] disjunct [from the body].

<header>Subjugation of the primary cause [-iii. 49</header>

The place is Kashmir or some other [place]. The time is the past or some other [time]. The object is subtile or other. As a result of the subjugation of the organ and of the inherence, [there follows] mastery of all evolving-causes and evolved-effects, a subjugation of the <term>primary cause</term><note>original: "Pradhāna"; the fundamental, unmanifested state of all material nature.</note>. An objector says ‘This may be true. By subjugation of the organs, the organs together with their objects may be mastered. ### 49. He who has only the full discernment into the difference between the **sattva** and the Self is one who has authority over all states-of-existence and is one who knows all.

He who is grounded in only the full discernment into the difference between the <term>sattva</term><note>The highest and purest quality of nature, characterized by light, clarity, and harmony.</note> and the Self, and who is in the higher consciousness¹ of being master in the higher clearness, and who has the *sattva* of his thinking-substance cleansed from the defilement of <term>rajas</term><note>The quality of energy, passion, and movement.</note> and <term>tamas</term><note>The quality of darkness, inertia, and delusion.</note> is one who has authority over all states-of-existence. The <term>aspects</term><note>original: "guṇa"; the three fundamental qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas) that constitute the material and mental world.</note> which are the essence of all things, which have both the determinations and the objects-of-determinations as their essence, present themselves as being the essence of the object-for-sight in its totality to their Owner, the <term>Soul</term><note>original: "kṣetrajña"; literally the "knower of the field," the conscious witness of all experience.</note>. This is the meaning.—Being <one who knows all> refers to the [intuitive] knowledge, produced by discrimination and rising instantaneously [into consciousness], of the aspects (*guṇa*) which are the essence of all, whether they be [iii. 14] quiescent or uprisen or indeterminable. This is the meaning. It is this perfection that is termed [i. 36] the ‘undistressed,’<note>original: "viśokā"; a state of mind free from all sorrow and suffering.</note> by attaining to which the yogin who knows all, whose hindrances and bondages have dwindled, takes his recreation as having mastery.

One whose <term>karmas</term><note>original: "karmas"; the accumulated effects of past actions.</note>, both hindrances [ii. 3] and bonds [i. 24], have dwindled away. He is of that kind.

**50. As a result of passionlessness even with regard to these perfections there follows, after the dwindling of the seeds of the defects, <term>Isolation</term><note>original: "Kaivalya"; the state of absolute liberation and independence of the Self from nature.</note>.**

When, after the dwindling of hindrances and of past actions, intuitive knowledge comes to him thus: ‘This presented-idea of discrimination is an external-aspect of the <term>purity</term><note>original: "sattva".</note>. And this purity is to be reckoned with those things that are to be escaped. The Self moreover is immutable, undefiled (<term>çuddha</term><note>original: "śuddha"; pure or unstained.</note>) by the aspects of nature, and other than the mind’s purity,’—when he is thus unaffected by these aspects, those seeds of the hindrances which, like **burned** <gloss>1</gloss> **seeds** of rice, are incapable of growing again, go together with the central-organ to their rest,—and when, these being resolved into the primary cause, the Self does not again have the experience of the **three pains** (<term>tāpa</term><note>original: "tāpa"; the three types of suffering: those caused by oneself, by other living beings, and by natural forces.</note>),—then these aspects, in that they are manifested in the central-organ as being karma and hindrances and fruitions, have **fulfilled** <gloss>2</gloss> **their purpose**, and invert-the-process-of-generation. Then there is the absolute absence of correlation of the Self with nature.

<header>Sensual temptations [-iii. 52</header>

“Of these [four], 1. . . . the observant-of-practice.” <note>original: "prathama-kalpika"; a beginner who has just started to experience the "light" of yoga.</note> This is one for whom the light of knowledge is just beginning to dawn but has not yet been fully mastered; their <term>intuitive knowledge</term> is focused on objects like the minds of others. 2. He describes the second type as one having “truth-bearing insight.” <note>original: "ṛtambharā-prajñā"; a state of mind that perceives only truth, previously discussed in Sūtra i. 48.</note> For this yogin, it has been said that “In this concentrated <term>mind-stuff</term><note>original: "citta"; the mental field of thoughts and emotions.</note>, the insight is truth-bearing.” This person wishes to master the physical elements and the sensory organs. 3. He describes the third class as “he who has subjugated the elements and the organs.” <note>original: "bhūtendriyajayin".</note> This yogin has gained mastery through <term>constraint</term><note>original: "saṃyama"; the focused application of attention, contemplation, and concentration.</note> upon the coarse elements of the world and upon the very process of knowing. This same yogin is further described as “all that,” meaning he has established the means to retain everything he has cultivated or acquired, such as the knowledge of other minds, as a direct result of his mastery over the elements and senses. Consequently, he does not lose these powers. He is one whose methods are not yet perfected for what is still to be achieved—specifically the “undistressed” state of perfection that leads to the highest state of desirelessness. Human effort only leads to the final goal when it is applied to the proper tools of acquisition. 4. He describes the fourth kind of yogin as “the fourth.” <note>original: "atikrānta-bhāvanīya"; one who has transcended even the practice of meditation.</note> This Exalted yogin is liberated while still living in the body; this is his final physical incarnation, and his only remaining goal is the final dissolution of the mind-stuff into its primary cause.

So, from among these four types of practitioners, the author determines which one is actually the target of the gods' invitations: “among these [four], the [second] <term>Honeyed Stage</term>.” <note>original: "madhumatī bhūmi"; the stage where knowledge is as sweet and direct as honey.</note> Regarding the first stage (the beginner), there is no possibility of them receiving an invitation from the Great <term>Indra</term><note>The king of the Vedic gods.</note> and the other deities. The third class also cannot be tempted, because through their mastery over the elements and senses, they have already obtained the powers the gods would offer. As for the fourth, because they have reached the highest state of passionlessness, the possibility of any attachment is far-removed. Thus, by a process of elimination, only the second type—the yogin of truth-bearing insight—is a proper <term>recipient</term><note>original: "viṣaya"; the subject or object of a particular action.</note> of this celestial invitation.

The phrase “Passes through air” refers to the power of traveling through the sky. “Unfading” means that which is imperishable. “Unaging” means that which is always fresh and new. He describes the spiritual danger caused by pride: “Such a one, if in his pride.” A person who, out of pride, considers themselves safe and secure will fail to realize the impermanence of all things and will not reflect on the dangers. The rest of the passage is straightforward.

### 52. As a result of constraint upon moments and their sequence [there arises the intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination.

Just as the <term>atom</term><note>original: "paramāṇu"; the smallest indivisible unit of physical matter.</note> is the minimal limit of matter,¹ so the <term>moment</term><note>original: "kṣaṇa"; the smallest indivisible unit of time.</note> is the minimal limit of time.

And time is an endless succession of these moments. ### iii. 52—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or Manifestations <note>original: "Vibhūti"</note> [288

...the minimal limit of time. Or, the time taken by an atom in motion in order to leave one point and reach the next point is a moment <note>original: "kṣaṇa"</note>. But the continuous flow of these [moments] is a sequence <note>original: "krama"</note>. Moments and the sequences of these [moments] cannot be combined into a [perceptually] real object <note>original: "vastu"</note>. Hours-of-eight-and-forty-minutes <note>A "muhūrta," a traditional Indian unit of time.</note>, days-of-thirty-such-hours and so on are combinations created by a mental-process <note>original: "buddhi"</note>. Thus time, being of this nature, does not correspond to anything [perceptually] real, but is a structure created by a mental-process and follows as a result of perceptions or of words. [Thus] to the ordinary thinking of the emergent mind it might appear as if it were [perceptually] real. But the moment does come within the [real] objects¹ and rests² upon the sequence. Furthermore the sequence has its essence in an uninterrupted succession of moments. This [sequence] is called time by experts in time. So the <term>yogins</term> <note>Practitioners of yoga who seek spiritual liberation.</note> use the term. For two moments cannot occur simultaneously. Because it is impossible that there be a sequence between two things that occur simultaneously. When a later moment succeeds an earlier without interruption, there is a sequence. Thus in the present there is a single moment and there are no earlier or later moments. Therefore there is no combination of them. But those moments which are past and future are to be explained as inherent in the mutations <note>The constant changes or transformations of matter.</note>. Accordingly the whole world passes through a mutation in any single moment. So all those external-aspects of the world are relative to this present moment. By <term>constraint</term> <note>original: "saṃyama"; the unified practice of concentration, meditation, and absorption.</note> upon moments and their sequence both are directly perceived. And as a result of this, the [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination comes about.

It has been stated in one place and another that as a result of constraint upon certain objects, knowledge of all follows. This [knowledge of all] is not a knowledge of everything whatsoever without remainder. But it only emphasizes what—

<page-num>289</page-num>
<header>Reality of the time-sequence [—iii. 52</header>
<sig>37 [H.O.S. 17]</sig>

...the kind of knowledge it is, just as in the expression "Eaten with all the condiments." For in this expression, the sense is that the meal was eaten with as many kinds of condiments as were served, but not every possible condiment in existence without remainder. For all that, the word "all" has in some cases the sense of "without remainder," in the sentence for instance, "The glutton has eaten all the food that was brought to him." For here it is understood as meaning "nothing was left over." So now here the author describes the meditative constraint <note>The practice of *saṃyama*, or combined focus.</note> which leads to the intuitive knowledge <note>original: "vivekaja-jñāna"</note> proceeding from discrimination and characterized as being a knowledge of everything without exception. 

**52. Moments . . . [intuitive] knowledge.** 

He describes the meaning of the word "moment" <note>original: "kṣaṇa"</note> by means of an analogy and in the words "Just as." When a clod of earth is being broken up, that smallest bit of it wherein the gradations of smallness reach their minimal limit is the atom. So similarly, the moment is the minimal limit of time. In other words, it is a particle of time which has no "prior" or "subsequent" within itself. This same moment is illustrated in another way by the words "Or, the time taken." The meaning is the time it would take for an atom to traverse a distance measured by the width of an atom.

He now describes the meaning of the word "sequence" <note>original: "krama"</note> by saying "the flow of these [moments]." The word "these" refers to the moments. And a sequence of this kind is not perceptually real; it is abstractly real. Because, when so combined, it cannot possibly be thought of as a single physical reality <note>original: "vastu"</note> in the case of things which do not occur simultaneously. This has been said in the words "Moments and the sequences of these." 

Since a sequence consists of moments which do not arise at the same time, and since a combination of moments is not a physical reality, therefore also a combination of moments and of their sequences is not perceptually real. Ordinary persons—who have neither the natural excellence of the thinking-substance <note>The "thinking-substance" refers to *citta*, or the mind-stuff.</note> nor that resulting from philosophical debate¹—whose emergent way of thinking is new every moment, and who deem such time to be a physical reality, are in error. 

So then, is the moment—as contrasted with time—unreal? Not so, as he says in the words "But the moment." "Does come within the perceptually real" means that the moment is a real thing. It is the basis <note>original: "ālambana"</note> for the sequence. It is supported by the sequence only in terms of how we describe or predicate it. This is the meaning. 

He gives the reason why the sequence should be the basis for the moment by saying "Furthermore the sequence." He gives the reason for the perceptual unreality of the sequence in the words "For . . . not." The word "for" <note>original: "ca"</note> expresses the idea of reason. To those who might suppose that moments occur simultaneously, he says they belong to different classes and such simultaneity is "impossible between two things." Why is this impossible? To this he replies that there must be "an earlier" moment. He brings the discussion to a close in the word "Thus." So then,

---

¹ Referring to a type of debate where one contends without sound reasons. See the *Nyāya-sūtra* i. 2. 3 (entry 44) <note>A foundational text of the Nyāya school of Indian logic.</note>.

<summary>This page defines the "moment" as the indivisible atom of time and "sequence" as its flow, arguing that while the moment is real, the sequence is a mental construct. It explains that true intuitive knowledge arises from understanding this distinction through meditative focus.</summary>

The words "inherent in" mean inseparably connected with the generic form. He sums up the discussion by saying "Accordingly." The particular object of this intuitive knowledge, which proceeds from discrimination, is now brought forward.

**53. As a result of this, there arises a deeper knowledge of two identical things which cannot be distinctly qualified by species, characteristic marks, or their position in space.**

<margin>² The Secret Treatise <note>original: "Rahasyam"</note> says that cows with white eyes are lucky.</margin>
If two identical things resemble each other in their position in space and in their characteristic marks, it is the difference in species which allows us to distinguish between them—for instance, "This is a cow; that is a mare." If the place and the species are the same, it is the characteristic mark that allows us to distinguish between them—for instance, "This cow has black eyes; that cow is lucky."² Since two <term>myrobolan</term> fruits <note>original: "myrobolan"—a bitter, plum-like fruit often used as a logical example in Indian philosophy.</note> resemble each other in species and in characteristic marks, it is the difference in their position in space that allows us to distinguish between them—for instance, "This one is in front; this other is behind." 

But consider a case where the <term>myrobolan</term> which was in front is moved to the place of the one behind while the observer's attention is occupied elsewhere. If the positions are then identical, one would mistakenly think, "That is the one that was in front; that is the one that was behind." In such a case, a <term>right classification</term> <note>original: "pravibhāga"</note> is impossible for the ordinary mind. Since the <term>knowledge of reality</term> <note>original: "tattva-jñāna"</note> must be free from doubt, it was said, <As a result of this there arises the deeper-knowledge,> as a result, that is, of the intuitive knowledge proceeding from discrimination. How is this? The point in space occupied by the <term>myrobolan</term> in front is distinct from the point in space occupied by the <term>myrobolan</term> behind. The two <term>myrobolans</term> remain distinct because they each pass through the specific moments and incidents unique to their own points in space. However, it is this process of passing through an incident belonging to another point in space...

<summary>This page explains Sūtra 3.53, which describes how a yogi’s intuition can distinguish between two objects that are identical in species, appearance, and position. It uses the analogy of two identical fruits to show that while ordinary perception fails when objects are swapped, yogic discrimination tracks the unique relationship between an object and its specific point in space and time.</summary>

<page-num>291</page-num>
<header>Intuitive knowledge of identical things [Continuing Book 3, Sūtra 53]</header>

...that is the cause of the distinction between the two. This example illustrates how the supreme <term>yogin</term> <note>an advanced practitioner of yoga who has attained supernormal perception</note> has a mental representation <note>original: "pratyaya"</note> of the difference between two atoms. This is a result of his direct experience of the specific point in space occupied by the atom in front, even when that atom is identical to another in its species, its characteristic marks, and its position in space. The reason for this is that the only remaining distinction is based on which atom occupies which point in space. Since it is impossible for an atom located "behind" to occupy the same point in space as the one "in front," the movement of the rear atom through its own specific point in space is distinct from the front atom's movement through its own. 

Others—specifically the <term>Vāiçeṣikas</term> <note>a school of Indian philosophy focused on naturalism and atomism</note>—describe the same matter in this way: "These ultimate particulars <note>original: "viçeṣa"</note> are what produce the idea of difference." Even in their view, the difference in the point of space, the characteristic marks, the physical extent, the intervening space between them, and the species might be considered a sufficient cause for making a distinction. However, the minute difference regarding the specific occurrence or "incident" is accessible only to the refined mind of the <term>yogin</term>. Therefore, it has been said by the teacher <term>Vārshagaṇya</term>,² "Since there is no difference in physical extent, or by reason of intervening space, or of species, there is no distinction in the primary root of things."

Although the knowledge that arises from such discrimination will be described later as encompassing all things entirely, this specific knowledge is so incredibly subtle that it is introduced first in the words of this <term>sūtra</term> <note>an aphorism or concise rule</note>. 

**53. Species . . . deeper-knowledge.** 

To ordinary people, a distinction in the species—that which is perceivable by the mind <note>original: "intelligibilis"</note>—is the standard way to know the difference between things. But when the mental category of the species (such as the "common nature of a cow") is identical, and when the location (whether in front or elsewhere) is also identical, the distinguishing factor <note>original: "differentia"</note> becomes the specific characteristic marks, such as the difference between a black-eyed cow and one marked as "lucky."

---

¹ <term>Vijñānabhikṣu</term> <note>a 16th-century philosopher and commentator</note> interprets this passage as referring to the teachings of the <term>Vāiçeṣikas</term>. He argues that while factors like physical extent distinguish permanent substances, there is no separate "entity" called a "particularity" (*viçeṣa*) that exists as a property of those substances. In his view, there is no extra attribute of difference beyond the actual differences in size, location, or similar qualities. The context of the argument determines which interpretation is correct.

² See the <term>Sāṁkhya Tattva Kāumudī</term> <note>The Moonlight of Sankhya Principles, a classic philosophical commentary</note>, section 47, for another quotation from <term>Vārshagaṇya</term>.

### iii. 53—] *Book III. <term>Supernormal Powers</term> <note>original: Vibhūti</note>*

In the case of two myrobolans <note>a type of medicinal fruit, often used in Indian philosophy as an example of objects that look identical</note>, the common nature of the myrobolan—the species [perceivable by the mind] <note>original: intelligibilis</note>—is equivalent; the characteristic mark, such as roundness, is also equivalent. However, the difference in the "point of space" is the distinguishing factor <note>original: differentia</note>. 

When, however, one wishes to test the <term>yogin’s</term> knowledge, and, while the <term>yogin</term> who possesses [intuitive] knowledge has his attention occupied elsewhere, one puts the myrobolan which was in front behind, and removes or hides the one that was behind, then—inasmuch as the places are equivalent so that an observer would think, "That fruit is the one that was in front, and that one is the one that was behind"—a correct classification is impossible for an ordinary person, however wise, who is conversant with only the three sources of valid ideas <note>perception, inference, and testimony</note>. 

Whereas the right view of things must be free from doubt. And in the case of the <term>yogin</term> who has [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination, there cannot be the possibility of doubt. So the author of the <term>sūtra</term> <note>Patañjali</note> says: <As a result of this there arises the deeper knowledge.> 

[The Comment] explains the words <As a result of this> by the words <<as a result [that is] of the [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination.>> 

A question is asked: "How can [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from <term>constraint</term> <note>original: saṃyama; the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and absorption</note> upon moments and upon their sequences discriminate one myrobolan from another when they have an equivalent species, characteristic mark, and point of space?" 

This is asked by the words <<How is this?>> 

The reply is given in the words: <<The point of space coincident with the myrobolan in front.>> The point of space which characterizes the myrobolan in front is limited to one moment of that myrobolan. Or we may say that there is an incessant mutation <note>original: pariṇāma; the constant transformation of matter</note> [of the point of space as compared] with it [the moment]. And this is distinct from the incessant mutation of the myrobolan which is behind—distinct, that is, <<from the point of space coincident with the myrobolan behind.>> 

Very well then, let there be a distinction as to points of space. How does this bear upon the distinction between the myrobolans themselves? 

The answer is in the words: <<And the myrobolans are distinct in that they pass through the incidents peculiar to their own points of space.>> The coincidence with its own point of space is that "digit of time" belonging to the myrobolan which, with respect to its own point of space, is characterized by a kind of mutation in terms of nearness or distance. That is its "incident" peculiar to its point of space. Its <<passing through>> is either its arriving at a point of space or it is knowledge itself. The two myrobolans are different in so far as there is this [passing through]. 

When the two myrobolans had a moment of mutation in terms of nearness and distance—insofar as the two points of space are in front or behind—then the <term>one who practices constraint</term> <note>original: saṃyamin</note> experiences the particularity of the incident of the mutation belonging to the two, in terms of nearness and distance with reference to another point of space. And he admits that they are quite different. Although at present [one of the myrobolans has such] a mutation that it is in the point of space of this [other myrobolan], still, up to the present moment, it had its mutation with reference to a different point of space. So it is the moment...

<summary>This page uses the example of two identical fruits to demonstrate how a yogin distinguishes between objects that appear the same. By focusing on the unique "moment" and "point of space" occupied by an object, the yogin can track its identity even if the objects are moved or swapped.</summary>

### Coincidence of the time and the space series [—iii. 53]

...of the change <note>original: "mutation," referring to *pariṇāma*</note> of this specific point in space which distinguishes it [from any other point in space]. And it is this "moment" which is directly perceived by meditative constraint <note>The practice of *samyama*, or the combined application of fixed attention, contemplation, and concentration</note>. So it was said, "But it is this passing through the moments belonging to another point in space that is the cause of the distinction between the two." With the help of this example and by dialogues between laymen and experts and others, one comes to believe that the distinction between even such types of atoms is accessible to the thinking-substance <note>the mind or *citta*</note> of the <term>yogin</term>, as he says "This." 

"Others [<term>Vaiçesikas</term> <note>A school of ancient Indian philosophy known for its atomism and logic</note>], however, describe" [that is, they set forth this]
<margin>Dasgupta, Yoga Philosophy, 194.</margin>
description by saying "which." For the <term>Vaiçesikas</term> say that there are "ultimate particulars" <note>unique, indivisible qualities called *viśeṣa*</note> functioning in permanent substances. So they say. To explain: <term>Yogins</term>, [when they consider] liberated beings who are equivalent in respect of species, point in space, and time, and who are also free from any specific defining characteristics, have a [deeper] knowledge of each person as he really is, distinct from other persons. Therefore, they [the <term>Vaiçesikas</term>] say, there must be some "ultimate particular" that differentiates them. And if so, this same [principle of distinction] is one that serves to distinguish permanent substances such as atoms. 

The author controverts this in the words, "Even in this opinion of theirs." Species, point in space, and characteristic marks have already been illustrated. "Limitation-in-extent" refers to an arrangement of parts (<term>samsthāna</term>). In this case [of limitation-of-extent], imagine a thing with a flawless arrangement of parts is removed, and another thing with a defective combination of parts is put in its place while the observer is occupied elsewhere. There is a mental perception of the difference because there is a difference in the arrangement of parts of this [thing]. Or, "limitation-in-extent" might refer to the physical body. There is a distinction between persons caught in the cycles of rebirth—whose souls (<term>ātman</term>) are bound to specific bodies—and those whose souls are liberated [from the round of rebirth], based on their different relations with various elemental forces. 

So, in all cases, the mental perception of a difference is established on grounds other [than the existence of "ultimate particulars"]. [Consequently] there is no [need to assume the existence] of ultimate particulars. <note>The author argues that space, time, and specific arrangements are enough to explain differences without needing the *Vaisheshika* category of *viśeṣa*.</note>

Intervening space (<term>vyavadhi</term>) also makes a difference between things, as in the case of the mythical lands of <term>Kuça</term> and <term>Puṣkara</term> <note>Two of the seven continents in ancient Hindu cosmology</note>, which are distinct simply by being two different points in space. Because differences in species, point in space, and other respects are accessible by the ordinary mind, it was said, "But the difference as to the incident <note>the specific momentary state</note> is accessible to the <term>yogin</term> only." The word "<term>eva</term>" <note>meaning "only" or "exclusively"</note> limits the words "difference as to the incident," but not the words "accessible to the thinking-substance of the <term>yogin</term>." It follows then that the distinction between liberated souls with respect to their relations with their...

<page-num>294</page-num>
<header>iii. 53—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or Manifestations <note>original: *Vibhūti*</note></header>

Knowledge of bodies that have existed in the past¹ is also accessible to the <term>yogin</term>. But in the case of one who has not yet identified the grounds for distinction mentioned above, there is no perceived division in the <term>primary-cause</term> <note>original: *prakṛti*, the fundamental material substrate of the universe</note>. This is what the Master has concluded. For this reason, it was said previously [ii. 22]: 
> “Though it has ceased to be seen by one whose purpose is fulfilled, it has not ceased to be entirely, since it is common to others beside him.” 

This is expressed by the phrases "limitation-in-extent" and "intervening-space." This statement should be understood as a partial explanation and should be applied to the various causes of difference already described, such as species, location, and time. The meaning is that within the <term>primary-cause</term>—which is the root of the entire world—there is no inherent distinction or difference.

### 54. The intuitive knowledge proceeding from discrimination is a deliverer; it has all things as its object, it has all times for its object, and it is an inclusive whole without sequence.

The word <term>deliverer</term> <note>original: *tāraka*, meaning "that which rescues" or "crosses over"</note> means that this knowledge arises out of its own vivid light without needing further external suggestions. It has "all things for its object," meaning there is nothing in existence that it cannot perceive. It has "all times for its object," meaning it possesses intuitive knowledge of the whole <note>original: *sarvam*</note> at all times—past, future, and present—including all its various states and transformations.³ The phrase "an inclusive whole without sequence" means that it grasps the entirety of reality at once, striking the <term>thinking-substance</term> <note>the mind or *citta*</note> in a single moment, encompassing all time. This is the complete form of intuitive knowledge born of discrimination. The "lamp of yoga" is merely a part of this greater light, beginning from the <term>Honeyed Stage</term>⁴ <note>original: *madhumatī*, a stage of spiritual attainment where knowledge is pure and sweet</note> and continuing until it reaches final perfection.

Having thus shown a part of the object of intuitive knowledge proceeding from discrimination, the author now provides the distinguishing characteristics of the knowledge itself. 
**54. Deliverer . . . intuitive knowledge.** 
He identifies this intuitive knowledge as the subject of his statement; the rest of the sentence describes its nature. It is called the "deliverer" because it rescues the practitioner from the ocean of the <term>round-of-rebirths</term> <note>original: *saṃsāra*</note>. He distinguishes this from the "Vividness" <note>original: *Prātibha*</note> mentioned previously [iii. 33] by stating it "has all times for its object." The phrase "with the sum of its states" means it includes all subordinate details. Therefore, the knowledge born of discrimination is complete. There is nothing—in any place, in any manner, or at any time—which is not within its view.

sphere. Why speak of <note>original: *āstām*</note> other kinds of knowledge? For even concentration conscious of objects is a part of this completed intuitive knowledge. So then there is nothing more complete than this, as he says: "Of this same, the lamp of yoga is a part." The lamp of yoga is concentration conscious of an object. **55. When the purity of the <term>purity-aspect</term> <note>original: *sattva*, the quality of light, clarity, and goodness in the mind</note> and of the Self are equal, there is Isolation.**

When the purity-aspect of the thinking-substance is freed from the defilement of the <term>passion-aspect</term> <note>original: *rajas*, the quality of activity and restlessness</note> and the <term>darkness-aspect</term> <note>original: *tamas*, the quality of lethargy and ignorance</note>, and when it has no task other than maintaining the presented-idea of the difference between the purity-aspect and the Self, and when the seeds of the hindrances within itself have been burned, then the purity-aspect enters into a state of purity equal to that of the Self. When this is so <note>original: *tadā*</note>, purity is the cessation of the experience which is falsely attributed to the Self. In this state of purity, <term>Isolation</term> <note>original: *Kaivalya*, the state of absolute freedom or spiritual detachment</note> follows for <term>one who possesses supremacy</term> <note>original: *īśvara*</note> or for one who does not, and for one who partakes of the intuitive knowledge proceeding from discrimination or for another. For if there be intuitive knowledge in the case of one whose hindrances have become "burned seeds," there is no further need of any supernormal power. As being the means of purifying the purity-aspect, both the <term>supremacy</term> <note>original: *āiçvarya*</note> proceeding from concentration and the intuitive knowledge have been introduced into the discussion. But strictly speaking, the intuitive knowledge represses <term>lack of vision</term> <note>original: *adarçana*</note>. When this is repressed, there are no more hindrances. Because there are no more hindrances, there is no <term>fruition of karma</term> <note>original: *karmavipāka*, the ripening of past actions into consequences</note>. In this state, the aspects—

their task done, do not again submit themselves as objects-for-sight to the Self. That is the Self's Isolation <note>The state of absolute freedom where consciousness is no longer entangled with the material world</note>. Then the Self having its light within itself becomes undefiled and isolated.

->Of the Exposition of the Comment on the <term>Pātañjalan</term> [Treatise], the Book on Supernormal Powers, the Third.<-

Having thus described the [various] constraints <note>original: *saṃyama*, the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and absorption</note> together with their supernormal powers, all of which indirectly prepare the way for Isolation, with the intent to show that the [intuitive] knowledge of the difference between the <term>sattva</term> <note>the aspect of the mind that is pure, clear, and light-giving</note> and the Self leads directly to Isolation, he here introduces the <term>sūtra</term> by the words «whether one has attained.» Whether [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination has been attained or not, nevertheless the insight into the difference between the <term>sattva</term> and the Self always brings Isolation to pass. This is the meaning. 

**55. When the purity of the <term>sattva</term> and of the Self are equal [there is] Isolation.** 

[The last word] <term>iti</term> <note>original: a Sanskrit particle marking the end of a quote or section</note> is meant to indicate the end of the <term>sūtras</term> [of this Book].—

1. The words «one-who-has-supremacy» refer to one who has the powers of action and of [intuitive] knowledge by reason of the constraints previously described. 
2. The words «or for one-who-has-not-supremacy» refer to one who partakes of the [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination by reason of the constraint described [ii. 52] immediately before. 
3. The words «or for another» refer to one in whom this [intuitive] knowledge has not risen [into consciousness]. 

In these cases there is no need at all for supernormal powers. Therefore he says «For . . . no.» And if it should be objected that there is no need of supernormal powers in connexion with Isolation, and that therefore instruction in them is useless, the reply is «As being the means of purifying the <term>sattva</term>.» The instrumental case is used to indicate such a kind of a mark <note>original: a reference to Pāṇini's grammar rule ii. 3. 21, explaining why a specific grammatical ending was used to show a characteristic</note>.—For the attainment of Isolation the supernormal powers are not absolutely useless, but they are not directly causes. This is the meaning. But it is the [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination that is the topic-under-discussion. And that which is a cause indirectly [the powers] is only figuratively a cause, not a principal cause. Strictly speaking, however, insight alone is the principal cause; [and not the discrimination]. This is the meaning. By the words «[intuitive] knowledge» he means the Elevation <note>original: *prasaṅkhyāna*, the highest state of meditative reflection</note>.

In this [Book] the indirect aids and the aids and the mutations have been treated at length, and the attainment of supernormal powers, and among these [powers] the [intuitive] knowledge proceeding from discrimination.

Such is the stanza which summarizes the contents of [this] Book.

## BOOK FOURTH

# ISOLATION

<vocab>Isolation, Book Fourth</vocab>

<page-num>296</page-num>
<header>iii. 55—] Book III. Supernormal Powers or <term>Vibhūti</term> <note>original: Vibhūti; refers to the "manifestations" or "glories" of power achieved by a yogi</note> [296</header>

Once their task is finished, [the forces of nature] no longer present themselves as objects of experience to the Self. That is the Self's Isolation <note>original: *Kaivalya*; the state of absolute freedom where consciousness is no longer entangled with the material world</note>. Then the Self, having its light within itself, becomes undefiled and isolated.

->This concludes the Exposition of the Commentary on the <term>Pātañjalan</term> <note>The work attributed to the sage Patañjali</note> Treatise, specifically the Third Book on Supernormal Powers.<-

Having thus described the various forms of "constraint" <note>original: *saṃyama*, the technical term for the combined practice of concentration, meditation, and spiritual absorption</note> together with their supernormal powers—all of which indirectly prepare the way for Isolation—the author now introduces the final <term>sūtra</term> <note>an aphorism or concise rule</note> with the intent to show that the intuitive knowledge of the difference between the <term>sattva</term> <note>the aspect of the mind that is pure, clear, and light-giving</note> and the true Self leads directly to Isolation. He begins with the words "whether one has attained." Whether this intuitive knowledge born of discrimination has been fully attained or not, it is the insight into the difference between the <term>sattva</term> and the Self that always brings Isolation to pass. This is the intended meaning.

**55. When the purity of the <term>sattva</term> and of the Self are equal, there is Isolation.**

The final word <term>iti</term> <note>a Sanskrit particle used here to mark the end of a section</note> is meant to indicate the end of the aphorisms for this Book.

**1. Perfections proceed from birth or from drugs or from spells or from self-castigation or from concentration.**

1. The power of having another body is the perfection by birth <note>Refers to being born as a god or a celestial being who possesses these powers naturally</note>. 2. [Perfection] by drugs is by an elixir-of-life¹ [got] in the mansions of the demons <note>original: asuras; refers to subterranean realms in Hindu cosmology where such elixirs were said to be found</note>, and by the like. 3. By spells, such as the acquisition of [the power of] passing through space and atomization <note>The ability to become as small as an atom</note> [iii. 45]. 4. [Perfection] by self-castigation <note>original: tapas; intense spiritual discipline or asceticism</note> is the perfection² of the will, the faculty of <term>taking on any form at will</term> <note>original: kāmarūpin</note> [or] of going anywhere at will, and so on. 5. Perfections proceeding from concentration <note>original: samādhi</note> have been explained.

Thus, in the First and Second and Third Books, concentration and the means of this [concentration] and the supernormal powers [produced] by it have been especially discussed. Of these, with the intent first to determine-the-nature-of mind-stuff which is conducive to Isolation, in the case of persons whose mind-stuff is perfected, he states the five-fold perfections by the words [of the aphorism]. **1. And so, with a view to exclude the possibility of any accidental [difference between cause and effect], he supplies the following words, "As to these [perfections], with regard to those bodies and organs which enter into the mutation of another birth." And then recites the <term>aphorism</term> <note>original: sūtra</note> 2. **The transformation into another birth is the result of the filling-in of the evolving-cause.**

When the body and organs, which have entered into the mutation of a human birth, enter into a birth as god or animal, the mutation is the result of the filling-in of the evolving-cause <note>The underlying material substance of the universe that allows for physical change</note>. Now the evolving-cause of the body is earth and other [coarse] elements, and the evolving-cause of the organs is the <term>personality-substance</term> <note>The psychological "I-sense" that shapes our individual identity</note>. An objection might be made to the effect that if this aid is to follow from mere filling-in, why is it not eternally so? To which the reply would be "such . . . as merit." So we have explained<note>1</note> how the same body can attain to the different stages of childhood and boyhood and young manhood and age and so on, or how a <term>banyan</term> <note>original: nyagrodha</note> seed can become a <term>banyan</term> tree, or how a particle of fire when placed on a pile of grass can envelop the region of the sky by the flaring forth of thousands of flames.

### **3. The efficient cause gives no impulse to the evolving-causes; but [the mutation] follows when the barrier [to the evolving-causes] is cut, as happens with the peasant.**

For an efficient cause <note>A secondary cause that triggers a change rather than being the substance of the change itself</note> such as merit gives no impulse to the <term>evolving-causes</term> <note>original: prakṛti; the fundamental potential of nature</note>, since a cause is not set into activity by an effect. In that case, how is this? [The answer is,] but in that case there is a cutting of the barrier, as happens with the peasant. Just as a peasant wishing to overflow<note>2</note> one meadow-plot, whether it be on the level or below or still lower, by filling-in with water from another meadow-plot, does not remove the waters with his hand, but cuts [the rim-of-turf which is] the <term>barrier</term> <note>original: āvaraṇa</note> of them. And after this is cut, the water itself overflows the other meadow-plot. So similarly <term>merit</term> <note>spiritual credit from good deeds</note> cuts <term>demerit</term> <note>spiritual debt from bad deeds</note>, the <term>barrier</term> <note>original: āvaraṇa</note> of the evolving-causes; and after this is cut, the evolving-

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how physical and spiritual transformations occur. This page uses a famous agricultural analogy to explain that our moral actions (merit and demerit) do not "force" nature to change, but rather remove the obstacles that allow nature to transform itself.</meta>

<header>iv. 3—] Book IV. Isolation or Liberation [302</header>

causes themselves overflow each its own appropriate <term>transformation</term> <note>original: vikāra; an evolved effect or change in form</note>. Or again, just as the same peasant, after the same [rim-of-turf] is cut, cannot force the watery or earthen essences to interpenetrate the roots of the different kinds of grain. In that case, what [can he do]? He removes from among them the pulse or maize or red rice or what not. And when they are thus removed, the essences interpenetrate of themselves the roots of the grain. Similarly, <term>merit</term> <note>original: dharma; moral or spiritual excellence</note> is an efficient cause in the sense that it follows upon nothing more than the mere cessation of <term>demerit</term> <note>original: adharma; moral or spiritual failing</note>, by reason of the absolute opposition between purity and impurity. But merit is not the cause which sets the <term>evolving-causes</term> <note>original: prakṛti; the fundamental material substance of nature</note> into activity. Of this <term>Nandishvara</term> <note>A legendary figure who, through extreme devotion, transformed from a human into a divine being</note> and others may be cited as examples. And conversely, demerit inhibits merit; and as a result of this, there is a transformation of impurity. And of this <term>Nahusha</term>¹ [the king who was changed into] a serpent, and others may be cited as examples.

The statement was that this "filling-in" is by the evolving-causes. With regard to this a doubt arises: "Is the filling-in by the evolving-causes natural, or is it due to merit? Which seems plausible [to the objector]? It seems plausible that even when the evolving-causes are there, the filling-in is accidental; and since we are traditionally taught that merit [and demerit] are causes, [the filling-in] is due to these causes." To this he replies [in the <term>aphorism</term> <note>original: sūtra</note>]:

### 3. The efficient cause gives no impulse to the evolving-causes; but [the transformation] follows when the barrier [to the evolving-causes] is cut, as happens with the peasant.

True—merit [and demerit] are efficient causes. But they are not impelling causes, since even these causes are the effects of the evolving-causes. And an effect does not impel a cause, forasmuch as this [effect] (in so far as its coming into existence is dependent upon this [cause]) is dependent on a cause, and [forasmuch as] the function of impelling belongs to what is independent. For surely when the potter is not there, the clay and the rod and wheel and the water and so on are not impelled by the jar which is to be produced or which has been produced. But they are impelled by a potter who is independent of them. Nor again can it even be supposed that it is the purpose of the Self that sets all in motion. But <term>the Lord</term> <note>original: Içvara; the Supreme Being or Divine Will</note> [sets all in motion] as being the <term>final objective</term> <note>original: uddeçya</note> of this [purpose of the Self]. For the purpose of the Self is described as setting all in motion only as being the final end² (<term>final objective</term> <note>original: uddeçya</note>). While this purpose of the Self is—

---

¹ By virtue of knowledge and asceticism and the power of yoga, **Nahusha** was equal to the task of ruling the Three Heavens. ² In the sense of being the object of desire. See the <term>Dictionary of Logic</term> <note>original: Nyāya-Koça</note> under the entry for <term>Objective-ness</term> <note>original: Uddeçatvam</note>, section 3.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of how a highly advanced practitioner of yoga (a yogin) can manifest multiple physical forms simultaneously. It concludes the discussion on "merit" and "demerit" from the previous page, explaining that even the Supreme Lord does not create from scratch but rather clears the path for nature’s inherent potential to unfold. It then addresses the technical question of how one person can inhabit multiple minds at once.</meta>

<page-num>303</page-num>
<header>Mind-stuff pervades many bodies [-iv. 5</header>

...yet to be, it is right that the unmanifested matter should be the cause of stability. But it does not follow from this that merit [and demerit] are not primary causes at all. Since it is quite consistent that they, like the peasant in the earlier analogy, should only remove obstructions. And in the case of the <term>Supreme Lord</term> <note>original: Içvara; the divine being who serves as a model for yogins</note> we must understand that his activity is limited to the removal of obstructions with a view to securing a basis for merit. All this, stated by the Commentary, is clear upon a mere reading.

---

But [if it be asked], while the <term>advanced practitioner</term> <note>original: yogin</note> creates many bodies for himself, do these bodies then have a single <term>internal organ</term> <note>original: antaḥkaraṇa; the mental faculty comprising mind, intellect, and ego</note>, or have they several? The answer is:

### 4. Created mind-stuffs result from egoism, and from this alone.

Assuming nothing more than <term>egoism</term> <note>original: asmitā; the "I-sense" or sense-of-personality</note> as the cause of <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>original: citta; the substance of the mind</note>, the practitioner makes these created minds. As a result of this, each of the bodies has its own separate mind.

Having finished the subject of <term>spiritual powers</term> <note>original: siddhi; perfections attained through yoga</note> occurring through the "filling-in" of nature's causes, the author now raises the question as to whether the mind-stuff residing in these various created bodies is one or many, by asking, "But [if it be asked], while..." If the practitioner creates multiple bodies, there would naturally be many internal organs. And because the intention and will would vary according to each individual mind within those bodies, they would not follow a single plan, and there would be no way to unify their memories—just as if they were entirely distinct people. Therefore, one might argue that there is only one mind-stuff which, like a lamp with a wide-reaching light, spreads out to pervade many created bodies. To this view, the author replies: **4. Created mind-stuffs result from egoism, and from this alone.** Each body, so long as it is alive, is clearly connected to its own individual mind-stuff—take, for instance, the separate minds of people like <term>Chaitra or Maitra</term> <note>traditional Indian placeholder names, similar to "John Doe and Richard Roe"</note>. The same rule applies to the bodies created by a practitioner. Thus, it is established that each created body has its own separate mental center. With this in mind, he says: *from egoism and from this alone.*

### 5. While there is a variety of actions, the one mind-stuff which impels the many is one.

How can many separate mind-stuffs have their actions coordinated for a single purpose by just one mind? [The answer is]: the practitioner creates a single "master" mind-stuff which directs and impels all the other individual mind-stuffs. From this central mind, the variety of actions in the different bodies is harmonized.

---

$^1$ Compare <term>Samkhya Sutra</term> <note>a foundational text of the Samkhya school of philosophy, closely related to Yoga</note> vi. 64.

<summary>This page explains how a yogi can manifest multiple bodies, each with its own mind derived from the "ego-sense," while a single master mind coordinates them all. It also clarifies that even the Supreme Lord works by removing obstacles to nature's flow rather than by forceful creation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how an advanced practitioner (yogin) coordinates multiple bodies. The previous page established that a practitioner uses their "sense of self" to create multiple distinct minds for these bodies. This page explains how a single primary mind directs those many secondary minds.</meta>

<page-num>304</page-num>
<header>iv. 5—] Book IV. Absolute Freedom [304</header>

Regarding the argument that if there are many minds, they could not all follow a single intention [of the practitioner who occupies these many bodies], nor could memories be properly coordinated, the reply is given in the following aphorism:

**5. While the various activities differ, the single mind-stuff is the director of the many.**

This coordination would be a flaw in the argument if the practitioner did not create one primary <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>original: citta; the functional mind-substance</note> to guide the <term>internal organs</term> <note>original: antaḥkaraṇa; the mental faculty</note> residing in the various created bodies. However, when such a primary mind is created, the argument remains sound. One should not argue that a practitioner, having one primary mind, has no need for separate internal organs for each body; nor should one claim there is no need to create a "guide" because the practitioner’s own original mind acts as the guide. This is because what is proven by logical evidence is not subject to simple dismissal <note>1</note> or questioning. On this point, there is a passage from the <term>Purāṇas</term> <note>original: Purāṇa; ancient records of legend and philosophy</note>:

->“By virtue of his authoritative power the <term>Supreme Lord</term> <note>original: Içvara</note>, though one, becomes many. Then being many he becomes one. From him also proceed all these variations of the internal organ. The <term>Lord of Yogins</term> <note>original: Yogiçvara</note> makes the bodies one-fold or two-fold or three-fold or manifold and again un-makes them. With some he may experience objects, with others he may practice intense self-discipline. All these he may eventually draw back into himself, just as the sun draws in its multitude of rays.”<-

It is with this same intention that the author speaks of "many mind-stuffs."

---

### 6. Of these [five perfections], the one that proceeds from meditation leaves no karmic residue.

The <term>constructed</term> <note>3</note> mind-stuff is of five kinds, for <term>perfections</term> <note>original: siddhi; spiritual powers</note> can arise from birth, from medicinal herbs, from sacred chants, from self-discipline, or from deep concentration. Of these five types, only the mind-stuff that results from <term>meditation</term> <note>original: dhyāna; contemplation</note> leaves no <term>latent-deposit</term> <note>original: āśaya or vāsana; the subconscious "stain" or "residue" left by actions</note>. Only that mind is free from residue which acts without being driven by passion or similar states. Consequently, it has no connection to merit or sin, since the practitioner's internal obstacles have been dissolved. For the other four types of mind, however, a latent-deposit of <term>karma</term> <note>the law of cause and effect regarding actions</note> remains.

Now, from these five [iv. 1] types of perfected minds that have been described, the author selects the specific mind-stuff that leads toward ultimate liberation. **6. Of these [five perfections] that which proceeds from contemplation leaves no latent-deposit.** The latent—

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the mind of a highly realized practitioner (yogin). <page-num>305</page-num>
<header>Action of the practitioner <note>original: karma of the yogin</note> [---Book IV. 7</header>
<sig>39 [Harvard Oriental Series 17]</sig>

Latent deposits are things that lie hidden, namely the subconscious impressions of our actions and the subconscious impressions of the obstacles <note>original: kleśa; the five hindrances such as ignorance and egoism</note> that cloud our judgment. A mind in which these impressions are not present is said to have no latent deposit. In other words, such a mind is conducive to ultimate liberation. Because this mind does not act out of passion or similar emotions, it is not connected to merit <note>good deeds</note> or to evil. But why is there no activity triggered by passion or similar states? The answer is found in the phrase: "since the practitioner's obstacles have dwindled away." To show that the mind-stuff <note>original: citta</note> produced through deep meditation—which contains no latent deposits—is distinct from other types of minds, the author states that all other minds possess these deposits with the words: "For the others, however."

---

For—

**7. The action <note>original: karma</note> of a practitioner <note>original: yogin</note> is neither white nor black; the actions of others are of three kinds.**

Action as a category is, as is widely known, four-parted <term>catuṣpāt</term> <note>original: four-footed or four-fold</note>: black, mixed (white-and-black), white, and neither-white-nor-black. Among these four:

1. The **black** actions are found in those who are wicked. 
2. The **white-and-black** actions are achieved through external means. The accumulation of subconscious impressions in this category occurs through either causing injury or providing benefit to others.
3. The **white** actions belong to those who engage in self-discipline <note>original: tapas; ascetic heat or castigation</note>, the recitation of sacred texts, and the practice of meditation. Because this kind of action is restricted to the internal mind alone, it does not depend on external tools and does not result in harm to others.
4. The **neither-white-nor-black** actions <gloss>1</gloss> are found in the renunciants <term>sannyāsin</term> <note>original: those who have cast aside worldly life</note> whose obstacles have faded away and who are inhabiting their final physical bodies. 

Among these four types, the practitioner of yoga alone possesses "not-white" action, because they have renounced <term>sannyāsāt</term> even the rewards of good deeds, and they possess "not-black" action because they want nothing to do with evil. However, the first three kinds of action mentioned are found in all other living beings.

On this same point, the author introduces an aphorism <term>sūtra</term> with the word "For" to provide the underlying reason: **7. The practitioner’s action is neither-white-nor-black; the action of others is of three kinds.** A division <term>pada</term> refers to a specific topic. An action that is contained within four divisions is called "four-divided" <term>catuṣpadā</term>.

On the other hand, there is benefit in this action, in that the Brahmans <note>the priestly class</note> and others receive their gifts. 

3. The **white** action belongs to those who castigate themselves <note>practice austerities or tapas</note> and recite sacred texts and practice contemplation,¹ to those who are not yet mendicant-saints <note>renunciates who have reached the highest stage</note>. He gives the reason for the whiteness in the words "Because this" <note>referring to the internal, non-injurious nature of these mental disciplines</note>. 

4. The **neither-white-nor-black** action is found in the mendicant-saints. He refers to the mendicant-saints when he says "have dwindled away" <note>referring to the dwindling of their obstacles/kleshas</note>. Because persons who have renounced all action <note>original: karma</note>, do not come into activity with reference to any action which can be attained by outer means-of-attainment. And accordingly, they have no latent-deposit <note>original: karmāśaya; the accumulated 'stock' of past deeds</note> of black action. And because they have altogether offered up to the Lord <note>original: Īśvara</note> the fruition <note>the ripening or results</note> of the latent-deposit of action, which is attainable by the following up of yoga, they have no latent-deposit of white action. For that action, the fruit of which is indestructible—that is, Isolation—is called white. The meaning is: for one who seeks no fruit at all,²—how can he have that specific action whose fruit is indestructible? Having thus described the four-fold kinds of action, he determines which belongs to which by saying "Of these four . . . the not-white."

---

**8. As a result of this there follows the manifestation of those subconscious-impressions only which correspond to the fruition of their action.**

"As a result of this" means as a result of the three kinds of action <note>black, white, and mixed</note>. The words "of those only which correspond to the fruition of their action" means that those subconscious-impressions <note>original: vāsanā; latent memories or tendencies</note> which correspond to the ripening of that specific action which is compatible with them, dwell upon the fruition of that action. The manifestation of these only follows. 

For when the action of the gods is ripening, it is not the efficient cause for the manifestation of hellish or of brutish or of human subconscious-impressions. It does, however, make manifest those subconscious-impressions only which correspond to a divine state. And the reasoning is the same with regard to hellish or brutish or human subconscious-impressions.

Having discussed in detail the latent-deposit of action, he tells what the outcome of the latent-deposit of the hindrances <note>original: kleśas</note> will be.

**9. There is an uninterrupted causal relation of subconscious-impressions, although remote in species and point-of-space and moment-of-time, by reason of the correspondence between memory and subliminal-impressions.**

Why is this? Because, although those subconscious-impressions are remote, the action [which produces] the same [result] becomes their manifester, [that is] efficient-cause; and so there is an uninterrupted causal relation. And wherefore is this? # iv. 9-] Book IV. Isolation or Kāivalya <note>original: Kaivalya; the state of absolute freedom or liberation in Yoga</note>

and subliminal impressions <note>original: samskaras; deep-seated mental imprints</note> are manifested <note>literally "phenomenalized," or brought into the realm of experience</note> by virtue of the fact that the latent deposit of action <note>original: karmashaya; the "stock" of accumulated past deeds</note> assumes a fluctuation <note>original: vritti; a modification or wave in the mind-stuff</note>.
