An objector says, “This may be true. But in the case of a man who immediately after his death passed into an existence as a cat, one would expect a manifestation of human subconscious impressions, in that these came immediately before. For it cannot be that one should not remember what was experienced on the day immediately preceding, but should remember what was experienced in the days before the intervention.” In reply to this, he says:

**9. There is an uninterrupted [causal] relation [of subconscious impressions], although remote in species and point of space and moment of time, by reason of the correspondence between memory and subliminal impressions.**

Although the subconscious impression of the cat may pass through intervening births and so on, still there is an uninterrupted succession of this subconscious impression with respect to its fruit <note>the specific result or experience</note>. For in consequence of the action <note>original: karma</note> whose ripening <term>vipaka: the maturation or "cooking" of past actions into results</term> was a birth as a cat, that particular subconscious impression which corresponds to its ripening would become manifest, and the memory of that subconscious impression would be produced, as he says, <<the rise [into consciousness] of the ripening [which results in a birth] as a cat.>> 

The "rise [into consciousness]" means that from which something rises into consciousness, [that is] the latent deposit of action. The words, <<and if again just that observable [form] by the operation of the conditions which manifest <term>vyañjaka: external triggers or catalysts</term> that given thing should rise [into consciousness]>> would mean that it would be manifested [that is] it would be brought near to the beginning of its ripening. This is the meaning. <<Subliminally existent>> means activities [of certain impressions]. <<In association with>>: it would be manifested after having seized [its object]. The meaning is that if it is to be manifested, it would be manifested only after having seized the subliminal impressions which correspond to its own ripening. 

Having explained that the result is in immediate succession with respect to the cause, he now explains the same with respect to the effect [memory] in the words <<And wherefore is this? . . . memory.>> There is similarity since both [memory and impression] correspond. This same thing he says by the word <<like.>> 

It is objected: “If the subliminal impressions are of the nature of experience, then in that case, since experiences are transitory, so also should the subliminal impressions be transitory. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Sutra 4.9, which explains how latent mental imprints (vasanas) persist across different lifetimes. It now transitions into Sutra 10, which argues that these imprints have no beginning in time because the fundamental will to live is eternal.</meta>

<page-num>309</page-num>

### Priority of desire [—iv. 10]

The <term>mental imprint<note>original: vasana; the lingering "perfume" or habit left by past experiences</note></term> is stable, even though it was caused by a fleeting experience. This similarity between a past experience and a present memory is actually based on a subtle difference; otherwise, if they were identical in essence, the comparison of "similarity" would be impossible. The rest of this argument is easy to follow.

**10. Furthermore, these <term>latent tendencies<note>original: vasanas; subconscious impressions</note></term> have no beginning in time, since the desire for life is permanent.**

These latent tendencies have no beginning because the desire for existence is eternal. This well-known desire—as mentioned in [Sutra ii. 9]—for one’s own self, expressed as "May I never cease to be! May I continue to exist!" is found in every living being and is not caused by the current life alone. 

Why is this so? How could the fear of death—which is driven by the memory of previous hatred and pain—arise in a <term>living creature<note>original: jantu; any sentient being</note></term> that has only just been born? In its current life, it has never experienced death. Furthermore, something that is self-caused does not need an external trigger. 

For these reasons, the <term>consciousness-field<note>original: citta; often translated as "mind-stuff"</note></term>, filled with these beginningless latent tendencies, uses a <term>triggering cause<note>original: nimitta; an efficient or instrumental cause</note></term> to activate certain memories, presenting them for the experience of the <term>Pure Awareness<note>original: Purusha; the witnessing Self</note></term>. 

Some other thinkers have concluded that the consciousness-field has a physical size corresponding to the dimension of the body—much like <gloss>1</gloss> the light of a lamp which is condensed when placed in a jar and spread out when placed in a palace. These thinkers argue that there is an intermediate state for the mind during the <term>cycle of reincarnation<note>original: samsara; the round of rebirths</note></term>. 

However, the Master <note>referring to the traditional commentator Vyasa</note> teaches that it is only the "fluctuation" or activity of this all-pervasive consciousness-field that contracts and expands. This mind also requires specific triggering causes, such as <term>merit<note>original: dharma; right-living or virtue</note></term>. 

This triggering cause is of two kinds: that which is external and that which is internal. The external kind involves the body and outside actions, such as receiving praise, giving alms, and performing respectful salutations. The internal kind, such as faith or belief, belongs solely to the consciousness-field itself. In this sense, it has been said:

> "As for friendliness and such <term>exalted states of mind<note>referring to the four virtues: friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity</note></term>, they are the joyful practices of <term>yoga practitioners<note>original: yogins</note></term>; they do not require external tools; they bring virtue to perfection."

Of these two—the inner and the outer methods—the work of the <term>inner mind<note>original: manas; the central-organ of thought</note></term> is the more powerful.

<page-num>310</page-num>
<header>iv. 10-] *Book IV. Liberation or Kāivalya* [310</header>

How is this? [The answer is, that intuitive] knowledge and <term>detachment<note>original: vairāgya; also translated as passionlessness</note></term> are unsurpassed by any other [force]. Who, by bodily action alone and without the power of the <term>mind-stuff<note>original: citta; the field of consciousness</note></term>, could empty¹ the Daṇḍaka Forest [of its inhabitants], or like the sage Agastya,² drink up the entire sea?

An objector says, “This may be true. But <term>subconscious impressions<note>original: vasanas; latent mental tendencies or habits</note></term> that were formed in a previous or even more distant birth might only manifest if there were a <term>source of valid knowledge<note>original: pramāṇa; a standard of proof</note></term> to prove that a previous birth even existed. But such proof does not exist. Furthermore, it should not be argued that the simple experience of joy or grief in a newborn animal is proof of a previous birth. This could be explained as being naturally self-caused, much like the rhythmic closing and opening of a lotus flower.” In reply to this objection, the author states:

**10. Furthermore, these [subconscious impressions] have no beginning [in time], since the desire for life is permanent.**

The "beginninglessness" of these subconscious impressions—rather than just their continuous causal relationship—is what is meant by the word "Furthermore." This is because the "desire for self" (the will to live) never loses its eternal character; therefore, these impressions have no assignable beginning. 

If someone objects that the eternal nature of this desire is unproven (arguing instead that it is simply self-caused), the reply points to "this well-known desire." A skeptic might ask, "Why should we assume this?" The answer lies in the behavior of "an animal just brought into life," a creature in a condition where it has not yet experienced death in this current birth. In other words, it is a being that has not yet encountered the event of dying. 

How, then, could a child—having just fallen forward from its mother’s lap and trembling with fear—possess a fear of death? This fear is rooted in the memory of past pain and the aversion to it. We can infer this fear from the specific way the child quivers as it tightly grasps the thread³ (adorned with a protective disk and other auspicious charms) hanging around its mother’s neck. 

If the skeptic again argues that this reaction is merely self-caused, the reply is "Furthermore, no." A self-caused event does not require an efficient cause to bring it into existence. What the author means is this: the trembling seen in a small child is grounded in fear. It is a specific kind of trembling, exactly like our own when we are afraid. And because the child's fear is identical to our own, it must be based on the memory of past pain. This fear, characterized by the expectation of future suffering, does not arise from thin air. Having instinctively inferred that the thing it fears is a cause of suffering—

<meta>This page continues the logical proof for the existence of past lives, specifically refuting the "naturalist" argument that instinctive behaviors are uncaused. It then transitions into a debate between philosophical schools regarding the physical size or "extent" of the mind-stuff (citta).</meta>

<page-num>311</page-num>
<header>Extent of the mind-stuff [-iv. 10</header>

Even a newborn child is afraid of something disagreeable. This fear is a result of the memory of a specific kind of pain, accompanied by a dislike for the cause of that fear which was experienced in the past. When the child encounters that cause now, he infers it will cause pain and becomes afraid. 

The child has had no opportunity in this current life to conclude that falling causes pain, nor has he experienced that specific pain yet. Therefore, the only logical conclusion remaining is that these experiences relate to previous births. 

This can be formally argued as follows: The memory of a newborn is based on a previous experience, because it is a memory—just like our own adult memories. 

One cannot argue that the opening and closing of a lotus flower is "self-caused" (happening without external influence). If something were truly self-caused, it would require no other conditions. If that were true, even the heat of a fire would require no cause. In reality, the expansion of a lotus is triggered by an accidental cause—such as contact with the rays of the morning sun—and its closing is caused by a <term>latent impression<note>original: saṁskāra; a subconscious habit or tendency that remains in the mind</note></term> which leads it to return to its original state. 

Similarly, when we see a child laugh or show signs of physical distress, we must infer that joy or grief experienced in a previous life is the cause of these actions. 

Having established this, the author brings the discussion to a close by saying, "It is for these reasons." By the term "efficient cause," he refers to <term>karma<note>The law of cause and effect where past actions dictate current circumstances</note></term> that has reached the point of fruition. "Laying hold of" refers to the moment these traits manifest.

Next, to resolve the various conflicting opinions regarding the dimensions of the <term>mind-stuff<note>original: citta; the field of conscious and subconscious mental activity</note></term>, he describes the different views using the analogy of "a water-jar... a palace."

### [The Sāṁkhya School's View]

The <term>Sāṁkhya<note>One of the oldest schools of Indian philosophy, which focuses on the duality of consciousness and matter</note></term> perspective is as follows: Since we only see the mind-stuff functioning within the boundaries of the physical body, there is no proof that it exists outside the body. 

However, it is not the size of an atom. If the mind were an infinitesimal atom, it would be impossible to experience multiple sensations at once. For instance, when eating a <term>festive snack<note>original: kōḍaboḷe or karanjī; a long, spiced cake or pastry eaten during Hindu festivals like Diwali. The author uses this to show how we feel the texture, taste, and smell of the food simultaneously over a large surface area of the tongue and mouth.</note></term>, we experience a five-fold sensation through our organs simultaneously. There is no evidence for the claim that these sensations actually happen in a rapid sequence that only *appears* simultaneous. Furthermore, a single "atomic" mind could not contact different organs located in different parts of the body at the exact same moment.

Therefore, the only remaining alternative for the Sāṁkhya school is that the mind-stuff is the same size as the body. Whether in the body of an ant or an elephant, the mind-stuff expands or contracts to fit its container, much like the light of a lamp expands or contracts depending on whether it is placed inside a small water-jar or a vast palace.

<header>iv. 10—] Book IV. Isolation or Liberation [312</header>

a [large] palace.' [So it is that] others have come to the conclusion that the form [of the mind-stuff] is the dimension of the body itself; it is that of which the dimension [is the body]. The <term>Sāṁkhya<note>One of the six major schools of Hindu philosophy, focusing on the dualism between consciousness and matter.</note></term> objector continues. 'If this [atomic theory] were true, how can this [mind-stuff] come into relation with the <term>womb<note>original: kṣetra; literally "the field," often used to refer to the physical body or the womb in the context of rebirth.</note></term> or the seed? Since [this mind-stuff] is dependent. For certainly when posts and such things do not move, their shadows do not move; nor when the canvas is not moving does the picture which rests upon it move. Therefore he says «And thus [they say] there is an intermediate state and there is ground for the round-of-rebirths.» The words «And thus» mean when [the mind-stuff] is of the dimension of the body, there is, in order to get into another body, both the leaving of the first body and the getting into the other body, by means of a correlation, while on the way <note>original: antarā; used here as an adverb meaning "in between."</note> with a migratory body. <note>This refers to a temporary vehicle for the soul between physical incarnations.</note> For of course by this [correlation] he would pass into another body as the <term>Sacred History<note>original: Purāṇa; ancient texts containing mythology and philosophy.</note></term> passage also says, "**Yama** <note>The God of Death.</note> by force drew forth a man the size of a thumb." This is what is meant by saying that there is an intermediate state and that consequently there would be ground for the round-of-rebirths.' Not tolerating this opinion, he gives his own by saying «the fluctuation.» It is only the all-pervasive mind-stuff's fluctuation which contracts and expands. So the Master, the **Self-born**, <note>A title for the creator or a supreme teacher; here identified as Patañjali.</note> set forth. His point [in rejecting the other theory] is this. If the mind-stuff without something-in-which-it-resides cannot get into a body, how does it [in the first place] find this something-in-which-it-resides in the migratory body? And if we imagine another body in this case, that would involve an infinite regress. Further, it is not possible that this migratory body be drawn forth from the body, since it is only when drawn forth that the mind-stuff can come into correlation with [the migratory body]. Therefore let there be a <term>subtle body<note>original: sūkṣma-çarīra; an ethereal body that carries the mind and vital energies between physical births.</note></term> from the moment of creation and up to the time of the great [mundane] dissolution. It would be limited in its function to the six-sheathed body, which would be the locus of the mind-stuffs. For so the mind-stuff could pass about in one body after another up to the Truth-world <note>The highest heavenly realm.</note> and down to **Avīci**. <note>The lowest and most painful of the Buddhist and Hindu hells.</note> And one could explain the drawing forth of this subtile body from the six-sheathed body. For in this case there is [no difficulty as to an] intermediate state of this [subtile body], because this [subtile body] is always necessarily there. <page-num>313</page-num>
<header>No migratory body [-iv. 10</header>

There is no ocular demonstration <note>visible proof</note> for this. Nor can the cycle of rebirth be used as a logical proof for the existence of this [subtle body]. This cycle can be explained just as well by the Master’s theory. While as for the Tradition (<term>āgama</term> <note>Sacred scripture or inherited wisdom</note>), it speaks of "drawing out" a person (<term>puruṣa</term> <note>The true Self or pure consciousness</note>). But a "person" is neither the mind-stuff nor a subtle migratory body; it is the Energy of Intellect <note>original: citi-śakti</note> which does not merge with physical objects. Since it is impossible to literally "draw out" this energy, we must understand the scriptural quote as being merely metaphorical. Thus, the explanation of the metaphor is that "drawing out" simply means the cessation of a fluctuation <note>vṛtti; the active movement or thoughts of the mind</note> belonging to both the Intellect and the mind-stuff regarding this or that object. 

As for what has been said in the <term>Smṛti</term> <note>Traditional legal and social texts</note>, the <term>Itihāsa</term> <note>Epics like the Mahabharata</note>, or the <term>Purāṇas</term> <note>Ancient lore and mythologies</note> regarding the mind-stuff just after it enters the body of a <term>Preta</term> <note>A "hungry ghost" or spirit of the deceased</note>, and how it is liberated from that state through the performance of commemorative feasts (<term>sapiṇḍīkaraṇa</term> <note>A ritual performed a year after death to unite the deceased with their ancestors</note>) and so on—all of this we accept. However, what we cannot tolerate is the idea that the mind-stuff itself is migratory <note>physically moving from one place to another</note>. There is no Tradition to support your theory. For the messengers of <term>Yama</term> <note>The god of death and justice</note> carry the person bound in chains only because he possesses a body in a general sense. It is never stated that there is a specific "migratory body." 

Hence, since the mind is an effect of the personality-substance <note>original: asmitā; the sense of "I-am-ness"</note>, and since this personality-substance pervades the three worlds like the sphere of the atmosphere, the central-organ <note>the mind or psyche</note> is also all-pervasive. <note>The Mīmāṁsā school holds that the self (ātman) is omnipresent. The Sāṁkhya-sūtras deny that the mind is all-pervasive, arguing it has a "middle dimension." The Vāiçeṣika and Nyāya schools see the self as atomic. The Yoga school taught here argues the mind-stuff is all-pervasive, but its activities expand and contract.</note> 

An objector says, "If this is true, then the fluctuations of this mind-stuff would also be all-pervasive, and everyone would be omniscient." 

The reply to this is: "only this . . . fluctuation." 

The objector replies, "This may be true. But how does this fluctuation, which depends only on mind-stuff, experience its contraction and expansion from time to time?" 

In reply to this, he says, "This [mind-stuff] furthermore." And this mind-stuff requires an efficient cause, such as right-living <note>dharma</note>, for its fluctuation to occur. He classifies this cause by saying, "And this efficient-cause." By the words "such . . . as," we are to understand things like energy and wealth. By the words "like belief, for instance," we are to understand qualities like energy and mindfulness <note>as discussed in Yoga Sūtra i. 20</note>. 

Regarding these being internal means, he cites the agreement of the Teachers by saying, "And in this sense it has been said." "Diversion" refers to functional activity. "Perfection" means whiteness <note>purity</note>. "Of these two" refers to the inner and the outer means. "[Intuitive] knowledge and passionlessness" refer to the qualities produced by them. By what quality of outer attainment are these outer means surpassed or overwhelmed? It is the qualities resulting from intuitive knowledge and passionlessness that overcome them, removing the mind from its previous condition.

<summary>This page argues that the mind-stuff (citta) is all-pervasive rather than a small body that travels between lives. It explains that "rebirth" and scriptural descriptions of souls being moved are metaphorical descriptions of changes in mental activity driven by karma and spiritual practice.</summary>

# Book IV. Isolation or Kaivalya

...of seed <note>The "seed" refers to the potential for future rebirth stored within the mind's subconscious traces</note>. This is the meaning. On this point he gives a well-known illustration in the words “the Daṇḍaka Forest” <note>A legendary forest in Indian epics, used here to illustrate how a vast area can be affected or transformed by a single cause</note>.

**11. Since [subconscious-impressions] are associated with cause and motive and mental-substrate (āśraya <note>The foundation or support upon which something rests</note>) and stimulus, if these cease to be, then those [subconscious-impressions] cease to be.**

1. **As to cause.** From right-living <note>original: dharma; acting in accordance with cosmic and moral law</note> results pleasure; from wrong-living <note>original: adharma</note>, pain; from pleasure, passion; from pain, aversion; and from this, struggle. Quivering in the central-organ <note>the mind-stuff or thinking faculty</note> or in the vocal-organ or in the body with this [struggle], a person either helps or injures another. From this again result right-living and wrong-living, pleasure and pain, passion and aversion. Thus revolves <gloss>1</gloss> the **six-spoked wheel** <gloss>2</gloss> of the round-of-rebirths <note>original: saṃsāracakram; the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth</note>. And as it ceaselessly revolves, undifferentiated-consciousness (**avidyā** <note>spiritual ignorance; the inability to distinguish the permanent Self from the temporary world</note>), the root of all the hindrances, is its motive-power. Such is cause. 

2. **But motive** is that [human purpose] with reference to which any condition (*yasya*) such as right-living becomes operative [in the present]. For it is not the rise of anything new <note>it is the manifestation of what was already latent in the mind</note>. 

3. **The central-organ**, however, while its task is yet unfulfilled, is the **mental-substrate** of subconscious-impressions. For when the task of the central-organ is fulfilled <note>meaning, when the mind has achieved its goal of providing experience and liberation for the Soul</note>, the subconscious-impressions, now without a mental-substrate, are not able to persist. 

4. **When a thing** confronted [with some object] brings to the surface any subconscious-impression [in itself], then [that object] is the **stimulus** of that [subconscious-impression]. 

Thus all subconscious-impressions are associated with these causes and motives and mental-substrates and stimuli. If they cease to be, the subconscious-impressions cohering with them also cease to be.

The question is raised: if these fluctuations of mind-stuff and the subconscious-impressions are without beginning, how can they be destroyed? For surely the **Energy of Intellect** (**citi** <note>pure consciousness or the power of the Soul</note>) which is without beginning cannot be destroyed. In reply to this he says, **11. Since [subconscious-impressions] are associated with cause and motive and mental-substrate (āśraya) and stimulus,**

<header>The principles of individuation</header>
<meta>iv. 12</meta>
<sig>A</sig>

if these cease to be, then those [subconscious-impressions] cease to be. Even a thing that has no beginning can evidently perish; for instance, the state of a thing being yet to come <note>original: anāgatatva</note>. [This is prior non-existence <note>original: prāg-abhāva; the logical state of a thing before it is created</note>.] So, being "without beginning" is not a valid logical proof <note>original: sādhana; the middle term in a syllogism</note> for eternal existence, because it applies to too many things <note>i.e., it is a "too wide" definition because things like "prior non-existence" have no beginning but do have an end</note>. As to the Energy of Intellect <note>the eternal, unchanging power of pure consciousness</note>, on the other hand, since there is no cause which could make it perish, it does not perish. But the reason for this is not simply that it has no beginning. And it has been stated in the aphorism <note>original: sūtra</note> that there is a cause which brings about the destruction of subconscious-impressions, although they have existed from time without beginning. 

Helping and injuring others are partial expressions for the efficient-cause of right-living <note>original: dharma; merit</note> and wrong-living <note>original: adharma; demerit</note> and so on. Under this expression, the drinking of spirits and similar prohibited acts are also included. The motive-power <note>original: netrī</note> is that which keeps the wheel of rebirth moving <note>original: nāyikā; the leader or directress</note>. He gives the reason for this in the words "the root" <note>referring to spiritual ignorance or avidyā</note>. Becoming operative is "presentness"; but it does not mean that right-living as such is made to grow from nothing. Of this very point the reason is given in the words "For it is not." That thing with which one is confronted would be an object of desire, such as contact with a maiden. So the meaning of the aphorism is that where the more extensive cause is absent, there the less extensive effect is also absent.

Since there is no production of that which is non-existent, nor destruction of that which is existent <note>a core principle of Sāṅkhya-Yoga philosophy called Satkāryavāda: effects pre-exist in their causes</note>, how will subconscious-impressions, by reason of their existence as real things, cease to exist?

**12. Past and future as such exist [in their own nature]; [therefore subconscious-impressions do not cease to be]. For the different time-forms belong to the various qualities of the objects.**

The future is that the manifestation <note>original: phenomenalization</note> of which is yet to come. The past is that the individual manifested form of which has already been experienced. The present is that which has entered into its functional activity. And this three-fold existence is the object for the intuitive knowledge of the practitioner <note>original: yogin</note>. And if they did not exist as real entities, this intuitive knowledge, having no real object to grasp, would not emerge <gloss>1</gloss> [in the mind-stuff]. Therefore, past and future exist as real things. Moreover, if the result of one's actions <note>original: karma</note>—either that which leads to worldly experience or that which leads to spiritual liberation—were entirely without any describable existence when it has yet to emerge, then the actions of the wise, directed towards achieving or avoiding these results, would have no logical ground. A cause is capable of making a result that already exists in potentiality become present, but it is not capable of producing <gloss>2</gloss> [something out of nothing].

<page-num>317</page-num>
# Past and future exist [-iv. 13

When one thing is the cause of another, it can bring its particular function into play only when the effect is [already] existing. For instance, consider the chapters of the <term>Veda</term> <note>The most ancient and sacred scriptures of Hinduism, containing hymns and ritual instructions.</note> referring to the [cutting of] sacrificial reeds (*kāṇḍalāva*). For certainly these cuttings of reeds do not bring into existence what is not already existing. Instead, they cause modifications or they bring near a thing which is already existing.

Similarly, the potter and the [efficient causes] <note>The "efficient cause" is the person or force that acts upon matter, like a baker (efficient cause) acting on flour (material cause).</note> lead to the present existence of a water-jar which already exists, just as the author says, “an already existent thing.” But if the past and future are to be supposed as being non-existent simply because they are not in the present, then, goodness gracious! the present would also be non-existent, because it is not currently in the past or the future. 

But as to existence, regardless of its relation to a specific time-form or to substance, it equally holds for all three states, as he says: “A substance, moreover.” The words “are in successive states” mean belonging to each state one by one. The expression “as a material thing” means in a substance which is a material thing. The grammatical ending *-tas* <note>A Sanskrit suffix used to denote various case relationships, often meaning "from" or "in regard to."</note> is used here for all case-endings. 

If the past and the future only exist so far as they are "past" and "future," then at the present moment they "are not," because at this time they are not yet past or no longer future, as he says, “And while one.” He brings the discussion to a close with the words, “state-of-existence after having-been-in-a-state-of-non-existence.” <note>This philosophical argument rejects the idea that things can pop into existence from total nothingness; everything is a transformation of what came before.</note>

**13. These [external aspects with the three time-forms] are manifest [individuals] or subtle [generic forms], and their essence is the qualities (*guṇas*).**

"These" refers to those external aspects with the three time-forms: those which are manifest <note>original: phenomenalized; appearing in the physical world.</note> are the present; those which are subtle are the past and the future—specifically the six non-particulars. <note>In this system of philosophy, the "non-particulars" are the intermediate stages of evolution between pure consciousness and the physical world.</note> Since this whole world is nothing more than a particular arrangement of the qualities <note>original: guṇa; the three fundamental forces of nature—balance (sattva), activity (rajas), and inertia (tamas).</note>, it has, in the strict sense, these qualities as its essence. And in this sense, the Exposition of the System <note>Refers to a foundational commentary on the Yoga Sutras.</note> has said:

->“The qualities, even from their greatest height,<-
->Do not come within the range of sight.<-
->But all that comes within the range of sight<-
->Seems like a phantom and is empty quite.”<-

### Book IV. Isolation or Liberation <note>original: *Kaivalya*, the final state of freedom and detachment in Yoga philosophy.</note>

iv.13—]

An objector says, "This may be true. But this manifold amplification <note>original: *prapañca*, the diversification or unfolding of the world from its basic state.</note> of the varied forms of the universe <note>original: *viśva*</note>, having as its essence the kinds of mutation which are the states of the substance and its external aspects, cannot properly come out of one primary substance. For from a cause which has no diversity, diversities of effect cannot come to pass." In reply to this he says:

**13. These [external aspects with the three time-forms] are manifest [individuals] or subtle [generic forms], and their essence is the primary qualities.** <note>original: *guṇa*. In this philosophy, all matter is composed of three qualities: *sattva* (purity/light), *rajas* (activity/passion), and *tamas* (darkness/inertia).</note>

These external aspects with the three time-forms <note>The past, present, and future.</note>, both the manifest and the subtle, have the primary qualities as their essence. For they have no other cause than the three-fold qualities. But as to their diversity, it follows from the diversity attending upon the beginningless subconscious impressions from hindrances produced by these primary qualities. In which sense it has been said in the **Vāyu Purāṇa**,¹ "Because the primary cause has manifold forms, there is a marvelous mutation." Of the earth and the other manifest individuals, and of the eleven organs <note>The five senses, the five organs of action, and the mind.</note>, which are present forms, there are past and future forms, which are the six non-particularized forms; and these arise according to their capacity.

Making now a distinction between the permanent and the impermanent forms of the universe, he gives first its permanent form in the words "this whole world." "This" [that is] the visible [world]. "A collocation" means a mutation with a particular arrangement of parts. On this point there is a specific mention of the **Shaṣṭitantra**² text. It is like a phantom <note>original: *māyā*, often translated as illusion or a magical display.</note>, but not quite a phantom. "Empty quite" means perishable. For just as a phantom in no time assumes different shapes, so those evolved effects whose external aspects become visible and invisible change from moment to moment. Whereas primary matter is permanent, and thus not homogeneous with a phantom, and is accordingly an ultimate reality.

---

But if all things are merely the three primary qualities (*guṇa*), how is it that there is a single sound and a single organ of sense?

**14. The identity of a thing is due to the unity of its mutation.**

When the qualities—disposed to vividness <note>sattva</note>, activity <note>rajas</note>, and inertia <note>tamas</note>—have as their essence the processes of knowing, insofar as they are instruments [of perception], there is a single mutation; for instance, the organ of hearing. When their essence is objects for—

### **14. The reality of a thing is due to the unity of its transformation.** <note>original: *Pariṇāmaikatvād vastutattvam*</note>

# Why is this incorrect?

**15. Because, while the [physical] thing remains the same, the mind-stuffs are different, [therefore the two are upon] distinct levels-of-existence.**

A single [physical] object is the common basis for many <term>mind-stuffs <note>original: "citta"; the individual mental field including intellect and ego</note></term>. It is not, of course, created by a single mind-stuff, nor yet is it created by many mind-stuffs. It is rather grounded in itself. Why is this? Because, while the [physical] thing remains the same, the mind-stuffs are different. When the mind-stuff is in relation with <term>virtue <note>original: "dharma"</note></term>, the mind-stuff has thoughts of pleasure, even though the [physical] thing remains the same. When in relation with <term>vice <note>original: "adharma"</note></term>, from the same [physical thing] it has thoughts of pain. When in relation with <term>delusion <note>original: "avidyā"</note></term>, from the same [physical thing] it has thoughts of infatuation. When in relation with complete insight, from the same thing it has thoughts of detachment.² If this is so, by whose mind-stuff would this thing be formed? Nor would it be sound to say that one person's mind-stuff is affected when brought into relation with an object formed by the mind-stuff of another person. Consequently, the [physical] thing and the thought—distinct because of their dissimilarity, in that the thing is the object-for-knowledge and the thought is the process-of-knowing—[exist upon] distinct levels-of-existence. There is not even a trace³ of a blending of the two. 

But from the point-of-view of the <term>Sāṃkhya <note>A school of philosophy that views the world as a real evolution of matter (Prakṛti) independent of the soul</note></term>, since a thing has three <term>aspects <note>original: "guṇa"; the three fundamental qualities of nature: goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas)</note></term> and since the changes of these aspects⁴ are unstable, the object comes into relation with the mind-stuffs [of different people]. Dependent [for its effect in this case or the other] upon such determinants as virtue [or vice or delusion or complete insight], it becomes the cause, in one form...

...or another, of presented-ideas, as they rise [into consciousness], corresponding [in quality] to the [determining] efficient-cause.

So having in this manner, independently of the <term>sūtra <note>original: "sūtra"; a concise aphorism or rule</note></term>, given the reason for setting up [the physical thing] as something over and above the mental-act, the author of the Comment introduces the reason as given in the <term>sūtra</term> itself by the words “Why is this?”

**15. Because, while the [physical] thing remains the same, the mind-stuffs <note>original: "citta"; the individual's field of consciousness</note> are different, [therefore the two are upon] distinct levels-of-existence.**

Whatever units are in the manifold these differ absolutely from the manifold. For instance, a single thought in <term>Chāitra <note>Chāitra, Māitra, Devadatta, and Vishṇumitra are generic names used in Sanskrit logic, much like "John Doe" or "Jane Smith."</note></term> or in <term>Māitra</term> is distinct from the presented-ideas in <term>Devadatta</term> and in <term>Vishṇumitra</term>, which are dissimilar. And since the intended-object is not different, even when the thoughts about it are manifold, it is other than the mental-acts. And further, the identity of the intended-object, although the thoughts of those who know it validly are different, is determined by the connection of one [thought] with another [in memory]. For in the case of a single woman who is presented-to-the-minds of several persons—one enamored, one ill-disposed, one infatuated, or one detached—we see a reciprocal connection so that one thinks, “She who is seen by you is seen by me also.”

Consequently, while the [physical] thing remains the same, because the mind-stuffs are different, because there is a difference of thoughts, [therefore] the two—the intended-object and the thought—[are upon] distinct levels-of-existence [that is] [distinct] means of distinguishing the essential attributes. In the lover, a thought of pleasure with reference to the woman loved; in rival mistresses, a thought of pain; but in <term>Chāitra</term> who has not obtained her, a thought of infatuation, a depression.

“This may be so,” the objector says, “but that intended-object with the distinguishing characteristic of being loved is figured forth by a mind-stuff of one person. And this same [intended-object] affects the mind-stuff of the others also. So [this mind-stuff] might be supposed to be common.” In reply to this he says, “nor would it be . . . another.” For if that were so, when one person has the thought of blue, all would have the thought of blue.

A further objection would be this: “Even according to the view which maintains the distinct existence of objects <note>original: "arthavāda"; here referring to the philosophical realism that objects exist independently of the mind</note>, how can one and the same object be the cause of mental-acts differing according to the difference in pleasure and the other [experiences]? For from a cause which is not different in its distinguishing characteristics, there should be no difference in effects.” In reply to this he says, “from the point-of-view of the <term>Sāṁkhya <note>The Sāṁkhya school is a dualist philosophy that identifies two eternal realities: Puruṣa (pure consciousness) and Prakṛti (matter/nature).</note></term>.” It is quite consistent to say that the same external thing which is a mutation of the three aspects <note>original: "guṇa"; the three fundamental qualities of nature: Sattva (purity/light), Rajas (activity/passion), and Tamas (inertia/darkness).</note> has three forms.

The objector says, “Even if it be so, then all without distinction would have a mental-act of pleasure and of pain and of infatuation.” In reply to this he says, “dependent [for its existence] upon such determinants as right-living.” The <term>sattva <note>The quality of light, goodness, and harmony.</note></term> accompanied by the <term>rajas <note>The quality of energy, movement, and passion.</note></term> and determined by right-living produces the sensation of happiness. But this same <term>sattva</term> when determined by knowledge <note>original: "vidyā"</note>, after the <term>rajas</term> has been removed, gives rise to a sensation of detachment. And right-living and the other [experiences]...

There are some who say that a thing is coextensive with its thought, in so far as like pleasure and the other [experiences] it is experienced. In this way when they thus reject the quality of being common [to several mind-stuffs], they deny the existence of the thing in both its earlier and its later moments. <note>The argument here is that if an object only exists when it is being thought about, it has no past or future existence outside of that momentary thought.</note>

### 16. And a thing is not dependent upon a single mind-stuff, [for then in certain cases] it could not be proved [by that mind-stuff], [and] then what would it be?

<margin>As the <term>School of Consciousness-Only <note>original: "Vijñānavāda"</note></term> maintains.</margin> If a thing were dependent upon a single mind-stuff, then if the mind-stuff be distracted or restricted <note>meaning the person is focused on something else or in a deep meditative trance</note>, it itself would be untouched by that mind-stuff. And not coming within the range of that [mind-stuff], and not being proved [by that mind-stuff], and unperceived in its nature by any one, would it then be at all? <margin>Compare de la Vallée Poussin: *The Negation of the Soul* (Journal Asiatique, 9th series, volume 20, 1902, pages 248 and 254).</margin> And how could it be produced again in relation to the mind-stuff? It would not possess those parts of it which are not apparent. So that if one says the back does not exist, neither could the belly be known. <note>This is a classic argument for the permanence of objects: if you only see the front of a jar, the back must still exist for the jar to be a "jar."</note> Consequently an intended-object is independent [of mind-stuff] and common to all the <term>Selves <note>original: "Purusha"; the eternal witnesses or souls of individuals</note></term>. And again independent mind-stuffs function differently for each <term>Self</term>. As a result of a relation between these two [the intended-object and the mind-stuff] there follows an apperception <note>the process by which the mind becomes aware of its own perceptions</note>, an experience of the <term>Self</term>.

The intended-object might be admitted to be distinct from knowledge, still since it is insensate (*insensate <note>original: "jada"; lacking its own consciousness or light</note>*), it cannot be perceived in the absence of knowledge, but must be illumined by the knowledge. Accordingly [the object] is only at the time of the idea, and not at other times. Since there is no evidence that it exists at other times. This the author of the Comment confutes independently of the <term>aphorism <note>original: "sūtra"</note></term> in the words «In this way when they.» For a [physical] thing (*physical thing <note>original: "vastu"</note>*) is experienced by ordinary observers <margin>This would be the point of view of the <term>School that All Things Exist <note>original: "Sarvāstivādin"</note></term>.</margin> as common to all mind-stuffs and as persisting <margin>Compare <term>Logic Aphorisms <note>original: "Nyāya-sūtra"</note></term> book 1, section 1, aphorism 40.</margin> in the succession of various moments and as consisting of a mutation. <page-num>326</page-num>
<header>iv. 16—] Book IV. Isolation or <term>Kāivalya <note>The state of absolute spiritual independence or "aloneness" where the soul is freed from the influence of matter.</note></term></header>

[If the object were merely an idea, then its] disappearance would be coexistential with the appearance and disappearance of the idea. If so, how can one act in accordance with (<term>anurodha <note>acting up to or conforming with</note></term>) this objective-factor (<term>idamañça <note>literally "the 'this' part," referring to the external object as perceived</note></term>) so that one shall not at the same time deny its existence? This is the meaning. Or we may suppose that there is not a denial of this objective-factor. Let the intended-object be coexistential with the knowledge of it. To this also the reply is in the <term>sūtra <note>an aphorism or concise rule in Sanskrit literature</note></term>. 

**16. And a thing is not dependent upon a single mind-stuff, [for then in certain cases] it could not be proved [by that mind-stuff], [and] then what would it be?** 

For the same <term>mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the collective mental functions of intellect, ego, and memory</note></term> which perceives a water-jar, when distracted by another substance such as a piece of cloth, does not remain fixed upon the water-jar; or when the mind-stuff which has <term>discrimination <note>the ability to distinguish between the eternal Self and the temporary physical world</note></term> as its object, attains at that very time to <term>restriction <note>original: "nirodha"; the meditative state where mental fluctuations are stilled</note></term>;—at these times, since there is no knowledge of the water-jar or of the discrimination, the water-jar and the discrimination, being dependent for their existence upon one particular knowledge only, would surely cease to exist when this knowledge ceases. 

This he says in the words "dependent upon a single mind-stuff." The words "how could it be" mean that it could not be. How does it happen that the mind-stuff is in relation to this thing whether it be a water-jar or discrimination? For the effects invariably are where the cause is, and invariably are not where the cause is not. Without regard to their own peculiar cause they cannot be produced by another cause. And if they are supposed to be causeless, then one would have to deny such an inconsistency as their accidental existence. And there is no ground for saying that whatever causes the knowledge of the thing also causes the physical thing itself. For then it would follow that the taste, the medicinal power, the digestion, and so on would be the same whether one makes use of an actual sweetmeat or of a "sweetmeat of hope" <note>an imaginary or desired object</note>. 

Therefore the point is well taken when he says "And how could it be produced again in relation to the mind-stuff?" Furthermore, the front part of any object implies the existence of the middle and hind parts. But if the existence of the thing were to depend entirely upon the knowledge of it, then the upper and middle parts would not exist at all, since the idea of them is not currently in the observer's experience. And accordingly, since the "pervader" (the upper and middle parts) does not exist, the lower part, which is "pervaded" (the part being looked at), would also not exist. And thus if the whole object be absent, how could it be urged that the intended-object is coexistential with the knowledge? As he says, "It would not possess those parts." The words "are not apparent" mean they are not perceived. He brings the discussion to a close by saying "Consequently." The rest is easy.

<page-num>327</page-num>
<header>Objects are sometimes known and sometimes unknown [—IV. 17</header>

## 17. A thing is known or not known by virtue of whether or not it colors the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: "citta"; the mental mirror consisting of the intellect, ego, and sensory mind.</note></term>.

External objects, like magnets, pull the mind-stuff toward them—as if the mind had the properties of iron—and leave an impression upon it. An object is "known" only when the mind-stuff is affected or "colored" by it. However, the <term>Self <note>The Purusha or pure consciousness, which observes the mind without being changed by it.</note></term>, who is distinct from the mind, is not known in this same way. The mind-stuff is subject to <term>mutations <note>original: "pariṇāma"; constant changes or transformations in state.</note></term> because the nature of an external thing is sometimes known <note>See Book II, section 20, page 152 of the Calcutta edition.</note> and sometimes not known.

This point might <note>The purpose of this aphorism (sūtra) is to dismantle the arguments of "Idealism," which claims objects only exist as ideas in the mind.</note> be conceded. "But," as an opponent might argue, "if an object is independent and lacks its own consciousness (insensate), it could never 'throw out light'—that is, make itself known. If it did produce its own light, it would no longer be unconscious. If it lost its unconscious nature, it would cease to be what it is, for a thing cannot exist if it casts off its own essential nature. Furthermore, one cannot claim that 'throwing out light' is a property of the object that is simply activated by our sense organs. If being 'lit up' were a property of the object itself, then once one person perceived it, that 'light' would be visible to everyone, just as the color blue is visible to all. Thus, if a single scholar understood a complex philosophical system, every person in the world would instantly become a scholar, and there would be no one left who is ignorant. Nor is it logical to say that an object's current appearance exists in its past or future. Therefore, the idea that an object exists independently outside of our conscious perception is nothing more than a wishful thought." 

In reply to this objection, the author recites the seventeenth sūtra: **17. A thing is known or not known by virtue of its affecting [or not affecting] the mind-stuff.**

Even though an object is itself unconscious, it affects the mind-stuff through the "channels" of the sense organs. The **Energy of Intellect** <note>original: "citi-çakti"; the pure power of consciousness.</note> casts its reflection into the "mirror" of the mind-stuff when the mind is in this affected state. By **enlivening** <note>original: "cetayamānā"; making the unconscious mind appear conscious through reflection.</note> the mind-stuff that has been colored by the object, the Energy of Intellect "experiences" the object. 

The Intellect does not actually give the object the property of "visibility." Nor is the Energy of Intellect ever truly "out of relation" with the mind-stuff, because we have established that its reflection is joined with the mind. Even though the mind-stuff is theoretically omnipresent, and the senses (made of "personality-substance") might not be in direct physical contact <note>Reading the Sanskrit "viṣaye nāsti" as "is not [directly] in the object."</note> with the distant object, the specific "fluctuation" or activity of the mind within a particular body creates that connection. This is why objects are compared to magnets: because the mind-stuff has properties like iron, the objects draw the mind toward them through the senses and leave an impression. Thus, the mind-stuff is capable of constant change or mutation, as the author states when he refers to the "mutations of the thing."

<summary>This page explains the Yoga philosophy of perception: objects are independent of the mind, but become "known" only when they leave an impression on the mind-stuff, which is then illuminated by the reflection of pure consciousness.</summary>

<page-num>328</page-num>
<header>iv. 18—] Book IV. Isolation or <term>Kāivalya <note>The state of ultimate spiritual liberation or "aloneness," where consciousness is completely detached from the material world.</note></term></header>

But as for the <term>Self <note>original: Puruṣa; the pure, eternal witness-consciousness.</note></term> for whom this same mind-stuff is an object-of-sense—

**18. Unintermittently the Master of that [mind-stuff] knows the fluctuations of mind-stuff [and thus] the Self undergoes-no-mutations.**

If, like the <term>mind-stuff <note>original: citta; the mental apparatus comprising the intellect, ego, and sensory mind.</note></term>, the Master also—that is, the Self—should undergo <term>mutation <note>original: pariṇāma; constant change or transformation in state.</note></term>, then the fluctuations of the mind-stuff which are its objects would be like external objects-of-sense, such as sounds and other perceptible things: they would be sometimes known and sometimes not known. The fact, however, that the <term>central organ <note>The mind-stuff (citta) acting as the hub of all sensory and intellectual processing.</note></term> is unintermittently known by its Master, the Self, leads us to infer that the Self is an entity that undergoes no mutations.

Thus, he has established the existence of the intended object as distinct from mind-stuffs. Now, with the intent of showing that the Self is distinct from these mind-stuffs whose nature is to enter into mutation, he asserts the Self’s immutability—the quality which differentiates it from these mind-stuffs. This he does by supplying some words and by reciting the *sūtra* <note>An aphorism or concise rule in Sanskrit literature.</note>: "But as for [the Self] for whom this same mind-stuff is an object-of-sense."

**18. Unintermittently the Master of that [mind-stuff] knows the fluctuations of mind-stuff [and thus] the Self undergoes-no-mutations.**

The mind-stuff—whether it be restless, infatuated, distracted, or in a state of focusedness—is always, up to the time of <term>restriction <note>original: nirodha; the cessation of mental activity in deep meditation.</note></term>, experienced by the Self as being in a state of mutation. Why is this so? Because the Self does not undergo mutation. If the Self entered into mutations, then the Self also, like the mind-stuffs, would sometimes know objects-of-sense and sometimes not. In reality, objects-of-sense are only known to him <note>Meaning the Self is a constant witness; it never "loses" the mind.</note>. Therefore, he does not undergo mutation. As a result, he is something distinct from things that are in mutation.

He says the same in the words: "If like the mind-stuff." It is the central organ, when in fluctuation, that he unintermittently knows. Of this he is the Master and Owner—in other words, the <term>Experiencer <note>The one who perceives the results of thoughts and actions.</note></term>. Regarding this Master, the Self, the fact of constant awareness leads us to infer his immutability. To explain: The point is that this Self, which does not enter into mutation, is distinct from the mind-stuff, which does.

<page-num>329</page-num>
<header>Things distinct from thoughts [—IV. 19]</header>

In the same way, the <term>central organ <note>The mind-stuff or *citta*, which serves as the processing hub for thoughts and sensations.</note></term> is also to be represented. And accordingly, the example of fire could not apply to it. For fire does not throw light upon its own self, which [previously was something] without light. In this context, light is thrown [only] when there is a relation between the light-giver and something [which is yet] to be lighted. Furthermore, such a relation [of a thing] does not occur with the thing itself. Besides, the meaning of the words "the mind-stuff illumines itself" is simply that it is not an object-for-knowledge for anyone else. It is like saying "the air is grounded in itself," which merely means it is not grounded in something else. Because living beings are aware—by reflection—of the processes of their own thinking-substances, they can say, "I am angry, I am afraid, I feel a passion for that person, I am angry with that person." This leads to purposive action. Such action would be impossible unless there were a knowledge of one’s own thinking-substance.

With the words "Should the doubt arise," the author introduces a <term>Destructionist <note>original: *vaināśika*; a term used here for a Buddhist philosopher who believes in the momentary nature of all things and denies a permanent Self.</note></term> as an opponent, who argues as follows: "All this may be so, provided the mind-stuff is an object for the Self. But it is not. On the contrary, this [mind-stuff] throws light upon itself [and] illumines its objects [and] originates in dependence upon previous mind-stuff. How then can the Self always have the objects perceived? And still more, how can it be distinct from the mind-stuff which enters into mutation?"

**19. It does not illumine itself, since it is an object-for-sight.**

It might be so [self-illumining], provided that the mind-stuff had consciousness of itself. This, however, it does not have. It is, like the color blue, [an object] capable of being included in experience insofar as it undergoes <term>mutation <note>original: *pariṇāma*; the process of change and transformation.</note></term>. And whatever is capable of being included in experience cannot throw light upon itself. For a thing cannot act upon itself [rather than upon the mind-stuff]. This is because the same thing cannot simultaneously be the act, the object of the act, and [one of] the <term>relations <note>original: *kāraka*; the grammatical relationships (like "by" or "for") that connect a noun to the action of a verb.</note></term>¹ of the act. For the act of cooking is not cooked; nor is the act of chopping chopped.

On the other hand, the <term>Self <note>original: *ātman*; the pure witness-consciousness.</note></term> does not undergo mutation and is not an object of experience. Therefore, with reference to him, self-enlightenment is not inexplicable. For his self-enlightenment is nothing but an enlightenment² which is not dependent on any other; it is not the result of his being an object of experience. Therefore, because it is an **object-for-sight**, the mind-stuff which is the object of the seeing does not illumine itself. Only the objects of the fluctuations of that mind-stuff which receives the reflection of the light of the <term>self <note>original: *ātman*</note></term> throw light. This is the point. An objector says, "But don’t you see that fire is an object-for-sight and yet has [its own light?]"

self-illumination in itself. "It is not with a fire as it is with water-jars and so on, which may be made manifest by [the light of a] fire; for a fire is not [made manifest] by another fire." In reply to this he says "And so, fire as an example." Why? "For fire does not." The meaning is that fire does not require any other fire to throw light upon it, but has light thrown upon it by a conscious mental act. So it does not throw light upon itself. Thus [fire] is not an exception to the general principle <note>original: *vyabhicāra*; a logical deviation where a rule fails to apply</note> stated in the aphorism. This is the meaning. The word "here" in the expression "And here light is thrown" distinguishes [fire] from the light which is the nature of the Self, in other words, the light which is of an active kind. What he means to say is this: Wherever there is an action, it is in all cases seen to exist as related to an agent, to an instrument of action, and to an object. Just as we see the act of cooking as related to the person <term>Chāitra <note>a generic name used in Indian logic, similar to "John Doe"</note></term> and to the fire and to the rice. Similarly, throwing light is an action. And this [action] too must be in the same threefold relation. Now, a relation must be based upon a difference between the parts. It is impossible where there is no difference. This is the meaning. 

When it is said "Besides, the meaning of the words <the light-stuff illumines itself> is that it is not an object of knowledge for any one," the objector grants, "This may be so. But let it not be said that the mind-stuff is an object of knowledge. For when the process of knowing—which is neither the cause nor the pervader [of the mind-stuff]—is suppressed, it does not follow that the mind-stuff itself must be suppressed." To this he replies, "of their own thinking-substance." The "thinking substance" means the mind-stuff.¹ "Movements" mean the functional activities <note>original: *vṛttis*; the waves or patterns of thought</note>. "Beings" mean living beings. The different fluctuations of mind-stuff—anger or greed, for instance—are, together with their basis the mind-stuff and with their objects, experienced by each individual; this refutes the statement that the mind-stuff is not an object of knowledge. He makes clear this same perception of the movements of one’s own thinking-substance by the words "I am angry."

# 20. And there cannot be a cognition of both [thinking-substance and thing] at the same time.

And it is impossible in a single moment to cognize one's own form and another's as well. It is a supposition² of the <term>Momentarists <note>original: *Kṣaṇikavāda*; Buddhist philosophers who believed that all things exist only for a fleeting moment before being replaced</note></term> that whatever exists is both the action and the means related to that action.

**20. And there cannot be a cognition of both [thinking-substance and thing] at the same time.** He who says that mind-stuff illumines itself and illumines objects of sense cannot at least say that mind-stuff cognizes itself by the same functional activity as that by which it cognizes objects. For a—

<page-num>331</page-num>
<header>Criticism of the Momentarists <note>original: "Vaināśika"; those who believe that all things are destroyed and recreated every moment</note> [—IV. 21</header>

A functional activity that does not possess a distinct, identifying characteristic is not capable of producing a different result. Therefore, we must assume a difference exists in the functional activity itself. In the view of the Destructionists <note>A term for certain Buddhist schools that argue for the momentariness of all existence</note>, there is no activity beyond the various acts of coming-into-being. And from a single act of coming-into-being—which lacks any distinct identifying characteristics—it is impossible for different effects to arise. If they did, such differences would be entirely accidental. Nor can it be argued (as in the final alternative) that the same single thing can have two separate moments of coming-into-being. Therefore, at one moment of time (<term>samaya <note>a specific unit of time or a "moment" in Indian philosophy</note></term>), the mind-stuff cannot both determine external objects and also its own state of thought; in other words, it cannot illuminate itself. The Commentary confirms this: "And it is impossible in a single moment." In this regard, the Destructionists have said, "Whatever constitutes the being of a thing, that itself is the action and the means-to-action." Consequently, the fact that the mind-stuff is an object-to-be-seen—which is a constant truth—proves it does not illuminate itself. Instead, it points toward a separate "Seer" (the Self), and to the fact that this Seer does not undergo change or mutation.

If one holds the opinion that a mind-stuff, though naturally limited, is known by another mind-stuff that exists immediately next to it in time, the answer is:

### 21. If [one mind-stuff] were the object-of-sight for another, there would be an infinite regress from one thinking-substance to another, as well as a confusion of memory.

If one mind-stuff were perceived by another mind-stuff, then who would perceive the thinking-substance of that second thinking-substance? Because that would have to be perceived by yet another, and that by another still, there would be an infinite regress <note>original: *anavasthā*; a logical flaw where an explanation requires an endless chain of prior causes</note>. Furthermore, there would be a confusion of memory. As many memories would exist as there were experiences across these various thinking-substances. As a result of the confusion between these different memories, there would be no limit to the memory of a single thinking-substance. Thus, everything is thrown into disorder by the Destructionists’ "prattling" about a Self that is only conscious by reflecting the thinking-substance. However, those who assume that the Experiencer exists as a pure witness do not fall into these logical traps. There are some who assume a "pure existence" that discards those five divisions-of-existence (<term>skandha <note>the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—that Buddhists believe constitute a "person"</note></term>) and assembles new ones. But—

<sup>2</sup> Compare section ii. 9.

### 22. The Intellect <note>original: "citi"</note> which unites not [with objects] is conscious of its own thinking-substance when [the mind-stuff] takes the form [by reflecting it].

The Intellect's consciousness of its own thinking-substance takes place when the thinking-substance, in so far as it is a receptacle for the reflection of the Intellect, passes into the form of that [Intellect], [that is], passes into a resemblance <note>original: "rūpātā"</note> of the Intellect <note>original: "citi"</note>. The transforming of itself into an object of experience makes this [Energy of Intellect] an experiencer. This is the meaning of the <term>sūtra</term>. This is also the meaning of the Comment. **23. Mind-stuff affected by the Seer and by the object-for-sight [leads to the perception of] all intended-objects.**

For the central-organ <note>Refers to the internal mental faculty (antahkarana) that processes experience</note> is affected by the object-for-meditation, and is itself on account of its objectivity connected by one of its own fluctuations with the subject, with the Self also. Assuming a form both intelligent and unintelligent, appearing (although really an object) as that which is not object, while unintelligent it appears to be intelligent, [and] like a crystal, is described as [perceiving] all intended-objects. 

Accordingly there are some, deceived by this resemblance to mind-stuff, who say that [mind-stuff] itself is intelligent. There are others <note>A reference to the Buddhist school of Idealism (Vijnanavada), which argues that external objects do not exist independently of the mind</note> who say that this whole universe is nothing more than mind-stuff, and that this world of things, cows and water-jars and other things, together with their causes, does not exist. They are to be pitied. Why so? Because their mind-stuff, shining forth [in consciousness] in all kinds of forms is the source of error.—Consequently in concentrated insight <note>original: "samadhi" or "prajna"</note> the object-for-the-insight when once reflected is other than [the mind-stuff] because this [Self] is that upon which [the insight] rests. If this object were the mind-stuff and nothing more than that, how could the insight by itself ascertain its form as being insight? Accordingly when in the insight an object is reflected it is the Self who determines [the object]. Thus, by dividing mind-stuff as such into knower and process-of-knowing and object-for-knowledge, they classify it according to its kinds [i. 41] as a triad also. These are men of complete insight. By them the Self has been reached.

**23. Mind-stuff affected by the Seer and by the object-for-sight [leads to the perception of] all intended-objects.** 

For just as when affected by blue or another [color], the mind-stuff makes a blue or other object stand before us by direct perception, so the mind-stuff affected by the Seer <note>The pure, unchanging consciousness or the True Self</note>, in that it has changed into an image of the Seer, makes the Seer also stand before us, by direct perception. For knowledge has two¹ kinds of forms: ‘I am aware of—the blue.’ So although the knower also, like the object known, can be established by direct perception, still special pains were not taken to give a distinct proof of it. Just as the statement ‘the image of the moon is in the water’ does not mean that the image cannot be directly perceived. And further if you say that this [image] which has entered the water does-not-validate <note>original: "apramāṇa"; lacking the status of valid knowledge or truth</note> this [moon], you have no right to say that the [actual] form also of the moon is-not-validated. 

Consequently the fluctuation of the mind-stuff, in so far as the mind-stuff reflects the Intelligence <note>The power of pure awareness</note>, has Intelligence as an object. Still we are able to say that [the fluctuation of the mind-stuff] does not contain Intelligence as an object. This is what is meant by saying that mind-stuff [leads to the perception] of all objects. This same is expressed by the words «For the central-organ.» The central-organ <note>The internal faculty or mind that organizes sensory data</note> is affected not only by the [external] object-for-meditation, by assuming the form of the intended-object, but as he says «itself ... also.» The word «also» comes in the wrong place and should be after «the Self.» The fluctuation of the Self is [this] change so that it is reflected in this [mind-stuff]. 

And this identity of the mind-stuff with the reflection of the Intelligence must have been assumed by the <term>Destructionists</term> <note>original: "vāināçika"; a term used by ancient Indian philosophers to refer to Buddhist schools that believe all things are momentary and have no permanent substance</note>. How otherwise could these have attributed Intelligence to mind-stuff—as he says «Accordingly»? The word «some» refers to those Destructionists who hold the theory that there are external things. The word «others» refers to those who hold the theory that there are <term>mental-acts</term> <note>original: "vijñāna"; the stream of consciousness or cognitive events</note> and nothing more. 

An objector says ‘If the mind-stuff only is experienced as having the form of the Seer and the form of the object-for-sight, then surely the Seer and the object-for-sight must be not different from the mind-stuff, as they say, “For although the <term>soul</term> <note>original: "ātman"</note> is not different from the thinking-substance, [still] by wrong-headed persons it is characterized as if it were possessing-a-difference [brought about by] the <term>recognition</term> <note>original: "saṁvitti"; direct awareness</note> of the object-for-knowledge and the <term>knower</term> <note>original: "grāhaka"</note>.” So then how is it that these Destructionists deserve our pity?’ In reply to this he says «in concentrated insight.» Because in accordance with the arguments already stated they should be led to assume that the Self is something different from the mind-stuff. its eight aids <note>The eight limbs of yoga practice</note> which would introduce them to concentrated insight <term>samādhi: a state of intense meditative absorption</term> the object of which is the self—they should be awakened. To explain: In the concentrated insight, the object-for-the-insight, the self, is other [than the mind-stuff] when [the self] is reflected. Why so? And if, although instructed by this argument, the opponent perversely should say, ‘Why should not that upon which it rests be the mind-stuff itself,’ he replies «If this object.» If this object, which is the self <note>original: "ātman"</note>, be merely the mind-stuff and not something over and above this [mind-stuff], then how could the insight by itself ascertain its form as being insight? And for what reason is this?

**24. This [mind-stuff], although diversified by countless subconscious-impressions, exists for the sake of another, because its nature is to produce [things as] combinations.**

Although diversified by absolutely countless subconscious-impressions <term>saṃskāra: latent mental imprints from past actions</term>, this same mind-stuff exists for the sake of another, for the sake of the experience and the release of another; not for its own sake. Because like a house¹ its nature is to work as a combination <note>Meaning that anything made of parts must serve a purpose for a conscious being who is not part of that combination</note>. The mind-stuff must act as a combiner [for the Self] and not for its own sake. Pleasurable mind-stuff is not for the pleasure [of the mind-stuff]. The mind-stuff of thought is not for the thought [of the mind-stuff]. But both of these two kinds exist for the sake of another. And that very Self which has its purpose in the two purposes of experience and liberation is this <other>, not any other in general. Any indefinite other as such which the Destructionists <note>original: "Vāitāṇḍikas"; philosophers who argue only to disprove others without establishing their own position</note> set forth in general terms, would all still exist for the sake of some other, since [after all] they [too] act [only] to produce things to be combined. But that particular other which is the Self does not act as a combination.

He introduces another reason for the existence of the self <note>original: "ātman"</note> over and above the mind-stuff by asking, «And for what reason is this?»

**24. This [mind-stuff], although diversified by countless subconscious-impressions, exists for the sake of another, because its nature is to produce [things as] combinations.**

<page-num>337</page-num>
<header>Mind-stuff exists for the Self [-iv. 25</header>
<sig>43 [H.O.S. 17]</sig>

Although countless subconscious-impressions <term>saṃskāras: latent mental traces from past lives</term> of karma <term>actions and their consequences</term> and subconscious-impressions of hindrances <term>kleśas: mental afflictions like ego and attachment</term> remain attached to <note>original: "adhiçerate"</note> the mind-stuff only, but not to the Self—and although, accordingly, the fruitions which depend upon subconscious-impressions, in so far as they are contained in the mind-stuff, would lead one to suppose that mind-stuff is the experiencer—and although, because all objects-of-experience are for the experiencer, everything would be supposed to be for the mind-stuff—still the mind-stuff diversified as it is by countless subconscious-impressions must be supposed to exist for the sake of another. Why? Because it acts as a combination. <note>The "argument from composition": anything made of combined parts, like a house or a tool, exists for the use of someone else who is not part of that combination.</note> This is the meaning of the aphorism <note>original: "sūtra"</note>. He explains the aphorism by saying “this same.” An objector asks, ‘This may be true. But what contradiction is there in supposing that the mind-stuff acts in combination and yet still for its own sake?’ If some one were to urge this, he replies “since it acts in combination.” The words “Pleasurable mind-stuff” are a partial expression for experience in general. Painful mind-stuff also is to be understood as expressed by these words. And when he says “thought” he means release. What he means to say is this: Pleasure and pain may be in essence both counteractive and coactive with reference to the mind-stuff, but cannot be so with reference to themselves. For there cannot be a fluctuation <term>vṛtti: a modification or movement of the mind</term> with reference to itself. <note>Just as a knife cannot cut itself, the mind cannot be the subject of its own experience.</note> Neither is there any other thing acting as a combination and itself giving rise, directly or indirectly, to pain and pleasure, for which the pain and the pleasure can be counteractive or coactive. Therefore he who is in no wise concerned either directly or indirectly with pleasure or pain, can be brought into a state of counteraction to them or of coactivity with them; and that one is the permanently detached Self. Similarly that thought <note>original: "jñāna"</note> which leads to liberation, in so far as it also depends upon objects-of-knowledge, and because a fluctuation cannot exist with reference to itself, is not for thought itself. And it cannot be that release would arise when this thought has reference to another. For this would make release impossible in the case of the discarnate and of those whose bodies are resolved into primary matter. <note>Referring to beings in high spiritual states who are not yet fully liberated.</note> Therefore intuitive thought also is for the sake of the Self only; and it is not for its own sake; neither for any other whatsoever. And if it were for the sake of any other who acted as a combination, the result would be an infinite regress. <note>A logical error where one explanation requires another, never reaching a final cause.</note> So it is settled that thought is for another who does not act as a combination.

**25. For him who sees the distinction, the pondering upon his own states-of-being ceases.**

Because a blade of grass sprouts during the rains we infer the existence of seed. Just so in the case of him who betrays thrills of joy and falling tears in hearing of the way of release, we may likewise infer that there is in him good karma rooted in the knowledge of the difference between the sattva <note>original: "sattva"; here referring to the highest clarity of the mind</note> and the Self, conducive to liberation, and brought to completion in the past. In him, the pondering—

<summary>This page argues that because the mind is a complex "combination" of parts, it must exist for a higher, unified observer—the Self. It concludes that once a seeker realizes the distinction between the mind and the Self, their existential anxieties and self-questioning disappear.</summary>
