...upon his own states-of-being which is natural <note>original: "natural to him," comparing similar expressions in Book 4, aphorism 10</note> to him comes into activity. When there is none of this [good karma <term>karma: the accumulated merit or influence of past actions</term>], this has been said: "For those who, after having renounced their own nature [of pondering upon themselves], there is by reason of lack [of good karma], a liking <note>original: "ruci"</note> for the opposing view and no liking for the ascertainment of truth—for them there is no sight of the distinction and no cessation of the pondering." 

Now as to this point <note>original: "tatra"</note>, the pondering upon his own states-of-being <note>referring to Book 2, aphorism 39</note> is in this fashion: 'Who was I? How was I? What is this birth? How is this birth? What shall we become? Or how shall we become?' But this pondering ceases for one who sees the distinction [between the mind-essence <term>sattva: the purest and most transparent quality of the mind-stuff</term> and the Self]. 

For what reason is this? Since it is this mind-stuff <note>original: "cittasyāivāiṣa," emphasizing that these changes belong only to the mind</note> which undergoes this diversified mutation. But when there is no longer undifferentiated-consciousness <term>avidyā: spiritual ignorance or the failure to distinguish between the eternal Self and the temporary world</term>, the Self is purified and untouched by the conditions of the mind-stuff. For this reason, this skillful person ceases pondering upon his own states-of-being.

Having thus enunciated the doctrine about the Self, as based upon reasonings, which is the primary source of Isolation, he discriminates the man who is competent for this teaching from the other man who is not competent. 

**25. For him who sees the distinction, the pondering upon his own states-of-being ceases.** 

For one who ponders upon the existence of the Self—for him, after his instruction in the eight aids to yoga <term>eight aids: the systematic steps of yoga practice including ethics, posture, and meditation</term>, if he follow the instruction up and practice yoga, as a result of that [following and practice] and after he sees the difference between the Self and the mind-essence of the mind-stuff, there comes a cessation of pondering upon the being of the self. 

For one who does not ponder at all upon the existence of the self, the heretic—for him, incompetent to receive the instruction, and failing to make out the existence of the self in this or the other world, there is no instruction, no seeing of the distinction, and no cessation of pondering upon the existence of the self. Such is the meaning of the aphorism <term>sūtra: a concise rule or thread of wisdom</term>. 

An objector asks, "How may we conclude that there is in the mind-stuff a pondering upon the states of the self?" In reply to this he says, "in the rains... just so." <note>This refers to a traditional analogy where the presence of certain effects allows one to infer a hidden cause.</note> It is inferred that there has been performed in a previous existence a karma which was the following up of the eight aids to yoga, or of a part of them, which is the seed of the sight of the fundamental truth <term>tattva: reality or the thing-as-it-is</term> and which is conducive to release. In such a person, unavoidably, the pondering upon the states of the self naturally goes on, even when there is no current practice <note>Compare the commentary on Book 3, aphorism 51</note> in concentration upon the thing. He shows who these persons are who, according to the statements of...

This realization is only possible for those with the necessary spiritual merit (karma) to pursue the higher stages of yoga.</summary>

<header>The Self becomes isolated [—iv. 27</header>

The traditionalists are not competent to explain this, saying: «When there is none of this (*yasya*) <note>original: "yasya," meaning "of whom" or "of which," referring to the lack of merit</note> [good karma <term>karma: the law of moral cause and effect; here, the merit that leads to spiritual insight</term>], this happens.» The opposing view is that there is no fruition of karma because there is no one in any other world, since no other world exists. There are those who have a liking for this [materialistic doctrine] and no liking for the demonstrated truth of the twenty-five entities <note>The twenty-five entities of the Samkhya philosophy, which describe the evolution of the universe from primordial nature to the individual self</note>. The pondering upon one’s own states-of-being has already [ii. 39] been explained. He refers to the man who sees the distinction by saying «since it is this mind-stuff.» For him who is skillful in the sight of the distinction, pondering upon his own states-of-being ceases.

### 26. Then the mind-stuff is borne down to discrimination, onward towards Isolation.
<gloss>is carried forward</gloss> <gloss>forward</gloss>
That mind-stuff of his which formerly was borne onward towards objects-of-sense, down to non-thinking, becomes changed for him. It is borne onward towards Isolation <term>Kaivalya: the state of absolute spiritual freedom where the Self is detached from the material world</term>, down to the thinking which comes from discrimination <note>original: "viveka," the ability to distinguish between the eternal Self and the temporary mind</note>.<sup>1</sup>

Now to the question ‘What kind of mind-stuff has the man who sees the distinction?’ he replies: **26. Then the mind-stuff is borne down to discrimination, onward towards Isolation.** [This is] explained by merely reading.

### 27. In the intervals of this [mind-stuff] there are other presented-ideas [coming] from subliminal-impressions.
The mind-stuff which is [borne] down towards discrimination of the presented-idea and the flow of which is towards nothing but discernment of the difference between the *sattva* <term>sattva: the quality of light, purity, and intelligence in the mind</term> and the Self, has in its intervals other presented-ideas, either ‘It is I’ or ‘It is mine’ or ‘I think’ or ‘I do not think.’ From what source? <gloss>residual traces</gloss> From the dwindling seeds, from previous subliminal-impressions <term>samskaras: subconscious imprints left by past actions and thoughts</term>.

An objector says ‘This may be so. But if the sight of the distinction has as its final goal (*niṣṭhā*) the discrimination, then the mind-stuff would at no time be emergent <note>meaning "active" or "distracted" by the world</note>. Whereas we see that [the mind-stuff] of one who goes the rounds for alms is emergent.’ To which the reply is this. **27. In the intervals of this [mind-stuff] there are other presented-ideas [coming] from subliminal-impressions.** A presented-idea is that by which a thing is presented [to the Self]. It is the *sattva* of the mind-stuff. From this [*sattva*] the Intelligence is discriminated. By this it is [borne] down to [discrimination]. By the words ‘I think’ liberation is plainly indicated as distinct [from infatuation]. By the words ‘I do not think’ infatuation is [plainly shown]. By the words ‘It is I’ or the words ‘It is mine’, the sense-of-personality (*ahāṃkāra*) <term>ahāṃkāra: the "I-maker" or ego-sense</term> and the sense-of-property (*mamakāra*) <term>mamakāra: the sense of ownership or "mine-ness"</term>, which are the sources of infatuation, are indicated.—

<header>iv. 27—] Book IV. Isolation or Kaivalya [340</header>

The compound (*kṣīyamāṇabīja* <note>original: "kṣīyamāṇabīja," literally "seeds in the process of being destroyed"</note>) is to be analyzed [as meaning] seeds which are dwindling. The words «from previous subliminal-impressions» <term>subliminal-impressions: saṃskāras; the latent mental traces or habits formed by past actions and thoughts</term> means from subliminal-impressions of emergence <term>emergence: vyutthāna; the state of mind when it is active and engaged with the world, rather than in deep meditation</term>.

### 28. The escape from these [subliminal-impressions] is described as being like [the escape from] the hindrances. <note>Referencing Book II, sutras 10-12 regarding the removal of mental afflictions</note>

The hindrances <term>hindrances: kleśas; the five afflictions (ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live) that cause suffering</term> when in the condition of burned seed <note>A traditional metaphor for mental seeds that have been so thoroughly neutralized by wisdom that they can no longer "sprout" into new thoughts or rebirths</note> are unfit <note>Compare Book II, sutras 4 and 13</note> for generation. Just so a previous subliminal-impression, when in the condition of seed burned by the fire of [intuitive] thinking <term>intuitive thinking: prasaṅkhyāna; the highest form of meditative insight</term>, does not generate presented-ideas <term>presented-ideas: vṛttis; the active fluctuations or thoughts in the mind</term>. But because the subliminal-impressions of [intuitive] knowledge are dormant <note>See Book II, sutra 7</note> until the task of the mind-stuff <term>mind-stuff: citta; the totality of the psychological mind</term> is completed, they are not considered here.

‘This might be granted,’ the objector says; ‘but even if there be discriminative thinking <term>discriminative thinking: vivekakhyāti; the clear realization of the difference between the true Self and the material mind</term>, supposing the subliminal-impressions of emergence generate other presented-ideas,—what means is there then for escaping them to the end that they in turn shall not generate other presented-ideas?’ In reply to this he says:

**28. The escape from these [subliminal-impressions] is described as being like [the escape from] the hindrances.** In the case of one whose discriminative thinking is not thoroughly mature, the subliminal-impressions of emergence not having dwindled away generate other presented-ideas. Whereas in the case of one in whom discriminative thinking is mature, the subliminal-impressions have dwindled and are not capable of generating other presented-ideas, just as the hindrances, although arising in the intervals of the discrimination, do not generate other subliminal-impressions. Why is this so? Because in that case these hindrances are in the condition of seeds burned by the fire of discriminative thinking. Similarly also the subliminal-impressions of emergence. —Now these subliminal-impressions of emergence must be restricted by the subliminal-impressions of discriminative thinking, and the subliminal-impressions of discrimination by the subliminal-impressions of restriction. But as for the subliminal-impressions of restriction, we have shown that they are outwardly objectless. The means of restriction must in all cases be considered, [but not the subliminal-impressions <note>These are not considered because they eventually cease on their own</note> of intuitive knowledge], as he says «of intuitive knowledge.» He refers to the subliminal-impressions of the higher passionlessness <term>passionlessness: vairāgya; the state of being free from all desire for worldly or even heavenly rewards</term>.

is to say] he is not looking for anything [as a reward] even from that <note>original: "tato 'pi"</note>; [and] if, even in respect of that, he is free from passion, in every case nothing-less-than discriminative discernment <term>discriminative discernment: viveka-khyāti; the profound realization of the difference between the pure Self and the material world</term> becomes his. So the author of the sutras, after describing Elevation <term>Elevation: prasaṁkhyāna; the highest state of meditative insight or reflection</term> as the means for restricting the emergence of worldly thoughts, gives the means for restricting Elevation itself. 

**29. For one who is not seeking a reward even in respect of Elevation, there follows in every case, as a result of discriminative discernment, the concentration [called] the Rain-cloud of Virtue.** 

[This seeker] looks for nothing—not even, for example, dominion over all things. «Even from that» means even from Elevation. [When] on the contrary, he is hindered even in respect of that state and is dissatisfied with it because he sees the defects of constant change, in every case nothing-less-than discriminative discernment becomes his. This same point he explains in the words «even in respect of that.» Whenever ideas of worldly emergence arise, then this seeker has not yet attained discriminative discernment at all times. But after he has no other ideas, he has attained discriminative discernment at all times. Then the concentration called the Rain-cloud of Virtue becomes his. What the author means to say is this: When the seeker becomes dissatisfied with Elevation and longs for its restriction, he should devote himself to the concentration called the Rain-cloud of Virtue. And by thus devoting himself to this "Rain-cloud," he attains discriminative discernment at all times. And thus he is capable of making that discernment restricted <note>i.e., bringing even the highest thoughts to a state of complete stillness</note>.

**30. Then follows the cessation of the hindrances and of karma.**

After the attainment of this Rain-cloud of Virtue, ignorance <term>ignorance: avidyā; the foundational misconception of the true nature of reality</term> and the other hindrances <term>hindrances: kleśas; the five mental afflictions that cause suffering</term> are pulled out by the roots. And the latent deposits of karma <term>karma: the accumulated results of past actions</term>, both good and bad, are destroyed along with their roots. Upon the cessation of the hindrances and of karma, the wise man, even while yet alive, is released <note>This refers to the state of Jivanmukti, or liberation while still in a physical body</note>. Why is this? Because misconception is the cause of existence <note>original: "bhavasya," referring to the cycle of worldly becoming or rebirth</note>. For surely no one has ever seen the birth of anyone whose misconceptions have dwindled away. And he tells what the purpose of this is.

**31. Then, because of the endlessness of knowledge from which all obscuring defilements have passed away, what is yet to be known amounts to little.**

The knowledge which is freed from all obscurations by hindrances and by karma becomes endless. The <term>sattva: the quality of purity, light, and harmony</term> of the obscured knowledge overwhelmed by the <term>tamas: the quality of darkness, inertia, and ignorance</term> which obscures it, and kept in motion here and there only by the <term>rajas: the quality of energy, passion, and movement</term>, is set free [from the *tamas*] and becomes fit for the process-of-knowing. In this case when it has become rid of defilement by any of the defilements of the covering, it becomes endless. In consequence of the endlessness of knowledge what is yet to be known amounts to little, to no more than a firefly in the sky. On which point this has been said <note>original: Tāitt. This is a famous Vedic riddle or paradox describing the impossible nature of spiritual realization.</note> “A blind man pierced a jewel; one without fingers strung it on a cord; one without a neck put it on; a dumb man paid honour to it.”

Then, because of the endlessness of knowledge from which all obscuring defilements have passed away, what is yet to be known amounts to little.** The obscurations are those things by which the *sattva* of the mind-stuff is obscured. The defilements are the hindrances and the karma. The compound is to be analysed into "all" and "obscuring-defilements." All these obscuring defilements have passed away from the *sattva* of the mind-stuff. Knowledge is that by which we know—this is the derivation. Because of the endlessness, by reason of its immeasurability, what is yet to be known amounts to very little. For just as in the autumn when the rays of the moon are freed from a dense veil [of cloud], and when they are brilliant in all directions, the light is so endless that water-jars and other things which are to be lightened up [amount to very] little,—similarly owing to the endlessness of light from the *sattva* of the mind-stuff from which all *rajas* and *tamas* have passed away, the things to be lightened up [amount to] little. This same he says in the words "from all." He makes this clear from the negative side by the words, "overwhelmed by the *tamas* which obscures it." Kept in motion by the *rajas*, whose disposition is to activity, and hence set free, [because] the *tamas* is removed from the spot. This is the meaning. Hence because by its

<page-num>343</page-num>
<header>Subsidence of aspects</header>

Because it rains—that is, it pours down—all kinds of knowable things, it is called the Rain-cloud of knowable things <note>original: Dharma-megha-samādhi; a high state of concentration where the yogi is showered with wisdom and virtue</note>. The objector says, "We may admit the existence of this Rain-cloud of knowable things, the concentration which is the cause of the subsidence of the hindrances with their subconscious impressions and of the latent deposit of karma. But even when this concentration exists, why should a creature not be reborn?" In reply to this, he says: "On which point this has been said." If an effect were to take place even when the cause is totally uprooted, then—my goodness!—the piercing of jewels by blind men and similar performances would take place before our eyes. And so this proverb, popular with reference to any inexplicable thing, would be explicable:

->A blind man pierced a jewel. He strung it, that is, put it on a thread. A man without fingers caught it. One without a neck wore it. And a mute spoke in praise of it.<- 
<note>This famous Vedic riddle from the Taittiriya Aranyaka describes a series of impossible actions to illustrate that once the cycle of rebirth is broken, the impossible becomes the reality of liberation, and the "impossible" rebirth can no longer occur.</note>

**32. When as a result of this the aspects (*guṇa*) have fulfilled their purpose, they attain to the limit of the sequence of mutations.**

<margin>Sequence of mutations; see Dasgupta, Yoga Philosophy page 213 and Table 37</margin>
As a result of the rise into consciousness of the Rain-cloud of knowable things, when the aspects <term>guṇa: the three fundamental qualities of nature—sattva (purity), rajas (activity), and tamas (inertia)</term> have fulfilled their purpose, they end the sequence of their mutations. For the aspects, having completed their work of providing experience and liberation to the Self, and having attained the limit of their sequence, are incapable of lingering even for a moment.

The objector says, "The last limit of the Rain-cloud of knowable things—the undisturbed calm of thought and the higher passionlessness—may remove to their very roots the subliminal impressions of emergent concentration, the latent deposits of hindrances, and of karma. Still, since the aspects of themselves are naturally disposed to form evolved effects, why do they not, even in the case of such a liberated Self, produce a body and organs and the rest?" The reply is this: **32. When as a result of this the aspects (*guṇa*) have fulfilled their purpose, they attain to the limit of the sequence of mutations.** The disposition of the aspects is such that when they have fulfilled their purpose with reference to any specific Self, they do not continue to be active with reference to that Self. This is the point.

### What now is this so-called sequence?

**33. The positive correlate to the moment, recognized as such at the final limit of the mutation, is a sequence.**

<margin>See Stcherbatsky, Central Conception of Buddhism, page 44.</margin>
A sequence has as its essence a continuous series of moments and is recognized as such at the final limit or termination of the mutation. For when a new garment has come to the end of its "newness," there is no "oldness" unless the oldness has passed through a continuous sequence of moments of change.

It also defines "sequence" as the continuous flow of moments that results in a visible change over time.</summary>

There are moreover two kinds of permanences, the **absolutely unchanging permanence** and the **permanence in mutation**. Of these two the Self’s <note>original: Puruṣa; the pure, unchanging consciousness</note> permanence is the absolutely unchanging, and the aspects’ <note>original: guṇa; the three fundamental qualities of nature—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas</note> permanence is in mutation. A thing is permanent when its essence is not destroyed while it is passing through mutations <note>A mutation is a change in form while the underlying substance remains the same, like gold being shaped into different jewelry</note>. Both of these two kinds have a [certain] permanence, because the essential nature of them is not destroyed. 

Of these two: with regard to the external-aspects of the aspects (*guṇa*), the thinking-substance <note>original: citta; the mind-stuff or collective mental functions</note> and the others for example, the sequence, having reached its end, is recognizable at the final limit of the mutation; with regard to permanent substances [that is] the aspects (*guṇa*), the end has not been reached; with regard to the absolutely unchanging permanent, the liberated Selves grounded in themselves and in nothing else, the being in themselves is experienced, to be sure, as a sequence, yet it has not reached its end [and is not recognizable at the final limit]. [The sequence is] abstracted from the act of existence and is based upon words [only].

Now has this round-of-rebirths <note>original: saṃsāra</note> as it exists in the aspects (*guṇa*), either in [actual] motion or in [potential] equilibrium, a final consummation of the sequence or not? This is incapable of answer. How then? A question capable of answer is this, ‘*Will every one who is born die?*’ ‘*Yes, sir.*’ There is [however] a question capable of alternative answers, ‘*Will every one after he has died be born again?*’ The skilful man upon whom discernment has dawned <note>original: viveka; the ability to distinguish the Self from the mind</note> <insert>Compare book i. 16 and book ii. 27 of the Calcutta edition.</insert> and whose craving has dwindled will not be born again; but any other will be born again.

Meanwhile he asks what a <term>sequence of mutations</term> <note>original: pariṇāma-krama; the orderly succession of changes a thing undergoes over time</note> is by saying «What now is this ?» 

**33. The positive correlate to the moment, recognized as such at the final limit of the mutation, is a sequence.**

The sequence of the mutation is that which has the <term>moment</term> <note>original: kṣaṇa; the smallest, indivisible unit of time in Yogic philosophy</note> as its positive correlate ; it is that to which the moments are related. It is that in which the accumulation of moments inheres. This is the meaning. And a sequence can never be explained unless there be that which the sequence contains. Neither can there be a sequence of only a single moment. Therefore the remaining alternative is that in which the accumulation of moments inheres. As he says in the words, «a continuous series of moments.» He gives the source-of-the-valid-idea for the sequence of the mutation by saying «of the mutation.» The final limit or termination of the mutation is the observed fact that even a new garment, although kept with care, after a time looks old. So then there is a sequence of the mutation. And before this point is reached the successive stages of oldness, the slightest, very slight, slight, noticeable, more noticeable, most noticeable, are inferred [already to exist]. This same he sets forth by a negative argument in the words «For when.» The words «unless . . . has passed through» refers to [an oldness] in which a [particular] moment in the sequence has not been reached. 

The objector says ‘Such a sequence is impossible in the case of <term>primary matter</term> <note>original: prakṛti; the fundamental, unconscious substance from which the material world evolves</note> since that is permanent.’ In reply to this he says «In permanent things also.» By the use of the plural he asserts that the sequence is to be found among all permanent things. As to this he shows first what the different kinds of permanent things are, and then explains how the sequence is found among permanent things in the words «two kinds.» The objector says ‘The absolutely unchanging, because it does not swerve from its own nature, may be conceded to be permanent. But how can that which is in mutation, which unceasingly swerves from its own nature, be permanent ?’ In reply to this he says «When.» External-aspects and time-variations and intensities, of these it is the nature to rise and fall. But for a substance there is no dislodging it from its essential nature. And to the question whether all the sequences are cognizable at the final limit of mutation, he says No. «Of these two : with regard to the external-aspects of the <term>qualities</term> <note>original: guṇas; the three fundamental threads or forces—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—that make up all physical and mental phenomena</note>, the <term>thinking-substance</term> <note>original: citta; the mind-stuff or individual consciousness</note> and the others for example.» Since it has reached the end because of the destruction of the properties, [therefore the sequence is cognizable at the end of the mutation]. In the case of the <term>primary cause</term> <note>original: pradhāna; another term for primary matter or Prakṛti</note>, however, the sequence of mutations does not reach an end.—The objector says ‘Since the original substance undergoes mutation in the form of external aspects, it may have a sequence of mutation. But how can the <term>Self</term> <note>original: Puruṣa; the pure, unchanging spiritual consciousness that is distinct from the mind and body</note> who does not enter into mutation have a sequence of mutation ?’ In reply he says «with regard to

<vocab>rebirth (saṃsāra), sequence (krama), mutation (pariṇāma), moment (kṣaṇa), termination, primary matter (prakṛti), permanent, qualities (guṇa), thinking-substance (citta), primary cause (pradhāna), Self (Puruṣa)</vocab>

<summary>This page defines the "sequence of mutation" as a succession of moments that becomes perceptible only when a change is complete, such as a garment becoming visibly old. It distinguishes between the changing sequence of the material world and the unchanging nature of the pure Self (Puruṣa).</summary>

--- Page 392 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of whether the sequence of change ever ends. It addresses the philosophical problem of whether the cycle of rebirth can truly be infinite or if it must eventually conclude for all souls, thereby potentially making nature itself temporary.</meta>

<page-num>346</page-num>
<header>iv. 33—] *Book IV. Isolation or <term>Kāivalya</term>* [346</header>

...the absolutely unchanging permanent. Persons who are in bondage, because they assume that they are not separate from their own <term>mind-stuff</term> <note>original: citta; the mental mirror that reflects consciousness</note>, have the <term>mutations</term> <note>original: pariṇāma; the constant changes or transformations of matter</note> of this mind-stuff attributed to them. And in the case of the liberated, a transformation based upon the mere act of existence—which has no physical substance—is mistakenly claimed to exist. Since "existence" is only a word, if we say that the liberated exist, the description that follows is based only on the act of existence and nothing more, as when the author says "from the act of existence." Regarding the <term>aspects</term> <note>original: guṇa; the three fundamental strands of nature—sattva, rajas, and tamas—which constitute all material reality</note>, it has been said that their sequence of transformation never reaches an end.

Not being satisfied with this, someone asks, "What now?" The words "in equilibrium" refer to the state of a <term>great mundane dissolution</term> <note>original: mahā-pralaya; the periodic cosmic event where the universe dissolves back into its primal state</note>; "in motion" refers to the time of creation. What the questioner means to say is this:

"If, because it is endless, there is no end to the transformations of the <term>round-of-existence</term> <note>original: saṃsāra; the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth</note>, then how, sir, could it suddenly cease for all souls at the time of a great cosmic dissolution? And how, at the beginning of a new creation, could the cycle of rebirth suddenly be produced? Furthermore, if souls are liberated one by one in a sequence, eventually everyone would be set free; the cycle of rebirth would be destroyed, meaning it would reach a final end to the transformations of the <term>primary cause</term> <note>original: prakṛti; the fundamental material nature of the universe</note>. And if this were so, the primary cause itself would be proven to be impermanent. Since you are also unwilling to admit that a completely new principle could just appear, you cannot say that these transformations are truly endless. For if you did, the idea that nature has no beginning would be contradicted, and you would be breaking all the rules of the <term>sacred books</term> <note>original: śāstra; authoritative philosophical or legal treatises</note>."

This is the central point. The author gives his reply with the words, "This is incapable of answer." This specific argument does not deserve a direct "yes" or "no" reply. To demonstrate that it is absolutely incapable of being answered in that way, he shows there is a different type of question that *is* absolutely answerable by saying, "A question . . . is." The question is: "Will everyone who is born die?" He gives the answer: "Yes, sir." In other words, "Certainly, sir."

Having asked a question that allows for only one answer, he then asks a question that allows for <term>alternative answers</term> <note>original: vibhajya-vacanīya; a question that must be analyzed and answered differently depending on the context</note> with the words, "Will every one [be liberated]?" He shows how this requires several different answers. He provides another question which also requires specific, different answers to make the meaning clear: "Likewise . . . the human race." 

But the original problem is incapable of an absolute, one-size-fits-all answer. It is not possible to say generally whether the cycle of rebirth for all people—whether they are fortunate or unfortunate—has a single end or not. We cannot determine the total bliss or lack of bliss for every living being with the same absolute certainty as the fact that everyone who is born will die. Instead, the question must be answered in alternative ways, as he says, "for the fortunate being." His intention is this: the logic suggests that if there is a series of liberations, eventually all would be set free and the cycle would stop. Now, this logic is based on the idea of liberation established by the Sacred Text...

<summary>This page discusses the philosophical debate over whether the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) and the transformations of nature (prakṛti) have an ultimate end for all beings. It distinguishes between questions with certain answers (like the inevitability of death) and complex questions regarding liberation that require a nuanced, case-by-case analysis.</summary>

<keywords>Kāivalya, mind-stuff, mutation, guṇa, cosmic dissolution, creation, saṃsāra, śāstra, rebirth, unanswerable questions</keywords>

--- Page 393 ---
<meta>This page concludes the Fourth Book of the Yoga Sūtras. It resolves the debate from the previous page regarding whether the entire universe ceases to exist once liberation is achieved. The text argues that because souls are infinite and reach enlightenment at different times, the cosmic cycle continues for others even after one individual attains absolute freedom.</meta>

<page-num>347</page-num>
<header>The Independence of Absolute Freedom [-iv. 34</header>

Sacred Tradition <note>original: āgama; authoritative spiritual knowledge passed down through the ages</note>. So how can the fact of the validity of the Sacred Tradition—which establishes the liberation we assume to be true—invalidate that same Sacred Tradition when it speaks of the permanence of the effects evolved from the primary cause? Therefore, this logical inference, which contradicts the Sacred Tradition, is not a valid source of knowledge. For it is taught in the Sacred Word <note>original: śruti</note>, the Tradition <note>original: smṛti</note>, the Legends <note>original: itihāsa</note>, and the Ancient Chronicles <note>original: purāṇa</note> that the succession of cosmic creations and resolutions <note>original: pratisarga; the periodic re-absorption of the universe into its primal state</note> is without beginning and without end. 

And so, first of all, it is not possible for all true selves <note>original: ātman; the eternal spark of consciousness</note> to experience a simultaneous destruction of the round-of-rebirths. Even learned men are not always grounded in discriminative discernment <note>original: viveka-khyāti; the ability to distinguish between pure consciousness and the material world</note>, even though it is meant to be acquired through the labor of study over many successive lifetimes. How much less likely is it, then, that all living creatures in general—both those that move and those that do not—would reach this state suddenly all at once! If causes do not happen at the same time, their effects cannot happen at the same time. Rather, discriminative discernment occurs in a sequence; and when countless beings are liberated one after another, there is no total destruction of the round-of-rebirth for the universe as a whole. Living beings are endless in number because they are truly beyond counting. Thus, the matter is cleared up.

Absolute Freedom <note>original: Kaivalya; also translated as "Isolation"</note> is said to follow after the sequence of the work of the fundamental qualities <note>original: guṇa; the three strands of nature: balance, activity, and inertia</note> has been completed. The nature of this state is now defined:

**34. Absolute Freedom is the "inverse generation" of the fundamental qualities once they are no longer providing a purpose for the Self; or, it is the Power of Consciousness grounded in its own nature.**

When the fundamental qualities <note>original: guṇa</note>—whose essence consists of causes and effects—undergo "inverse generation" <note>original: pratiprasava; the process of effects dissolving back into their causes</note>, they do so because experience and liberation have finally been accomplished for the Self. Once a purpose is no longer provided for the Self, this is Absolute Freedom. The Self’s Power of Thought becomes "isolated" or "absolute," since it is grounded in itself and is never again related to the clarity of the mind-substance <note>original: citta-sattva</note>. Its continuance in this state forevermore is Absolute Freedom.

In this authoritative book on yoga by Patañjali, in the Exposition of the Sāṁkhya philosophy <note>original: Sāṁkhya; the dualistic school of thought upon which Yoga is built</note>, this concludes the Fourth Book, the Book on Absolute Freedom.

The scholar notes the connections between this final verse—which determines the nature of Absolute Freedom—and previous topics with the words "task of the fundamental qualities." **34. Absolute Freedom is the inverse generation of the fundamental qualities, no longer provided with a purpose by the Self, or it is the Power of Consciousness grounded in itself.** Insofar as their work is done, the fundamental qualities, no longer serving a purpose for the Self, are inversely generated. They are resolved back into their original cause, which is the primary-matter <note>original: pradhāna; the unmanifested source of the physical universe</note>. Of these qualities, whose...

<summary>This final page defines Kaivalya (Absolute Freedom) as the state where nature's qualities finish their work for an individual soul and dissolve back into their source, leaving pure consciousness to stand alone. It clarifies that while individuals find liberation, the universe continues its cycles for the infinite number of other beings yet to reach enlightenment.</summary>
<keywords>Kaivalya, Absolute Freedom, Guṇas, Inverse Generation, Power of Consciousness, Patañjali, Sāṁkhya, liberation, cosmic dissolution</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the Fourth Book of the Yoga Sūtras. It completes the discussion on the process of liberation, explaining how the various layers of the mind and matter dissolve back into their source when a soul achieves absolute freedom. It also provides a final summary of the topics covered in the entire treatise.</meta>

<page-num>348</page-num>
<header>iv. 34] Book IV. Isolation or Absolute Freedom <note>original: Kaivalya</note></header>

When their purpose as the building blocks of cause and effect is finished, the deep-seated mental impressions <note>original: saṃskāra; the subconscious residues of past actions and thoughts</note> created by the restraint of distracting thoughts are dissolved back into the mind-stuff; and the mind-stuff is absorbed into the sense of "I-ness" <note>original: asmitā; the substance of personality</note>; and this personality-substance is absorbed into manifest nature; and manifest nature is finally absorbed into the unmanifest source <note>original: prakṛti; the primal matter of the universe</note>. This reverse-process of creation <note>original: pratisarga; the backward movement where effects return to their causes</note> of the fundamental qualities of nature <note>original: guṇa</note>, whose essence had been to act as causes and effects, is Absolute Freedom. It is the liberation of an individual Self <note>original: puruṣa</note> from the primary cause of the material world.

—Or, liberation is simply the Self remaining grounded in its own true nature, as the author says: "Grounded in itself." It is true that the Power of Pure Consciousness <note>original: citi-śakti</note> remains grounded in itself even during a great cosmic dissolution <note>original: pralaya; the periodic end of the universe</note>. But that state is not true liberation <note>because the soul eventually returns to the cycle of rebirth</note>. Therefore, the author adds the word "permanently" <note>indicating a state from which there is no return to suffering</note>. The word *so it is* <note>original: iti</note> in the aphorism <note>original: sūtra</note> signifies the end of this authoritative work.

***

In this Book, the author has described first the state of mind required for liberation, then the supernatural powers of other realms, the nature of external objects, and the nature of the Knower <note>original: jña; the conscious subject</note>. He has explained the "Cloud of Virtue" <note>original: dharma-megha; the highest state of meditative wisdom that showers peace and merit</note>, the nature of concentration, the two types of liberation, and various other incidental topics. There has also been a description of the source of mental afflictions <note>original: kleśa; the causes of human suffering like ignorance and ego</note>, and those afflictions themselves have been recounted. Here also, the two kinds of Yoga—the yoga of action and the yoga of meditation—along with the eight limbs of practice <note>original: aṣṭāṅga; the foundational steps of yoga including ethics, posture, and breath</note> have been set forth. The path to freedom, which relies on the distinction between the qualities of nature and the pure Self, has also been made clear. Absolute Freedom has been defined, and the Pure Consciousness <note>original: citi</note> has been made free from all suffering.

->In the *Clarification of the Entities* <note>original: Tattva-vāiçāradī</note>, which is an explanation of the commentary on Patañjali’s Yoga Treatise, and which was composed by the Venerable Vācaspati Miśra, the Fourth Book, on Absolute Freedom, is now finished.<-

# APPENDIX 7

## INDEX OF WORDS IN THE APHORISMS <note>The "Sūtras" are the pithy, foundational threads of wisdom that make up the text of Patanjali’s Yoga system.</note>

An alphabetic index of the Aphorisms themselves is given in the edition of the Bombay Sanskrit Series, and in that of the Ānandāçrama Series of Poona.—This index is designed to include all the words of the text of the Aphorisms, and no others. The text used is that of the Calcutta edition from the year 1891 <note>original: "Saṃvat 1947; Baptist Mission Press"</note>; and accordingly the word **five** <note>original: "pañca"</note>, for example, is included. The numbers refer to the chapter-quarter <note>term: "pāda"; the Yoga Sūtras are divided into four quarters or chapters.</note> and the specific aphorism.

The Aphorisms contain almost no finite verb-forms (such as **is** <note>original: "asti"</note>, **might be** <note>original: "syāt"</note>, **is diminished** <note>original: "kṣīyate"</note>, or **are born** <note>original: "jāyante"</note>), and I have therefore put the participles in their proper alphabetic place rather than under their verbal roots: for example, **past** <note>original: "atīta"</note>, **escaped** <note>original: "apeta"</note>, **arisen** <note>original: "udita"</note>, and **gone** <note>original: "vīta"</note> are listed under the letter **A**, **U**, and **V**, not under the root **i** (to go). Similarly, words like **born into** <note>original: "abhijāta"</note>, **near** <note>original: "āsanna"</note>, **produced** <note>original: "utpanna"</note>, **spoken** <note>original: "ukta"</note> (not under the root *vac*), and **unattained** <note>original: "a-labdha"</note> are listed as they appear; this applies to other negatives beginning with **an-** or **a-**. On the other hand, pronoun forms are grouped in the usual way: **that**, **of that**, **those**, and **he** <note>original: "tat", "tasya", "tāḥ", "sa"</note> are all under the base form **that** <note>original: "tad"</note>; while **his** and **of these** <note>original: "asya", "eṣām"</note> are under **this** <note>original: "idam"</note>; and **by this** <note>original: "etena"</note> is under **this** <note>original: "etad"</note>.

---

- **one-pointedness** <note>original: "ekāgratā"</note>, the one-pointedness of the mind <note>original: "cittasya_ekāgratā"</note> iii. 12; [the transition from] all-objectness to one-pointedness <note>original: "sarvārthatā_ekāgratā"</note> iii. 11.
- **one-pointed focus** <note>original: "ekāgrya"</note>, high-mindedness, one-pointedness, and mastery over the senses <note>original: "saumanasya_ekāgrya_indriya-jaya"</note> ii. 41.
**this** <note>original: "etad"</note>, by this same process, the reflective [absorption is explained] <note>original: "etayaiva savicārā"</note> i. 44; by this, [the changes] in the elements and senses [are explained] <note>original: "etena bhūtendriyeṣu"</note> iii. 13.

**that** or **it** <note>original: "tad"</note>, 1. their restraint <note>original: "tan-nirodhaḥ"</note> i. 12; that highest <note>original: "tat paraṁ"</note> i. 16; for the sake of that <note>original: "tad-artha"</note> i. 28; colored by that <note>original: "tad-añjana"</note> i. 41; born from that <note>original: "taj-jaḥ"</note> i. 50; their fluctuations <note>original: "tad-vṛttayaḥ"</note> ii. 11; their fruition <note>original: "tad-vipāka"</note> ii. 13; for its sake <note>original: "tad-artha"</note> ii. 21; common to others than that [person] <note>original: "tad-anya-sādhāraṇa"</note> ii. 22; for the sake of its seeing <note>original: "tad-dṛśeḥ"</note> ii. 25; from the absence of that <note>original: "tad-abhāvāt"</note> ii. 25; in its presence <note>original: "tat-sannidhau"</note> ii. 35; that alone <note>original: "tad eva"</note> iii. 3; from mastery of that <note>original: "taj-jayāt"</note> iii. 5; that also <note>original: "tad api"</note> iii. 8; the distinction between them <note>original: "tat-pravibhāga"</note> iii. 17; that with its support <note>original: "tat sālambanam"</note> iii. 20; the graspability of that <note>original: "tad-grāhya"</note> iii. 21; from equality with that <note>original: "tat-sāmyamāt"</note> iii. 22; its movement <note>original: "tad-gati"</note> iii. 28; its qualities <note>original: "tad-dharma"</note> iii. 45; from detachment from that <note>original: "tad-vairāgyāt"</note> iii. 50; of that and its sequence <note>original: "tat-kramayoḥ"</note> iii. 52; their ripening <note>original: "tad-vipāka"</note> iv. 8; the absence of those <note>original: "tad-abhāvaḥ"</note> iv. 11; that is without proof <note>original: "tad apramāṇakam"</note> iv. 16; its coloring <note>original: "tad-uparāga"</note> iv. 17; of its lord <note>original: "tat-prabhoḥ"</note> iv. 18; it is not self-luminous <note>original: "na tat svābhāsam"</note> iv. 19; when it assumes that form <note>original: "tad-ākāra-āpattau"</note> iv. 22; that [mind] with its countless [latent impressions] <note>original: "tad asaṁkhyeya-"</note> iv. 24; in the gaps of that <note>original: "tac-chidreṣu"</note> iv. 27.

2. [genitive singular] its cause <note>original: "tasya hetuḥ"</note> ii. 24; its designator <note>original: "tasya vācakaḥ"</note> i. 27; not the object of that <note>original: "tasya-aviṣayī"</note> iii. 20; in its stages <note>original: "tasya bhūmiṣu"</note> iii. 6; its peaceful flow <note>original: "tasya praśānta-"</note> iii. 10; its sevenfold [insight] <note>original: "tasya saptadhā"</note> ii. 27; even with the restraint of that <note>original: "tasya-api nirodhe"</note> i. 51.

3. [locative singular] that being so or present <note>original: "tasmin sati"</note> ii. 49.

[masculine plural] those are the obstacles <note>original: "te antarāyāḥ"</note> i. 30; they are to be abandoned by resolving back to the source <note>original: "te pratiprasava-heyāḥ"</note> ii. 10; they have joy and sorrow as their fruits <note>original: "te hlāda-paritāpa-phalāḥ"</note> ii. 14; they are obstacles in samādhi <note>original: "te samādhāv upasargāḥ"</note> iii. 37; they are manifest or subtle <note>original: "te vyakta-sūkṣmāḥ"</note> iv. 13.

**there / in that** <note>original: "tatra"</note>, there, in the state of stability <note>original: "tatra sthitau"</note> i. 13; there [in God], the unsurpassed [seed of omniscience] <note>original: "tatra niratiçayam"</note> i. 25; there, by the conceptualizations of word, object, and knowledge <note>original: "tatra çabda_artha-jñāna-vikalpaiḥ"</note> i. 42; in that state, the insight is truth-bearing <note>original: "ṛtambharā tatra prajñā"</note> i. 48; there, the one-pointedness of the mental content [is meditation] <note>original: "tatra pratyaya_ekatānatā"</note> iii. 2; of those, the mind born of meditation is without latent impressions <note>original: "tatra dhyāna-jam anāçayam"</note> iv. 6.

**but / indeed** <note>original: "tu"</note>, but that [practice], when maintained for a long time <note>original: "sa tu dīrghakāla"</note> i. 14; but the breaking of the obstacles [is from the fullness of nature] <note>original: "varaṇabhedas tu"</note> iv. 3.

<margin>-</margin> **suffering / pain** <note>original: "duḥkha"</note>, suffering yet to come is to be avoided <note>original: "heyaṃ duḥkham"</note> ii. 16; to the wise, all is indeed suffering <note>original: "duḥkham eva sarvam"</note> ii. 15; resulting in endless suffering and ignorance <note>original: "duḥkha_ajñāna_ananta-phalāḥ"</note> ii. 34; regarding the impure, the painful, and the non-self [as their opposites] <note>original: "açuci-duḥkha_anātmasu"</note> ii. 5; regarding objects of happiness, suffering, virtue, and vice <note>original: "sukha-duḥkha-puṇya_apuṇya-viṣayāṇām"</note> i. 33; aversion is that which follows suffering <note>original: "duḥkha_anuçayī dveṣaḥ"</note> ii. 8; suffering and despair <note>original: "duḥkha-daurmanasya"</note> i. 31; by the suffering caused by latent impressions <note>original: "saṃskāra-duḥkhaiḥ"</note> ii. 15.

<header>Appendix 7</header>

<margin>-</margin>**eternal** <note>original: "nitya"</note>, the appearance of the self, happiness, and purity in what is non-eternal, impure, and painful <note>original: "nitya-cuci-sukha_ātma-khyāti"</note> ii. 5.

**eternity** <note>original: "nityatva"</note>, because of the eternity of the desire [to live] <note>original: "āçiṣo nityatvāt"</note> iv. 10.

<margin>-</margin>**sleep** <note>original: "nidrā"</note>, sleep is the mental fluctuation supported by the absence of any content <note>original: "abhāva-pratyaya_ālambanā vṛttir nidrā"</note> i. 10; the [five] fluctuations are right knowledge, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory <note>original: "nidrā-smṛtayaḥ"</note> i. 6; or [attain stability] by leaning on the knowledge gained from dreams and sleep <note>original: "svapna-nidrā-jñāna_ālambanam"</note> i. 38.

**binding** <note>original: "nibandhanin"</note>, anchoring the state of stability <note>original: "sthiti-nibandhanī"</note> i. 35.

**cause** <note>original: "nimitta"</note>, the cause does not set the nature in motion [but removes obstacles] <note>original: "nimittam aprayojakam"</note> iv. 3.

**inclined toward** <note>original: "nimna"</note>, flowing toward discernment <note>original: "viveka-nimnam"</note> iv. 26.

<margin>-</margin>**observance** <note>original: "niyama"</note>, restraints and observances <note>original: "yama-niyama-"</note> ii. 29; purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to God are the observances <note>original: "çauca-samtoṣa-tapaḥ-svādhyāya-īçvarapra-ṇidhānāni niyamāḥ"</note> ii. 32.

**unsurpassed** <note>original: "niratiçaya"</note>, the unsurpassed seed of omniscience <note>original: "niratiçayaṃ sarvajñabījam"</note> i. 25.

**without immediate result** <note>original: "nirupakrama"</note>, action is either fast-fruiting or dormant <note>original: "sopakramaṃ nirupakramaṃ ca karma"</note> iii. 22.

<margin>-</margin>**cessation** <note>original: "nirodha"</note>, Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind <note>original: "yogaç citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ"</note> i. 2; their cessation comes through practice and dispassion <note>original: "abhyāsa-vairāgyābhyāṃ tan_nirodhaḥ"</note> i. 12; when even that is restricted, because all is restricted, seedless concentration is attained <note>original: "tasya_api nirodhe sarva-nirodhān nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ"</note> i. 51; the transformation of cessation is the moment of the mind's connection with cessation, when the impressions of the outgoing state disappear and the impressions of cessation appear <note>original: "vyutthāna-nirodha-saṃskārayorabhi-bhava-prādurbhāvau nirodha-kṣaṇa-citta_anvayo nirodhapariṇāmaḥ"</note> iii. 9.

**discernible** <note>original: "nirgrāhya"</note>, the sequence is discernible at the very end [of a transformation] <note>original: "aparānta-nirgrāhyaṃ kramaḥ"</note> iv. 33.

**seedless** <note>original: "nirbīja"</note>, because all is restricted, seedless concentration is attained <note>original: "sarva-nirodhān nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ"</note> i. 51; even that [concentration with a seed] is external to the seedless <note>original: "tad api bahiraṅgaṃ nirbījasya"</note> iii. 8.

<margin>-</margin>**shining forth** <note>original: "nirbhāsa"</note>, where only the object shines forth <note>original: "artha-mātra-nirbhāsam"</note> i. 43, iii. 3.

**creation** <note>original: "nirmāṇa"</note>, created minds [proceed from the sense of "I-am-ness"] <note>original: "nirmāṇa-cittāni"</note> iv. 4.

**without reflection** <note>original: "nirvicāra"</note>, the reflective and the non-reflective states are explained as having subtle objects <note>original: "savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣma-viṣayā"</note> i. 44; in the proficiency of the non-reflective state, the inner light of the self dawns <note>original: "nirvicāra-vāiçāradye 'dhyātmaprasādaḥ"</note> i. 47.

**without reasoning** <note>original: "nirvitarka"</note>, when the memory is purified, the mind is as if empty of its own form, and only the object shines forth; this is "without reasoning" <note>original: "smṛti-pariçuddhau svarūpa-çūnyā_iva_arthamātra-nirbhāsānirvitarkā"</note> i. 43.

<margin>-</margin>**cessation / turning back** <note>original: "nivṛtti"</note>, cessation of hunger and thirst <note>original: "pipāsā-nivṛtti"</note> iii. 30; the cessation of afflictions and karma <note>original: "kleça-karma-nivṛttiḥ"</note> iv. 30; the cessation of the dwelling on the nature of the self <note>original: "ātma-bhāva-bhāvanā-nivṛttiḥ"</note> iv. 25.

**uninterruptedness** <note>original: "nairantarya"</note>, [practice is grounded when] maintained for a long time without interruption <note>original: "dīrghakāla-nairantarya-"</note> i. 14.

**placement** <note>original: "nyāsa"</note>, by placing the light [of the higher mind upon an object] <note>original: "āloka-nyāsāt"</note> iii. 25.

---

**mud** <note>original: "paṅka"</note>, [mastery over the upward breath prevents contact with] water, mud, or thorns <note>original: "jala-paṅka-kaṇṭaka"</note> iii. 39.

**five** <note>original: "pañca"</note>, there are five afflictions <note>original: "pañca kleçāḥ"</note> ii. 3.

**fivefold** <note>original: "pañcataya"</note>, the fluctuations of the mind are fivefold <note>original: "vṛttayaḥ pañcatayyaḥ"</note> i. 5.

**path** <note>original: "panthan"</note>, the two paths [of object and mind] are distinct <note>original: "vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ"</note> iv. 15.

**other / higher** <note>original: "para"</note>, 1. *other*, the mind also exists for another's purpose <note>original: "cittam api para_artham"</note> iv. 24; experience exists for another's purpose [the Self] <note>original: "bhogaḥ para_arthatvāt"</note> iii. 35; entering into another's body <note>original: "para-çarīra_āveçaḥ"</note> iii. 38; knowledge of another's mind <note>original: "para-citta-jñānam"</note> iii. 19; lack of contact with others <note>original: "parāir asaṃsargaḥ"</note> ii. 40;
2. *higher*, that is the higher [dispassion] <note>original: "tat paraṃ [vairāgyam]"</note> i. 16.

**ultimate / highest** <note>original: "parama"</note>, the highest mastery [of the senses] <note>original: "paramā vaçyatā"</note> ii. 55; extending from the smallest to the ultimate greatness <note>original: "parama-mahattva_anta"</note> i. 40.

<margin>-</margin>**infinitesimal** <note>original: "paramāṇu"</note>, from the infinitesimal atom to the ultimate greatness <note>original: "paramāṇu-paramamahattva"</note> i. 40.

<margin>-</margin>**transformation** <note>original: "pariṇāma"</note>, the transformations of essential character, temporal state, and condition <note>original: "dharma-lakṣaṇa_avasthā-pariṇāma"</note> iii. 13; the three transformations <note>original: "pariṇāma-traya"</note> iii. 16; the sequence of transformations <note>original: "pariṇāma-krama"</note> iv. 32; the difference in sequence is the cause for the difference in transformation <note>original: "krama_anyatvaṃ pariṇāma_anyatve hetuḥ"</note> iii. 15; the very end of a transformation <note>original: "pariṇāma_aparānta"</note> iv. 33; [the wise see all as painful] due to the pains of transformation, anxiety, and habituation <note>original: "pariṇāma-tāpa-saṃskārair"</note> ii. 15; the transformation into another species <note>original: "jāty-antara-pariṇāma"</note> iv. 2; the reality of an object is due to the uniqueness of its transformation <note>original: "pariṇāma_ekatvād vastutattvam"</note> iv. 14; the transformation of the mind's one-pointedness <note>original: "cittasya_ekāgratā-pariṇāmaḥ"</note> iii. 12; the transformation of cessation <note>original: "nirodha-pariṇāma"</note> iii. 9; the transformation of concentration <note>original: "samādhi-pariṇāma"</note> iii. 11.

**anguish** <note>original: "paritāpa"</note>, [the fruits of action are] joy or anguish <note>original: "hlāda-paritāpa"</note> ii. 14.

**measured / observed** <note>original: "paridṛṣṭa"</note>, measured by numbers <note>original: "saṃkhyābhiḥ paridṛṣṭa"</note> ii. 50.

**purification** <note>original: "pariçuddhi"</note>, the purification of memory <note>original: "smṛti-pariçuddhi"</note> i. 43.

**termination / conclusion** <note>original: "paryavasāna"</note>, the subtle world ends at the unmanifest <note>original: "aliṅga-paryavasānam"</note> i. 45.

**level / stage** <note>original: "parvan"</note>, the stages of the qualities [of nature] <note>original: "guṇa-parvāṇi"</note> ii. 19.

**thirst** <note>original: "pipāsā"</note>, hunger and thirst <note>original: "kṣut-pipāsā"</note> iii. 30.

<margin>-</margin>**merit** <note>original: "puṇya"</note>, merit and demerit <note>original: "puṇya_apuṇya"</note> i. 33, ii. 14.

**again** <note>original: "punar"</note>, then again, the quieted and the arisen [mental contents] <note>original: "tataḥ punaḥ çāntoditāu"</note> iii. 12; because of the possibility of undesirable attachment again <note>original: "punar aniṣṭaprasaṅgāt"</note> iii. 51.

<margin>-</margin>**the Self / Pure Consciousness** <note>original: "puruṣa"</note>, though the intellect and the Self are absolutely distinct <note>original: "sattva-puruṣayor atyanta-saṃkīrṇayoḥ"</note> iii. 35; of that [mind], the Self is the master <note>original: "tat-prabhoḥ puruṣasya"</note> iv. 18; only the discernment of the difference between the intellect and the Self <note>original: "sattva-puruṣa_anyatā-khyātimātra"</note> iii. 49; from the vision of the Self comes a lack of thirst for the qualities of nature <note>original: "puruṣa-khyāter guṇa-vāitṛṣṇyam" </note> i. 16; from concentration on its own purpose comes knowledge of the Self <note>original: "sva_artha-saṃyamāt puruṣa-jñānam"</note> iii. 35; [liberation is] the state where the qualities of nature are devoid of any purpose for the Self <note>original: "puruṣa_artha-çūnyam"</note> iv. 34.

# Index of Words in the Sūtras

**of the pure intellect and the Self** <note>original: "sattva-puruṣayoḥ"</note>, liberation occurs when the purity [of the intellect] is equal [to that of the Self] <note>original: "śuddhi-sāmye kaivalyam"</note> iii. 55; the Lord is a special Self <note>original: "puruṣa-viśeṣa īśvaraḥ"</note> i. 24.

**former** <note>original: "pūrva"</note>, [the higher state] is preceded by the practice [of the notion of cessation] <note>original: "abhyāsa-pūrvaḥ"</note> i. 18; the internal [limbs] compared to the former ones <note>original: "antaraṅgaṃ pūrvebhyaḥ"</note> iii. 7; previous births <note>original: "pūrva-jāti"</note> iii. 18; the teacher even of the ancients <note>original: "pūrveṣām api guruḥ"</note> i. 26.

**preceded by** <note>original: "pūrvaka"</note>, preceded by wisdom <note>original: "prajñā-pūrvaka"</note> i. 20; preceded by delusion <note>original: "mohapūrvakaḥ"</note> ii. 34.

<margin>-</margin> **light** <note>original: "prakāśa"</note>, illumination, activity, and stability [are the qualities of nature] <note>original: "prakāśa-kriyā-sthiti"</note> ii. 18; [mastery] over the light of the eye <note>original: "cakṣuḥ-prakāśā"</note> iii. 21; the destruction of the covering of the light <note>original: "prakāśā_varaṇa-kṣaya"</note> ii. 52, iii. 43.

<margin>-</margin> **sacred syllable** <note>original: "praṇava"</note>, its designator is the sacred syllable [Om] <note>original: "vācakaḥ praṇavaḥ"</note> i. 27.

<margin>-</margin> **involution** <note>original: "pratiprasava"</note>, the involution of the qualities <note>original: "guṇānāṃ pratiprasavaḥ"</note> iv. 34; to be abandoned by involution [resolution into their cause] <note>original: "pratiprasavaheyāḥ"</note> ii. 10.

**inward** <note>original: "pratyak"</note>, inward-turned consciousness <note>original: "pratyak-cetanā"</note> i. 29.

**withdrawal of senses** <note>original: "pratyāhāra"</note>, withdrawal and concentration <note>original: "pratyāhāra-dhāraṇā"</note> ii. 29; when the senses, by withdrawing from their objects, imitate the nature of the mind, it is withdrawal <note>original: "svaviṣaya_asaṃprayoge cittasya svarūpa_anukāra iva_indriyāṇāṃ pratyāhāraḥ"</note> ii. 54.

**primary matter** <note>original: "pradhāna"</note>, from the mastery of primary matter <note>original: "pradhāna-jayāc ca"</note> iii. 48.

**activity** <note>original: "pravṛtti"</note>, an activity involving objects <note>original: "viṣayavatī pravṛttiḥ"</note> iv. 5 <note>Note: usually cited as i. 35</note>; by placing the light of activity <note>original: "pravṛtty-āloka-nyāsāt"</note> iii. 25; one mind is the director of the many in their various activities <note>original: "pravṛtti-bhede prayojakaṃ cittam ekam anekeṣām"</note> iv. 5.

**peaceful** <note>original: "praśānta"</note>, the peaceful flow [of the mind] <note>original: "praśānta-vāhitā"</note> iii. 10.

**exhalation** <note>original: "praśvāsa"</note>, inhalation and exhalation <note>original: "śvāsa-praśvāsa"</note> i. 31, ii. 49.

<margin>-</margin> **element/creature** <note>original: "bhūta"</note>, 1. element, *elements and sense organs* <note>original: "bhūta_indriya"</note> ii. 18, iii. 13; *mastery over the elements* <note>original: "bhūta-jayaḥ"</note> iii. 44.
2. creature, *the sounds of all living beings* <note>original: "sarva-bhūta-ruta"</note> iii. 17.
3. participle in *not having become an object [of the mind]* <note>original: "aviṣayībhūtatvāt"</note> iii. 20.

-**deliberation** <note>original: "vitarka"</note>, 1. deliberation [upon coarse objects], *[cognitive absorption accompanied by] deliberation, reflection, joy, and the sense of 'I-am'* <note>original: "vitarka-vicāra-ānanda-asmitā-rūpa-anugamāt samprajñātaḥ"</note> i. 17. 2. perverse consideration, *perverse considerations such as violence etc., whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved* <note>original: "vitarkā hiṃsādayaḥ kṛta-kārita-anumoditāḥ"</note> ii. 34; *when oppressed by perverse considerations, the cultivation of the opposite [should be practiced]* <note>original: "vitarka-bādhane pratipakṣa-bhāvanam"</note> ii. 33.

**free from desire** <note>original: "vitṛṣṇa"</note>, *of one who is free from desire for objects [seen or heard]* <note>original: "viṣaya-vitṛṣṇasya"</note> i. 15.

-**bodiless** <note>original: "Videha"</note>, *[absorption] for the bodiless and those merged in primary nature* <note>original: "Videha-Prakṛtilayānām"</note> i. 19; *the external, unimaginable activity of the mind is the "Great Bodiless" state* <note>original: "bahir-akalpitā vṛttir mahāvidehā"</note> iii. 43.

**the wise** <note>original: "vidvāṃs"</note>, *[attachment to life is found] even in the wise* <note>original: "viduṣo 'pi"</note> ii. 9.

**retention** <note>original: "vidhāraṇa"</note>, *by the expulsion and retention [of the breath]* <note>original: "pracchardana-vidhāraṇābhyāṃ"</note> i. 34.

**application** <note>original: "viniyoga"</note>, *its application is in stages* <note>original: "bhūmiṣu viniyogaḥ"</note> iii. 6.

-**cessation** <note>original: "vinivṛtti"</note>, *the cessation of the cultivation of the self's nature* <note>original: "bhāvanā-vinivṛttiḥ"</note> iv. 25.

-**misconception** <note>original: "viparyaya"</note>, *[the mind's activities are] right knowledge, misconception, and verbal delusion* <note>original: "pramāṇa-viparyaya-vikalpa-"</note> i. 6; *misconception is false knowledge not established in the true form [of the object]* <note>original: "viparyayo mithyājñānam atadrūpapratiṣṭham"</note> i. 8.

-**fruition** <note>original: "vipāka"</note>, *[God is] untouched by afflictions, actions, fruition, or latencies* <note>original: "kleśa-karma-vipāka-aparāmṛṣṭaḥ"</note> i. 24; *as long as the root exists, its fruition is birth, lifespan, and experience* <note>original: "sati mūle tad-vipāko jāty-āyur-bhogāḥ"</note> ii. 13; *of the subconscious impressions favorable to the fruition [of those actions]* <note>original: "vipāka-anuguṇānām . . . vāsanānām"</note> iv. 8.

-**remote** <note>original: "viprakṛṣṭa"</note>, *knowledge of the remote* <note>original: "viprakṛṣṭa-jñānam"</note> iii. 25.

**distinct** <note>original: "vibhakta"</note>, *their paths are distinct [due to the difference in minds]* <note>original: "vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ"</note> iv. 15.

-**cessation** <note>original: "virāma"</note>, *[the absorption] preceded by the practice of the notion of cessation* <note>original: "virāma-pratyaya-abhyāsa-pūrvaḥ"</note> i. 18.

**conflict** <note>original: "virodha"</note>, *and because of the conflict of the activities of the primary qualities [Gunas]* <note>original: "guṇa-vṛtti-virodhāc ca"</note> ii. 15.

-**discrimination** <note>original: "viveka"</note>, *the mind is then inclined toward discrimination and gravitates toward liberation* <note>original: "viveka-nimnaṃ kaivalya-prāgbhāraṃ cittam"</note> iv. 26; *discriminative discernment* <note>original: "viveka-khyāti"</note> ii. 26, ii. 28, iv. 29; *knowledge born of discrimination* <note>original: "viveka-jaṃ jñānam"</note> iii. 54; *meditation born of discrimination* <note>original: "viveka-jaṃ dhyānam"</note> iii. 52.

-**distinction** <note>original: "viśeṣa"</note>, 1. the particular, *a special soul* <note>original: "puruṣa-viśeṣa"</note> i. 24; *because it has a particular purpose* <note>original: "viśeṣa-arthatvāt"</note> i. 49; *the particular and the non-particular* <note>original: "viśeṣa-aviśeṣa"</note> ii. 19. 2. the distinction, *thence follows a further distinction* <note>original: "tato 'pi viśeṣaḥ"</note> i. 22; *for one who sees the distinction* <note>original: "viśeṣa-darśinaḥ"</note> iv. 25.

**sorrowless** <note>original: "viśoka"</note>, *or the sorrowless and luminous [state]* <note>original: "viśokā vā jyotiṣmatī"</note> i. 36.

-**object** <note>original: "viṣaya"</note>, *an experienced object* <note>original: "anubhūta-viṣaya"</note> i. 11; *of one free from desire for objects* <note>original: "viṣaya-vitṛṣṇasya"</note> i. 15; *when the mind is not in contact with its own objects* <note>original: "sva-viṣaya-asamprayoge cittasya"</note> ii. 54; *the knowledge born of discrimination has all things as its object in all ways* <note>original: "tārakaṃ sarva-viṣayaṃ sarvathā-viṣayam akramaṃ ceti vivekajaṃ jñānam"</note> iii. 54; *having a different object than the two [scripture and inference]* <note>original: "prajñābhyām anya-viṣayā"</note> i. 49; *reflective and non-reflective [absorptions] having subtle objects* <note>original: "savicārā nirvicārā ca sūkṣma-viṣayā"</note> i. 44; *of objects of vice* <note>original: "apuṇya-viṣayāṇām"</note> i. 33; *external and internal objects* <note>original: "bāhya-abhyantara-viṣaya"</note> ii. 51; *having as its object those who are free from desire* <note>original: "vitarāga-viṣayam"</note> i. 37.

**state of having an object** <note>original: "viṣayatva"</note>, *the state of having subtle objects extends up to the "unmarked" [Prakṛti]* <note>original: "sūkṣma-viṣayatvaṃ ca-aliṅga-paryavasānam"</note> i. 45.

**possessing an object** <note>original: "viṣayavant"</note>, *or a higher activity concerning an object [brings steadiness]* <note>original: "viṣayavatī vā pravṛttiḥ"</note> i. 35.

**free from** <note>original: "vīta"</note>, *having as its object [one who is] free from desire* <note>original: "vītarāga-viṣayam"</note> i. 37.

-**energy** <note>original: "vīrya"</note>, *faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom* <note>original: "śraddhā-vīrya-smṛti-samādhi-prajñā"</note> i. 20; *upon being established in continence, energy is gained* <note>original: "brahmacarya-pratiṣṭhāyāṃ vīrya-lābhaḥ"</note> ii. 38.

-**fluctuation** <note>original: "vṛtti"</note>, *Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind* <note>original: "yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ"</note> i. 2; *the fluctuations are fivefold, painful or non-painful* <note>original: "vṛttayaḥ pañcatayyaḥ kliṣṭa-akliṣṭāḥ"</note> i. 5 [the list follows in the next sutra]; *the fluctuation known as sleep* <note>original: "vṛttir nidrā"</note> i. 10; *the fluctuations of the mind are always known to its master because of the soul's changelessness* <note>original: "sadā jñātāś citta-vṛttayas tat-prabhoḥ puruṣasya-apariṇāmitvāt"</note> iv. 18; *conformity with the fluctuations* <note>original: "vṛtti-sārūpyam"</note> i. 4; *and because of the conflict of the fluctuations of the primary qualities [Gunas]* <note>original: "guṇa-vṛtti-virodhāc ca"</note> ii. 15; *external, internal, or suppressed fluctuations* <note>original: "bāhya-abhyantara-stambha-vṛttiḥ"</note> ii. 50; *their fluctuations are to be abandoned through meditation* <note>original: "dhyāna-heyās tad-vṛttayaḥ"</note> ii. 11; *of one whose fluctuations have dwindled* <note>original: "kṣīṇa-vṛtteḥ"</note> i. 41; *the external, unimaginable activity* <note>original: "bahir-akalpitā vṛttiḥ"</note> iii. 43.

-**sensation** <note>original: "vedana"</note>, *[from that arise] sensation, vision, and taste* <note>original: "vedana-ādarśa-āsvāda-"</note> iii. 36.

**to be experienced** <note>original: "vedanīya"</note>, *to be experienced in birth* <note>original: "janma-vedanīyaḥ"</note> ii. 12.

**freedom from desire** <note>original: "vaitṛṣṇya"</note>, *freedom from desire for the primary qualities [Gunas]* <note>original: "guṇa-vaitṛṣṇyam"</note> i. 16.

**hostility** <note>original: "vaira"</note>, *the abandonment of hostility* <note>original: "vaira-tyāgaḥ"</note> ii. 35.

-**detachment** <note>original: "vairāgya"</note>, *detachment is the consciousness of mastery in one free from desire for objects seen or heard* <note>original: "dṛṣṭa-ānuśravika-viṣaya-vitṛṣṇasya vaśīkārasaṃjñā vairāgyam"</note> i. 15; *through practice and detachment* <note>original: "abhyāsa-vairāgyābhyām"</note> i. 12; *through detachment even from that, comes liberation* <note>original: "tad-vairāgyād api doṣa-bīja-kṣaye kaivalyam"</note> iii. 50.

**lucidity** <note>original: "vāiśāradya"</note>, *upon the lucidity of the non-reflective [absorption]* <note>original: "nirvicāra-vāiśāradye"</note> i. 47.

**manifest** <note>original: "vyakta"</note>, *the manifest and the subtle* <note>original: "vyakta-sūkṣmāḥ"</note> iv. 13.

**designatable** <note>original: "vyapadeśya"</note>, *non-designatable [the future]* <note>original: "a-vyapadeśya"</note> iii. 14.

**hidden** <note>original: "vyavahita"</note>, *separated by time* <note>original: "kāla-vyavahita"</note> iv. 9; *the subtle and the hidden* <note>original: "sūkṣma-vyavahita"</note> iii. 25.

**explained** <note>original: "vyākhyāta"</note>, *transformations are explained* <note>original: "pariṇāmā vyākhyātāḥ"</note> iii. 13; *[absorptions] with subtle objects are explained* <note>original: "sūkṣma-viṣayā vyākhyātā"</note> i. 44.

# HARVARD ORIENTAL SERIES

**Harvard Oriental Series.** Edited, with the coöperation of various scholars, by **CHARLES ROCKWELL LANMAN**, Bachelor of Arts and Doctor of Laws <note>original: "A.B. and LL.D."</note> (Yale), Doctor of Laws (Aberdeen), Wales Professor of Sanskrit at Harvard University; Honorary Member of the Asian Society <note>original: "Asiatic Society"</note> of Bengal, the Asian Society <note>original: "Société Asiatique"</note>, the Royal Asian Society <note>original: "Royal Asiatic Society"</note> of Great Britain and Ireland, and the German Oriental Society <note>original: "Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft"</note>; Member of the American Philosophical Society; Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences; Foreign Member of the Royal Bohemian Society of Sciences; Honorary Correspondent of the Archaeological Department of the Government of India; Corresponding Member of the Institute of Bologna, of the Royal Society of Sciences at Göttingen, of the Imperial Russian Academy of Sciences, and of the Institute of France (Academy of Inscriptions and Humanities <note>original: "Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres"</note>).

Published by **The Harvard University Press, Cambridge, Massachusetts, U.S.A.**
To be bought, in America, of GINN & COMPANY, 29 Beacon Street, Boston, Mass.; in England, of GINN & Co., 9 St. Martin's Street, Leicester Square, London, W.C.; in Continental Europe, of O. Harrassowitz, Leipzig.—The price of volume 3 is $1.20. Price of volumes 7 and 8 (not sold separately) is $5. Price of volume 10 is $6. The price of each of the other volumes is $1.50.—One dollar ($1.00) = 4.18 Marks = 5.15 francs or lire = 4 shillings and 2 pence = 3 rupees.—Volume 10 is royal quarto <note>original: "4º"</note> (32 cm.), volumes 7 and 8 are super-royal octavo <note>original: "8º"</note> (28 cm.); the rest are royal octavo (26 cm.). All are now bound durably in full buckram with gilt top.

**Volume 1. Jātaka-Mālā**, Stories of Buddha's former incarnations, by <term>Ārya Çūra</term> <note>A famous Buddhist poet known for his elegant Sanskrit style.</note>. Edited in Sanskrit (Nāgarī letters <note>The traditional "city-script" used for sacred and scholarly Indian texts.</note>) by Professor H. KERN, University of Leiden, Netherlands. 1891. Second issue, 1914. Pages, 270. (Translation by Speyer, London, 1895, Frowde.)

**Volume 2. Sānkhya-Pravachana-Bhāshya**, or Commentary on the exposition of the Sānkhya philosophy <note>One of the oldest systematic philosophies of India, focusing on the dualism between consciousness and matter.</note>, by <term>Vijñāna-Bhikshu</term> <note>A 16th-century philosopher who sought to harmonize different schools of Indian thought.</note>. Edited in Sanskrit (Roman letters) by Professor R. GARBE, University of Tübingen, Germany. 1895. Pages, 210. (Translated by Garbe, Leipzig, 1889, Brockhaus.)

**Volume 3. Buddhism in Translations.** By the late **HENRY CLARKE WARREN**, of Cambridge, Mass. 1896. Fifth issue, 1909. Pages, 540. (Over 100 extracts from the sacred books of Buddhism, so arranged as to give a connected account of the legendary life of Buddha, of his monastic order, of his doctrines on karma and rebirth, and of his scheme of salvation. The work has been widely circulated and has been highly praised by competent authorities.)

**Volume 4. Karpūra-Mañjarī.** A drama by the Indian poet <term>Rājaçekhara</term> <note>A prominent playwright and critic of the late 9th and early 10th centuries.</note> (900 A.D.). Critically edited in the original <term>Prākrit</term> <note>A group of natural or vernacular languages used in ancient India, often appearing in dramas alongside Sanskrit.</note> (Nāgarī letters), with a glossarial index and an essay on the life and writings of the poet, by STEN KONOW, of the University of Christiania, Norway; and translated into English with notes by C. R. LANMAN. 1901. Pages, 318.

**Volumes 5 and 6. *The Great Deity-Index*** <note>original: "Brihad-Devatā"</note> (attributed to Çāunaka), a summary of the deities and myths of the **Rig-Veda** <note>The oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational sacred scriptures of ancient India</note>. Critically edited in the original Sanskrit (**Nāgarī** <term>Nāgarī: The script used for writing Sanskrit, often called Devanāgarī</term> letters) with an introduction and seven appendices (volume 5), and translated into English with critical and illustrative notes (volume 6), by Professor A. A. MACDONELL, University of Oxford. 1904. Pages, 234 + 350 = 584.

**Volumes 7 and 8. *Atharva-Veda*** <note>The fourth Veda, containing hymns, spells, and philosophical discourse</note>. Translated, with a critical and explanatory commentary, by the late Professor W. D. WHITNEY, of Yale University; revised and brought nearer to completion and edited by C. R. LANMAN. 1905. Pages, 1212. (The work includes critical notes on the text, with various readings of European and Indian <note>original: "Hindu"</note> manuscripts; readings of the Kashmirian version; notices of corresponding passages in the other Vedas, with report of variations; data of the **scholiasts** <term>Scholiasts: Ancient commentators who provided word-for-word explanations and context for sacred texts</term> as to authorship, divinity, and meter of each verse; extracts from the secondary <note>original: "ancillary"</note> literature concerning ritual and explanation; literal translation; elaborate critical and historical introduction.)

**Volume 9. *The Little Clay Cart*** (**Mṛcchakaṭika**), a Hindu drama attributed to King Shūdraka. Translated from the original Sanskrit and **Prākrits** <term>Prākrits: Ancient regional dialects used alongside Sanskrit in literature, often spoken by commoners or women in plays</term> into English prose and verse by A. W. RYDER, Instructor in Sanskrit in Harvard University. 1905. Pages, 207.

**Volume 10. *Vedic Concordance***: being an alphabetic index to every line of every stanza of the published Vedic literature and to the ritual <note>original: "liturgical"</note> formulas thereof, that is, an index (in Roman letters) to the Vedic **mantras** <note>Sacred chants or verses</note>, together with an account of their variations in the different Vedic books. By Professor MAURICE BLOOMFIELD, of the Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore. 1906. Pages, 1102.

**Volume 11. *The Pañchatantra*** <note>literally "The Five Treatises," a famous collection of Indian animal fables and wisdom stories</note>: a collection of ancient Hindu tales, in the version <note>original: "recension"</note> (called **Pañchākhyānaka**, and dated 1199 A.D.) of the Jaina monk, Pūrṇabhadra, critically edited in the original Sanskrit (in Nāgarī letters; and, for the sake of beginners, with word-division) by Dr. JOHANNES HERTEL, Professor at the Royal Secondary School <note>original: "königlichen Realgymnasium"</note>, Doebeln, Saxony. 1908. Pages, 344.

**Volume 12. *The Pañchatantra-text of Pūrṇabhadra***: critical introduction and list of variations <note>original: "variants"</note>. By Professor HERTEL. 1912. Pages, 245. (Includes an index of stanzas.)

**Volume 13. *The Pañchatantra-text of Pūrṇabhadra***, and its relation to texts of allied versions as shown in Parallel Specimens. By Professor HERTEL. 1912. (Nineteen sheets, mounted on guards and issued in atlas-form. They give, in parallel columns, four typical specimens of the text of Pūrṇabhadra's **Pañchatantra**, in order to show the family <note>original: "genetic"</note> relations in which the Sanskrit versions of the **Pañchatantra** stand to one another, and the value of the manuscripts of the single versions.)

**Volume 14. *The Pañchatantra***: a collection of ancient Hindu tales, in its oldest version, the Kashmirian, entitled **Tantrākhyāyika**. Sanskrit text, reprinted from the critical major edition by Professor HERTEL. Minor edition. (Nearly ready.)
